We also see how helping and caring for others during hard times is an important part of being Christlike. Trust, faith, and kindness can help us face trials, knowing Heavenly Father has a plan, even when it is hard to see in the moment.
d06.matters: The Plague of Justinian matters because it changed the course of history. With so many lives lost and entire regions weakened, the dream of a single, powerful Roman Empire in the West ended. Europe broke into smaller kingdoms and local powers. This political change led, over centuries, to the rise of modern nations – each with its own culture and government. For families of faith, it's important to know that, though such suffering was great, Heavenly Father’s higher purposes can move forward. Over time, the division of power made it possible for different ideas, including true religious freedom, to take root, setting the stage for later blessings, including the Restoration of the Gospel.

sources.name: CDC – Plague History
World History Encyclopedia – Plague of Justinian
Britannica – Justinian I: The Plague
The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints – Enduring Trials with Faith

d06.evidence: Archaeologists and historians have found strong evidence for the plague’s impact. Ancient texts by writers like Procopius describe in detail the disease’s horrors, the deaths in Constantinople, and the fear it caused. Modern science has confirmed these stories through genetic testing of graves from the period, finding DNA from Yersinia pestis, the bacterium that causes bubonic plague. Connecting written records with these biological findings gives us confidence in what happened. The numbers lost are estimates, but the scale of the tragedy and its effects on the empire and beyond are well supported by both historical and scientific research.
d06.happened: In the year 541 AD, a terrible disease swept through the great cities and countryside of the Byzantine Empire, which we call the Plague of Justinian. The plague likely started in Egypt and by sea trade reached Constantinople, the bustling capital ruled by Emperor Justinian. People began to fall ill with high fevers, chills, and painful swellings called buboes. The sickness moved quickly, and within only a few months, thousands were dying every day in the city. It did not stop there; the disease spread through the lands around the Mediterranean Sea – places where millions lived. Families lost parents, children, and neighbors. Fields went untended and markets were empty, because so many could not work. Historians today estimate that between 25 to 50 million people died during these years – perhaps one out of every four people in the region. The empire was weakened for many years. Justinian himself fell sick but survived. His dream to rebuild what once was the Roman Empire faded, changed forever by the plague's shadow.
d06.scripture: While the scriptures do not mention the Plague of Justinian directly, principles that help us in times of disaster appear throughout them. For example, in Doctrine and Covenants 101:16, the Lord teaches, 'Be still and know that I am God.' The Book of Mormon also describes times when people suffered and turned to God for comfort and help, like in Alma 31:31–38, where Alma prays for his people in their trials. These verses remind families that even in hard times, God is aware of us, and history moves with His purposes.
d06.background: Before the plague, the Byzantine Empire was the strongest power in Europe and the Mediterranean. Ruling from Constantinople, Emperor Justinian set out to restore the Roman Empire's former greatness. This meant wars in Italy, building great churches like the Hagia Sophia, and creating fair laws to help govern so many people. Most people in the empire were farmers, fishermen, merchants, and artisans living in small villages or busy cities. They grew food, baked bread, sailed ships, and worshiped in Christian churches. Trade moved goods and ideas along Roman roads and over the sea, but these connections also allowed diseases to travel quickly across great distances. Life was challenging, yet there was hope for peace and unity – hopes dashed by the swift and devastating arrival of the plague.

d07.talk: If something scary happened in our neighborhood, how could we help others, even people we don't know very well?
d07.child: A big earthquake happened in a city called Aleppo a long time ago. Many people got hurt or lost their homes. It didn’t matter what church they went to—everyone needed help, and people had to take care of each other.
d07.learn: We can learn from the Aleppo earthquake that life can change suddenly and that we should be ready to help others when hard things happen. It teaches us that our differences become much smaller when we face a problem together, and that God cares for all His children equally. Talking about old disasters can help families prepare for emergencies and build faith that with kindness, faith, and cooperation, we can get through even very hard times.
d07.matters: The Aleppo earthquake matters because it shows how natural disasters do not care about the differences that separate people, such as religion, nationality, or power. During a time of great division and violence, the earthquake struck everyone alike, reminding us that we all rely on the same earth. This is a powerful lesson for families of faith: in the face of suffering or loss, we are called to see each other as Heavenly Father’s children, regardless of background. Remembering disasters like this can help families teach compassion, preparedness, and unity, especially when so much of the world’s history is marked by conflict.

sources.name: Encyclopedia Britannica: Aleppo Earthquake of 1138
U.S. Geological Survey: Historic Earthquakes – Aleppo, Syria 1138
World History Encyclopedia: Aleppo

d07.evidence: Historians and researchers agree that the earthquake near Aleppo in 1138 was one of the most deadly in recorded history. Medieval Arabic and Christian writers wrote about the event, estimating a staggering number of deaths, sometimes as high as 230,000, though exact numbers are uncertain. Archaeological evidence confirms that earthquakes have often struck the region, known for its fault lines. While some early details and numbers might be exaggerated by frightened survivors, the destruction in Aleppo and its surroundings was real and long lasting. Modern scientists can study the region’s geology and ancient ruins to confirm that major earthquakes did and still do occur there.
d07.happened: On October 11, 1138, one of the deadliest earthquakes in history struck near the city of Aleppo in present-day Syria. The ground shook so powerfully that many buildings, including large stone castles and city walls, collapsed in seconds. Homes, mosques, churches, and markets were destroyed. People from every walk of life were caught in the disaster, with hundreds of thousands either killed outright or left without shelter. Reports from the time tell of whole neighborhoods flattened, and many families never saw their loved ones again. Though the city and surrounding villages had faced wars and sieges during the Crusades, this was a calamity neither sword nor shield could stop. The earthquake’s force spread across a wide area, touching both Christian and Muslim communities without distinction. For weeks and months after, survivors faced hardship as food, clean water, and medical care ran short. The region was forever changed, with so many dead that entire communities disappeared.
d07.scripture: Scriptural teachings do not mention the Aleppo earthquake specifically, but several passages remind us that the earth is the Lord’s and sometimes He allows natural events to humble mankind and draw us together. In Matthew 5:45, we read that God "maketh his sun to rise on the evil and on the good, and sendeth rain on the just and on the unjust." Similarly, the Book of Mormon (3 Nephi 8) describes cities destroyed by earth’s power and counsels people to remember God in times of disaster. Doctrine and Covenants 88:87 also speaks about the power of natural forces. These passages help us understand that tragedies can unite us and help us turn our hearts to God and each other.
d07.background: Aleppo was one of the oldest and most important cities in the world at the time, known for its busy markets, tall stone walls, and strong castles. People there lived in houses built from thick rock, which helped keep out enemies during wars but could be dangerous in an earthquake. The area had a mix of cultures and religions—Christian and Muslim leaders were at odds due to the Crusades, fighting over control of the Holy Land. Families grew wheat, made cloth, and cared for animals. Daily life was shaped by traditions, faith, and the constant worry of war. At the time, most people traveled by foot or donkey and rarely went far from home. News of events like the earthquake spread by word of mouth or from travelers passing through. There were no warning systems or modern hospitals, so people were especially vulnerable when disaster struck without warning.

d08.talk: Why do you think people might look for God more during very hard times?
d08.child: Long ago, a sickness called the Black Death made many people in Europe and nearby lands very sick, and many died. It was a sad and scary time, but people tried to help each other and learned new ways to live. Even when hard things happen, God still loves us and helps us learn.
d08.learn: From the Black Death, we learn about human resilience and God’s care, even in the hardest times. Suffering can lead to change, new beginnings, and a more personal faith. Families may talk about how the Lord can use trials for good and prepare people for great things to come. It also helps us be grateful for modern medicine and reminds us to care for the sick and lonely today.
d08.matters: The Black Death matters for many reasons. It dramatically reduced Europe’s population, leading to labor shortages, changes in land use, and eventually better wages for workers. It also deeply shook people’s trust in their leaders—both those in government and in the church. With so much suffering, many started to look for God in a more personal way, hoping for answers and comfort. For families of faith, this moment shows how even tragic hardships can lead people to seek the Lord and question old traditions, eventually helping prepare the world for changes like the Reformation and, centuries later, the Restoration. It is a story about grief, survival, and searching for meaning.

sources.name: CDC: History of Plague
The British Museum: The Black Death
Encyclopaedia Britannica: Black Death

d08.evidence: The reality of the Black Death is confirmed by a wealth of historical sources: written records of deaths, letters, and city chronicles all describe the same terrible events. Modern science has helped too—researchers have discovered mass graves and traced DNA from the victims’ teeth, confirming they carried Yersinia pestis, the plague bacterium. These findings match what was described in those years. There is still some discussion among historians about all the ways the disease spread and why it was so deadly, but the core facts are very well established by both history and science.
d08.happened: The Black Death was a terrible outbreak of disease that swept across much of Asia, the Middle East, and Europe between 1347 and 1351. It began when ships arrived in Sicily from the Crimea, carrying cargo—both goods and fleas that lived on black rats. These fleas carried a bacterium called Yersinia pestis, which causes bubonic plague. The disease spread rapidly along trade routes, quickly reaching towns and cities across Europe. People would become sick very quickly with painful swellings, fever, and sometimes, within days, would die. Entire families and villages were wiped out. In some places, there were not enough people left to bury the dead. Estimates say 75 to 200 million people lost their lives worldwide in just a few years. This disaster was so massive that in many towns, one in every three people died. It wasn’t just a medical crisis—it changed everything about life, work, and community, causing deep fear, broken families, and loss throughout the known world.
d08.scripture: While the Black Death is not spoken of directly in scripture, the Bible does talk about times of great suffering and plagues, such as in Exodus 7–12, where the Lord allows plagues in Egypt. In the Book of Mormon, Alma 33:19 teaches healing through looking to God in faith, as Moses lifted the brazen serpent. In Doctrine and Covenants 61:36, the Lord offers comfort, saying, “I, the Lord, am with you.” These passages remind us that through all pain and trial, God remains aware and offers hope.
d08.background: Europe in 1347 was a land of small villages, bustling market towns, and great walled cities. Most people were peasants, working land owned by nobles or the church. The Catholic Church was the center of village life; priests led prayers, gave comfort, and taught about God. People traded goods, news, and rumors across continents on growing networks of roads and ships. Hygiene and medical knowledge were limited: people didn’t know about germs or the importance of clean water or managing waste. Life was close to the earth—hard but full of tradition and faith. Travel, war, and trade had already spread smaller outbreaks, but nothing like what was to come.

d09.talk: What can we do to make sure our home is safe if an earthquake happens?
d09.child: A long time ago, a big earthquake shook a place in China, and many people got hurt because their homes were not strong enough. This teaches us to build safe houses and help each other when bad things happen.
d09.learn: The 1556 Shaanxi earthquake teaches us the critical importance of constructing homes and buildings that can withstand natural disasters. It also reminds us of the need for community preparedness and the value of supporting one another during times of crisis. By learning from past events, we can better protect our families and communities in the future.
d09.matters: The 1556 Shaanxi earthquake stands as a somber reminder of the immense power of natural forces and the vulnerability of human societies. For families of faith, it underscores the importance of preparedness and resilience in the face of unforeseen disasters. It also highlights the need for compassion and aid to those affected by such tragedies. Reflecting on this event can inspire us to strengthen our communities, support one another, and trust in Heavenly Father's plan, even during times of great trial.

sources.name: 1556 Shaanxi earthquake
The Deadliest Earthquake Ever Recorded | HISTORY
What Were The World's Deadliest Earthquakes?

d09.evidence: Historical records from the Ming Dynasty provide detailed accounts of the earthquake's impact, describing the extensive destruction and high death toll. Modern seismological studies estimate the earthquake's magnitude to be around 8.0, based on the scale of the damage and geological evidence. The collapse of the yaodong dwellings significantly contributed to the high number of fatalities, as these structures were particularly susceptible to seismic activity. The event remains a focal point in the study of earthquake hazards and the importance of building practices that consider local geological conditions.
d09.happened: In the early hours of January 23, 1556, a catastrophic earthquake struck the Wei River Valley in Shaanxi Province, China. Modern estimates place its magnitude around 8.0, making it one of the most powerful earthquakes recorded. The tremors were so intense that they caused mountains to shift, rivers to change course, and massive fissures to open in the ground. Entire villages were obliterated, and in some counties, up to 60% of the population perished. The death toll is estimated at approximately 830,000 people, making it the deadliest earthquake in recorded history. The devastation extended across an area of about 520 miles, affecting 97 counties in provinces including Shaanxi, Shanxi, Henan, Gansu, Hebei, Shandong, Hubei, Hunan, Jiangsu, and Anhui. The earthquake also triggered landslides, floods, and fires, further compounding the destruction and loss of life.
d09.scripture: While the scriptures do not specifically mention the 1556 Shaanxi earthquake, they do speak to the principles of compassion and service in times of disaster. In Mosiah 4:26, we are taught to "succor those that stand in need of your succor." This principle encourages us to assist and support those who are suffering, reflecting the love and care that Heavenly Father has for all His children.
d09.background: During the mid-16th century, China was under the rule of the Ming Dynasty, a period marked by cultural flourishing and economic growth. The Shaanxi region, situated in central China, was densely populated, with many inhabitants living in yaodongs—artificial caves carved into the soft loess cliffs of the Loess Plateau. These dwellings provided insulation and were economical to construct, making them popular among the rural population. However, their structural vulnerability became tragically evident during the earthquake, as the shaking caused widespread collapse of these homes, leading to significant loss of life. The region's economy was primarily agrarian, with communities relying on farming and local trade. The sudden and massive destruction disrupted daily life, leading to food shortages and economic hardship in the aftermath.

d10.talk: How can we help others when something scary or sad happens?
d10.child: A big earthquake hit Lisbon a long time ago while people were at church, and many people were hurt or lost their homes. After the shaking, big waves and fires made things even worse. Even though it was sad, people learned to ask good questions and help each other.
d10.learn: The Lisbon Earthquake teaches us that disasters can happen suddenly and change lives in an instant, even for people who are trying to do good. We learn to be prepared for hard times, to care for one another, and to trust that God is close, even when we do not understand why things happen. Honest questions and searching for meaning are important parts of faith. Hard times can prepare us to receive greater truths and develop compassion for others who suffer.
d10.matters: The Lisbon Earthquake is remembered not just for its destruction but for the deep questions it raised about faith and the nature of suffering. Many people across Europe wondered how such a disaster could take place in a city full of faithful people on a sacred day. Philosophers like Voltaire began to question old ideas about God and suffering, and this started a larger movement called the Enlightenment, which focused on reason and individual thought. These big questions prepared the world for new spiritual movements, including the Restoration of the gospel, by encouraging honest searching for truth and a more personal relationship with God. For families of faith, the Lisbon Earthquake is a reminder that even during tragedy, God is still present and that asking questions can lead to greater understanding.

sources.name: US Geological Survey: The Lisbon Earthquake
Encyclopaedia Britannica: Lisbon Earthquake of 1755
Smithsonian Magazine: How the Lisbon Earthquake Changed the World

d10.evidence: Scientists and historians have carefully studied the Lisbon Earthquake. Geological studies show Lisbon sits near the boundary of two tectonic plates, which caused the massive earthquake and tsunami. Written accounts from survivors describe the shaking, flooding, and fires with much detail. Archaeologists have found layers of burned material and collapsed buildings from that day. The death toll is estimated between 30,000 and 40,000, though exact numbers are debated. This disaster was one of the first to be studied for its scientific causes as well as its moral and philosophical meaning, helping to shape the modern study of earthquakes and natural disasters.
d10.happened: On the morning of November 1, 1755, as the people of Lisbon, Portugal gathered to celebrate All Saints Day, a great earthquake struck. Most families were in church, giving thanks and worshiping together. Around 9:40 am, the ground began to rumble. Buildings shook and crashed to the ground, trapping many inside. Some people ran to the river or the open market squares, hoping to find safety. But the shaking was only the beginning. Soon after, enormous waves—known as a tsunami—swept over the shores, dragging away homes and people. Fires then broke out all across the city, feeding on the ruined houses and churches. The flames quickly spread, burning for days. By the end, between 30,000 and 40,000 people had died. Much of Lisbon was left in ruins. People around the world heard about this disaster, wondering how such a thing could happen on such a holy day.
d10.scripture: While the scriptures do not speak directly about the Lisbon Earthquake, many passages deal with suffering and God's presence in hard times. In the Book of Mormon, Alma 7:11-12 teaches that Jesus Christ took upon Himself all our pains and afflictions. Romans 8:28 in the Bible reminds us, 'All things work together for good to them that love God.' Doctrine and Covenants 122:7-9 records the Lord telling Joseph Smith that trials can work for our growth and that God will always be with us. These passages assure us that God does not cause suffering but can work within it to bring blessings and understanding.
d10.background: Lisbon in 1755 was one of Europe's most powerful cities, the capital of Portugal and the center of a vast global empire. The people were mainly Catholic and deeply religious, and All Saints Day was one of the most important holy days of the year. Families dressed in their best clothes and attended mass in grand stone churches. Portugal was wealthy from its colonies overseas, especially in South America, Africa, and Asia. Daily life for most people, though, was still simple. Most families worked hard, and cities like Lisbon were crowded and filled with traders, sailors, and craftsmen. The city was full of tall stone buildings and narrow streets, making it especially dangerous when the earthquake struck.

d11.t: Tambora Eruption — Year Without a Summer
d11.talk: How do you think people felt when the weather changed and they couldn't grow enough food?
d11.child: A long time ago, a big volcano called Mount Tambora erupted and sent so much ash into the sky that it made the world colder. This made it hard for farmers to grow food, and many people had to move to new places to find better lives.
d11.learn: The eruption of Mount Tambora teaches us about the profound impact natural events can have on the world. It reminds us of the importance of preparedness, the resilience of communities in the face of adversity, and the interconnectedness of global systems. For families of faith, it also serves as a testament to the ways in which God's creations are interwoven and how challenges can lead to growth, adaptation, and deeper faith.
d11.matters: The eruption of Mount Tambora had profound global consequences. The massive amount of ash and sulfur dioxide released into the atmosphere led to significant climatic changes, including the "Year Without a Summer" in 1816. This period of global cooling resulted in crop failures, food shortages, and economic hardship across Europe and North America. For families of faith, this event serves as a reminder of the interconnectedness of God's creations and the unforeseen ways in which natural events can influence human history. It also underscores the importance of resilience and faith in the face of adversity.

sources.name: Smithsonian Magazine: 200 Years After Tambora, Some Unusual Effects Linger
NASA Earth Observatory: Mount Tambora Volcano, Sumbawa Island, Indonesia
USGS: Hazards and Climatic Impact of Subduction-Zone Volcanism

d11.evidence: Scientific studies have extensively documented the 1815 eruption of Mount Tambora. Geological evidence includes the massive caldera formed by the eruption and the widespread distribution of volcanic ash found in ice cores and sediment layers worldwide. Climatic data from tree rings and historical records confirm the global temperature drop and the resulting agricultural failures. Historical accounts from various regions detail the immediate and long-term impacts on human populations, including famine, disease outbreaks, and migration patterns. These converging lines of evidence provide a comprehensive understanding of the eruption's magnitude and its far-reaching effects.
d11.happened: In April 1815, Mount Tambora on Sumbawa Island, Indonesia, erupted in the most powerful volcanic event in recorded history. The eruption began on April 5 and reached its climax on April 10–11. The explosion was so immense that it was heard over 2,600 kilometers away. The eruption ejected approximately 150 cubic kilometers of tephra—exploded rock and ash—into the atmosphere, reducing the mountain's height from about 4,300 meters to 2,850 meters and creating a caldera 6 kilometers wide and 1,250 meters deep. The immediate impact was catastrophic: pyroclastic flows and falling ash destroyed villages, and an estimated 60,000 to 92,000 people lost their lives due to the eruption and subsequent famine and disease. The eruption also had far-reaching climatic effects, leading to the "Year Without a Summer" in 1816, which caused global temperature drops, crop failures, and widespread famine.
d11.scripture: While the scriptures do not directly reference volcanic eruptions, they do speak to the power of natural events and their role in God's plan. In the Book of Mormon, 3 Nephi 8 describes great destruction, including tempests, earthquakes, and fires, that occurred at the time of Christ's crucifixion. These events led to darkness and mourning among the people. This passage illustrates how natural disasters can serve as catalysts for reflection, repentance, and a deeper understanding of divine purposes.
d11.background: In the early 19th century, the world was largely agrarian, with communities heavily dependent on local agriculture for sustenance. The Indonesian archipelago, including Sumbawa Island, was part of the Dutch East Indies, a colony under Dutch control. The region was home to various indigenous kingdoms and communities, many of whom lived in close proximity to active volcanoes, which were both revered and feared. Daily life was deeply connected to the land and sea, with fishing, farming, and trade forming the backbone of local economies. However, the lack of modern communication and scientific understanding meant that communities were often unprepared for natural disasters like volcanic eruptions.

d12.talk: How would you help someone who didn't have enough to eat?
d12.child: Long ago in Ireland, potato plants got sick, so there wasn't enough food and many people grew hungry or had to leave their homes. Lots of Irish families moved far away to America or other places to make a new start. Some later found the Church and became pioneers in Utah.
d12.learn: From the Irish Potato Famine, we learn how important it is to watch for and care for those who suffer—neighbor or stranger. We also see that even the hardest experiences can, in time, bring new growth and hope. Families that suffered so much in Ireland built new lives in America and strengthened their faith. Remembering their story helps us find courage and compassion in hard times, and teaches us to trust Heavenly Father, believing He can turn our struggles into blessings.
d12.matters: The Irish Potato Famine matters because it changed millions of lives and even the course of nations. Immigrants from Ireland spread out across the world, especially to America, bringing their culture, faith, and hopes with them. For families of faith, the famine’s legacy is part of many family trees. Among those who fled to America were people who would hear the message of the Restoration and join the early Church. Their journey reminds us that Heavenly Father can bring about new blessings, even through heartbreak and loss. The famine’s story helps us see how much we depend on each other and how we can share Christlike love with those in need.

sources.name: Irish Potato Famine – Britannica
National Museum of Ireland – The Irish Famine
Encyclopedia of Emigration and Migration in History
The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints: Irish Migration and the Church

d12.evidence: Today, historians know the famine happened because many records—letters, newspapers, government reports, and even scientific samples—have survived. Scientists have shown that Phytophthora infestans, the blight fungus, ruined the potatoes. Graveyards and ship logs confirm how many lives were lost and how many people left Ireland. There are still buildings, ships, and even empty villages left from that time. Recent research has confirmed the causes and effects, including social and economic hardships, and the role of political decisions that made things worse by limiting relief and emigration options. Scholars agree the numbers are huge: close to a million and a half deaths and as many as two million leaving Ireland. These facts are not debated—historians are certain about the main details, though they continue to learn more about the people and their stories.
d12.happened: In 1845, something terrible began in Ireland, a green country where many families depended almost entirely on potatoes to eat. That year, a disease called potato blight—a kind of fungus—struck the fields. Almost overnight, potato plants turned black and mushy, rotting in the ground before they could be harvested. Year after year, for seven long years, the blight kept returning, destroying the main food crop. With so little else to eat, people grew weaker each season. Hunger quickly led to sickness and disease. The disaster became known as the Irish Potato Famine. Nearly one and a half million people died—not just from hunger, but also from illnesses that followed. Many families, desperate to survive, left everything behind and emigrated. Over a million sailed across the ocean to America, Canada, and Australia on overcrowded ships, hoping for a better life. By the time the famine ended, Ireland had lost almost half its people, dropping from about eight million to five million souls. It’s remembered as one of the greatest human disasters in European history.
d12.scripture: Though no scripture speaks directly about the Irish Famine, many verses teach about caring for those who suffer. The Bible tells us in Matthew 25:35, "For I was an hungered, and ye gave me meat..." In the Book of Mormon, Mosiah 4:26 invites us to "impart of your substance to the poor." The Doctrine and Covenants, D&C 81:5, says, "succor the weak, lift up the hands which hang down, and strengthen the feeble knees." These passages teach us to notice those who are hungry or sad, and to help however we can, just as the Savior would.
d12.background: Before the famine, Ireland was a lush but poor country under British rule. Most Irish families were farmers, but they didn’t own the land—they rented it from wealthy British landlords. Potatoes grew well in Ireland’s cool, wet climate, and could feed large families from small plots of land. The potato became the single most important food for poor people; many ate little else. Families lived in small cottages, often crowded and simple, with few comforts. Daily life was hard, with children helping in the fields and mothers working to stretch what food they had. Irish society was also deeply Christian, with most people belonging to the Catholic faith, while many of the landowners practiced a different religion and lived in England, far removed from their tenants’ lives. This meant when disaster came, many Irish families were left without help from the people whose land they worked.

d13.talk: How do you think people felt when they saw the red sunsets after the volcano, and how could we help if something hard happened in our town?
d13.child: A big volcano called Krakatoa exploded so loudly people far away could hear it. The explosion made huge waves and changed the sky’s colors around the world. Even though it was scary, people helped each other, and the sunsets were beautiful for a long time.
d13.learn: From Krakatoa, we learn that the earth’s wonders can bring both beauty and trial. Disasters may come, but after difficulty, there can also be hope, new beginnings, and shared compassion. The world is deeply connected; what happens in one place often touches many others. We can teach our families to be prepared, to trust in God’s care, and to see how, through both storms and sunsets, we can find evidence of His hand and opportunities to serve.
d13.matters: Krakatoa’s eruption shows how one moment in nature can change life for people across the whole planet. For families of faith, it’s a reminder that all God’s children share one earth, and that caring for each other in times of trouble is part of His plan. Krakatoa’s sunsets inspired artists and caught the world’s attention, showing beauty mixed with tragedy. Today, by remembering Krakatoa, families can talk about preparing wisely for emergencies and noticing the wonders of God's world—sometimes, even after disaster, there are moments of surprising beauty and lessons in how we are all bound together.

sources.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica – Krakatoa eruption of 1883
Smithsonian Museum – The Aftermath of Krakatau
US Geological Survey – Impact of the 1883 eruption of Krakatoa

d13.evidence: Scientists have studied records from ships, local witnesses, and global weather observations to understand Krakatoa’s eruption. The sound was measured more than 4,800 kilometers away, making it the loudest sound ever recorded. Tsunami marks, written survivor accounts, and changes in climate data confirm the eruption’s effects—much of the globe saw colorful sunsets, and global temperatures dropped around 1.2°C for several years. Paintings from that time, along with diary entries and even tree rings, show the event was felt all over the earth. Today, modern volcano monitoring uses lessons learned from Krakatoa to help warn people in similar situations, showing the value of careful historical and scientific study.
d13.happened: On August 27, 1883, the volcano Krakatoa, which sits on an island in the Sunda Strait between Java and Sumatra in Indonesia, erupted in one of the most powerful explosions in recorded history. The eruption was so massive that it was heard thousands of kilometers away—people in Australia and even on Rodrigues Island in the Indian Ocean could hear the roar. The force of the blast was about 200 million tons of TNT. As the volcano exploded, much of the island itself collapsed into the sea, and waves as high as a 10-story building raced across the ocean. These tsunamis swept over nearby coastlines, destroying towns and villages and killing more than 36,000 people. Ash from the explosion shot high into the sky, blocking sunlight and changing weather patterns for several years. People all across the world saw the sky change, with sunsets turning vivid shades of red and orange for months to come. The ash and gases from Krakatoa's eruption cooled the earth and made global temperatures drop for a few years, reminding all how the natural world is connected.
d13.scripture: There is no scripture that tells of Krakatoa directly, but the Bible speaks often of the earth and its power. In Doctrine and Covenants 88:45-47, it says "the earth rolls upon her wings, and the sun giveth his light by day... All these are kingdoms, and any man who hath seen any or the least of these hath seen God moving in his majesty and power." The scriptures also teach that Heavenly Father is aware of all His children and invites us to love and help one another (Mosiah 2:17, Matthew 25:40). When the earth groans or changes, as it did with Krakatoa, we see the power of creation and are reminded to reach out, comfort, and care for others.
d13.background: Life in 1883 was marked by steam engines, growing cities, and new technologies, but most people still depended on nature for food, trade, and travel. Java and Sumatra were part of the Dutch East Indies, a colony of the Netherlands, with many people living in small coastal villages, fishing and farming as their ancestors had done. Telegrams and newspapers were spreading information faster than ever, so news of the disaster reached distant lands more quickly than it would have a generation earlier. Across the ocean, the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints had been founded only a few decades earlier in the United States. By the 1880s, the Church was beginning to send missionaries into far-off places like the Pacific Islands, showing the first signs of becoming a global faith family.

d14.talk: What is something we could do to help someone if there was a big storm in our town?
d14.child: A huge storm called a hurricane hit the city of Galveston and many people lost their homes and families. Neighbors and even strangers helped each other to be safe and start over. God wants us to help whenever someone is in trouble.
d14.learn: From the Galveston Hurricane, we learn that disasters can bring out courage and kindness in people. We see the need for preparation, for caring for our neighbors, and for working together through hard times. Our faith teaches us that we should help and comfort each other, especially when trouble comes suddenly, trusting in Heavenly Father’s love and doing our best to be His hands by serving others.
d14.matters: The Galveston Hurricane matters today because it showed how quickly life can change, and how communities respond to disaster. It taught the importance of preparing for natural hazards and led to advances in weather prediction and emergency planning. For families of faith, the story of Galveston also reminds us of our sacred responsibility to help others in times of need. Many people, including Latter-day Saint members and missionaries, helped rescue and care for survivors, showing Christlike compassion and service. The disaster tested—and revealed—the hearts of the people.

sources.name: National Weather Service: The Great Galveston Hurricane of 1900
Texas State Historical Association: Galveston Hurricane of 1900
Smithsonian Magazine: America’s Deadliest Disaster

d14.evidence: Historians have gathered accounts from survivors and old photographs that show the extent of the devastation in Galveston. Scientific studies confirm the hurricane as a Category 4 storm, with winds likely around 130–145 miles per hour and a storm surge of about 15 feet. The city’s records show the massive loss of life and property, and archaeological digs have found remnants of vanished neighborhoods beneath later rebuilding. Weather records and government reports from the time provide reliable details of the event. Today, Galveston's history museums and the National Weather Service preserve documents, photos, and personal stories that confirm what happened and how the city rebuilt afterward.
d14.happened: On September 8, 1900, a powerful hurricane swept over the city of Galveston, Texas. Early that day, dark clouds and strong winds signaled a storm, but few realized just how severe it would be. By afternoon, the winds reached over 100 miles per hour, and the sea began to rise. Galveston, built on a low barrier island, had no protective sea wall at the time. As the evening wore on, a massive wave, called a storm surge, crashed into the city. Water rushed through streets and homes, sweeping away buildings and entire neighborhoods. Families climbed onto rooftops and held on to whatever they could to survive. By the time the waters receded the next morning, the hurricane had destroyed more than 3,600 buildings. The loss was overwhelming—somewhere between 8,000 and 12,000 people lost their lives, marking it as the deadliest natural disaster in U.S. history. Survivors faced devastation, searching for loved ones and beginning the long, hard work of rebuilding their lives and their city.
d14.scripture: Several scriptures connect to what happened in Galveston. The Savior teaches us to 'love thy neighbor as thyself' (Luke 10:27) and, in the Book of Mormon, Alma commands the church to 'mourn with those that mourn; ...comfort those that stand in need of comfort' (Mosiah 18:9). These principles guided the faithful as they aided each other after the hurricane. The scriptures do not directly mention hurricanes, but stories such as the Savior calming the storm (Mark 4:35-41) remind us that He has power over nature and cares for us in all trials.
d14.background: At the turn of the 20th century, Galveston was a busy and growing port city with around 37,000 residents. Children played in the sandy streets, while adults worked in shipping, fishing, and business. There was a strong sense of community, and the city offered electricity, streetcars, and fine homes—luxuries rare in many parts of the country at that time. Most people received news by telegraph or newspaper, but weather forecasting was still very basic. Few believed a hurricane could strike so hard, and almost no one left before the storm hit. Galveston was also a place where many faiths lived side by side, and people often turned to their churches for support, especially when trouble came. Life was often busy and hopeful, but also depended much on the weather and the sea.

d15.talk: How can we help someone who is having a hard time, like people did after the earthquake?
d15.child: A big earthquake made San Francisco shake and burn, and many people lost their homes. Neighbors and helpers from far away worked together to help those in trouble. When something scary happens, being kind and working together can help us feel safe again.
d15.learn: We can learn that disasters can happen to anyone, no matter how strong or busy a city—or a family—might seem. What matters most is how people care for each other when trouble comes. The example of neighbors reaching out, sharing food and shelter, and working together to rebuild, shows what it means to love our neighbors as ourselves. These lessons help us remember to be prepared, to serve others, and to keep faith that even after hard times, with God’s help and each other's support, better days can come.
d15.matters: This event matters for many reasons. It showed how, even in strong and growing places, unexpected disaster can change everything in moments. Thousands of families lost their homes and loved ones, and the city had to be almost completely rebuilt. For families of faith, it is a reminder that trials can come without warning, but also that people and communities can reach out to help each other through kindness and service. When the earthquake struck, people—including members of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints—gathered food, clothing, and shelter for survivors. Their willingness to serve is an example families can follow today when others are in need.

sources.name: USGS Earthquake Hazards Program: 1906 San Francisco Earthquake
Encyclopedia Britannica: San Francisco Earthquake of 1906
National Archives: The San Francisco Earthquake and Fire, 1906
Church History: Early Church Humanitarian Work

d15.evidence: Scientists have long studied the 1906 earthquake, using modern tools to understand why it happened. The quake was caused by a sudden slip along the San Andreas Fault—a crack in the earth that runs through California. By looking at old photos, diaries, and news reports, historians have pieced together an accurate picture of the earthquake’s destruction and the many ways people responded to it. Archaeologists have even used the burned layers under the city as clues to how San Francisco was rebuilt afterward. The number of deaths and the vast extent of the destruction are well documented, and the rebuilding of the city was one of the largest efforts of its kind in American history.
d15.happened: On the morning of April 18, 1906, San Francisco was shaken by one of the most powerful earthquakes in American history. At 5:12 AM, families all over the city were awakened by the ground rolling and buildings swaying. The earthquake had a magnitude of about 7.9, and lasted less than a minute, but the destruction was immediate and severe. Streets split open, train tracks twisted, and entire neighborhoods buckled. But this was only the beginning. Gas pipes broke and fires sparked across the city, quickly spreading out of control. Over the next three days, these fires burned block after block, destroying 25,000 buildings. Water pipes had burst in the quake, making it nearly impossible for firefighters to stop the flames. When the fires finally died, most of San Francisco was in ruins. Between 3,000 and 6,000 people lost their lives, and most people in the city were left without homes. Out of about 410,000 residents, around 300,000 became homeless and needed shelter, food, and help from their neighbors.
d15.scripture: The scriptures teach us about helping others during times of trouble. In the Bible, the story of the Good Samaritan (Luke 10:25-37) reminds us to be kind and help those who are suffering, even when it is hard. The Book of Mormon encourages us to mourn with those that mourn and comfort those in need of comfort (Mosiah 18:8-9). While no scripture tells the story of the San Francisco earthquake and fire directly, these principles of love and service are at the heart of what many did for each other during and after the disaster.
d15.background: In 1906, San Francisco was a busy city full of people from all over the world. The city was known for its cable cars, its lively neighborhoods like Chinatown, and its hills looking out over the bay. Most people worked hard, whether running small shops, working on ships, or running newspapers that told of the latest gold discoveries. It was a time of great invention—telephones, electric lights, and streetcars were changing daily life. Many families lived in wooden houses, as buildings were often made from materials that were easy to find and quick to build with. San Francisco was also becoming a center for trade and travel on the West Coast, pulling in newcomers from across the United States and around the world. The city’s mix of cultures and new ideas made it a bright spot in California, though it meant many did not yet know each other well when disaster struck.

d16.talk: If someone in our family or neighborhood was sick, what could we do to help them feel loved and cared for?
d16.child: A sickness called the Spanish Flu made many people very sick all over the world. Families had to help each other, and even people who were strong and young could get very sick. People learned to be kind and take care of others during hard times.
d16.learn: From the Spanish Flu, we learn how quickly sickness can change the world, and how important it is to care for others, especially in scary times. We see how faith, patience, and working together can help families and communities heal, both in body and spirit. Preparing for difficulties, serving those in need, and trusting in Heavenly Father's love are all lessons that came from this challenging time.
d16.matters: The Spanish Flu matters because it shows how fragile human life can be, even in a time when people thought they were making great progress in science and technology. For families of faith, especially those who believe that God can work through both joy and hardship, it was a time to serve, mourn together, and rely on each other. For the Church, the organizational lessons learned in caring for hundreds of ill members helped inspire later programs for welfare and humanitarian aid, which serve millions today. This history reminds us to prepare both spiritually and practically for hard times, and trust in God's love and guidance.

sources.name: U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention: 1918 Pandemic (H1N1 virus)
Smithsonian Magazine: Why the Second Wave of the 1918 Spanish Flu Was So Deadly
National Museum of American History: The Deadliest Flu

d16.evidence: Scientists have studied the Spanish Flu using old medical records, letters, and newspapers from around the world. Researchers have even recovered pieces of the 1918 virus from bodies buried in Alaska's permafrost and examined them using modern science. This has helped us understand why it was so deadly and why it spread so fast. Historians agree that the estimates of people infected and killed are based on careful study of local and national reports, even though some places kept better records than others. All major histories and health organizations confirm the global scale and impact of the Spanish Flu. The record-keeping and evidence for this event are very strong and widely accepted.
d16.happened: The Spanish Flu pandemic began in early 1918 and swept across the world with alarming speed. It was caused by a new strain of the influenza virus, which spread from person to person through coughs, sneezes, and even by talking in close contact. This disease was especially dangerous because it did not just make older, frail people sick—it struck down healthy young adults and even children, which was very unusual. In just about two years, it infected around 500 million people, a third of the world’s population at that time. Between 50 and 100 million people died, making it the deadliest pandemic in recorded history. Whole communities were devastated. Streets seemed empty, shops closed, and funerals often happened without families able to gather. Hospitals were overwhelmed and doctors and nurses bravely cared for many more than they could manage. School buildings and churches were used as makeshift hospitals. The pandemic ended as suddenly as it began, leaving behind families who mourned and communities that had changed forever.
d16.scripture: While none of the scriptures speak directly about the Spanish Flu or pandemics, many passages in scripture talk about afflictions, compassion, and comforting the sick. James 5:14 in the Bible says, 'Is any sick among you? Let him call for the elders of the church; and let them pray over him.' In the Book of Mormon, Mosiah 18:9 teaches to 'mourn with those that mourn; yea, and comfort those that stand in need of comfort.' The Doctrine and Covenants 81:5 says to 'succor the weak, lift up the hands which hang down, and strengthen the feeble knees.' These scriptures encourage caring for others in times of trial, just as many did during the Spanish Flu.
d16.background: The world in 1918 was still reeling from the terrible costs of World War I. People had just lived through years of fighting, hunger, and fear. In towns and cities, families hoped to rebuild their lives after the war's end. However, life was not calm or easy. Most people did not have access to the modern medicine or good antibiotics we have today. News traveled slowly, and many did not know how to protect themselves except by staying away from crowds. Many lived in close quarters, especially in cities, which made the spread of sickness fast and hard to control. Children often helped take care of siblings, and neighbors sometimes gave comfort or food to each other. For members of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, this was also a time when missionary work was spreading across the globe. That important effort halted because missionaries brought illness home or became very sick themselves.

d17.t: China Floods — Deadliest Disaster in History
d17.talk: What can we do to help people who are affected by big storms or floods?
d17.child: A long time ago, in 1931, big rivers in China overflowed and caused a huge flood. Many people lost their homes, and some got very sick because the water was dirty. It was a very sad time for many families.
d17.learn: The 1931 China floods teach us the importance of disaster preparedness and the need for strong community support systems. They remind us that natural disasters can have far-reaching consequences, especially when compounded by political and economic instability. As families, we can learn to be more self-reliant, to plan for emergencies, and to extend help to others in times of need, embodying the principles of charity and service.
d17.matters: The 1931 China floods highlight the profound impact natural disasters can have on societies, especially those already facing political and economic challenges. For families of faith, this event serves as a reminder of the importance of preparedness and community support in times of crisis. It also underscores the need for compassion and aid to those affected by such tragedies, reflecting the gospel principle of loving and serving our neighbors.

sources.name: 1931 China floods
Central China flood, 1931 | DisasterHistory.org
Highest death toll from a flood | Guinness World Records

d17.evidence: Historical records from the time, including reports from the National Flood Relief Commission and studies by scholars like John Lossing Buck, provide detailed accounts of the 1931 floods. These documents describe the extent of the flooding, the number of people affected, and the subsequent famine and disease outbreaks. While exact death tolls vary among sources, the consensus is that the disaster had a catastrophic impact on central China, affecting millions and leading to significant loss of life.
d17.happened: In the summer of 1931, central China experienced one of the deadliest natural disasters in recorded history. The Yangtze, Yellow, and Huai Rivers overflowed due to a combination of heavy rainfall, snowmelt, and previous drought conditions. This led to widespread flooding that submerged vast areas, including major cities like Wuhan and Nanjing. The floodwaters destroyed homes, farmland, and infrastructure, leaving millions homeless. The immediate impact was catastrophic, with an estimated 150,000 people drowning in the initial stages. However, the aftermath proved even more devastating. The destruction of crops and food supplies led to severe famine, and the unsanitary conditions caused outbreaks of diseases such as cholera, measles, and dysentery. Estimates of the total death toll vary widely, ranging from 422,499 to as many as 4 million people, making it possibly the deadliest natural disaster in human history.
d17.scripture: The scriptures teach us about the importance of preparedness and caring for others in times of need. In the Doctrine and Covenants 38:30, the Lord advises, "If ye are prepared ye shall not fear." This emphasizes the need for physical and spiritual readiness. Additionally, in Mosiah 2:17, we are reminded that "when ye are in the service of your fellow beings ye are only in the service of your God," encouraging us to assist those who are suffering.
d17.background: In the early 20th century, China was undergoing significant political and social changes. The country was transitioning from the Qing Dynasty to the Republic of China, leading to political instability and civil unrest. Many regions were impoverished, and infrastructure was underdeveloped. The Yangtze River Basin, a densely populated area, was particularly vulnerable to natural disasters due to its geography and the reliance of its inhabitants on agriculture. The combination of political turmoil and economic hardship left the population ill-prepared to handle a disaster of such magnitude.

d18.talk: How do you think people can help others when a big disaster happens, even if they live far away?
d18.child: A giant storm called a cyclone hit Bangladesh long ago. Huge waves covered the land and many people lost their homes. Afterward, people from around the world helped those who needed it most.
d18.learn: We can learn to watch out for one another, especially in times of trouble. Families and communities are safer when they are prepared and when they work together. This event encourages us to be ready to help, whether by sharing, giving, or comforting. It also teaches the importance of listening to warnings and seeking ways to prevent harm before tragedy strikes. Caring for others, especially those far away or different from us, brings us closer to our Heavenly Father’s ways.
d18.matters: The Bhola Cyclone matters because it showed how vulnerable people can be when living with nature’s dangers and without enough help or warning. The tragedy led the world to see how important it is to prepare for disasters and care for those who are suffering. For families of faith, this event reminds us that our call to help others can cross oceans and borders. The global response to the Bhola disaster laid groundwork for humanitarian aid efforts that many, including Latter-day Saints, continue today. It showed that loving our neighbor means reaching out both near and far, just as Heavenly Father desires.

sources.name: Encyclopedia Britannica: Bhola cyclone
National Centers for Environmental Information (NOAA): The 1970 Bhola Cyclone
BBC: Bangladesh’s deadliest storm remembered
Humanitarian aid - Newsroom, churchofjesuschrist.org

d18.evidence: Scientists have studied weather data, historical records, and surviving eyewitness accounts to confirm the scale and impact of the Bhola Cyclone. Satellite images and meteorological records show how quickly the storm gained strength over the Bay of Bengal. Studies of the storm’s aftermath found that most deaths came from the storm surge flooding that swept over the flat land. Aid organizations and news agencies from around the world kept records of how people responded and how much international help was sent. This event is well documented through photos, interviews with survivors, and official reports, leaving little doubt about what happened or why it was so devastating.
d18.happened: On November 12, 1970, one of the most powerful and deadly cyclones ever recorded slammed into the coast of what was then East Pakistan, now called Bangladesh. The Bhola Cyclone struck overnight, carrying winds estimated up to 115 miles per hour and pushing a wall of ocean water—the storm surge—deep into the low-lying Ganges-Brahmaputra delta. Villages, rice fields, and small islands crowded with families were swept over by waves, destroying homes and crops, leaving very little behind. Most of the 300,000 to 500,000 people who died were killed by the sudden rush of water. Many survivors lost loved ones and everything they owned. In the days that followed, emergency help was slow to reach the hardest hit areas due to destroyed roads and lack of preparation. The heartbreaking scale of the disaster made headlines around the globe and moved many to send aid and support. It also led to deep anger in East Pakistan against the distant government in West Pakistan, where decisions and resources were controlled but much help did not arrive. This disaster became one of the sparks that led to the struggle for independence that created Bangladesh the next year.
d18.scripture: Though no scripture speaks directly of cyclones, the Savior’s commandment to 'love thy neighbour as thyself' (Matthew 22:39) urges us to care for those in need, especially in times of disaster. Mosiah 4:26 in the Book of Mormon teaches believers to 'administer of your substance unto him that standeth in need.' Both verses remind us that helping in times of great distress is a sacred duty and reflects God’s love in our actions.
d18.background: At the time of the Bhola Cyclone, East Pakistan was one of the most crowded and poor parts of the world. Most people lived in small villages and farmed rice, fish, or jute near the rivers and the sea. Families counted on the yearly rains and the land’s rich soil, but they were always at risk from storms and floods. The local government had little power, and most major decisions were made in West Pakistan, the other half of the country, far across India. Many in East Pakistan felt neglected, especially when it came to safety and disaster planning. Before 1970, weather warnings were basic, and few families had strong homes or ways to escape incoming storms. Life was often difficult and uncertain, but communities tended to be close and families relied on each other.

d19.talk: What is something we can do to help others when something hard happens, even if it’s far away?
d19.child: A giant wave called a tsunami crashed into the land and hurt many people. People from all over the world helped those who needed it. Helping others makes families strong and shows love.
d19.learn: From this disaster, we learn that both nature and life are unpredictable and sometimes terribly hard. We also see how quickly people can come together, share, and comfort one another when tragedy strikes. For families who trust in God, it’s a reminder to reach out to help, as we are all part of His family. It’s also wise to teach children and families ways to be ready and caring when emergencies happen. Above all, we learn that hope and kindness can shine even in the darkest of times.
d19.matters: The Indian Ocean tsunami matters to the world because it showed how quickly life can change and how deeply connected people are, no matter their country or background. For families of faith, the disaster is a reminder that in moments of overwhelming loss, the goodness in others can bring hope and healing. The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints and many other faith groups came together, sending aid and support, which showed that love and service cross all boundaries. It reminds us to be prepared for emergencies, to help those in need, and to trust that God is mindful of all His children, even in very hard times.

sources.name: Smithsonian Ocean: Indian Ocean Tsunami
United States Geological Survey (USGS): Indian Ocean Tsunami
The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints Newsroom: Tsunami Relief
Encyclopedia Britannica: Indian Ocean Tsunami 2004

d19.evidence: The story of the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami is thoroughly documented in scientific studies, survivor accounts, and international reports. Geological evidence confirms the massive earthquake off the coast of Sumatra, which is part of a known subduction zone where two plates of the earth’s crust meet. After the earthquake, deep-sea sensors and satellite imagery recorded the speed and scale of the tsunami waves. Scientists have used these records to model how the water moved and to learn how to better prepare for future tsunamis. International aid agencies and news reports, as well as local records, support the totals of deaths, injuries, and massive displacement. The widespread, collaborative response is also well-recorded, with organizations like the United Nations, Red Cross, and dozens of governments participating.
d19.happened: On the morning of December 26, 2004, a massive underwater earthquake with a magnitude of 9.1 struck off the coast of Sumatra, Indonesia. The energy released by this quake was so intense that it caused the entire planet to vibrate slightly. Within minutes, giant waves known as a tsunami raced across the Indian Ocean at the speed of a jet plane. These waves crashed into the shores of 14 different countries, including Indonesia, Sri Lanka, India, Thailand, and as far away as Somalia in Africa. Towns and villages close to the ocean were hit hardest, with homes and entire communities swept away. More than 227,000 people lost their lives, making it the deadliest tsunami in recorded history. About 1.7 million people became homeless, losing nearly everything in a single day. In the weeks that followed, families searched for loved ones, and local survivors—often working together with strangers—did everything they could to rescue the injured and take care of the living. The disastrous scale of the tsunami touched the hearts of people all over the world, leading to an immense outpouring of support and aid.
d19.scripture: While no scripture describes a tsunami exactly, many scriptures teach about caring for those in need and responding to suffering. In the New Testament, Jesus teaches, 'Verily I say unto you, Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me' (Matthew 25:40). The Book of Mormon recounts times of great destruction, such as at the death of Christ, but always emphasizes turning to God and helping one another (see 3 Nephi 8–9). Doctrine and Covenants 81:5 teaches, 'Succor the weak, lift up the hands which hang down, and strengthen the feeble knees.' These passages point us to compassion, quick action, and faith during disaster.
d19.background: In 2004, the nations around the Indian Ocean included vast areas of rich natural beauty, from Indonesian rainforests to the sandy beaches of Thailand and the hill country of Sri Lanka. Many families lived near the coast, relying on fishing, farming, or tourism for their daily bread. December is a holiday season for many, so the beaches were busy with visitors as well as locals. This part of the world had experienced earthquakes before, but very few people in these countries had learned about tsunamis or how to recognize the warning signs, like the sudden retreat of the ocean. The communities affected were made up of many faiths and traditions, all bound by family and neighborhood ties. On ordinary days, children went to school, adults worked hard, and local markets bustled from sunrise onward.

d20.talk: How can we help someone who is having a hard time, like the people in Haiti did after the earthquake?
d20.child: A huge earthquake hit Haiti in 2010 and many homes fell down. Lots of people needed help, and many helpers came. Even when it’s hard, people can help each other and feel God’s love.
d20.learn: We can learn from the Haiti earthquake how important it is to look out for each other, especially in hard times. It teaches us to be grateful for what we have and to be prepared for emergencies. We also learn that even when things seem hopeless, serving others brings hope. Faith in Jesus Christ can help people heal and rebuild, no matter how difficult their trials are.
d20.matters: The Haiti earthquake matters because it was one of the deadliest disasters in recent history, happening to a nation already facing deep poverty. It reminds us of how suddenly life can change, and how important it is to care for each other when tragedy comes. For families of faith, it’s a lesson in showing compassion and being ready to help. The Church’s response—offering aid and comfort—shows that Heavenly Father’s love reaches everywhere, even in the hardest times. The resilience and growth of the Church in Haiti since the earthquake also testify that faith can bring light even after the darkest days.

d20.evidence: Scientific studies confirm that the 2010 earthquake in Haiti measured magnitude 7.0 on the Richter scale. The epicenter was only 25 kilometers from Port-au-Prince, which made the shaking extremely strong in the capital and surrounding areas. Engineers explain that many buildings in Haiti were not built to withstand earthquakes, which led to so much damage and loss of life. Satellite images and ground surveys from after the event show massive destruction. Relief agencies, governments, and historians have all carefully recorded what happened and worked together to help Haiti recover, showing strong evidence of the earthquake’s effects and response.
d20.happened: On January 12, 2010, a powerful earthquake struck near the city of Port-au-Prince, Haiti’s capital. The ground shook violently, and within only about thirty seconds, thousands of buildings collapsed. Hospitals, schools, and homes were turned to rubble. Streets filled with dust and cries for help. Many people were trapped inside fallen buildings, and neighbors rushed to help each other before rescue teams could reach them. It is estimated that between 100,000 and 316,000 people lost their lives, though the exact number remains debated because of the chaos and lack of records. About 1.5 million people were left without homes. In the days after the earthquake, families slept outdoors, desperately searching for their loved ones. Relief arrived from around the world, but the damage was so wide and deep that recovery was painfully slow. For Haiti, already one of the poorest countries in the world, this disaster made life even harder, but it also showed the world how much people can care and help when something terrible happens.
d20.scripture: When thinking of the Haiti earthquake, certain scriptures about comfort, service, and compassion feel important. In the Book of Mormon, Mosiah 18:9 teaches us to "mourn with those that mourn" and "comfort those that stand in need of comfort." In the New Testament, Matthew 25:40 says, "Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me." These passages teach us to serve and lift others in their hard times, just as Christ would.
d20.background: Before the earthquake, Haiti was already facing many hardships. It is located on the western part of the island of Hispaniola in the Caribbean and is the poorest country in the Western Hemisphere. Most Haitian families lived in simple homes, often made of weak materials like cinder blocks and tin roofs. Jobs were hard to find, and many people did not have access to clean water, good schools, or health care. Everyday life required creativity and courage, as people worked hard to provide for their children. Despite these challenges, Haitian culture is rich in music, faith, and strong family ties. Many Haitians belong to different Christian faiths, and The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints had a growing presence, with missionaries and local members actively serving their neighbors.

e01.fall: The fall of the Akkadian Empire happened over many years, beginning around 2193 BC. As the empire grew, keeping control over distant lands became harder. Local governors sometimes rebelled, and the cost of constant warfare strained the empire’s resources. Sargon’s descendants faced growing unrest among the people, hardships brought by drought, and changes in the rivers that hurt farming. Archaeologists have found signs of a sudden change in climate—possibly a long, severe drought—called the '4.2-kiloyear event,' which led to famine and the weakening of cities. Meanwhile, groups from the north called the Gutians invaded, taking advantage of the weakened Akkadian state. Internal divisions and the growing pride of later kings may have led to loss of respect and loyalty among the people. As these troubles stacked up, the empire could not hold together. By about 2154 BC, the Akkadian Empire had fallen, and much of Mesopotamia returned to smaller, separate kingdoms, though the memory of Akkad lived on and shaped later Babylonian and Assyrian empires.
e01.rise: The rise of the Akkadian Empire began with Sargon, around 2334 BC. Sargon was born in humble circumstances, possibly as a cupbearer to the king of Kish, a Sumerian city-state. He came to power through clever leadership, military skill, and perhaps some luck in the political struggles of the Sumerian cities. The fertile land between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers made large cities possible, providing a strong base for agriculture and trade. Sargon’s idea was new for his time: instead of ruling just a single city, he set out to conquer and unify all the Sumerian cities, using his army, which became the first professional standing army in history. Sargon established a central government, built a capital at Akkad, and appointed loyal governors over the cities he conquered, tying them together under a common administration. The Akkadian language was used in all official business, helping people from different backgrounds to work together. Through trade, alliances, and force, Sargon’s rule stretched from the Persian Gulf to the Mediterranean, opening new routes for goods and ideas. His grandson Naram-Sin later took these ideas farther, even declaring himself divine. Belief in the king’s greatness, the promise of organized rule, and new ways of using language and power all helped the Akkadian Empire rise.
e01.talk: Why is it important to remember and share the good things people learned in the past?
e01.child: Long ago, Sargon became the first king to unite many cities in a land called Mesopotamia. His empire helped people share ideas and writing, and some of Abraham’s family lived there too. God’s people can help keep good things safe for everyone.
e01.learn: From the Akkadian Empire, we learn how language, law, and leadership can shape the future, and how pride, wisdom, and humility might decide what endures. Just as the Akkadians preserved earlier knowledge, we can protect what is good and true for those who follow. Families can talk about how choices and unity matter—whether in empires or at home.
e01.matters: The story of the Akkadian Empire matters because it teaches how people can work together to create something bigger than themselves. Families of faith can see the hand of Heavenly Father in how the spread of writing, law, and government made it possible, long after, to protect and share holy writings such as the Bible. The Akkadian legacy also reminds us that power can bless many or harm many, depending on the choices of those who hold it. For the world, the Akkadian Empire showed how ideas, language, and law can knit many different people together—a lesson that still shapes societies today.

e01.evidence: Archaeologists have uncovered vast cuneiform tablet libraries, royal inscriptions, city ruins, and cylindrical seals from Akkadian times. Sargon's conquests and administrative reforms are recorded in these texts and echoed in Sumerian king lists. The famous 'Stele of Naram-Sin' shows his grandson as a mighty conqueror. Clay tablets and monumental inscriptions prove the wide use of the Akkadian language. However, the exact location of the city of Akkad itself has not yet been found. Despite this, historians widely agree about the empire, thanks to thousands of matching records and ongoing archaeological discoveries across Mesopotamia.
e01.happened: Around 2334 BC, a man named Sargon rose to power in Mesopotamia, a land known today as Iraq and Syria. Sargon, whose name meant 'the true king,' united the once-separated Sumerian city-states under his rule, leading to the creation of the Akkadian Empire. This was the first time in recorded history that a single ruler governed such a wide span of cities and lands in the ancient world. Sargon built a new capital, Akkad, and through wars and careful alliances, extended his rule from the Persian Gulf all the way to the Mediterranean Sea. After Sargon, his grandson Naram-Sin carried the empire to even greater heights, calling himself 'King of the Four Quarters' and building grand temples and monuments. The Akkadian Empire made Akkadian the language of government and trade, laying the foundation for future empires. Over 180 years, it weathered rebellions and challenges. Yet, its great cities, organized government, and strong armies could not last forever. Eventually, pressures from invaders, climate changes, and internal unrest would bring it to an end, but the Akkadian Empire left a deep mark on history.
e01.scripture: While the Bible does not specifically name the Akkadian Empire, it tells of Abraham, born in Ur of the Chaldees (Genesis 11:28, Abraham 1:1), which was an important Sumerian-Akkadian city. The Lord called Abraham to a special covenant, showing that even in the world's greatest cities and empires, He remembers His people and His promises. The scriptures teach that when nations remember God and uphold righteous principles, they prosper (Ether 2:12; Proverbs 14:34), and when pride and selfishness take over, decline often follows.
e01.background: Before the Akkadian Empire, Mesopotamia was a land of independent city-states, each with its own ruler, its own gods, and its own walls. The Sumerians, living in cities like Ur, Uruk, and Lagash, built the earliest known cities and invented cuneiform writing, the world’s first recorded written language. People farmed the rich soil between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers, raised livestock, and traded goods. They worshiped in grand temples called ziggurats, and their lives turned around the rhythms of planting, harvest, and festival. The Akkadians were a Semitic-speaking people living nearby, merging their culture with the older Sumerian traditions. Life was not always easy: floods, rivalries, and scarcity often led to fighting and alliances. Into this world, Sargon transformed the region by forging the first empire, bringing a new era of unity and shared culture.

e02.fall: After Hammurabi's death in 1750 BC, the Babylonian Empire faced challenges that led to its decline. His successors lacked his leadership qualities, resulting in weakened central authority. Internal strife and administrative inefficiencies emerged, undermining the stability he had established. Externally, the empire faced invasions from neighboring peoples, such as the Hittites, who sacked Babylon around 1595 BC. These combined internal and external pressures eroded the empire's cohesion, leading to its eventual fall and the fragmentation of Mesopotamia into smaller, competing states.
e02.rise: Hammurabi's rise to power was facilitated by several factors. Geographically, Babylon was situated along the Euphrates River, providing fertile land for agriculture and a strategic position for trade. Hammurabi's leadership was marked by military prowess and diplomatic acumen. He formed alliances with neighboring city-states and, over time, conquered them, expanding Babylon's territory. His ability to integrate diverse regions under a centralized administration allowed for efficient governance. The implementation of the Code of Hammurabi established a uniform legal system, reinforcing his authority and unifying the populace. These strategic choices and favorable conditions enabled Babylon to emerge as a dominant power in Mesopotamia during his reign from 1792 to 1750 BC.
e02.talk: Why do you think it's important to have rules that everyone knows and follows?
e02.child: A long time ago, a king named Hammurabi made rules to help people live together peacefully. He wrote these rules on a big stone so everyone could see them. This helped people know what was right and wrong.
e02.learn: From Hammurabi's unification of Mesopotamia and his codification of laws, we learn the significance of strong leadership and the establishment of clear legal frameworks in fostering societal stability and justice. It teaches us that laws, when applied fairly, can protect the vulnerable and promote harmony within diverse communities. This historical example encourages us to value justice and the rule of law in our own lives.
e02.matters: Hammurabi's unification of Mesopotamia under a centralized government marked a significant shift from fragmented city-states to a cohesive empire, setting a precedent for future civilizations. The Code of Hammurabi is one of the earliest examples of written law, emphasizing the importance of codified legal systems in maintaining social order. For families of faith, this historical event underscores the value of justice and the rule of law, principles that are foundational in many religious teachings. It also highlights the role of divinely inspired leadership in guiding societies toward righteousness and equity.
