Encyclopaedia Britannica - Abraham

g06.evidence: Today, historians and archaeologists do not have direct evidence proving that Abraham or Isaac lived or that this event happened exactly as described. Mount Moriah is linked by tradition to the Temple Mount in Jerusalem, an important site for Jews, Christians, and Muslims. Many ancient stories have roots in real places and peoples but may be retold and changed over centuries. Most scholars consider Abraham’s story as part of early sacred storytelling, deeply meaningful to many but difficult to confirm with scientific methods. Archeology in the area does show that people lived in tents, raised animals, and made sacrifices, matching the background the Bible describes.
g06.happened: Long ago, Heavenly Father asked Abraham to do something very hard. He told Abraham to take his beloved son Isaac to a mountain called Moriah and offer him as a sacrifice. Abraham loved Isaac dearly, and this request must have felt confusing and painful. However, Abraham trusted God and obeyed, taking Isaac up the mountain. When they arrived, Abraham built an altar and prepared everything. Just as Abraham was about to offer his son, an angel called out and stopped him, saying that he had shown his faith. At that moment, Abraham spotted a ram caught in the bushes, and God told him to offer the ram instead of Isaac. This story shows deep faith and obedience, and also hints at something important Heavenly Father would do in the future.
g06.scripture: The main story is found in Genesis 22:1-19 in the Old Testament. Jesus refers to Abraham and this event in John 8:56. In the Book of Mormon, Abraham's faith and the story of Isaac are mentioned in Jacob 4:5. The Doctrine and Covenants (D&C 132:36-37) and Pearl of Great Price (Abraham 1:15; 2:12) also discuss Abraham’s faithfulness. These passages tell about Abraham’s obedience and how this experience is a symbol, or a type, of Heavenly Father’s own sacrifice of Jesus Christ.
g06.background: This story happened in a time when people lived simple, close-to-the-earth lives, herding animals, growing crops, and living in tents or small homes. Abraham and his family believed in one God, very different from their neighbors who often believed in many gods. Offering sacrifices was a common practice in ancient times, meant to show devotion or to ask for blessings. Mount Moriah, where this event is said to have taken place, lies in what is now Jerusalem, an area that would later become very important for many faiths. Life in Abraham's day was full of traveling, seeking water and pasture, and relying on family and trust in God to get through hard times.

g07.talk: How do you think Joseph felt when he saw his brothers again after so many years, and why do you think he chose to forgive them?
g07.child: Joseph’s brothers sold him and he ended up in Egypt, far from home. He still chose to be good and helped many people when there was no food. God helped Joseph, and Joseph forgave his brothers.
g07.learn: Families can learn that choosing to forgive, trusting in God, and doing our best can make good things happen even after hard times. Joseph’s story also teaches us to be brave when we do not understand why things are hard and to look for ways to help others, just as Joseph helped his brothers and many nations.
g07.matters: Joseph’s story matters because it shows that God can turn hard times into blessings and cares about each person’s faith and choices. For families of faith, Joseph’s forgiveness and wisdom inspire us to trust God during unfair or painful moments. He is also considered a 'type' of Jesus Christ: betrayed, wronged, but then raised up to save others. Seeing God’s hand in Joseph’s life encourages us to believe that God’s purposes can still go forward, even when things look grim, and that our hardships can help others.

sources.name: The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints – Joseph in Egypt
British Museum – Life in Ancient Egypt
National Geographic – Who Was Joseph, the Biblical Dreamer?

g07.evidence: Archaeologists have found many things from ancient Egypt that teach us about life there, including records of famines and food storage, which match what the Bible describes. However, there is no direct archaeological evidence that names Joseph or proves every detail of his story—this is common for people who lived thousands of years ago. Ancient Egyptian records do mention foreign officials who rose to power, making Joseph’s rise possible within that society. Historians generally agree Egypt experienced famines and had foreign leaders, but whether Joseph’s exact story happened as told is still discussed among scholars.
g07.happened: Joseph was one of the youngest sons of Jacob, living first in Canaan with his large family. Because Joseph’s father favored him, his brothers became jealous and sold him to traders, who took him down to Egypt. In Egypt, Joseph was bought by Potiphar, an officer of Pharaoh. Although Joseph tried to do what was right, he was falsely accused by Potiphar’s wife and put into prison. Even in prison, Joseph tried to serve faithfully, and God blessed him with the ability to interpret dreams. When Pharaoh heard of this gift, he called Joseph out of prison to explain troubling dreams. Joseph, relying on God, interpreted them to mean seven years of plenty would be followed by seven years of famine. Pharaoh made Joseph a leader over all of Egypt to prepare for the famine. When the famine struck, Joseph’s own brothers came to Egypt to buy food, and Joseph forgave them, caring for his family and many others.
g07.scripture: Joseph’s story is told in the Bible in Genesis chapters 37 and 39–50. Stephen talks about him in Acts 7:9–16, connecting his life to God’s great work. The Book of Mormon (2 Nephi 3:4-15) also speaks about Joseph’s role in preparing for his descendants’ blessings. There are also lessons of forgiveness, patience, and trusting God, taught in Doctrine and Covenants 121:7–8, which reminds us that adversity can give greater understanding and strength.
g07.background: During Joseph’s time, both Canaan and Egypt were ancient lands with families who moved often with their flocks or worked long days building and farming. Families held traditions from their ancestors, and many people believed in many gods. Egypt was a powerful, organized place with a Pharaoh as king and officials to help him. Life for an ordinary person meant hard work—growing crops, gathering water, or caring for animals. Before Joseph’s story, his father Jacob had received special promises from God, and the family lived as shepherds. Disagreements and jealousy between brothers were common in many families, and it was not unusual then for people to move and even become servants or slaves in other countries because of war, famine, or family need.

g08.talk: How did God show His power when He helped Moses lead the Israelites out of Egypt?
g08.child: God helped Moses lead the Israelites out of Egypt, showing His power and love. He gave them commandments to follow, teaching them how to live. This story reminds us to trust God and follow His teachings.
g08.learn: The story of Moses and the Exodus teaches us about God's power to deliver His people from bondage and His desire for them to live according to His commandments. It emphasizes the importance of faith, obedience, and trust in God's promises. The narrative also highlights the significance of remembering and teaching God's acts to future generations, as seen in the institution of the Passover. For families, it serves as a reminder to rely on God's guidance during challenging times and to pass on the stories of faith to their children.
g08.matters: The Exodus is a foundational event in the history of Israel, symbolizing deliverance and God's faithfulness. It demonstrates God's power to save His people and His desire for them to live according to His commandments. For families of faith, the story teaches trust in God's promises and the importance of obedience. It also highlights the significance of remembering and teaching God's acts to future generations, as seen in the institution of the Passover. The Exodus narrative has inspired countless believers to rely on God's guidance during challenging times.

sources.name: World History Encyclopedia: Moses
Wikipedia: The Exodus
Jewish Bible Quarterly: Extra-Biblical Evidence of the Exodus

g08.evidence: The historicity of the Exodus is a subject of debate among scholars. While the Bible provides a detailed account, there is a lack of direct archaeological evidence confirming the event. Egyptian records from the period do not mention the Exodus or Moses. Some scholars suggest that the absence of evidence may be due to the Egyptians not recording defeats or events that portrayed them negatively. Others propose that the story may have a historical core, reflecting smaller-scale migrations or events that were later expanded upon. The Merneptah Stele, dating to around 1208 BC, mentions 'Israel' in Canaan, indicating the presence of the Israelites in the region at that time. However, this does not directly confirm the Exodus narrative. Overall, the lack of direct evidence leaves the historicity of the Exodus open to interpretation.
g08.happened: Around 1450 BC, the Israelites were enslaved in Egypt. Heavenly Father called Moses to lead them to freedom. Moses, with his brother Aaron, approached Pharaoh, asking him to release the Israelites. Pharaoh refused, so God sent ten plagues upon Egypt, each demonstrating His power. The final plague, the death of the firstborn, led Pharaoh to release the Israelites. They left Egypt in haste, crossing the Red Sea, which God parted for them. After crossing, the sea closed, drowning the pursuing Egyptian army. The Israelites then journeyed through the wilderness toward Mount Sinai. At Sinai, Moses received the Ten Commandments from God, establishing a covenant with the Israelites. They wandered in the desert for 40 years before reaching the Promised Land of Canaan.
g08.scripture: The Book of Exodus (chapters 1-15) details the story of Moses and the Israelites' departure from Egypt. In 1 Corinthians 10:1-4, Paul refers to the Israelites' journey, stating, '...they drank of that spiritual Rock that followed them: and that Rock was Christ.' This passage connects the physical sustenance provided during the Exodus to Jesus Christ, emphasizing the spiritual nourishment He offers. Additionally, Hebrews 11:24-29 highlights Moses' faith in leading the Israelites out of Egypt, underscoring the importance of faith in God's promises.
g08.background: Egypt during this period was a powerful kingdom, known for its monumental architecture and advanced civilization. The Israelites, living in Egypt, were subjected to harsh slavery, building cities like Pithom and Rameses. Daily life for the Israelites was grueling, involving heavy labor under oppressive conditions. Egyptian society was hierarchical, with Pharaoh at the top, considered a god-king. The Egyptians worshiped multiple deities, and their culture was rich in art, literature, and science. The Israelites maintained their distinct identity and faith in the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, despite their bondage.

g09.talk: How can trusting in God help us face our own challenges?
g09.child: David, a young shepherd, trusted God and defeated a giant named Goliath with just a stone and a sling. This shows that with faith, we can overcome big problems.
g09.learn: We learn that faith in God can empower us to face and overcome great challenges. David's example encourages us to trust in the Lord's strength rather than our own, reminding us that with His help, we can achieve what may seem impossible.
g09.matters: This story illustrates the power of faith and trust in God. David's victory over Goliath symbolizes that with divine support, even the seemingly insurmountable can be overcome. For families of faith, it teaches that courage and reliance on the Lord can lead to triumph over challenges, no matter how daunting they appear.

sources.name: Valley of Elah
David & Goliath - World History Encyclopedia
David and Goliath: truth or legend?

g09.evidence: Archaeological excavations in the Valley of Elah have uncovered sites like Khirbet Qeiyafa, a fortified city dating to the late 11th and early 10th centuries BC. This city features two gates, leading some scholars to identify it as Shaaraim, mentioned in 1 Samuel 17:52. Inscriptions found at Khirbet Qeiyafa, written in early Canaanite or Hebrew script, along with the absence of pig bones in animal remains, suggest an Israelite or Judean cultural identity. Additionally, a ceramic shard discovered at Tell es-Safi, identified as the biblical Gath, contains an inscription with names similar to "Goliath," indicating that such names were in use during that period. However, direct evidence linking these findings to the specific events of David and Goliath remains inconclusive.
g09.happened: In the Valley of Elah, a young shepherd named David faced Goliath, a giant warrior from the Philistine army. Goliath challenged the Israelites to send a champion to fight him in single combat. David, trusting in the Lord, stepped forward with only his sling and five smooth stones. With a single shot, he struck Goliath on the forehead, causing the giant to fall. David then used Goliath's own sword to kill him, leading to the Philistines' defeat and David's rise to prominence.
g09.scripture: The account of David and Goliath is detailed in 1 Samuel 17. This chapter describes the confrontation, David's faith, and the subsequent victory that led to his recognition among the Israelites.
g09.background: During this time, the Israelites and Philistines were in conflict over territory. The Philistines, originating from the Aegean region, had settled along the coastal plains of Canaan and were known for their advanced weaponry and military prowess. The Israelites, a confederation of tribes, were establishing themselves in the central highlands. Daily life for Israelites involved agriculture, herding, and adherence to their covenant with God. The Valley of Elah, a fertile region with significant strategic importance, was the setting for this pivotal encounter.

g10.talk: Why do you think having a special place to worship Heavenly Father is important for families?
g10.child: King Solomon built a beautiful temple long ago where people went to worship Heavenly Father. It was a special place filled with His presence. Today, temples are still places where families can feel close to God and each other.
g10.learn: The story of Solomon's Temple teaches us the importance of dedicating spaces and efforts to worship and connect with Heavenly Father. It reminds us that sacred places can strengthen our faith and bring communities together in devotion. For families, it underscores the value of creating environments where spiritual growth and unity can flourish.
g10.matters: Solomon's Temple holds profound significance as it established a central place for the Israelites to connect with Heavenly Father. For families of faith today, it serves as a reminder of the importance of sacred spaces dedicated to worship and communion with God. Temples are places where families can be sealed together for eternity, strengthening their bonds and commitment to divine principles. The story of Solomon's Temple encourages believers to seek and cherish their own sacred experiences and places of worship.

sources.name: Solomon's Temple - Wikipedia
A Rival to Solomon's Temple - Biblical Archaeology Society
Rare archaeological stone seal uncovered in Jerusalem - The Jerusalem Post

g10.evidence: Archaeological evidence directly confirming the existence of Solomon's Temple is limited, primarily due to the sensitivity of the Temple Mount site, which restricts extensive excavations. However, discoveries such as the Tel Motza temple, dated to the 9th century BC and located near Jerusalem, share architectural similarities with biblical descriptions of Solomon's Temple. Additionally, a rare stone seal from the First Temple period, bearing a name in paleo-Hebrew script, was discovered near the Southern Wall of Jerusalem’s Temple Mount, providing indirect evidence of the era's cultural and religious practices.
g10.happened: Around 970 BC, King Solomon, son of King David, built the first permanent temple in Jerusalem, known as Solomon's Temple. This sacred house was constructed on the Temple Mount and became the central place of worship for the Israelites. The temple was designed with great care, featuring a Holy of Holies where the Ark of the Covenant was placed. Upon its completion, it is said that Heavenly Father's glory filled the temple, signifying His presence among His people. This temple stood as a symbol of faith and devotion until its destruction by the Babylonians in 587 BC.
g10.scripture: The Bible provides detailed accounts of Solomon's Temple in 1 Kings 6–8 and 2 Chronicles 3–7. These passages describe the temple's construction, dedication, and the divine presence that filled it upon completion. In the Book of Mormon, temples are also central to worship, as seen in 2 Nephi 5:16, where Nephi builds a temple after the pattern of Solomon's Temple. Doctrine and Covenants 124:27 emphasizes the importance of building temples as places of holiness and worship.
g10.background: Before Solomon's Temple, the Israelites worshiped in a portable tabernacle as they journeyed through the wilderness. The construction of a permanent temple marked a significant shift, providing a stable and central location for worship. Jerusalem, the city chosen for the temple, was a bustling center of political and religious life. Daily life for the Israelites involved agricultural work, trade, and adherence to religious laws and festivals. The temple became the heart of their spiritual practices, hosting sacrifices, prayers, and gatherings that reinforced their covenant with Heavenly Father.

g11.talk: Why do you think God wanted people to know about Jesus before He was born?
g11.child: Isaiah was a prophet who told people that Jesus would come, even hundreds of years before He was born. His words about Jesus were saved for a very long time. God helped keep these words safe so we could read and learn from them today.
g11.learn: From Isaiah’s example, we learn the value of hope and patience. Even when world events are hard and the future seems unsure, God’s promises are sure. The words of His prophets are meant to guide, comfort, and prepare us to recognize and follow Jesus Christ. We also learn that the things God inspires and protects—like ancient prophecies—can bless whole generations of families who choose to remember and follow Him.
g11.matters: Isaiah’s prophecies are important because they show that God prepared the world for Jesus Christ long before He was born. For families of faith, this means Heavenly Father keeps His word, and hope can last for generations even through dark times. Because Isaiah’s words were kept safe and copied for centuries, we have proof that God’s messages can survive and bless us today. Studying his prophecies helps us see Christ’s life and mission more clearly, and reminds us that God’s plans are sure.

sources.name: Dead Sea Scrolls, The British Museum
Isaiah 53, ChurchofJesusChrist.org Bible Dictionary
Encyclopaedia Britannica: Isaiah
Smithsonian Magazine: What Are the Dead Sea Scrolls?

g11.evidence: The discovery of the Dead Sea Scrolls around 1947 gave us ancient copies of Isaiah’s writings that were made hundreds of years before Jesus was born. These scrolls, carefully preserved in jars near Qumran, show that the words of Isaiah 53 already existed long before Christ’s birth, exactly as found in our Bibles today. This confirms that Isaiah’s detailed prophecies about a suffering Savior were not written after the fact. Scholars agree that the Isaiah scrolls date from roughly the second century BC, supporting the idea that these were real prophecies, not later additions. The scrolls are now studied in museums and have strengthened the historical reliability of the Bible.
g11.happened: About 2,700 years ago, a prophet named Isaiah lived in Jerusalem, the capital city of ancient Israel. Isaiah was called by God to warn the people about their choices and to share messages of hope and salvation. One of the most remarkable things Isaiah did was to prophesy about the coming of the Messiah, whom Christians believe to be Jesus Christ. Isaiah’s words are found in the Bible, and they describe the life, suffering, and victory of Christ hundreds of years before His birth. In particular, Isaiah chapter 53 speaks of a servant who would suffer for the sins of others, be rejected, wounded, and ultimately bring healing and peace. Isaiah wrote these messages during a time of great trouble and change, sharing Heavenly Father’s promise that even though hard times would come, a Savior would one day make things right for all people who turn to Him.
g11.scripture: Isaiah 53 in the Old Testament describes the Savior’s suffering and Atonement in striking detail. In the Book of Mormon, several prophets including Abinadi and Nephi also quote or refer to Isaiah’s words (Mosiah 14, 2 Nephi 11, 2 Nephi 25). Jesus Himself referred to Isaiah during His ministry (Luke 4:16-21). These passages show how the ancient prophecies connect directly to Jesus and are recognized in both the Bible and the Book of Mormon.​
g11.background: Isaiah lived in a time when the kingdom of Israel was divided. The northern part, called Israel, and the southern part, called Judah, had separate kings and often faced wars, invasions, and trouble from powerful neighbors like Assyria. Jerusalem was a busy city, full of people trying to live, work, and worship while dealing with fear of enemies and the challenge of staying true to God. Most people grew their own food, lived in simple homes, and gathered at the temple for worship. Prophets like Isaiah were not always popular because their words, especially warnings, could be hard to hear. But many listened with hope, longing for a day when God’s promises would finally come true.

g12.talk: Why do you think Esther was brave, even though she was scared?
g12.child: Esther was a brave queen who saved her people by telling the king what was right. She trusted Heavenly Father and stood up for what was good, even when she was scared. Because of her, many people were safe.
g12.learn: We can learn from Esther that ordinary people can make a big difference when they trust in God and stand up for what is right, even when they are afraid. Esther’s story encourages us to be brave when we see something wrong and to believe that we may be in a certain place or situation for a reason. When we seek God’s help through prayer and fasting, we can have courage to face our own hard things and help others too.
g12.matters: Esther’s story matters greatly to the world and to families of faith today. Her courage showed that one person's prayers, faith, and bravery can change the course of history and protect many lives. For Christians, this moment kept the line of the Jewish people safe—a lineage that, according to belief, would lead to the birth of Jesus Christ many centuries later. Esther’s example teaches families that the right thing is often hard to do, but trusting in God and being brave can bless others long after we are gone.

sources.name: Bible Gateway – Book of Esther
Jewish Virtual Library – The Story of Esther
The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints – Old Testament Stories: Esther Saves Her People
Encyclopaedia Britannica – Esther

g12.evidence: Historians generally believe that a Persian king named Ahasuerus (often identified with Xerxes I) ruled during this time, and that Jews did live in Persia as exiles. The story of Esther is detailed in the Bible, and Persian records show the grandeur and customs of the royal court. However, there is not yet direct archaeological proof of Queen Esther herself or the exact events of the story. Some scholars debate whether the Book of Esther is a historical account or a story told to convey important values. Many features in the account do fit what is known about Persian life and laws, and the Jewish festival of Purim has been celebrated for over two thousand years to remember the events in the story.
g12.happened: Around 480 BC, a brave young woman named Esther found herself in a position very few could imagine. Born a Jewish exile in the land of Persia, Esther was chosen to become the new queen after King Ahasuerus (also known as Xerxes) sought a new wife. Though the king did not know about her Jewish heritage, Esther listened carefully to the advice of her cousin Mordecai, who had raised her like a daughter. Trouble soon came when Haman, a high official in the king's court, developed a hatred toward the Jewish people. Haman convinced the king to pass a law that would allow all Jews in the kingdom to be killed on a certain day. Mordecai urged Esther to speak to the king, even though the law said anyone who came before the king without an invitation could be killed. Esther fasted and prayed, and then courageously went before the king. She invited him and Haman to a special banquet, where she revealed her Jewish identity and Haman’s evil plan. The king was shocked and upset. He stopped the decree, punished Haman, and allowed Esther's people to be safe. Esther’s courage and wisdom saved her people from destruction.
g12.scripture: The story of Esther is told in the Old Testament, in the Book of Esther, particularly in chapters 4–7. The famous phrase, “Who knoweth whether thou art come to the kingdom for such a time as this?” is found in Esther 4:14. While the Book of Mormon and other scriptures do not mention Esther directly, her courage echoes the teachings found in Doctrine and Covenants 121:7–9, which remind us to be faithful and to trust God in times of danger or difficulty, trusting that He prepares us for special purposes.
g12.background: The story of Esther took place in the ancient city of Susa, the capital of Persia, a vast empire that stretched from India to Egypt. The Jewish people were living in Persia as exiles, having been taken from their homeland years before when Jerusalem fell to Babylon. Life in Susa was busy, with people of many nations and religions. Persian kings like Ahasuerus lived in luxury, holding banquets and making important decisions from vast palaces. For the Jewish people in exile, daily life required wisdom and carefulness. They gathered with their families, remembered their traditions, and tried to honor God while living under foreign rule.

g13.talk: What would you do if you had to choose between following God or following what everyone else is doing?
g13.child: Daniel prayed to God, even when it was scary, and God kept him safe from the lions. He helped a king understand his dreams and showed that God’s promises come true. God can help us be brave too.
g13.learn: We can learn that Heavenly Father can help us be brave and faithful, even when life seems scary or strange. Daniel shows that keeping our trust in God opens the way for miracles and blessings, not just for ourselves but for many others. His story invites families to pray, keep faith, and look for ways they can help God’s work. Even when the world changes, God’s promises do not.
g13.matters: For families of faith, Daniel’s story is more than just an adventure—it is a lesson about standing up for what is right, even when it’s hard. Daniel’s faith in God helped him survive trials and become a force for good, showing that Heavenly Father can protect and guide His children wherever they are. The dream Daniel interpreted is also important for Latter-day Saints. The stone cut without hands is often seen as a symbol of the Restoration—the reestablishing of Christ’s church in our day, starting small and spreading across the world. The story invites each family to trust God and to see their part in His bigger plans.

sources.name: Bible Dictionary: Daniel
Encyclopedia Britannica: Daniel
The British Museum: Babylon

g13.evidence: Archaeologists have found records and ruins from ancient Babylon, including its impressive city gates and inscriptions from King Nebuchadnezzar’s time. These findings confirm the setting and some events, such as the exile of people from Judah. However, there is no direct historical evidence that Daniel himself lived in Babylon or that the lions’ den event happened exactly as told. Many scholars see Daniel’s stories as faithful accounts meant to teach important lessons, though historical details can be debated. There is strong evidence of Babylonia’s grandeur and the Jewish exile, but the personal stories from the Book of Daniel are mostly supported by religious tradition and the text itself.
g13.happened: Daniel was a young man from Judah who, along with his friends, was taken captive by the Babylonians when King Nebuchadnezzar conquered Jerusalem. Living in Babylon, Daniel grew up far from home, learning the language and customs of a foreign land. Because he loved God and kept His commandments, Daniel was blessed with wisdom, which set him apart in the king’s court. Daniel became known as someone who could interpret dreams and mysteries. The most famous story tells how Daniel was thrown into a den of hungry lions because he prayed to God, even when it was against the law. God protected him, and the lions did not harm him. Daniel also interpreted King Nebuchadnezzar’s dream about a large statue made of different materials, which represented future empires. In this dream, a stone was cut out without hands and smashed the statue, growing into a mountain that filled the earth. Daniel explained that this stone symbolized God setting up His kingdom—one that would never be destroyed. Through it all, Daniel’s faith and courage helped him bless many people, showing that God can use His faithful children to do great things, even in difficult times.
g13.scripture: Daniel chapters 1 through 6 tell about Daniel’s experiences in Babylon—including the lions’ den and the dream of King Nebuchadnezzar in Daniel 2. Latter-day Saints connect Daniel 2:34-45, with its stone cut without hands, to Doctrine and Covenants 65:2, which talks about the gospel filling the whole earth. While the Book of Mormon and Pearl of Great Price do not mention Daniel by name, the principle of God working through faithful people is found throughout scripture. These stories remind us that God’s kingdom will succeed, no matter what challenges come.
g13.background: This story takes place in ancient Babylon, in what is now Iraq, during the late 7th and early 6th centuries BC. After the Babylonian army destroyed Jerusalem, many people from Judah, including young nobles, were taken captive. Life in Babylon was very different from home—the people spoke a different language, worshipped different gods, and had new ways of living. Babylon was a rich and powerful city, famous for its tall walls and beautiful gardens. The Jewish captives had to decide whether to hold on to their beliefs or give in to Babylonian culture. For Daniel and his friends, trusting Heavenly Father became central to their daily lives.

i01.talk: How do you think learning to use fire changed the way early people lived?
i01.child: Long ago, people learned to use fire to stay warm, cook food, and keep safe from animals. This helped them grow smarter and live better lives.
i01.learn: The mastery of fire teaches us about human ingenuity and adaptability. It reminds us that with the tools and knowledge provided by Heavenly Father, we can overcome challenges and progress. Fire's dual nature—as a source of warmth and a potential hazard—also teaches us to use our gifts responsibly, ensuring they serve to uplift and not harm.
i01.matters: The control of fire was a transformative milestone that shaped human evolution. It enabled cooking, which improved nutrition and supported brain growth, leading to the development of complex societies and cultures. For families of faith, this event can be seen as part of Heavenly Father's plan, providing humans with tools to progress and fulfill their divine potential. Fire symbolizes both physical and spiritual enlightenment, guiding humanity toward greater understanding and communion with God.

sources.name: Guinness World Records: First use of fire by humans
PMC: The discovery of fire by humans: a long and convoluted process
History.com: Why Did Early Humans First Use Fire?
American Bible Society: Fire

i01.evidence: Archaeological findings provide substantial evidence of early human use of fire. In Wonderwerk Cave, South Africa, researchers discovered charred bones and plant ash dating back approximately one million years, located deep within the cave, indicating human control of fire. Similar evidence has been found at sites like Chesowanja in Kenya and Gesher Benot Yaaqov in Israel, where burned materials suggest fire use by early humans. These discoveries highlight the significance of fire in human evolution and its role in shaping our ancestors' lives.
i01.happened: Around one million years ago, early humans in Africa began to harness fire, marking a pivotal moment in human history. This mastery provided warmth, protection from predators, and a means to cook food, which made it easier to digest and unlocked more nutrients. Cooking not only improved health but also supported brain development, as the energy saved from digesting cooked food could be redirected to fuel a growing brain. Evidence of early fire use has been found in places like Wonderwerk Cave in South Africa, where charred bones and plant ash dating back about one million years have been discovered deep within the cave, suggesting human control of fire. This advancement laid the foundation for future technological and cultural developments, influencing the trajectory of human evolution.
i01.scripture: Fire is a significant symbol in the scriptures, representing God's presence, guidance, and purification. In Exodus 3:2, God appears to Moses in a burning bush, signifying His presence and calling. Hebrews 12:29 describes God as a "consuming fire," emphasizing His power and holiness. Additionally, Acts 2:3 recounts the Holy Spirit descending upon the apostles as "tongues of fire," symbolizing divine inspiration and empowerment. These passages illustrate fire's role as a conduit for divine interaction and transformation.
i01.background: Before mastering fire, early humans lived in a world where survival was a daily challenge. They relied on raw foods, which were harder to digest and less nutritious. Nights were cold and dark, and predators posed constant threats. The environment was harsh, and humans had to be resourceful to find food and shelter. The discovery and control of fire transformed their way of life, providing warmth, safety, and a new method to prepare food, which in turn supported their physical and cognitive development.

i02.talk: Why do you think Heavenly Father wants us to write things down and remember them?
i02.child: Long ago, people in Sumer started making marks on clay to keep track of things. This was the first writing, and it helped them save stories and messages for others. Because of writing, we can read about what happened long ago and learn from those stories today.
i02.learn: From this moment in history, we learn that simple needs and persistent work can lead to great blessings for everyone—like the ability to record and share truth. It also shows us that technologies, when used wisely, can help Heavenly Father’s work move forward by preserving His teachings. The invention of writing is a reminder to value the words we have been given, especially the scriptures, and to take care in how we record and share important things in our own lives.
i02.matters: Writing matters to all of us because it lets thoughts and teachings travel beyond a single person or place. Without writing, important lessons, stories, and especially the words of scripture would be easily lost. For families who cherish the scriptures, writing is the gift that made it possible for Heavenly Father’s words to reach us—first as marks on clay or parchment, and today as printed books or digital pages. Knowing how writing began helps us see its power and its purpose: to share, remember, and bless each generation.

sources.name: British Museum: Cuneiform
Encyclopedia Britannica: Cuneiform
The Metropolitan Museum of Art: The Invention of Writing

i02.evidence: Archaeologists have found thousands of clay tablets in Iraq from Sumerian cities, with some showing the earliest stages of cuneiform writing. The oldest ones date to just before 3,200 BC. By reading these tablets, which are stored in museums around the world, experts can track how simple picture writing became the cuneiform system. These records cover everything from farmer’s receipts to poems and stories. There is no doubt among historians that writing first appeared in this way and place, thanks to the huge number of surviving tablets and the fact that many different teams have studied them for well over a hundred years.
i02.happened: Around 3500 BC, in a place called Sumer, people created a way to write down their thoughts on clay tablets. This happened in Mesopotamia, which is now part of Iraq. The kind of writing they invented is called cuneiform, because it uses wedge-shaped marks pressed into the clay with a reed. Before this, people could only share stories and instructions by speaking, but now they could leave messages that lasted long after they were gone. At first, writing was used to keep track of goods, like how much barley was stored or how many sheep were traded. Over time, people wrote not just numbers, but words, lists, and even stories. This invention made it possible for information and stories to be saved and shared with people far away and long after the writers themselves had died. As writing grew, it helped people organize their communities, remember their history, and pass on knowledge, making life more connected and complex.
i02.scripture: The Bible often speaks of writing. In Exodus 24:4, Moses wrote all the words of the Lord. The Book of Mormon says in 1 Nephi 5:19-22 that written records help preserve commandments for future generations. Doctrine and Covenants 68:4 promises that what is spoken by the Spirit and written down will be scripture. Although there is nothing that directly describes the invention of writing, these verses show the importance Heavenly Father places on recording His word for His children.
i02.background: At the time writing was invented, Sumer was made up of small, busy cities, each with its own ruler and temple. People lived in mud-brick homes, farmed the river plains, raised animals, and traded goods along the rivers. They worked hard to grow crops like wheat and barley, and they relied on careful watering from the rivers to help their plants grow. Sumerians made many things by hand, including pottery, tools, and cloth. Before writing, people used tokens and counting boards to track trade and harvests, but as cities grew, that system was not enough. The need for a better way to remember and organize things led them to invent writing, a tool that changed how their whole society worked.

i03.talk: How do you think our life would be different if we didn’t have paper for books and scriptures?
i03.child: A kind man in China made the first real paper almost 2,000 years ago. It helped people write down stories and scriptures so families could read them more easily. Now, every book we use, even our scriptures, comes from that idea.
i03.learn: We can learn that even simple inventions, made with kindness and patience, can bless millions—even billions—of people for centuries. We can remember that learning and sharing truth is a gift, and it is good to treasure the tools that help us do it. Innovation often comes quietly, and sometimes the smallest changes open the biggest doors for families, communities, and future generations.
i03.matters: Paper is important because it made sharing stories, laws, knowledge, and scriptures far easier. Before paper, sacred writings and all kinds of records could only be kept by a few, often just rulers or priests. After Cai Lun’s invention, scriptures and teachings could be shared and read in homes and churches everywhere. For families who love the scriptures and value learning, we owe much to this Chinese invention. It’s a reminder that Heavenly Father knows how new ideas can bless His children, and that tools created in one part of the world can someday help everyone.

sources.name: The British Library – The history of paper
Smithsonian Magazine – How Paper Changed the World
Encyclopaedia Britannica – History of paper

i03.evidence: Records from Chinese history, including court documents from the Han Dynasty, tell us that Cai Lun presented the idea of paper to the emperor in 105 AD and was given credit as the inventor. Archaeologists have found very old sheets of paper in China, some dating back almost 2,000 years. Modern historians agree that while simple paper-like materials may have existed before Cai Lun, he improved the process and made it practical and popular. Museums around the world, including in China and Europe, show preserved samples of early Chinese paper, supporting these historical accounts. Cai Lun’s breakthrough stands as one of ancient history’s clear milestones.
i03.happened: In the year 105 AD, a man named Cai Lun, who worked for the royal court during China’s Han Dynasty, created something that would change the world: paper. Before this time, people wrote on things like bamboo strips, silk, or animal hides, but these were heavy, expensive, or hard to make. Cai Lun experimented with bits of bark, old cloth, and fishing nets. He mashed them up with water into a thin paste, pressed and dried them, and made sheets that were light, flexible, and easy to write on. Cai’s invention quickly spread throughout China, helping more people to write and share ideas. Over the centuries, the secret of making paper traveled slowly from China, through the Middle East, and finally into Europe. When paper reached Europe, it meant books could be made cheaply enough that regular people, not just the wealthy or the church, could own them. This changed how families, scholars, and faith communities learned together and helped knowledge to grow and spread in ways never seen before.
i03.scripture: The Bible teaches that the word of God should be written and remembered for future generations, such as in Deuteronomy 6:6-9 when families are told to write God’s words “upon the posts of thy house, and on thy gates.” The Book of Mormon describes prophets engraving their records on metal plates (1 Nephi 19:1), showing the importance of written scripture, even when hard to do. While ancient scripture speaks of stone, metal, or parchment, the principle is clear: preserving and sharing God’s word matters. Paper made this much easier and helped families to keep the teachings close.
i03.background: At the time of Cai Lun’s invention, China was under the reign of the Han Dynasty, a period marked by great growth in population, culture, and inventions. People mostly wrote on bamboo strips tied together like books, or on pieces of silk, both of which were not practical for everyday writing because they were either too heavy or too costly. Daily life in China was rooted in farming, family, and service to the emperor. Only scholars and officials could read or write, and they worked for the government, keeping important records. Books took up much space and were hard to carry. News and teachings were mostly passed by word of mouth or kept in sealed archives. The invention of paper opened up the chance for more people to learn, which would later change not only China, but also the rest of the world.

i04.talk: How do you think having our own copy of the scriptures helps us learn about Heavenly Father?
i04.child: Long ago, people had to copy books by hand, which took a very long time. Then, a man named Gutenberg made a special machine that could print many books quickly. This helped more people read the Bible and learn about God.
i04.learn: Gutenberg's invention teaches us the profound impact that technological advancements can have on society and faith. By making the scriptures more accessible, the printing press empowered individuals to seek personal understanding and develop a closer relationship with God. It reminds us of the importance of embracing tools and innovations that can enhance our spiritual growth and knowledge.
i04.matters: The invention of the printing press was a pivotal moment in history, leading to the rapid spread of ideas and knowledge. For families of faith, this meant that the Bible and other religious texts became more accessible, allowing individuals to read and interpret scriptures personally. This accessibility laid the groundwork for movements like the Protestant Reformation, where figures such as Martin Luther emphasized personal engagement with the scriptures. The ability to own and read the Bible at home empowered families to strengthen their faith and understanding of God's word, fostering a more personal and direct relationship with the divine.

sources.name: Printing Press - Invented, Gutenberg, Significance | HISTORY
The Gutenberg Bible - Library of Congress Bible Collection
The Invention of Printing | The Morgan Library & Museum

i04.evidence: Historical records, such as the Helmasperger Instrument—a legal document from 1455—provide evidence of Gutenberg's printing activities. Surviving copies of the Gutenberg Bible, with their uniform type and high-quality printing, demonstrate the capabilities of his press. Additionally, the rapid spread of printing technology across Europe after Gutenberg's invention indicates its effectiveness and transformative impact. Within fifty years, millions of books had been printed, significantly increasing the availability of written material and contributing to the rise in literacy rates across the continent.
i04.happened: In the mid-15th century, Johannes Gutenberg, a skilled goldsmith from Mainz, Germany, developed a revolutionary method of printing. Around 1439, he introduced a system that combined movable metal type, a wooden press adapted from wine presses, and oil-based inks. This innovation allowed for the mass production of books with unprecedented speed and consistency. By 1455, Gutenberg had completed the printing of the Bible, known as the 42-line Bible due to the number of lines per page. This marked the first major book produced using his press. The ability to produce multiple copies of texts efficiently transformed the dissemination of knowledge, making books more accessible and affordable to a broader audience.
i04.scripture: The scriptures emphasize the importance of seeking knowledge and wisdom. Proverbs 4:7 states, "Wisdom is the principal thing; therefore get wisdom: and with all thy getting get understanding." The Book of Mormon also highlights the value of learning: "But to be learned is good if they hearken unto the counsels of God" (2 Nephi 9:29). The Doctrine and Covenants encourages the study of various subjects: "Seek ye out of the best books words of wisdom; seek learning, even by study and also by faith" (D&C 88:118). The printing press facilitated the fulfillment of these scriptural admonitions by making sacred texts more accessible to individuals and families.
i04.background: Before Gutenberg's invention, books in Europe were laboriously copied by hand, primarily by monks in monasteries. This process was time-consuming and costly, resulting in limited availability of books, which were often large, ornate, and chained to library shelves to prevent theft. Literacy was confined mainly to the clergy and the wealthy elite. The scarcity of books meant that most people relied on oral traditions and the teachings of the Church for information. Daily life was predominantly agrarian, with limited access to education and written materials. The introduction of the printing press began to change this landscape by making books more widely available, thus promoting literacy and learning among the general populace.

i05.talk: Why do you think Samuel Morse chose a Bible verse as the very first telegraph message?
i05.child: A man named Samuel Morse sent the first message by telegraph in 1844. It was a Bible verse that said, 'What hath God wrought.' Thanks to this invention, people could talk to each other from far away very quickly.
i05.learn: From this event, we can learn that technology, when used wisely, can be a tool for good. It reminds us to be grateful for Heavenly Father’s help and to use our talents to bless others. The story of the first telegraph also encourages us to see new inventions not just as machines, but as ways to do good in the world and make life better for many.
i05.matters: The invention of the telegraph mattered to the world because it brought people and nations closer together. News could now be shared instantly across continents. For families of faith, the telegraph helped spread messages, scripture, and even the work of the Lord more quickly. It made it possible for missionaries to communicate faster and for leaders to respond in times of need. The fact that the first message sent was a verse from the Bible reminds us that technology can be used to serve God’s purposes. This moment shows how Heavenly Father’s children can use their talents, with His help, to do amazing things and bless others.

sources.name: Smithsonian National Museum of American History: Morse Telegraph
Library of Congress: Today in History - Samuel Morse
Encyclopedia Britannica: Samuel Morse and the Telegraph

i05.evidence: There is strong historical evidence confirming this event. Samuel Morse demonstrated the working telegraph in public before Congress and many witnesses. Records, letters, and newspaper articles from 1844 describe the event in detail, and the original message—“What hath God wrought”—is preserved in official histories and museums today. The physical remains of early telegraph machines and wires, as well as Morse’s own journals and notebooks, provide further evidence. Museums such as the Smithsonian display Morse’s telegraph equipment, and the moment is well-documented by historians. Scholars agree this was a turning point in communication technology.
i05.happened: In 1844, something remarkable happened in Washington, D.C., that changed the way people communicate forever. Samuel Morse, an American inventor and artist, sent the first message by electric telegraph over a long distance. He tapped out the words “What hath God wrought” from the U.S. Capitol in Washington to Alfred Vail, who was waiting in Baltimore, about 40 miles away. The message traveled along wires, carried by the pulses of electricity that spelled out the words in dots and dashes—what we now call Morse code. The words themselves were chosen from the Bible, Numbers 23:23, and showed both a sense of wonder and gratitude. This was the first time in human history that an instant message could travel far faster than any person, horse, or ship could carry it. After the message was received, cheers and excitement filled the rooms, and many knew they were witnessing history being made. It was the beginning of a new era in communication, making it possible to send information quickly across whole countries and, eventually, the world.
i05.scripture: The Bible verse used—Numbers 23:23—was sent in the first telegraph message, showing a link between faith and invention. The scriptures speak of the Lord hastening His work (Doctrine and Covenants 88:73), and the telegraph is one example of how technology can help make sharing the gospel and gathering information faster. Just as the Book of Mormon says about seeking learning by study and also by faith (Doctrine and Covenants 88:118), the telegraph showed how science and faith can work together.
i05.background: Before 1844, news and messages could only travel as fast as a horse could gallop, a ship could sail, or a person could walk or run. People used handwritten letters, stagecoaches, and messengers. While a few slower methods like semaphores (systems using flags or towers) helped send messages over short distances, none were fast or practical for long distances. Samuel Morse was already known as a painter, but after experiencing the pain of slow communication himself, he devoted years to inventing a better way. The telegraph used electromagnets and wires to send signals over vast distances, something brand new. Life during this time was full of change, with trains and factories beginning to transform cities and farms, yet people still lived much as they had for centuries—until technology like the telegraph began to shrink the distances between them.

t01.talk: What special thing from our life would you want to share if you traveled to another country?
t01.child: Long ago, people carried silk and spices a very long way from China to Rome. Along these big roads, they also shared stories and learned new things about God. The Silk Road helped people become friends, even if they lived far apart.
t01.learn: From the Silk Road, we learn that sharing with others can bless all involved. The things we create, discover, or believe can travel farther and help more people than we might ever guess. Just as Heavenly Father helped people long ago cross great distances to share knowledge and truth, He can use us and the tools we have today—like technology, kindness, and our testimonies—to help His work go forward.
t01.matters: The Silk Road is important because it brought the world together long before airplanes or the internet. For families of faith, it helps us see how God uses ordinary things—like roads and trade—to help His children learn from each other and spread His truth. The Silk Road made it possible for inventions like paper to travel to Europe, which later helped the Bible and other scriptures be printed and shared with many people. It’s a reminder that connecting with others can lead to wonderful changes and the spreading of good ideas.

sources.name: Smithsonian: The Silk Road
National Geographic: Silk Road
University of Pennsylvania: The Silk Road

t01.evidence: Historians and archaeologists have discovered coins, sculptures, ancient texts, and even the remains of caravans and inns along the route. Painted caves in China and ruins of old cities in Central Asia show what life was like for traders and travelers. Ancient Roman and Chinese records mention the exchange of silk and strange products, confirming much of what we know. DNA and artifact studies show that people and ideas truly mixed along these routes. Modern research continues to fill in our picture of how the Silk Road worked and how important it was for connecting continents.
t01.happened: The Silk Road was a series of ancient trade routes that stretched more than four thousand miles from China in the East all the way to Rome in the West. It wasn’t a single road but many paths and caravan trails, crossing high mountains, wide deserts, and busy cities. Starting around 200 BC and lasting until about 1450 AD, the Silk Road helped traders carry silk, spices, paper, and even new discoveries like gunpowder from Asia to Europe. Caravans of camels or horses would carry goods in both directions, and trading posts and cities grew at stopping places along the way. It wasn’t just material things that traveled—people shared stories, art, music, and beliefs. Through these travels, religions such as Buddhism, Christianity, and Islam spread across Asia and Europe. The Silk Road made the world feel smaller as faraway places became connected, helping ideas and inventions reach people who might never have imagined such things before.
t01.scripture: The Bible tells stories of travelers and journeys that changed the world, such as Paul’s missionary travels in Acts 13-21, where he brought the gospel across the Mediterranean, touching new lands and peoples. In Doctrine and Covenants 88:79, the Lord commands us to learn about “countries and kingdoms” so we can be prepared for His work. The movement of knowledge and the gospel along trade routes like the Silk Road shows how the Lord ‘prepares a way’ to spread truth and blessings, much as He did for His ancient servants.
t01.background: Long before the Silk Road, people lived in small villages or cities, usually trading only with nearby neighbors. Ancient China, Persia, India, and Rome were already great civilizations with their own rich cultures, foods, and ways of thinking. Most travel was slow and dangerous, often by foot or with animals, and people depended on the land and their crafts to survive. Families grew their own food, spun their own cloth, and rarely saw outsiders except during local markets or festivals. As empires grew and rulers wanted exotic goods like silk or rare spices, people began to look farther beyond their borders. Caravan routes started as simple trails taken by herders and traders but grew as more people saw the value in exchanging goods and stories with distant lands.

t02.talk: How did the search for spices lead explorers to discover new lands?
t02.child: Long ago, people loved spices like cinnamon and pepper because they made food taste better and helped keep it fresh. Traders traveled across oceans and lands to bring these spices from faraway places to Europe. Their journeys led to the discovery of new lands, including America.
t02.learn: The history of the spice trade teaches us about the interconnectedness of the world and how economic pursuits can lead to significant cultural and spiritual developments. It reminds us that our efforts, even when driven by temporal goals, can be guided by Heavenly Father to fulfill His greater purposes. This encourages us to seek His guidance in all our endeavors, trusting that He can lead us to outcomes that align with His divine plan.
t02.matters: The spice trade was a catalyst for global exploration and the eventual European colonization of various parts of the world. For families of faith, this period underscores how commercial pursuits can lead to unintended, yet divinely significant, outcomes. The search for spices led to the discovery of new lands, including the Americas, which would later become a haven for religious freedom and the birthplace of the Restoration. It serves as a reminder that Heavenly Father can use worldly endeavors to fulfill His greater purposes, guiding individuals and nations toward paths that align with His divine plan.

sources.name: Spice Trade - Wikipedia
The Spice Trade & the Age of Exploration - World History Encyclopedia
Spice Routes: History, Trade Goods & Maritime Geography | Geography Worlds

t02.evidence: Historical records and archaeological findings provide substantial evidence of the extensive spice trade routes that connected Southeast Asia to Europe. Ancient texts from various cultures document the high value placed on spices and the lengths to which traders would go to obtain them. Maritime archaeology has uncovered shipwrecks along these routes, revealing cargoes of spices and other goods, confirming the scale and significance of this trade. The establishment of European trading posts and colonies in spice-producing regions further attests to the lengths nations went to secure direct access to these valuable commodities.
t02.happened: Between the 11th and 16th centuries, the spice trade flourished as a vast network of maritime and overland routes connected Southeast Asia's spice-producing regions to Europe. Spices like pepper, cinnamon, cloves, and nutmeg were highly prized in Europe for their ability to flavor and preserve food, as well as for medicinal uses. These valuable commodities were transported from the Moluccas (Spice Islands) in Indonesia, through the Indian Ocean, and onward via the Red Sea or Persian Gulf to Mediterranean ports. Arab and Persian merchants played key roles in this trade, controlling the flow of spices and maintaining high prices by keeping their sources secret. European demand for these exotic goods grew, leading to significant economic and cultural exchanges between the East and West. The desire to find direct sea routes to the spice-producing regions eventually spurred the Age of Exploration, with navigators like Christopher Columbus seeking new paths to these lucrative markets.
t02.scripture: While the scriptures do not directly mention the spice trade, they do speak to the principle of seeking and finding. In Matthew 7:7, the Savior teaches, "Ask, and it shall be given you; seek, and ye shall find; knock, and it shall be opened unto you." This principle can be applied to the explorers' quests, where their search for spices led to the discovery of new lands and opportunities. Additionally, 2 Nephi 1:5 in the Book of Mormon speaks of a "land of promise" prepared by the Lord, which can be seen as a foreshadowing of the Americas becoming a land of religious freedom and restoration.
t02.background: In the medieval world, spices were not just culinary luxuries but essential commodities. They were used to enhance the flavor of food, preserve meats, and in various medicinal remedies. The high value of spices made them a form of currency and a symbol of wealth. The overland Silk Road and maritime routes facilitated the movement of these goods, but the journey was long and fraught with challenges, including taxing intermediaries and political conflicts. The fall of Constantinople in 1453 to the Ottoman Turks further complicated overland trade, prompting European nations to seek alternative routes to the East. This quest for direct access to spices led to significant advancements in navigation and shipbuilding, setting the stage for global exploration.

t03.talk: How might God use the things we build or use today, like roads or the internet, to help people learn about Him?
t03.child: Long ago, Rome built strong roads and sent ships far away so people could trade things like silk and gold. These roads also helped missionaries travel and tell others about Jesus. Heavenly Father sometimes uses things like roads to help His work happen.
t03.learn: From the Roman trade network, we learn that the Lord can use anything—even old roads or ship routes designed for business—to help people find truth and share it with others. We see that technology and travel, when used well, can bless many lives. Families can talk about how being connected with others is good, but it also means being wise about what we share and learn. As we use today’s technology, we can ask ourselves how we can use it to do good, just as early Christians did along the Roman roads.
t03.matters: The Roman trade network made the world feel connected in ways that had never happened before. People could experience new foods, colors, and ideas from faraway lands. For a family of faith, this mattered because the same roads and ships that carried silk and spices also made it possible for the message of Jesus Christ to travel quickly beyond its tiny beginning. The Apostle Paul and many missionaries could reach towns across the empire with relative ease. Today, we can see this as something Heavenly Father allowed—even planned for—so that the gospel could spread to all His children in those days. The ability for ideas to travel matters deeply in how faith grows and communities change.

sources.name: British Museum: Rome's Trade with India
World History Encyclopedia: Roman Trade
Smithsonian Magazine: How Ancient Trade Changed the World

t03.evidence: Historians and archaeologists have found strong evidence of the Roman trade network. The remains of stone roads with mile markers show just how far Roman construction reached. Ancient shipwrecks carrying Roman and Indian goods have been found in the Mediterranean and Indian Oceans, providing proof of trade. Old Roman coins have been discovered in India and even as far as China, showing that trade reached these distant places. Written sources from Rome, Egypt, and India describe goods, merchants, and sometimes missionaries traveling these routes. Modern studies using satellite images have even traced lost roads and busy ports that once made this global exchange possible. While not every single journey can be traced, the overall picture is strongly supported by physical and written evidence.
t03.happened: Between the first and fourth centuries AD, the Roman Empire created one of the largest and most effective trade networks the world had ever seen. Spanning from the heart of Rome itself, these routes stretched westward through Europe, looped eastward into India and even reached the far-off lands of China. Ships full of goods sailed the Mediterranean Sea, while caravans crossed long, dusty desert roads. Precious items like silk from China, spices from India, gold and ivory from Africa, and glassware, wine, and olive oil from Rome moved along these paths. Roman merchants exchanged goods, stories, and even ideas with traders from many nations. Along with traders, Christian missionaries traveled these paved roads and safe sea lanes, spreading the teachings of Jesus Christ far beyond the borders of Judea. The famous Roman roads—built strong for armies—now carried the hopes and messages of regular people, merchants, and believers alike. By the year 150 AD, this wide web of roads and sea routes bustling with travelers was among the greatest highways for both commerce and communication in ancient history.
t03.scripture: Several scriptures touch on the principle that Heavenly Father prepares people and circumstances to help His work move forward. In the Bible, Acts 9-28 tells about Paul's journeys using Roman roads to spread the gospel. Paul often traveled safely and could teach about Jesus in faraway cities because of this network. In Doctrine and Covenants 88:73, the Lord promises to 'hasten [His] work in its time,' showing that when the moment is right, the right means and paths are made ready. These passages remind us that God can use even government and trade systems, planned for other reasons, to bless His children.
t03.background: Before Rome's greatest reach, much trade was local, and travel between faraway nations was hard and dangerous. The people of Rome lived in cities filled with noise and activity. Most people were farmers, but there were also builders, soldiers, merchants, and teachers. Rome itself was the center of a huge empire, touching many lands, peoples, and languages. Daily life for many involved work and family, with markets offering goods from every part of the known world. Romans ate bread and olives, wore colorful fabrics, and looked up at stone buildings. The government was strong, and its armies protected long roads and busy ports, making travel and trade remarkably safe—for the time. The empire connected Europe, North Africa, and the Middle East, making the world seem smaller and more possible to cross than ever before.

w01.fall: The decline of Sumerian civilization resulted from both internal and external factors. Internally, the city-states often engaged in conflicts over resources and power, leading to political instability. Over time, the intensive irrigation practices led to soil salinization, reducing agricultural productivity and weakening the economic base. Externally, around 2334 BC, Sargon of Akkad conquered the Sumerian city-states, establishing the Akkadian Empire and diminishing Sumerian autonomy. Subsequent invasions by groups such as the Gutians further destabilized the region. By around 2000 BC, the Sumerian civilization had largely declined, with its cities either abandoned or absorbed into emerging empires. These factors—internal strife, environmental challenges, and external conquests—collectively led to the fall of Sumerian civilization.
w01.rise: The rise of Sumerian civilization was influenced by several factors. The geography of Mesopotamia, with its fertile land between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers, provided abundant resources for agriculture. Around 3500 BC, the Sumerians developed irrigation systems to control river flooding and support crop growth, leading to food surpluses. This agricultural abundance allowed populations to grow and urban centers to form. Leadership played a crucial role, with rulers organizing labor for large-scale projects like temple construction and city walls. The invention of cuneiform writing enabled efficient administration and record-keeping, facilitating complex governance. Additionally, the Sumerians' strategic location fostered trade with neighboring regions, bringing wealth and cultural exchange. These combined factors—fertile land, innovative leadership, technological advancements, and trade—contributed to the emergence and growth of Sumerian cities.
w01.talk: Why do you think it's important to have rules and ways to write things down in a city?
w01.child: Long ago, people called the Sumerians built some of the first cities in the world. They made a way to write called cuneiform and had rules to help everyone live together peacefully. Abraham, a man we learn about in the scriptures, was born in one of these cities called Ur.
w01.learn: Studying the rise of Sumerian cities teaches us about the origins of urban life, governance, and written communication. It highlights human ingenuity in developing systems to manage complex societies. For families of faith, it underscores how God's plans unfold within historical contexts, as seen in Abraham's story. Recognizing the interplay between divine guidance and human history can deepen our understanding of scriptural narratives and their relevance to our lives.
w01.matters: The emergence of Sumerian cities marks a pivotal moment in human history, representing the transition from rural communities to urban societies. This shift introduced organized governance, written language, and codified laws, elements that are fundamental to modern civilizations. For families of faith, the Sumerian context is significant because it is the backdrop of Abraham's early life. Understanding this setting enriches the appreciation of Abraham's journey and the covenant established by Heavenly Father, highlighting the interplay between divine guidance and human history.

sources.name: Ur of the Chaldees - Encyclopedia of The Bible - Bible Gateway
Ur of the Chaldees - BYU Studies
Ur - Archaeological Site | Biblexika
Ur of the Chaldees — Biblical Archaeology | The Scriptorium

w01.evidence: Archaeological excavations have uncovered extensive evidence of Sumerian cities. The city of Ur, identified with modern Tell el-Muqayyar in Iraq, has been extensively studied. Excavations led by Sir Leonard Woolley in the 1920s and 1930s revealed the Great Ziggurat of Ur, royal tombs, and numerous artifacts that attest to a sophisticated urban society. Cuneiform tablets found in these cities provide records of administrative activities, literature, and legal codes, confirming the Sumerians' advancements in writing and governance. These findings collectively affirm the historical reality of Sumerian civilization and its contributions to human history.
w01.happened: Around 3500 BC, the Sumerians in Mesopotamia, present-day Iraq, established some of the world's first cities, including Uruk and Ur. These urban centers were characterized by large populations, complex social structures, and monumental architecture. The Sumerians developed cuneiform, one of the earliest known writing systems, which they used for record-keeping, literature, and legal codes. Their legal systems, such as the Code of Ur-Nammu, are among the earliest recorded laws, reflecting a society with organized governance and justice. These advancements laid the foundation for future civilizations in the region.
w01.scripture: The scriptures mention Ur of the Chaldees as the birthplace of Abraham. In Genesis 11:31, it states, "And Terah took Abram his son... and they went forth with them from Ur of the Chaldees, to go into the land of Canaan." This passage situates Abraham's origins within the Sumerian city of Ur. Additionally, in the Book of Abraham 1:1, Abraham describes his residence in "the land of the Chaldeans." These references connect the patriarch's early life to the Sumerian civilization, providing context for his departure and the unfolding of God's covenant.
w01.background: Before the rise of Sumerian cities, human societies were primarily agrarian, with people living in small villages and relying on subsistence farming. The fertile land between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers, known as the Fertile Crescent, provided abundant resources that supported population growth and the development of complex societies. The Sumerians, believed to have migrated into this region, harnessed these resources to build irrigation systems, enabling surplus agriculture and the growth of cities. Daily life in Sumer involved farming, trade, and craftsmanship, with a social hierarchy that included rulers, priests, merchants, and laborers.

w02.fall: Egypt’s Old Kingdom, which built the Great Pyramid, didn’t last forever. Over the next centuries, the massive effort to build pyramids was hard to sustain. As the pharaohs spent more and more resources on giant monuments, local rulers called nomarchs gained power and became rivals. The economy weakened; droughts and failures of the Nile’s flood led to hunger and unrest. Over time, the pharaoh’s power grew weaker as ordinary people looked to their local leaders for help. Around 2181 BC, Egypt entered a period called the First Intermediate Period, when the central government broke down. Civil wars and the loss of trust in the pharaoh’s power followed. Inside, pride and competition pulled their unity apart. Over-reaching on tombs, forgetting the needs of the people, and losing touch with what made them strong led to their decline. Egypt would rise and fall many times, but the glory days of the original pyramid builders faded, leaving their monuments behind as reminders, but not as secure foundations for their people’s happiness.
w02.rise: Egypt's rise to build the Great Pyramid began with its special land. The Nile River made the soil rich and the fields productive, allowing Egypt to support a growing population. Over centuries, local villages joined into one kingdom under powerful rulers, with the first pharaoh Narmer (around 3100 BC) uniting Upper and Lower Egypt. Pharaohs claimed to be chosen by the gods, giving them deep authority and helping them organize people for big projects. Khufu, for whom the Great Pyramid was built, came from a long line of strong rulers and inherited a kingdom with plenty of workers, food, and resources. Egypt’s priests and scribes developed math, engineering, and writing—skills needed for building huge monuments. The belief that their king would live forever in the afterlife inspired Egyptians to devote years to finishing the Great Pyramid. The project showed the power of organization, shared belief, and human determination to tackle something never done before. By about 2560 BC, thanks to rich land, wise leaders, and a common vision, Egypt reached the height of its early glory with the pyramid’s completion.
w02.talk: What is something we can build together that is even more important than a pyramid?
w02.child: Long ago, people in Egypt worked together to build a giant pyramid for their king. It’s still standing after thousands of years, showing what people can do when they help each other. God wants us to build things that last, like love and kindness in our family.
w02.learn: The story of the Great Pyramid teaches us about teamwork, planning, and aiming for something beyond oneself. It’s a reminder that great things are made from many small efforts, and that faith, effort, and vision can build up families and communities. While the things we build with our hands may change or fade, the love and faith we build together can last.
w02.matters: The building of the Great Pyramid matters because it shows what people can achieve when they work together and use their gifts, even without modern machines. It still stands as a symbol of human dedication, planning, and faith in something lasting beyond one lifetime. For families of faith, this reminds us that while the world sometimes celebrates things we can see and touch, Heavenly Father’s work is about building faithful families and hearts. The invisible things we build together, like love and trust, can last longer than even the greatest stone monuments.

sources.name: British Museum: Building the Pyramids
Smithsonian Magazine: How the Pyramids Were Built
Encyclopaedia Britannica: Great Pyramid of Khufu

w02.evidence: Archaeologists have carefully studied the Great Pyramid, finding ancient records and remains of workers’ villages nearby. Hieroglyphs inside tombs and on stones explain the involvement of thousands of Egyptian workers who labored together, and not slaves as once commonly thought. Scientists have analyzed the types of stones used and how they were transported from quarries, showing that Egyptians used clever ramps, levers, and teamwork. Today, the pyramid’s inner passages and burial chambers can still be explored. Modern technologies, like 3D scans and muon imaging, have helped uncover hidden voids and passages within the pyramid, deepening our understanding while leaving some mysteries unsolved.
w02.happened: Around 2560 BC, the Great Pyramid of Giza was completed in Egypt. This enormous structure was built as a tomb for Pharaoh Khufu, the ruler of the time. The pyramid stands alongside other pyramids and the mysterious Sphinx on the Giza plateau, near the Nile River. Its construction took many years and required thousands of workers, including skilled builders, stone cutters, and laborers. The Great Pyramid was the tallest man-made building in the world for almost 4,000 years, reaching about 146 meters (480 feet) high. Its blocks, weighing several tons each, fit together with remarkable accuracy. The pyramid was covered in smooth, white limestone that shone brightly in the sun, making it visible from miles away. Even after thousands of years, it remains one of the most recognized symbols of ancient Egypt and a wonder of the ancient world.
w02.scripture: The scriptures do not mention the Great Pyramid or Egypt's pyramids directly, but principles in the Bible and other scriptures speak to it. In Matthew 6:19-21, Jesus taught, “Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth... but lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven.” Similarly, Doctrine and Covenants 6:7 reminds us to “seek not for riches but for wisdom.” These verses help us remember that while some people have devoted their lives to building stones that last, God calls us to build lives filled with love and service, which last forever.
w02.background: Before the Great Pyramid was built, Egypt was already a well-organized kingdom, known for its rich culture and powerful rulers called pharaohs. The land along the Nile was fertile, supporting villages and cities. Egyptians believed in many gods and had a special respect for the afterlife. Their society was divided into classes, with the pharaoh at the top, followed by priests, officials, craftsmen, and farmers. Most people lived in mud-brick homes and worked in agriculture, though large state projects like the pyramid brought workers from all over. Life was shaped by the rhythms of the Nile, with its yearly flooding feeding the crops that fed the people. Pharaohs built monuments to show their greatness and to honor their gods, hoping their names would be remembered forever.

w03.fall: The decline of Athens' Golden Age was precipitated by both internal and external factors.
