es10.learn: From this event, we can learn that even the greatest challenges can be overcome when people work together, share knowledge, and care about others’ well-being. God has given us minds to discover and hands to help, and sometimes the things we invent—like vaccines—can become tools to lift suffering and save lives. The end of smallpox teaches us that with faith, effort, and unity, enormous good can be done for families across the world.
es10.matters: Smallpox eradication matters deeply because it shows what is possible when humanity unites to solve a problem, regardless of politics or borders. For families of faith, this victory can be seen as a blessing made possible by the gifts of discovery, charity, and cooperation—blessings that come from God to help relieve suffering. It reminds us that technology, when used wisely and with care for others, can help fulfill God's commandment to love our neighbors. It also strengthens hope that other diseases could one day be eliminated, making the world a safer place for children everywhere.

sources.name: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC): History of Smallpox
World Health Organization: Smallpox eradication
Smithsonian Magazine: The Last Disease Eradicated

es10.evidence: The historical and scientific evidence for smallpox eradication is overwhelming and well documented. Detailed medical records, millions of vaccine vials, and personal testimonies from survivors and healthcare workers show the deadly impact smallpox once had and the painstaking efforts that led to its end. The World Health Organization coordinated the global campaign and kept careful records of every case and every vaccination effort. Surveillance teams traveled to remote villages and busy cities, helping ensure no case went unnoticed. Since 1980, there has not been a single naturally occurring case of smallpox, confirming its eradication. Laboratories still hold samples for study, but strict controls are in place. The story is confirmed in medical history books, museums, and by eyewitnesses still alive today.
es10.happened: On May 8, 1980, the World Health Assembly officially declared that smallpox, a deadly and ancient disease, had been eradicated from the world. This was the result of years of hard, careful work by scientists, doctors, and health workers from many countries. Smallpox was a terrible illness known for causing fever, a distinctive skin rash, and often death or lifelong scarring. The campaign to end smallpox included watching for any outbreaks and then quickly vaccinating anyone who might have been close to someone sick. This strategy, called 'ring vaccination,' helped contain outbreaks before they could spread. The last person to get smallpox naturally was Ali Maow Maalin, a cook in Somalia, in 1977. After that, scientists watched closely for any new cases. For three full years, none appeared. That proved the disease was truly gone. This achievement was historic, showing what people around the globe can do when they work together, even when their countries do not always get along. No other human disease has been wiped out on purpose as smallpox has.
es10.scripture: While the scriptures do not mention smallpox or diseases by name, they do teach about using knowledge to bless others. In the Doctrine and Covenants 88:118, we are told, 'seek ye out of the best books words of wisdom; seek learning, even by study and also by faith.' The Savior’s ministry often focused on healing and compassion for the sick and afflicted, as seen throughout the Gospels (for example, Matthew 14:14). The principle of loving and helping those in need is central to Christ’s teachings and can inspire efforts to end suffering, including through the wise use of technology and cooperation.
es10.background: Before smallpox was defeated, it was one of humanity’s worst enemies. In many parts of the world, seeing someone covered in the painful blisters of smallpox was tragically common. Families in villages and in cities lived with the fear that smallpox could strike at any time, killing young and old alike, or leaving people blinded or scarred for life. Hospitals in affected areas were often overwhelmed when outbreaks happened. Scientists and doctors devoted much of their work to finding better vaccines, treatments, and ways to keep smallpox from spreading. By the 1960s and 1970s, the world was changing rapidly—countries, even rivals like the United States and the Soviet Union, found ways to cooperate on global health. This unity made the eradication campaign possible and gave hope that diseases did not have to rule over people’s lives.

es11.talk: Why do you think it's important to help children around the world stay healthy?
es11.child: Long ago, many children didn't live to see their fifth birthday because of sickness and poor living conditions. Today, thanks to clean water, vaccines, and better care, more children are growing up healthy and strong.
es11.learn: The significant reduction in child mortality teaches us the value of persistent efforts in public health and the importance of global cooperation. It reminds us that challenges once thought insurmountable can be overcome through innovation, education, and compassion. As we continue to strive for further improvements, we are encouraged to support initiatives that promote the health and well-being of children worldwide, recognizing that each life is precious and worthy of protection.
es11.matters: The substantial decrease in child mortality is a testament to human ingenuity and compassion. For families of faith, this progress can be seen as a blessing and a reminder of our responsibility to care for the most vulnerable among us. It underscores the importance of continuing efforts to ensure that every child has the opportunity to grow and thrive. This achievement also highlights the power of collective action and the impact of combining scientific advancements with humanitarian efforts to improve lives globally.

sources.name: World Health Organization: Child mortality and causes of death
Central Statistics Office: World Child Mortality Rates 1950-2024
UNICEF Data: Neonatal Mortality

es11.evidence: Historical data clearly illustrates the dramatic decline in child mortality over the past two centuries. In 1800, approximately 43% of children worldwide died before their fifth birthday. By 1950, this figure had decreased to 22%, and by 2024, it had further dropped to around 3.7%. This progress is attributed to various factors, including improved sanitation, the development and distribution of vaccines, better nutrition, and enhanced medical care. Organizations like the World Health Organization and UNICEF have documented these trends and the interventions that have contributed to saving millions of young lives.
es11.happened: Over the past few decades, the world has witnessed a remarkable decline in child mortality rates. In 1990, approximately 93 out of every 1,000 children died before reaching their fifth birthday. By 2024, this number had fallen to about 36 per 1,000 live births, marking a significant reduction in child deaths worldwide. This progress translates to millions of young lives saved each year. The primary factors contributing to this decline include widespread vaccination programs, improved access to clean water and sanitation, better nutrition, the use of insecticide-treated bed nets to prevent malaria, and increased availability of skilled birth attendants. These interventions have collectively addressed the leading causes of child mortality, such as infectious diseases, malnutrition, and complications during birth.
es11.scripture: The scriptures teach us about the value of each child and the importance of caring for them. In the Bible, Jesus said, "Suffer the little children to come unto me, and forbid them not: for of such is the kingdom of God" (Mark 10:14). This passage emphasizes the preciousness of children and our duty to nurture and protect them. Similarly, in the Book of Mormon, we read about the Savior's love for children and His admonition to care for them (3 Nephi 17:21-23). These teachings inspire us to support efforts that safeguard children's health and well-being.
es11.background: In the early 19th century, child mortality rates were alarmingly high, with nearly half of all children dying before the age of five. This was largely due to poor sanitation, limited medical knowledge, and inadequate nutrition. Families often faced the heartbreak of losing multiple children to diseases that are now preventable or treatable. Over time, advancements in public health, medicine, and technology began to change this grim reality. The introduction of vaccines, improvements in sanitation and hygiene, and better understanding of nutrition played pivotal roles in reducing child deaths. By the mid-20th century, these efforts had already begun to show significant results, setting the stage for the dramatic declines observed in recent decades.

es12.talk: Why do you think it's important for us to learn to read and write?
es12.child: Long ago, most people couldn't read or write. Now, almost everyone can! This means we can read stories, learn new things, and understand our faith better.
es12.learn: The global rise in literacy teaches us the transformative power of education. It highlights the importance of providing learning opportunities to all individuals, regardless of background. For families, it reinforces the value of teaching children to read, not only for practical benefits but also to enable them to engage with their faith on a personal level, fostering a lifelong love of learning and spiritual growth.
es12.matters: The rise in global literacy has profound implications. Literate individuals have better access to information, can participate more fully in civic life, and have improved economic opportunities. For families of faith, literacy enables personal engagement with sacred texts, fostering a deeper understanding and personal connection to spiritual teachings. Teaching children to read not only equips them with essential life skills but also allows them to explore and internalize their faith traditions, continuing a legacy of learning and spiritual growth.

sources.name: Global literacy rate 2024 | Statista
This is how much the global literacy rate grew over 200 years | World Economic Forum
Was Weber Wrong? A Human Capital Theory of Protestant Economic History | The Quarterly Journal of Economics | Oxford Aca

es12.evidence: Historical studies have shown a strong link between Protestantism and higher literacy rates. Researchers Sascha O. Becker and Ludger Woessmann analyzed 19th-century Prussian data and found that Protestant regions had higher literacy and income levels. They attributed this to the Protestant emphasis on personal Bible reading, which necessitated literacy and led to the establishment of more schools. This suggests that religious motivations played a significant role in promoting education and literacy during that period.
es12.happened: Over the past two centuries, the world has witnessed a remarkable transformation in literacy. In 1820, only about 12% of the global population over the age of 15 could read and write. This meant that nearly nine out of ten people were unable to engage with written texts. By 1900, literacy rates had modestly increased to just over 20%. However, the mid-20th century marked a significant acceleration in literacy growth. By 1960, the global literacy rate had risen to 42%, and by 1983, it reached 70%. Today, approximately 87% of adults worldwide are literate, with youth literacy rates even higher. This progress reflects concerted efforts in education and the recognition of literacy as a fundamental human right.
es12.scripture: The scriptures emphasize the importance of learning and wisdom. In the Doctrine and Covenants, the Lord instructs, "Seek ye out of the best books words of wisdom; seek learning, even by study and also by faith" (D&C 88:118). This passage underscores the value of both secular and spiritual education, encouraging individuals to pursue knowledge to strengthen their faith and understanding.
es12.background: In the early 19th century, education was a privilege reserved for the elite. Most people lived in agrarian societies where formal schooling was scarce, and children often worked alongside their families from a young age. The Industrial Revolution began to change this landscape, as the need for a more educated workforce became apparent. Religious movements, particularly Protestantism, emphasized personal Bible reading, which spurred the establishment of schools and promoted literacy. Over time, governments recognized the economic and social benefits of an educated populace, leading to the implementation of compulsory education laws and the expansion of public schooling systems.

es13.talk: Why do you think it's special to have grandparents in our lives?
es13.child: A long time ago, most people didn't live very long, and many never met their grandparents. Now, people live much longer, so it's common to know and spend time with grandparents.
es13.learn: The remarkable increase in life expectancy teaches us the value of progress and the importance of utilizing knowledge and resources to improve human well-being. It reminds us to appreciate the time we have with our loved ones and to invest in building strong, supportive family relationships. Recognizing that such longevity is a relatively recent development encourages us to make the most of the opportunities it presents, fostering connections across generations and strengthening the fabric of our families and communities.
es13.matters: The doubling of life expectancy over the past century is a testament to human ingenuity and the blessings of modern advancements. For families of faith, this extended lifespan offers more opportunities to build and strengthen multigenerational relationships. Grandparents can play a pivotal role in the upbringing and spiritual education of their grandchildren, sharing wisdom and experiences that enrich family life. This shift underscores the importance of cherishing and nurturing family bonds, recognizing them as precious gifts that were less attainable in previous generations.

sources.name: World Health Organization: Life Expectancy
Our World in Data: Life Expectancy

es13.evidence: Historical and scientific data provide clear evidence of the dramatic increase in life expectancy. In 1900, global life expectancy was around 32 years. By 2021, it had risen to approximately 71 years. This improvement is attributed to advancements in medical care, such as the development of vaccines and antibiotics, improved sanitation, better nutrition, and public health initiatives. The World Health Organization reports that between 2000 and 2019, global life expectancy increased by more than six years, from 66.8 years to 73.1 years. These statistics underscore the significant progress made in enhancing human health and longevity.
es13.happened: Over the past century, the world has witnessed a remarkable transformation in human longevity. In 1900, the average global life expectancy at birth was approximately 32 years. By 2021, this figure had more than doubled, reaching around 71 years. This increase is not confined to wealthier nations; every region across the globe has experienced significant gains in life expectancy. Such progress reflects substantial advancements in medical care, public health initiatives, and overall living conditions. Notably, the improvement isn't solely due to a reduction in child mortality rates; individuals at all stages of life are now living longer. This means that today, it's common for people to know their grandchildren—a familial connection that was rare throughout most of human history.
es13.scripture: The scriptures emphasize the value of family and the blessings of longevity. In Psalms 128:6, it is written, "Yea, thou shalt see thy children's children, and peace upon Israel." This passage highlights the joy and fulfillment that comes from witnessing multiple generations within a family. Additionally, in Doctrine and Covenants 68:25, parents are counseled to teach their children the principles of the gospel, a responsibility that can now be shared more broadly across generations due to increased life spans.
es13.background: At the dawn of the 20th century, life was markedly different from today. Medical knowledge was limited, and many diseases that are now preventable or treatable were often fatal. Sanitation systems were rudimentary, leading to widespread outbreaks of illnesses. Infant and child mortality rates were alarmingly high, and many adults succumbed to infections or conditions that are now manageable. The concept of a multigenerational family living together was uncommon, as many individuals did not live long enough to see their grandchildren. Daily life was fraught with challenges that made survival into old age a rare achievement.

es14.t: Extreme Poverty Falls Below Ten Percent
es14.talk: Why do you think sharing what we have can help families far away who we may never meet?
es14.child: A long time ago, most people in the world were very poor and struggled each day just for food. Now, only a few do, because many people have found ways to help each other and make life better. We can all help by sharing what we have and being kind.
es14.learn: We can learn that great good can come over time when people wisely use resources, knowledge, and the gifts God has given. Even when problems seem huge and unending, steady efforts and wise choices can change the world for the better. This milestone encourages us to be hopeful, grateful, and willing to help lift those still in need.
es14.matters: This drop in extreme poverty means millions of families can now send their children to school, eat nutritious food, and live in safer homes. It's a powerful reminder that, with wise use of knowledge and working together, people can create real and lasting change. For families who believe God gave us talents and technology to lift each other, this moment is a testament to faith in action: when hearts and hands combine, suffering can be eased and opportunities can grow. Understanding this gives hope and encourages gratitude, inspiring us to use our blessings to help others.
