Our World in Data: Global Extreme Poverty
Encyclopaedia Britannica: Poverty

es14.evidence: The fall in global poverty is carefully tracked by institutions like the World Bank, which uses surveys and data collected from almost every country. Their research shows that in 2015, the number of people living on less than $2.15 a day (the international line for extreme poverty) dropped below 10 percent of the global population for the first time. Detailed studies show that China and India each lifted hundreds of millions out of poverty when they made big changes to their economies by opening trade, improving education, and protecting property rights. Though some scholars debate exactly which policies worked best, almost all experts agree the trend is real. Surveys in rich countries often show people think global poverty is getting worse, when the opposite is true.
es14.happened: In the year 2015, the world reached a remarkable milestone: for the first time in recorded history, fewer than 10 percent of people around the globe were living in what experts call “extreme poverty.” Extreme poverty is when a person has so little money that it's very hard to get enough food, clean water, shelter, or anything else day-to-day life requires. Back in 1820, almost everyone—about 90 out of every 100 people—lived under these conditions. Progress was slow at first. By 1950, about half the world still struggled, and even in 1990, more than one in three faced extreme poverty. But then, a wave of change swept through. New ideas about property, markets, and sharing knowledge spread. The two countries with the most people—China and India—shifted their economies and dramatically reduced poverty. By 2015, thanks to steady work by millions of families, governments, churches, schools, and charities, the world passed the threshold: less than one-tenth of all people lived on less than about two dollars a day.
es14.scripture: Scripture teaches us about caring for the poor and the blessings of working together to lift others. In the Bible, the Savior says, 'For ye have the poor with you always, and whensoever ye will ye may do them good' (Mark 14:7). The Book of Mormon urges that 'ye will administer of your substance unto him that standeth in need' (Mosiah 4:16). Doctrine and Covenants 104:17 explains, 'For the earth is full, and there is enough and to spare.' While the Bible predicts there will always be poor to care for, these scriptures also show God wants us to use what we have generously and wisely so far fewer need suffer.
es14.background: The world in the early 1800s was a very different place. Most people worked on farms or in simple labor, often just trying to survive. There were not many machines, and most families grew or made nearly everything they used. In many countries, disease, famine, and war made life even harder. Even as electricity, trains, and medicines appeared, the benefits came slowly to those in poverty. By the mid-1900s, countries began to share more ideas and inventions, and leaders worked toward peace and trade. Children went to school more often, and families started to have safer homes and more reliable sources of food. Still, for over a billion people, having enough to eat every day was not certain until changes sped up in the late 20th century.

es15.talk: How can we help people who don't have enough to eat or go to school?
es15.child: Many people in Africa don't have enough money for food, clothes, or school. We can help by sharing what we have and being kind to others.
es15.learn: This situation teaches us that while progress in reducing global poverty is possible, it requires sustained and targeted efforts, especially in regions facing structural challenges. It highlights the need for comprehensive strategies that address economic growth, education, healthcare, and governance. For individuals and communities, it serves as a reminder of the importance of compassion, service, and advocacy in supporting those in need.
es15.matters: The persistence of extreme poverty in Sub-Saharan Africa has profound implications for global development and humanitarian efforts. For families of faith, this situation underscores the moral imperative to assist those in need, reflecting the teachings of compassion and service. Addressing poverty aligns with the belief that all individuals are children of God, deserving of dignity and opportunity. Moreover, alleviating poverty contributes to global stability, as economic hardship often correlates with social unrest and migration pressures. Therefore, concerted efforts to reduce poverty are essential for fostering peace and prosperity worldwide.

sources.name: World Bank: Measuring Poverty
World Bank: Africa Overview
World Bank: Poverty Overview

es15.evidence: Historical and economic data indicate that while global poverty rates have declined over the past few decades, progress has been uneven. In 2024, the World Bank reported that 45.1% of Sub-Saharan Africa's population lived in extreme poverty, amounting to approximately 464 million people. This figure represented a significant portion of the global extreme poor. Factors contributing to this situation included rapid population growth, economic stagnation, and conflicts. Additionally, regions affected by fragility and weak governance structures experienced higher poverty rates, underscoring the complex interplay between economic development and political stability.
es15.happened: In 2026, the global fight against extreme poverty faced significant challenges, particularly in Sub-Saharan Africa. Despite efforts to reduce poverty, the region saw a rise in the total number of people living in extreme poverty. This increase was primarily due to population growth outpacing economic gains. By 2024, approximately 45.1% of Sub-Saharan Africa's population lived on less than $3.00 per day, the international threshold for extreme poverty. This equated to about 464 million individuals. The World Bank projected that, without substantial intervention, the number of people living in extreme poverty could remain high for decades, potentially increasing by 2040. This stagnation was attributed to factors such as economic stagnation, conflict, and fragile governance structures in many affected countries.
es15.scripture: The scriptures emphasize the importance of caring for the poor and needy. In the Bible, Proverbs 19:17 states, "He that hath pity upon the poor lendeth unto the Lord; and that which he hath given will he pay him again." Similarly, in the Book of Mormon, Mosiah 4:26 teaches, "And now, for the sake of these things which I have spoken unto you—that is, for the sake of retaining a remission of your sins from day to day—that ye may walk guiltless before God—I would that ye should impart of your substance to the poor." These passages highlight the spiritual significance of aiding those in poverty.
es15.background: Over the past few decades, the world witnessed a significant decline in extreme poverty, largely driven by economic growth in regions like East and South Asia. However, this progress was uneven. Sub-Saharan Africa, home to diverse cultures and rich natural resources, faced persistent challenges. Many communities lacked access to essential services like education, healthcare, and clean water. Daily life for those in extreme poverty often involved subsistence farming, limited employment opportunities, and vulnerability to economic shocks. Despite international aid and development programs, structural issues such as political instability, corruption, and inadequate infrastructure hindered substantial progress in poverty reduction.

ex01.t: Alexander the Great - East to India
ex01.talk: How can learning about other cultures help us understand and love our neighbors better?
ex01.child: Long ago, a leader named Alexander traveled from Greece to India, meeting new people and sharing ideas. His journey helped different cultures learn from each other, making the world more connected.
ex01.learn: From Alexander's journey, we learn the power of cultural exchange and the importance of communication. By sharing languages and ideas, societies can grow and enrich each other. This history teaches us to value and respect different cultures, recognizing that such interactions can lead to greater understanding and unity.
ex01.matters: Alexander's journey to India was more than a military expedition; it was a bridge between East and West. By establishing cities and encouraging the mingling of cultures, he set the stage for the Hellenistic period, where Greek language and ideas blended with those of the East. This fusion influenced art, philosophy, and governance, enriching both civilizations. For families of faith, this historical event underscores how diverse cultures can come together, sharing knowledge and traditions. It also highlights how the spread of a common language, like Koine Greek, can facilitate the sharing of important messages, much like the New Testament was later written in this accessible dialect, allowing the teachings of Jesus Christ to reach a broader audience.

sources.name: Alexander the Great
Indian campaign of Alexander the Great
Cultural Diffusion in Hellenistic Period

ex01.evidence: Historical records from ancient historians like Arrian and Plutarch provide detailed accounts of Alexander's campaigns, including his battles and interactions with local rulers. Archaeological findings, such as the remains of cities founded by Alexander, support these narratives. The spread of Hellenistic art and architecture in regions as far as India indicates a significant Greek influence. Additionally, the adoption of Koine Greek as a common language across these territories is evidenced by inscriptions and documents from the period. These pieces of evidence collectively confirm the historical reality of Alexander's journey to India and its lasting impact.
ex01.happened: Between 334 and 323 BC, Alexander the Great embarked on an ambitious campaign that extended from Greece to the edges of India. After uniting the Greek city-states, he crossed into Asia Minor, defeating the Persian Empire and continuing eastward. In 327 BC, Alexander entered the Indian subcontinent through the Khyber Pass, aiming to expand his empire further. He faced formidable resistance from local rulers, notably King Porus of the Paurava kingdom. In 326 BC, at the Battle of the Hydaspes River, Alexander employed strategic tactics to overcome Porus's forces, which included war elephants. Impressed by Porus's valor, Alexander reinstated him as a satrap, or governor, of his own territory, fostering loyalty among the local populace. Alexander's army, weary from years of campaigning and facing the prospect of confronting the powerful Nanda Empire further east, eventually refused to march beyond the Hyphasis River (modern Beas River). Respecting his soldiers' wishes, Alexander turned back, marking the easternmost extent of his conquests. On his return journey, he founded several cities, many named Alexandria, to serve as administrative centers and to spread Greek culture. His campaign facilitated significant cultural exchanges between the Greek and Indian civilizations, leaving a lasting impact on art, architecture, and language in the regions he traversed.
ex01.scripture: While the scriptures do not directly mention Alexander the Great, the principle of God preparing the way for His purposes is evident. In Doctrine and Covenants 88:78-79, the Lord instructs us to seek learning in various fields, including history and languages, to be better prepared to serve Him. Alexander's conquests, which spread the Greek language and culture, can be seen as part of this preparation, creating a common linguistic foundation that later facilitated the spread of the gospel through the New Testament.
ex01.background: Before Alexander's conquests, the Greek world was composed of city-states, each with its own government and culture, yet sharing a common language and religious beliefs. The Persian Empire, a vast and powerful entity, controlled much of the known world, including parts of Asia Minor and the Middle East. Daily life in these regions varied, with agrarian societies in the countryside and bustling trade centers in cities. The Indian subcontinent was home to diverse kingdoms and cultures, with advanced urban centers, rich traditions in art and science, and complex social structures. The interaction between these civilizations was limited, with trade being the primary form of contact. Alexander's campaign changed this dynamic, creating new routes for cultural and commercial exchange.

ex02.talk: What is something you would walk a long way to learn or find?
ex02.child: A brave monk named Xuanzang walked all the way from China to India to find special books about his religion. He brought these books back so everyone in China could learn from them. His story shows how important it is to look for truth, even when it is hard.
ex02.learn: Xuanzang teaches us that the search for truth and wisdom takes courage, patience, and trust in Heavenly Father. Even when the road is long and uncertain, good things can come from persistence and faith. Families can be inspired to treasure their own scriptures and seek to understand the beliefs of others with kindness and curiosity.
ex02.matters: Xuanzang’s journey matters because it shows us the power of seeking truth, even when it is hard or risky. His story reminds us that finding and sharing truth can bless whole nations—not just one community. For families of faith, Xuanzang’s devotion to gathering sacred writings is much like the faith of early Latter-day Saints who crossed great distances to have the scriptures and worship as they believed. Such journeys are powerful reminders that Heavenly Father honors great efforts to seek truth and share goodness with others.

sources.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Xuanzang
Smithsonian Magazine: The Monk Who Brought Buddhism to China
World History Encyclopedia: Xuanzang

ex02.evidence: Historical accounts and archaeological evidence both confirm Xuanzang’s journey. Xuanzang himself wrote a detailed record of his travels, called the 'Great Tang Records on the Western Regions.' Many places he described—like the ruins of Nalanda University—have been found by archaeologists, and match his descriptions closely. Chinese historical records from the Tang Dynasty also mention and honor Xuanzang upon his return. The impact of his translations and the lasting popularity of Journey to the West in China provide further proof of his importance. While some small details of his adventure are hard to verify, the main events of his journey are confirmed by multiple sources.
ex02.happened: Xuanzang was a Buddhist monk from China who, in 629 AD, left his home in the city of Chang’an and began an incredibly long journey all the way to India. He made this trip mostly on foot, leaving behind almost everything he knew, and facing deserts, tall mountains, hunger, and even dangers from robbers along the way. Xuanzang’s goal was to find original Buddhist scriptures and bring them back to China, so people at home could learn from them, too. Over 16 years, Xuanzang traveled roughly 10,000 miles, visiting many cities and famous Buddhist sites such as Nalanda, the great university of ancient India. He listened to teachers, copied many sacred texts, and learned new ideas about his faith. When Xuanzang finally returned home to China in 645 AD, he was welcomed warmly, and he spent many years carefully translating the scriptures he had gathered, sharing precious knowledge with many others. His adventure became one of the world’s most amazing stories, inspiring the beloved Chinese novel Journey to the West.
ex02.scripture: There is no direct mention of Xuanzang or Buddhist journeys in Latter-day Saint scripture, but the principle of seeking truth through diligent effort is seen throughout. In the Book of Mormon, Lehi’s family traveled far to retrieve the brass plates (1 Nephi 3-5), risking much to preserve God’s word. Doctrine and Covenants 88:118 teaches to 'seek ye out of the best books words of wisdom,' encouraging faithful study from all good sources. These scriptures show how Heavenly Father values our effort to gather and learn sacred truth.
ex02.background: Xuanzang lived during the Tang Dynasty, a time when China was strong, open to new ideas, and bustling with people from many lands. Chang’an, his home city, was a huge, lively place—often called the world’s largest city at the time. Chinese people in this era valued learning, and religions like Buddhism, Daoism, and Confucianism shaped daily life. Most people farmed, made crafts, or traded goods in busy markets; some became scholars or monks. Buddhism had taken root in China about 400 years earlier, but many Chinese Buddhists worried their teachings, copied and re-copied from ancient Indian sources, might not be complete or correct. The journey overland from China to India was dangerous—across the Silk Road and over the Himalayas—yet stories of India as Buddhism’s birthplace drew serious seekers like Xuanzang to undertake the risk.

ex03.t: Marco Polo - Silk Road to China
ex03.talk: Why do you think it mattered that Marco Polo wrote down what he saw and learned in China?
ex03.child: Marco Polo went on a long, dangerous trip from Italy to China. He saw many new things, like how the Chinese made paper and fireworks. Later, his stories helped people in Europe get excited about learning and exploring new places.
ex03.learn: From Marco Polo we can learn that exploring new lands and learning from others can lead to unexpected blessings for many. One person’s courage, questions, and careful record-keeping can help people see the world in a new way and bring knowledge that opens doors. Families can remember that curiosity, guided by faith and a desire to do good, can be one of Heavenly Father’s tools in preparing the world for greater light and truth.
ex03.matters: Marco Polo’s journey brought news of China and the East to a Europe hungry for discovery. His stories gave Europeans their first big look into Asian civilization and its advanced technology, like papermaking and printing. These inventions would later help bring about the Renaissance and the invention of the printing press. From a faith perspective, it’s remarkable that one man’s curiosity helped set off a chain of learning and exploration that would eventually help the Bible, and later the Book of Mormon, be printed, carried, and read by millions. Marco’s story reminds families that God can use even the simplest beginnings—like a merchant's journey—to bring greater light to the world.

sources.name: Metropolitan Museum of Art – Marco Polo and the Silk Road
Encyclopaedia Britannica – Marco Polo
History.com – Marco Polo

ex03.evidence: Scholars have examined Marco Polo’s book for hundreds of years. Most historians agree that he really did travel to China and witness many of the things he described. His detailed accounts of the size and richness of Beijing (then Khanbaliq), local customs, and technologies mostly match what Chinese records from the Yuan Dynasty say. Archaeologists and historians have found very few European artifacts or written evidence in China from that exact time, but the details and insights found in his book go well beyond what could have been known by hearsay in Europe. However, some minor errors and fanciful tales in his account have led some historians to wonder if Polo sometimes included second-hand stories he heard on his travels. On the whole, the journey and time at Kublai Khan’s court are considered well-attested by modern scholars.
ex03.happened: Marco Polo was a young man from Venice, Italy, when he began his famous journey in 1271 with his father and uncle. Their goal was to reach the court of Kublai Khan, the powerful ruler of China, whom Polo’s family had met years earlier. Their route took them along the fabled Silk Road, winding through deserts, mountains, and strange cities full of new sights and customs. After many hardships and years of travel, Marco Polo arrived in Khanbaliq, now Beijing, in 1275. There, he became a trusted envoy for Kublai Khan and spent about 17 years serving in the Khan's court, learning about the Chinese way of life, technology, and government. When he finally returned to Venice, Polo shared his stories of great cities, marvelous inventions, and nations that seemed almost magical to Europeans. His stories were gathered in a book called “The Travels of Marco Polo.” This book fascinated thousands of readers with tales of paper money, rapid communication across the empire, and everyday wonders like fireworks, printing, and spices unknown in Europe. These stories caught the attention of many, including explorers like Christopher Columbus.
ex03.scripture: No scripture mentions Marco Polo by name, but there are principles that connect with his story. In the Bible, the Lord often invites His disciples to go to new lands and learn from many peoples. In Doctrine and Covenants 88:78-80, God tells us to “seek learning, even by study and also by faith,” and to “be instructed more perfectly in theory, in principle, in doctrine, in the law of the gospel, in all things…of countries and of kingdoms.” Marco Polo’s journey is a good example of seeking learning from the world, and sharing it for the good of others.
ex03.background: Marco Polo lived during the Middle Ages, a time when most Europeans had little direct contact with the cultures of Asia. Venice, Marco’s home, was a bustling city of merchants and traders who exchanged goods with far-off lands. Travel was dangerous and slow, with many people spending their lives in the same towns or villages where they were born. China, on the other hand, was ruled by the Mongol Empire, the largest contiguous empire the world has ever seen. Under Kublai Khan, China was highly organized, with thriving cities, grand roads, and incredible new technologies like papermaking, printing, and gunpowder. Life for most Europeans in this era was simple and hard; they depended on farming, lived in small stone or wooden homes, and learned most things from local priests, merchants, or travelers with news from afar. The journey Marco Polo made was rare and risky, but it opened a window between two very different worlds.

ex04.talk: What do you think would happen if people shared what they learned with others from faraway places?
ex04.child: A Chinese leader named Zheng He once sailed big ships to faraway lands, meeting many new people. After his journeys, China stopped exploring and stayed at home. That gave other countries a chance to find new lands later on.
ex04.learn: We learn that the world changes in unexpected ways. Sometimes plans are set aside or great work is paused, and we don’t always know why. But looking back, we can often see God’s wisdom or preparation in the timing, even if it felt disappointing at first. We are also reminded to use the gifts and opportunities Heavenly Father gives us, knowing that He always cares for all His children around the world.
ex04.matters: Zheng He’s voyages changed the way the world connected, even if only for a short time. They showed how far humans can reach when they cooperate, plan, and trust in new ways of doing things. For families of faith, this story teaches that great opportunities come, but also that timing matters greatly in God’s work. The Chinese choice to turn inward after these voyages left room for others—like the Portuguese and Spanish—to explore and change the world. That opened the door for the Americas to be discovered by Europeans at a particular moment in God’s timing, when later, religious reformers would seek a new land for freedom. It reminds us to look for God’s hand in the way history flows, even if we can’t see the reasons right away.

sources.name: Smithsonian Magazine - Zheng He: The Ming Dynasty Admiral Who Explored the World
BBC - The voyages of Zheng He
Metropolitan Museum of Art - Zheng He’s Voyages

ex04.evidence: We have strong historical evidence for Zheng He’s voyages. Ancient Chinese records, including detailed logs of the fleets, names of the crew, and official orders, have survived. Archaeologists have found relics of Ming-era ceramics in places like East Africa and India—far from China’s shores—confirming the reach of the expeditions. The size of Zheng He’s largest ships, described as up to 120 meters long, is debated, but the grand scale is confirmed by shipyards found in Nanjing. Records from the countries Zheng He visited, such as inscriptions in Sri Lanka, also describe the arrival of the Chinese fleets. After the voyages, written imperial edicts show a clear shift to focus only on China’s lands and to curtail overseas journeys. Historians agree China could have easily continued exploring, but internal changes—such as the death of supporters at court and concern over costs—caused the sudden end.
ex04.happened: Between 1405 and 1433, a Chinese admiral named Zheng He led seven enormous sea voyages, some of the most ambitious in human history. Zheng He was appointed by the Yongle Emperor of the Ming Dynasty to take fleets as large as 300 ships—many times bigger than anything in Europe at the time—from the busy city of Nanjing out into the vast Indian Ocean. These fleets sailed to lands far from China, including what we now know as Vietnam, Indonesia, India, Arabia, and all the way to East Africa. Zheng He’s ships carried silk, porcelain, and gifts to show China’s wealth and peace, while bringing back rare animals and goods, and returning with visitors and ambassadors from those distant shores. People in foreign lands were amazed by the size and order of the fleets. By 1415, the world seemed closer together than ever, with China at the center of a buzzing network of trade and diplomacy. But after these voyages ended, the Chinese government made a surprising decision: they stopped building large ships, closed their harbors to most foreign trade, and future emperors focused only on the land within their borders. In this way, a door to the wider world was closed for China for centuries.
ex04.scripture: There is no scripture that directly tells the story of Zheng He or ancient Chinese explorers. However, principles from scripture do relate. Doctrine and Covenants 1:23 teaches that God acts in His own due time and in a way that the world might be prepared for His work. Likewise, in Acts 17:26, the Apostle Paul explains that Heavenly Father “hath determined the times before appointed, and the bounds of their habitation.” These verses remind us that the Lord is mindful of all nations and peoples, guiding the movements of history according to divine wisdom and purpose.
ex04.background: The world of early 1400s China was vibrant and powerful. The Ming Dynasty stood as one of the richest civilizations, famous for its beautiful art, advanced technology, and busy cities. Most people lived in small farming villages, growing rice and vegetables, but the great cities buzzed with markets, workshops, and government officials. The emperor was considered the ‘Son of Heaven’ and ruled over a vast land with millions of subjects. Other civilizations, such as the Indian kingdoms and the powerful trading cities of Arabia and East Africa, were also prospering. Travel by land and sea was slow and sometimes dangerous, but rare goods, stories, and ideas traveled far. At the time, no European ships had sailed around Africa, and few outside of Asia knew much about China or its mighty fleets. Daily life for Zheng He's sailors included strict routines, careful navigation by the stars, and the immense teamwork needed to sail across oceans.

ex05.t: Bartolomeu Dias - Cape of Good Hope
ex05.talk: Why do you think it's important to explore new places and learn about different people?
ex05.child: Long ago, a brave sailor named Bartolomeu Dias sailed around the bottom of Africa, finding a new way to reach faraway lands. This helped people trade and share ideas across the world.
ex05.learn: From Dias's journey, we learn the value of perseverance and courage in the face of the unknown. His expedition teaches us that seeking new paths can lead to significant advancements and blessings. It also reminds us that, with faith and determination, we can overcome obstacles and contribute to the greater good.
ex05.matters: Dias's successful navigation around the Cape of Good Hope was a monumental achievement that paved the way for a direct sea route from Europe to Asia. This breakthrough diminished the Islamic monopoly on overland trade routes, reshaping global economic and political dynamics. For families of faith, this event underscores the belief that Heavenly Father prepares the way for His purposes. The opening of new trade routes facilitated the spread of ideas, cultures, and, eventually, the gospel to distant lands, aligning with the divine plan to bring His children closer together.

sources.name: Bartolomeu Dias - Life, Legacy & Expeditions | HISTORY
Bartolomeu Dias: Biography, Expedition of the Cape of Good Hope
Cape of Good Hope

ex05.evidence: Historical records, including logs from Dias's expedition and accounts from the Portuguese court, provide detailed information about the voyage. Archaeological findings, such as the padrões (stone crosses) erected by Dias along the African coast, serve as tangible evidence of his journey. These markers, placed at key points, signified Portuguese claims and navigational achievements. The Cape of Good Hope itself remains a geographical testament to Dias's exploration, with its treacherous waters and strategic location continuing to be significant in maritime history.
ex05.happened: In 1488, Portuguese explorer Bartolomeu Dias led an expedition that became the first European venture to round the southern tip of Africa. Departing from Lisbon in August 1487, Dias commanded two caravels and a supply ship. The journey down the West African coast was arduous, with the crew facing strong storms that pushed them out to sea. After 13 days without sight of land, they turned northeast and, on February 3, 1488, anchored in what is now Mossel Bay, South Africa. This confirmed they had navigated around the continent's southernmost point. Dias continued eastward along the coast but, due to dwindling supplies and a restless crew, decided to return to Portugal. On the return voyage, they sighted the southern tip of Africa, which Dias named the "Cape of Storms" due to its treacherous weather. King John II of Portugal later renamed it the "Cape of Good Hope," reflecting the optimism of establishing a sea route to India. Dias returned to Lisbon in December 1488, having opened the way for future maritime trade between Europe and Asia.
ex05.scripture: While the scriptures do not directly mention maritime exploration, they emphasize the importance of seeking knowledge and understanding. Proverbs 25:2 states, "It is the glory of God to conceal a thing: but the honour of kings is to search out a matter." This suggests that exploration and discovery are noble pursuits that can lead to greater understanding of God's creations. Additionally, Doctrine and Covenants 88:79 encourages learning about "things which are at home, things which are abroad," highlighting the value of expanding our knowledge of the world.
ex05.background: In the late 15th century, European nations were eager to find new trade routes to Asia, especially after the overland routes became more perilous due to the rise of the Ottoman Empire. Portugal, under King John II, was at the forefront of maritime exploration, seeking a sea passage to the lucrative markets of India and the East. Bartolomeu Dias, a nobleman and experienced sailor, was chosen to lead this critical expedition. Daily life for sailors like Dias was grueling, with long months at sea, limited provisions, and the constant threat of unknown territories and hostile encounters. The success of such voyages depended on courage, navigational skill, and the ability to endure hardships.

ex06.talk: Why do you think Columbus felt God was helping him sail to new lands?
ex06.child: Columbus sailed far across the sea because he wanted to find new lands. When he landed, he met people he’d never seen before, and the world was never the same. His trips helped lead to where we live and what we enjoy today.
ex06.learn: From Columbus’s story, we learn that exploring new ideas and places can lead to great blessings, but also challenges. We can see that even big, world-changing events are filled with choices—some wise, some mistaken. Families can learn to recognize the ways Heavenly Father prepares people and places for His work, and also to act with care as we meet new people and places.
ex06.matters: Columbus’s voyages are important because they connected two parts of the world that had not known each other. This set in motion changes—some wondrous, some very hard. For families of faith, these events led to the founding of countries like the United States, where religious freedom later made the Restoration of the gospel possible. A family can see how Heavenly Father can use even ordinary people, with their strengths and weakness, to accomplish purposes that echo through history. We can talk about the blessings and also the great responsibilities that come with discovery and change.

sources.name: Smithsonian - Columbus’s Journeys Changed the World
National Park Service - Columbus’s Legacy in the Americas
Encyclopedia Britannica - Christopher Columbus
The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints - Columbus and the Restoration

ex06.evidence: Historians know a lot about Columbus’s voyages. His own journals and letters have survived, along with reports from his crew. Archaeological finds support stories about the places he landed. We have old maps showing where he sailed, and even today, experts study what the world was like before and after Columbus. Evidence shows there were already millions of people living in the Americas with their own societies. While Columbus opened the door for huge exchanges between continents, these contacts also brought diseases and conflict that had profound effects on native peoples. The date of his first landing (October 12, 1492) and his route are very well established by historical documents.
ex06.happened: In 1492, Christopher Columbus set sail from Spain with three ships: the Niña, the Pinta, and the Santa María. His goal was to find a shortcut to Asia by sailing west across the Atlantic Ocean. After weeks at sea, he and his crew finally spotted land, which turned out to be one of the islands now called the Bahamas. Over the next twelve years, Columbus made four voyages to the lands he discovered, visiting parts of what are now the Caribbean islands, Central America, and South America. Columbus met many people who already lived there, whom he called 'Indians,' thinking he had reached Asia. Though others would later understand this was actually a ‘New World’ unknown to Europeans, Columbus himself died believing he had found a new route to Asia. His voyages changed the world by opening up the Americas to European explorers, settlers, and traders, leading to big changes for the people and places on both sides of the Atlantic.
ex06.scripture: Doctrine and Covenants 101:80 says God raised up wise people to establish freedom in America. In 1 Nephi 13:12, the Book of Mormon prophet Nephi has a vision of a man guided by the Spirit across 'the many waters' to the promised land—many Latter-day Saints see this as describing Columbus’s voyage. Columbus’s own writings say he felt guided by God in his journey. The Bible also teaches that great journeys can be led by the Lord, such as with Abraham or Moses (see Genesis 12:1-3 and Exodus 3-4).
ex06.background: Before Columbus sailed, Europe, Africa, and Asia were connected by long trade routes, but the Americas were not known to these continents. Most Europeans had never heard of the large lands or the millions of people living there. Daily life in late 1400s Spain was shaped by farming, small towns, and the Catholic faith. People traveled by horse or by foot, and kings and queens ruled over the land. Ships were powered by wind and sailed based on the stars. The world felt smaller then, separated by huge oceans. The people Columbus met in the Americas had rich cultures, languages, and ways of living that had grown for thousands of years. Their daily lives included farming, fishing, building homes, and worshiping in their own traditions.

ex07.t: Vasco da Gama - Sea Route to India
ex07.talk: Why do you think Heavenly Father sometimes lets people find new places or ways to do things?
ex07.child: Vasco da Gama got in his boat and sailed all the way from Portugal to India. He found a new way to get spices and treasures by going around Africa, and that changed how people traded. His adventure helped more people in Europe learn and get new things, like books and Bibles.
ex07.learn: From Vasco da Gama’s story, we learn that courage and curiosity can open up new worlds. We also see how inventions and hard work can change many lives, not just the ones on the ships, but families and communities all over the globe. For a family of faith, it’s a reminder that Heavenly Father can use all kinds of events—even business and adventure—to bless His children and prepare the world for greater light and knowledge.
ex07.matters: Vasco da Gama’s journey changed the way the world traded. By finding a sea route to India, he helped end the monopoly that overland traders had on Asian goods, especially spices. The wealth from this trade helped fund many changes in Europe, including the printing of Bibles and books that supported the spreading of knowledge and faith. For families of faith, these events are reminders that Heavenly Father can use even simple things like ships, trade, and curiosity for His greater purposes—to help the gospel eventually reach more people.

sources.name: National Geographic - Vasco da Gama
BBC - Vasco da Gama
Encyclopaedia Britannica - Vasco da Gama

ex07.evidence: Historians have many records from Portugal about Vasco da Gama’s voyage, including ship logs, letters, and royal documents. Archaeologists have found remains of ships from similar journeys and traded goods in ports across Africa and India that match what was described from da Gama’s time. Portuguese writings and Indian accounts both describe the meeting between Vasco da Gama and the Zamorin of Calicut, showing that this contact really happened. There are also maps from the period that show the expanding knowledge Europeans gained about Africa and Asia after these voyages. The overwhelming agreement among historians is that Vasco da Gama’s journey to India by sea was a real and documentable event.
ex07.happened: In 1497, a brave Portuguese explorer named Vasco da Gama set sail from Lisbon, Portugal, on a mission to find a sea route to India. He and his crew sailed south along the coast of Africa, then around the stormy tip known as the Cape of Good Hope. After many months at sea, facing hunger, sickness, and storms, they finally reached the shores of Calicut, India, in 1498. This was the first time Europeans had sailed all the way from Europe to India by sea, instead of traveling over hard and dangerous land routes. Da Gama was welcomed by local rulers, though there were many challenges in making the new trade arrangements work. When he returned home, he brought back spices and valuable goods worth much more than the cost of his voyage. His successful journey opened the door for Europeans, especially the Portuguese, to trade directly with Asia, which changed world trade forever and started a new era of exploration.
ex07.scripture: The scriptures don’t mention Vasco da Gama or the sea route to India, but they do speak about the Lord preparing ways for His work to be done. In 1 Nephi 17:8-14, the Lord commands Nephi to build a ship to cross the ocean, promising guidance and protection. Acts 8:27-40 also tells us about Philip sharing the gospel with an Ethiopian traveler, showing that the Lord can use travel and trade to carry the gospel further. These passages teach us that new paths, discoveries, and technologies can serve God's purposes in preparing the world for more truth and light.
ex07.background: At the end of the 15th century, Europe was changing quickly. New inventions like the compass, better ships, and improved maps made it possible for sailors to travel farther than ever before. Most goods from Asia, like spices and silk, reached Europe over land through many middlemen on the Silk Road. This made them very expensive and rare. Ordinary families often never saw such goods. Portugal, a small but determined country, had already sent explorers like Bartolomeu Dias to the coast of Africa, hoping to find a path around it. Vasco da Gama’s voyage was like the next step in a long race. Most people in Europe lived in small towns or the countryside, working as farmers, fishers, or craftsmen, and news of da Gama’s journey would have been both exciting and strange to them.

ex08.talk: How do you think Magellan's journey helped people learn more about the world?
ex08.child: A long time ago, a man named Magellan sailed around the world, showing that the Earth is round. His journey helped people understand that we are all connected.
ex08.learn: Magellan's journey teaches us about the resilience and determination required to explore the unknown. It reminds us of the importance of faith and perseverance in the face of adversity. For families, it serves as an example of how courage and a desire to learn can lead to groundbreaking discoveries that benefit all of humanity.
ex08.matters: Magellan's expedition was a monumental achievement that provided tangible proof of the Earth's roundness and the vastness of its oceans. For families of faith, this journey underscores the unity of Heavenly Father's creation, demonstrating that all lands and peoples are interconnected. The successful circumnavigation paved the way for future exploration and missionary work, making it geographically possible to fulfill the divine mandate to spread the gospel to every nation.

sources.name: Ferdinand Magellan - Early Years, Expedition & Legacy | HISTORY
Magellan expedition - Wikipedia
Was Magellan the First Person to Circumnavigate the Globe? | HISTORY

ex08.evidence: Historical records, including the detailed accounts of Antonio Pigafetta, a member of the expedition, provide firsthand insights into the journey. Archaeological findings, such as artifacts from the voyage and the remains of the ship Victoria, corroborate these accounts. Additionally, navigational charts and maps from the era document the route taken, further validating the expedition's accomplishments.
ex08.happened: In 1519, Portuguese explorer Ferdinand Magellan set sail from Spain with a fleet of five ships and approximately 270 men, aiming to find a westward route to the Spice Islands. The journey was fraught with challenges, including treacherous waters, mutinies, and dwindling supplies. After navigating the strait at the southern tip of South America—later named the Strait of Magellan—the expedition entered the vast Pacific Ocean. They endured a grueling three-month crossing before reaching the Philippines in 1521. There, Magellan was killed during a conflict on the island of Mactan. Despite this loss, the expedition pressed on. Under the command of Juan Sebastián Elcano, the remaining crew continued westward, eventually returning to Spain in 1522 aboard the ship Victoria. Out of the original 270 men, only 18 completed the journey, marking the first recorded circumnavigation of the Earth.
ex08.scripture: The scriptures emphasize the unity and interconnectedness of all God's children. In Acts 17:26, it is stated, "And hath made of one blood all nations of men for to dwell on all the face of the earth." This passage highlights the shared heritage and unity of humanity, aligning with the realization brought about by global exploration that all people are part of a single, divine creation.
ex08.background: In the early 16th century, European nations were fervently seeking new trade routes to access the lucrative spices of the East Indies. The Treaty of Tordesillas in 1494 had divided the newly discovered lands outside Europe between Spain and Portugal, prompting Spain to explore westward routes. Daily life for sailors was arduous, with long voyages exposing them to the risks of scurvy, starvation, and shipwreck. Navigation relied on rudimentary tools, and uncharted waters posed constant dangers. The world was still largely unknown to Europeans, and voyages like Magellan's were ventures into the vast, mysterious expanses of the globe.

ex09.talk: Why do you think it was brave for Captain Cook to sail to places no one from his country had seen before?
ex09.child: Captain Cook sailed really far from England to islands in the big Pacific Ocean. He made maps so other people could find their way, too. Some of the places he visited later became homes for lots of church members, like Hawaii and New Zealand.
ex09.learn: From Cook’s story, we can learn the value of exploring, learning, and preparing the way for others. Sometimes, going into the unknown is part of how we keep growing, both in faith and as a family. Mapping new places took courage and careful attention, just like learning new things or serving others does today. We also learn how important it is to respect and learn from other cultures, as many of those Cook met had lessons and skills of their own, given by God.
ex09.matters: Captain Cook’s explorations opened new connections between peoples and lands that had long been apart. For families of faith, these voyages mattered because they made the way safer and clearer for those who would follow, including missionaries. Within about a lifetime after Cook’s arrival, missionaries—including those from The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints—came to share the gospel in New Zealand and Hawaii. Today, these islands are home to strong and vibrant Latter-day Saint communities. Cook’s careful mapping also set an example of preparing the way for others, much like how families prepare the way for each other in faith and love.

sources.name: Australian National Maritime Museum - James Cook
National Library of New Zealand - Captain Cook
Church of Jesus Christ - Church History in the Pacific
BBC - Captain Cook Timeline

ex09.evidence: Historians have many detailed records of Cook’s voyages, including his own journals, crew logs, and maps made during the trips. These documents match with the places he visited, and many locations in New Zealand, Australia, and Hawaii still remember his arrival. Archaeological digs have found evidence of his visits, and museums preserve objects collected on the voyages. Polynesian oral histories recall encounters with Europeans, often describing Cook’s ships and crew from the Islanders’ point of view. While there are debates about the effects of these meetings on island peoples, the events themselves are well documented. Cook’s charts of the Pacific were so precise that navigators used them for decades afterward.
ex09.happened: Between 1768 and 1779, Captain James Cook, a British naval officer and explorer, sailed across the vast Pacific Ocean on three separate voyages. Starting in Plymouth, England, Cook led the HMS Endeavour and later two other ships to places European maps hardly touched. On his first voyage, he sailed to Tahiti to observe the passing of Venus across the sun, which would help astronomers calculate the distance from Earth to the sun. Afterward, he mapped the coastlines of New Zealand, proving there were two main islands, and then charted much of the eastern coast of Australia, being the first European to do so in detail. Along these journeys, Cook and his crew made first European contact with many Pacific islanders, including the Māori of New Zealand and the Aboriginal Australians. On his later voyages, Cook traveled further north to the Hawaiian Islands, where he also became the first known European visitor. Sadly, during his third voyage, Cook died in Hawaii during a conflict. His voyages changed maps and brought the cultures, plants, and animals of the Pacific Islands into European awareness.
ex09.scripture: The scriptures do not mention Captain Cook, but the idea of exploring new lands and sharing knowledge is woven throughout. In Doctrine and Covenants 88:79, saints are told to seek learning "by study and also by faith"—including about the earth, its kingdoms, and peoples. In the Bible, the Lord often sends travelers to prepare His work, like Paul’s missionary journeys in Acts. The Book of Mormon also teaches that the Lord guides people across the waters to new lands (1 Nephi 18). These passages remind us that journeys, maps, and learning can serve Heavenly Father’s purposes.
ex09.background: Before Captain Cook’s voyages, European knowledge of the world’s oceans and distant lands was limited. Sailors and mapmakers from Portugal, Spain, and the Netherlands had charted parts of the Pacific, but vast regions were blank or filled with guesses. The people of Polynesia, Australia, and New Zealand had rich cultures, centuries-old traditions, and expert navigation skills, moving between islands by reading stars and ocean currents long before Europeans arrived. In places like Tahiti, life was guided by chiefs and priests, with fishing, farming, and gathering at the heart of daily tasks. In England, the Enlightenment was taking hold—an age of seeking knowledge, science, and discovery. Cook himself had risen from humble beginnings, learning navigation and math as a sailor before being chosen to lead these great voyages.

ex10.talk: How can learning new things help your family or someone who will come after you?
ex10.child: Lewis and Clark went on a long trip across wild country that no one from their country had seen before. They made maps and found out what animals and plants lived there, so other people could travel safely later. People could travel west because Lewis and Clark found the way.
ex10.learn: We can learn from Lewis and Clark that preparing, working together with people who have different strengths, and trusting in a good purpose can help us do things that seem impossible. Their teamwork with each other and with Native peoples made their survival possible. Just as they paved a path for others, we too might be preparing ways for others without realizing it, and Heavenly Father can guide us as we do hard things for His work.
ex10.matters: Lewis and Clark’s journey matters because it opened up the West for new families, settlers, and future explorers. Their maps and reports let others know the land could be crossed, and that it had rich resources and beauty. For families of faith, we can see this as an example of preparation—Heavenly Father let good people gather knowledge so others could follow safely later. Without their careful notes across Wyoming, Idaho, and the Rockies, it might have been much harder for pioneers—including those led by the Prophet Brigham Young—to make their way to the Salt Lake Valley.

sources.name: National Park Service: Lewis & Clark National Historic Trail
Smithsonian Magazine: The Legacy of Lewis and Clark
Library of Congress: Lewis & Clark
Church of Jesus Christ: Pioneers in the West

ex10.evidence: The story of Lewis and Clark is very well supported by evidence. Their journals, letters, and maps are preserved and studied by historians and scientists today. Many places along their route have been identified by the things they described—rivers, mountains, plants, and animals. Their discoveries, such as prairie dogs and grizzly bears, matched what scientists later found in those places. Archaeologists have found remains of forts, campsites, and trading sites where the Corps of Discovery passed, and museums display items and drawings from the expedition. Descendants of Native American tribes remember the visitors and keep their own records. Because of all this evidence, historians are certain the journey happened much as the journals describe.
ex10.happened: In 1804, two men named Meriwether Lewis and William Clark set out from a place called Camp Dubois in Illinois with a group called the Corps of Discovery. Their mission was to explore the huge stretch of land the United States had just bought from France—known as the Louisiana Territory—and try to find a route all the way to the Pacific Ocean. For over two years, Lewis, Clark, and their team traveled up the wide Missouri River, over the steep Rocky Mountains, and down the fast rivers to the Pacific coast. Along the way, they met many Native American nations, some of whom helped them with food and directions. The group carefully mapped the land, wrote down their discoveries, and collected plants and animals new to science—over 300 species in all. When they finally reached the Pacific Ocean, they built a home for winter called Fort Clatsop. When spring came, they made the long journey back to St. Louis. Their 8,000-mile trip helped the United States learn what the land was like, where rivers and mountains stood, and who lived there.
ex10.scripture: No scripture tells the story of Lewis and Clark directly, but their journey shows the value of seeking knowledge, exploring new lands, and preparing the way for others. In Doctrine and Covenants 88:78–80, the Lord commands us to seek learning by study and by faith and to prepare ourselves in all things. Their efforts can also remind us of Nephi’s journey into the wilderness, trusting the Lord would prepare a way (1 Nephi 3:7). Both stories teach how faith and diligent work can help people do hard things for good reasons.
ex10.background: In 1803, the United States doubled in size almost overnight by purchasing the land from France in the Louisiana Purchase. Most Americans lived east of the Mississippi River, in cities and towns, with few knowing what lay beyond. This was a time before cars, trains, or even good roads—most travel was by riverboat, horseback, or walking. Lewis and Clark were both former soldiers chosen for their experience and care. Their team included French interpreters, men skilled at hunting and carpentry, a young Native American mother named Sacagawea who helped them communicate and survive, and Clark’s enslaved man York. For many Native peoples, these new visitors marked the beginning of huge changes. Daily life for most Americans meant working farms, making clothes by hand, and living close to the land.

ex11.talk: What do you think we can learn from studying the different animals and plants that Heavenly Father created?
ex11.child: Long ago, a man named Charles Darwin sailed on a big ship to faraway places. He saw many different animals and plants and wondered how they became so different. His questions helped people learn more about how all living things are connected.
ex11.learn: Darwin's journey teaches us the value of curiosity and careful observation in understanding the world around us. It reminds us that seeking knowledge, both spiritual and scientific, can lead to profound insights about our existence and the wonders of creation.
ex11.matters: Darwin's work revolutionized our understanding of biology, introducing the concept that all species, including humans, share common ancestors and have evolved over time. For families of faith, this perspective can deepen appreciation for the complexity and diversity of life, reflecting the grandeur of Heavenly Father's creations. The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints has stated that it has no official position on the theory of evolution, emphasizing that the details of the physical creation are matters for scientific study, while affirming that humans are children of God.

sources.name: Church Publishes Topic 'Organic Evolution'
Darwin's finches
Timeline of the Voyage of the Beagle

ex11.evidence: Historical records, including Darwin's own journals and correspondence, provide detailed accounts of his observations and the development of his theories. The specimens he collected, particularly the finches from the Galápagos Islands, are preserved in museums and have been studied extensively, offering tangible evidence of the variations that inspired his ideas. Modern genetic research has further supported the concept of common ancestry among species, aligning with Darwin's conclusions.
ex11.happened: In December 1831, Charles Darwin, a young naturalist, embarked on a five-year journey aboard the HMS Beagle, a British naval ship set to survey the coastlines of South America and other regions. During this voyage, Darwin meticulously observed and collected a vast array of specimens, including plants, animals, and fossils. In 1835, the Beagle reached the Galápagos Islands, a remote archipelago in the Pacific Ocean. There, Darwin noted subtle differences among species from one island to another, particularly among finches. These observations led him to consider how species might change over time. Upon returning to England in 1836, Darwin collaborated with experts to analyze his collections. His studies culminated in the publication of "On the Origin of Species" in 1859, where he introduced the theory of natural selection, proposing that species evolve over generations through the survival and reproduction of individuals best suited to their environments.
ex11.scripture: While the scriptures do not provide specific details about the mechanisms of creation, they affirm that God is the Creator of all things. In the Book of Moses, it is written, "And I, God, created all things... spiritually, before they were naturally upon the face of the earth" (Moses 3:5). This passage emphasizes that all creation is divinely orchestrated, though the exact processes are not detailed.
ex11.background: In the early 19th century, the prevailing belief in Europe was that species were unchanging creations. The idea that species could evolve was not widely accepted. Charles Darwin, born in 1809, initially studied medicine and theology before developing a keen interest in natural history. The HMS Beagle's voyage provided him with an unparalleled opportunity to explore diverse ecosystems and gather extensive data, challenging existing notions about the natural world.

ex12.talk: How do you think the astronauts felt seeing Earth from the moon for the first time?
ex12.child: People from Earth flew to the moon in a rocket and walked on it. They were brave and worked with lots of helpers. God wants us to learn about all His amazing creations.
ex12.learn: The story of the moon landing teaches us to never stop reaching for worthy dreams, no matter how impossible they seem. With faith, teamwork, and hard work, barriers can be overcome. Exploring new frontiers—even the moon—can help us appreciate the beauty of our earth, the power of human unity, and the wonders of creation that Heavenly Father invites us to discover.
ex12.matters: For everyone on Earth, seeing humans land on another world made the impossible seem possible. Families realized how small and precious our planet is when photos showed the Earth floating like a blue marble in the vast dark of space. For families of faith, the moon landing echoes beliefs about human potential and our divine heritage. Exploring God's creations, even beyond our own world, can help us feel awe and gratitude for His handiwork. This moment also reminds us that curiosity and courage, when guided by righteous desires, can bless everyone.

sources.name: Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum - Apollo 11 Mission Overview
NASA - Apollo 11 Mission
Church of Jesus Christ – God Created the Heavens and the Earth (Genesis 1)

ex12.evidence: There is strong evidence confirming the Apollo 11 moon landing. Physical samples such as moon rocks, which are different from any material found on Earth, have been studied by scientists across the world. Thousands of photos and hours of video were broadcast during the mission, and the exact moment Armstrong stepped onto the moon was shown live to millions. Equipment left on the lunar surface by the astronauts, such as scientific instruments and the American flag, can still be observed using modern space cameras. Testimonies from astronauts, engineers, and international observers, plus detailed mission records, make it one of the best-documented events in history.
ex12.happened: On July 20, 1969, two American astronauts, Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin, became the first humans to walk on the moon. Their spaceship, Apollo 11, launched from Kennedy Space Center in Florida and traveled about 240,000 miles to reach the moon. After four days in space, their lunar module called the Eagle landed in a flat area named the Sea of Tranquility. Millions of people watched on television as Neil Armstrong stepped onto the lunar surface and spoke the famous words: "That's one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind." Buzz Aldrin joined him moments later, and together they spent about two and a half hours walking, collecting moon rocks, and taking photos. Their safe return to Earth was a huge moment for people everywhere, showing what can be achieved when many minds and hands work together. The moon landing became a symbol of hope, courage, and the power of technology to reach new heights.
ex12.scripture: The scriptures speak about the greatness of God's creations and the eternal potential of His children. In Doctrine and Covenants 130:10–11, it is taught that all the worlds and their inhabitants are part of Heavenly Father's plan, and that knowledge of these worlds will become known to the faithful. Genesis 1 in the Bible tells of God creating the moon and stars to give light and be signs for seasons. The experience of seeing the Earth from the moon also aligns with scriptures teaching that we are all one family under God, sharing a common home, as seen in Acts 17:26.
ex12.background: The 1960s were a time of immense change and challenge in the world. The United States and the Soviet Union were locked in a race to space, each determined to prove their strength and innovation. Yuri Gagarin from the Soviet Union became the first person in space in 1961, which inspired America's President John F. Kennedy to set a goal: land a man on the moon before the decade ended. Ordinary families watched news of these events on black and white TVs. Many people lived with the memory of recent wars and hoped science could bring peace and progress. The men who flew to the moon were test pilots, engineers, and scientists—brave, but also regular people with families waiting for them back home. They depended on thousands of ground crew, technicians, and planners, mostly in their twenties and thirties, showing that great things can happen when people work closely together.

fa01.talk: Why do you think God keeps telling families His promises, instead of just one person?
fa01.child: A long time ago, Heavenly Father made big promises to Abraham and his family. They trusted God, even when things were hard. Because of them, we have many stories and blessings, too.
fa01.learn: We can learn that being faithful, even when it’s hard or unpopular, can bless families and many others, just like Abraham’s family did. Technology, like scripture apps or family history tools, can help us remember and share our own family covenants and stories. Understanding Judaism reminds us that God keeps His promises and that every family is important in His plan.
fa01.matters: Judaism matters because it introduced the powerful idea that all people are children of one loving God who makes promises and calls people to live righteous lives. For families of faith, every story in the Old Testament is part of this history. Christianity comes from these same roots, believing Jesus is the fulfillment of God's promises to Abraham. Learning about Judaism helps us understand our own spiritual family tree, to respect others' faiths, and to see how God's work can move across centuries and cultures. It also teaches about staying true to beliefs even when living among those who believe differently.

sources.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica – Judaism
United States Holocaust Memorial Museum – Jewish History and Community
The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints – Abrahamic Covenant

fa01.evidence: Most historians agree that the stories of Abraham and the earliest patriarchs were passed down by word of mouth for many generations before being written. Archaeologists have found evidence of towns and practices in ancient Canaan that fit what the Bible describes. However, there is no direct archaeological proof for Abraham himself. Later figures, like King David and the existence of ancient Israel, have strong evidence, including inscriptions and buildings. The Jewish people's survival and traditions, even after thousands of years of being scattered and sometimes persecuted, are a testament to their deep faith and commitment. While the story's details are debated, Judaism’s ancient roots and influence are well supported historically.
fa01.happened: Judaism began about 4,000 years ago, around the time of Abraham, in a land called Canaan, which is now mostly Israel and nearby places. According to Jewish tradition and the Bible, Heavenly Father made a sacred promise called a covenant with Abraham and his family. The Lord promised to bless Abraham, give him many descendants, and to bless all the families of the earth through him. Abraham, his son Isaac, and his grandson Jacob are often called the patriarchs of Judaism. Over centuries, their families grew and became a people—later called Israelites—who believed in one God and followed His teachings. God gave them special laws and commandments, most famously through Moses, including the Ten Commandments. Life was not easy: they were sometimes slaves, sometimes wanderers, sometimes kings and then exiles. Even when scattered across many lands, Jews kept their faith, traditions, and hope in God's promises. Judaism remains a living faith, practiced by families all over the world, sharing many stories also found in the Christian Old Testament.
fa01.scripture: Many scriptures speak of the covenant the Lord made with Abraham. Genesis 12:1-3 describes God calling Abraham and promising to bless all nations through him. Galatians 3:8-9 in the New Testament teaches that this covenant found its fulfillment in Jesus Christ. The Book of Mormon often refers to the house of Israel and the promises given to Abraham and his children (see 1 Nephi 15:18, 3 Nephi 20:25-27). Doctrine and Covenants 110:11 mentions the return of the keys of the gathering of Israel, further connecting this ancient promise to the latter days.
fa01.background: Before Judaism, most people in the world worshipped many gods and followed the customs of their tribe or city. Canaan, where Abraham traveled, was filled with small villages and towns, each with their own idols and ways of life. Families lived in tents or small houses, raised animals like sheep, and grew crops. Society was organized around clans and families, and traditions were passed down by word of mouth. The idea of one God who cared for all people was very different from the beliefs of their neighbors. Since there were no written scriptures yet, stories of Abraham and his family were shared by telling and retelling them, especially as they traveled and moved to new places. Over time, these stories were written down and became the Jewish scriptures.

fa02.talk: What is one way we can show kindness or help someone who is having a hard time?
fa02.child: A long time ago, a man named the Buddha taught people how to be kind and wise so they could be happy and help others. Even today, many people try to follow his example and make the world a kinder place. Loving and helping others is something Jesus taught too.
fa02.learn: Buddhism teaches us that seeking peace and compassion is good for everyone. We learn that every person struggles, and that being gentle and understanding—rather than judging or ignoring others' pain—can help heal hearts. For Latter-day Saint families, seeing what is good and true in other religions helps us respect our neighbors and recognize God’s hand across the world. It reminds us to act with love, just as Christ would.
fa02.matters: Buddhism’s way of teaching compassion and wisdom has influenced how entire cultures think about respect, peace, and kindness for thousands of years. For families of faith, it offers a view of God’s love at work, planting seeds of truth in many places. Even though most Buddhists do not speak of Heavenly Father in the ways Christians do, their focus on kindness echoes what Jesus taught: to love others and care for those who suffer. Learning about Buddhism helps children see how Heavenly Father’s light can be found in every nation and culture, preparing people to receive more truth.

sources.name: Encyclopedia Britannica – Buddhism
BBC – The Story of Siddhartha Gautama
Smithsonian Magazine – Who Was the Buddha?
The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints – Principles of Compassion

fa02.evidence: Most historians agree that Siddhartha Gautama, later known as the Buddha, was a real person who lived in northern India and taught the ideas that we now call Buddhism. Ancient texts, such as the Pali Canon, were written down several hundred years after his life, preserving his teachings. Archaeological sites like Bodh Gaya, where he is said to have reached enlightenment, are visited by pilgrims to this day. Artifacts, such as ancient sculptures and carvings, show how early followers honored his memory. While the exact dates and some details of his life are still debated, scholars generally believe he lived in the sixth century BC and shaped world religion through his teachings.
fa02.happened: Around 563 BC, in a place called Bodh Gaya in India, a young prince named Siddhartha Gautama lived in a palace with every luxury. Yet, he was troubled by suffering he saw in the world—pain, old age, and death. Leaving behind his royal life, he traveled and sought answers through deep thinking and meditation under a tree known now as the Bodhi Tree. After much effort and reflection, Siddhartha gained insight, or 'enlightenment,' understanding the causes of suffering and how to overcome them. He became known as the Buddha, meaning 'The Awakened One.' The Buddha spent the rest of his life teaching others a path called the Dharma, which centers on living with wisdom, compassion, and moderation to end suffering and find true peace. His teachings spread widely, and today, millions follow this way of life, called Buddhism, striving to be kind and mindful wherever they live.
fa02.scripture: While the scriptures of the Church do not talk directly about the Buddha, several teachings from the Bible and Book of Mormon relate to the Buddhist focus on compassion and ending suffering. The Savior taught, "Blessed are the merciful: for they shall obtain mercy" (Matthew 5:7) and commanded, "Love your neighbor as yourself" (Matthew 22:39). In the Book of Mormon, Mosiah 18:9 invites believers to "bear one another’s burdens, that they may be light" and to "mourn with those that mourn." These principles encourage us to feel and show compassion, just as Buddhism teaches.
fa02.background: India in the sixth century BC was a land of many kingdoms, each with its own rulers, customs, and beliefs. Most people lived in small villages, farming the land or trading goods in busy town markets. Society was divided into castes, or social classes, with strict rules about one’s place and duties. Religion was important, centered largely on many gods, rituals, and sacrifices led by priests. It was also a time of great questioning, as some people started to wonder about deeper meaning beyond everyday struggles. The Buddha grew up during this period, surrounded by both great wealth and the stark realities of suffering, which made him wonder if there was a better way to live. He was not the only philosopher of his age; in other parts of the world, teachers like Confucius and Pythagoras were asking big questions, too.

fa03.talk: What can we learn from other people's beliefs that helps us be better friends and neighbors?
fa03.child: Long ago, a man named Muhammad said that God was sending him messages. His teachings became the religion of Islam, which many people follow today. Muslims believe Jesus was a prophet, but not that He is our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ.
fa03.learn: Studying the founding of Islam teaches us the power of faith to inspire societal transformation. It highlights the importance of compassion, justice, and community in addressing social inequalities. Recognizing the shared values among different faiths encourages mutual respect and understanding. This knowledge empowers families to engage in meaningful dialogues with people of diverse backgrounds, fostering a more inclusive and harmonious world.
fa03.matters: The founding of Islam has had a profound impact on world history, shaping cultures, laws, and societies across continents. For families of faith, understanding Islam's origins offers insights into the shared values and teachings among Abrahamic religions. Islam's emphasis on monotheism, compassion, and social justice resonates with principles found in other faith traditions. Recognizing these commonalities fosters mutual respect and understanding among diverse religious communities. Muslims honor Jesus and Mary, but they believe Jesus was a prophet, not our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ: they do not believe He is the Son of God who died for our sins and rose again. That is the great difference between Islam and Christianity.

fa03.evidence: Historical records provide a detailed account of Muhammad's life and the early development of Islam. Islamic tradition, preserved through oral and written histories, offers insights into his experiences and the societal changes he initiated. Archaeological findings, such as early Quranic manuscripts, support the textual preservation of the Quran. The rapid expansion of Islam after Muhammad's death is documented through various historical sources, illustrating its significant influence on subsequent civilizations. While some aspects of early Islamic history are debated among scholars, the core events surrounding Muhammad's life and the establishment of Islam are well-documented and widely accepted.
fa03.happened: In the early 7th century, a man named Muhammad lived in Mecca, a bustling city in present-day Saudi Arabia. Around the year 610 AD, during a period of deep reflection in a cave called Hira, Muhammad experienced a profound event. He reported that the angel Gabriel appeared to him, delivering messages from God. These messages, emphasizing the oneness of God and calling for moral and social reform, were later compiled into the Quran, the holy book of Islam. Initially, Muhammad shared these revelations privately, but as he began to preach publicly, he and his followers faced increasing opposition from Meccan leaders who felt threatened by his teachings. In 622 AD, to escape persecution, Muhammad and his followers migrated to the city of Yathrib, later known as Medina. This migration, called the Hijra, marks the beginning of the Islamic calendar. In Medina, Muhammad established a community based on the principles revealed to him, uniting various tribes under the new faith. Over the next decade, Islam spread throughout the Arabian Peninsula. By 632 AD, when Muhammad passed away, Islam had become a significant religious and social force in the region.
fa03.scripture: While the scriptures of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints do not directly reference the founding of Islam, they emphasize principles of seeking truth and understanding among all people. The Book of Mormon teaches, "All are alike unto God" (2 Nephi 26:33), underscoring the importance of recognizing the worth and contributions of diverse cultures and beliefs. Doctrine and Covenants encourages believers to "seek ye out of the best books words of wisdom" (D&C 88:118), promoting the pursuit of knowledge and understanding from various sources. These teachings inspire an attitude of respect and learning towards all of God's children, including those of different faith traditions.
fa03.background: Before Islam's emergence, the Arabian Peninsula was a land of diverse tribes and cultures. Mecca, Muhammad's birthplace, was a significant trade hub, attracting merchants and travelers from various regions. The city was also home to the Kaaba, a sacred sanctuary housing numerous idols worshiped by different tribes. Society was predominantly tribal, with loyalty to one's clan being paramount. While some communities practiced monotheistic beliefs, such as Judaism and Christianity, polytheism was widespread. The region lacked a centralized political authority, leading to frequent inter-tribal conflicts. Economically, the area relied heavily on trade, with caravans transporting goods like spices, textiles, and incense across vast deserts. Socially, there were stark inequalities, with a clear divide between the wealthy elite and the impoverished. Practices like infanticide, especially of female infants, and the marginalization of certain groups were common. This was the world into which Muhammad was born, a society ripe for the transformative messages he would later convey.

ff01.talk: Why do you think people want to choose what they believe, rather than being told what to believe?
ff01.child: A long time ago, an Egyptian king tried to make everyone worship just one god and forget their old gods. When he died, the people quickly went back to their own ways. This shows us faith is strongest when we choose it ourselves.
ff01.learn: This event teaches that belief forced from above seldom lasts. True faith grows best when it is chosen, taught patiently, and lived with sincerity. Akhenaten’s story gives an example from ancient history of why agency matters in religion. Even powerful rulers cannot make belief live in the hearts of people. This can help us remember to respect each person’s path in faith, and to teach what we know with patience and love.
ff01.matters: Akhenaten’s actions matter because they mark the first time in history a government forced everyone, by law, to follow a single state religion. He tried to erase choice in belief. This event teaches us how faith, if compelled by rulers rather than chosen, can struggle to take root among a people. For families of faith today, it reminds us that love for God and real belief cannot simply be passed by force or decree—they must grow in the heart, by agency. Once the pressure lifted, people returned to what they knew and loved. It shows the difference between faith offered and faith imposed.

sources.name: The British Museum: Akhenaten and Amarna Period
Metropolitan Museum of Art: Akhenaten
Encyclopaedia Britannica: Akhenaten

ff01.evidence: Historians know about Akhenaten’s religious revolution from stone carvings, remains of the city of Amarna, and letters from that time. Archaeologists have uncovered temples to Aten and ruins of Akhenaten’s capital. Inscriptions show the deliberate erasing of Amun’s name. After his death, later pharaohs restored old temples and destroyed Akhenaten’s monuments, which itself became evidence for his erasure. The story is clear from many archaeological finds and texts, though the reasons Akhenaten acted and what ordinary Egyptians truly felt are still studied. Akhenaten’s short-lived changes and the swift return to old ways leave a clear, if sometimes mysterious, record.
ff01.happened: Around 1350 BC, in ancient Egypt, Pharaoh Akhenaten made a remarkable and very strict change.
