He decided there should be just one god for all Egyptians to worship: the Aten, a form of the sun. Before this, Egyptians honored many gods and goddesses, and each temple was busy with festivals and offerings. Akhenaten shut down those temples, stopped their priesthoods, and removed the name of their greatest god, Amun, from monuments and writings. He even built a new city—Amarna—for the worship of Aten alone, and made everyone join in. This was not a gentle invitation; it was ordered. Priests and ordinary people lost their old ways of worship. While a few people, especially those close to the pharaoh, joined him, many others quietly held onto their traditional beliefs. Akhenaten led this new religion until he died, and soon after, Egypt’s leaders and people quickly went back to their old gods, erased Akhenaten’s memory, and left his city in ruins. His unique faith did not last beyond his rule.
ff01.scripture: The scriptures do not describe Akhenaten or ancient Egyptian religion directly, but they teach about agency and the right to choose. In the Book of Mormon, 2 Nephi 2:27 says, 'Wherefore, men are free according to the flesh... they are free to choose liberty and eternal life.' The Doctrine and Covenants teaches that 'no power or influence can or ought to be maintained by virtue of the priesthood, only by persuasion, by long-suffering, by gentleness and meekness, and by love unfeigned' (D&C 121:41). These principles tell us that faith must be chosen, not forced.
ff01.background: Ancient Egypt was a land of many gods, great temples, and royal families believed to be chosen by heaven. Most Egyptians lived along the Nile, farming and fishing, and their daily rhythms followed the river and seasons. Religion was part of everything—they prayed to different gods for crops, health, and safety. Powerful priests helped care for the gods’ temples and held much influence. When Akhenaten became pharaoh, Egypt was wealthy and its traditions seemed everlasting. People celebrated familiar festivals each year, made offerings to their favorite gods, and expected their rulers would do the same. Life was close-knit, with families working together, and every city had its special patron god.

ff02.talk: Why do you think Cyrus wanted people to be free to worship in their own way?
ff02.child: King Cyrus helped people go home and rebuild their temples, even though they were from different places. He made a rule that let families worship God in their own way again. God can use anyone to help others.
ff02.learn: We can learn that showing respect and kindness, even to those who are different from us, brings peace and blessings that reach far beyond what we might expect. God can use anyone to accomplish His work, and sometimes help comes through unexpected means. Families can remember that freedom—especially religious freedom—is something precious that we should protect and share. Just as Cyrus’s actions blessed many, our choices can bless others, too.
ff02.matters: The choice of Cyrus to let people return to their homes and worship as they wished opened the way for greater peace and allowed the rebuilding of faith and temples, including the Jewish temple in Jerusalem. For families of faith today, Cyrus’s example shows that God can work through many people and situations—even those who do not worship Him directly—to do good in the world. It also teaches about the important value of religious freedom, which helps people live in peace and follow the teachings of their own hearts without fear. The story of Cyrus is a reminder that acts of fairness and compassion can change the course of history for many peoples.

sources.name: British Museum - The Cyrus Cylinder
Encyclopaedia Britannica - Cyrus the Great
Church of Jesus Christ - Old Testament Study Guide: Ezra 1
Metropolitan Museum - The Cyrus Cylinder and Ancient Persia

ff02.evidence: The Cyrus Cylinder, made of baked clay and now kept in the British Museum, describes in cuneiform writing how Cyrus allowed exiled people to return to their lands and rebuild their temples. This artifact is considered a strong piece of archaeological evidence, because it matches the timeline and details found in the Bible. Historians largely agree that Cyrus followed a policy of tolerance toward different peoples and religions, supported by many records in Persian, Babylonian, and Greek sources. While the Cylinder doesn’t name the Jews specifically, its policies match what Ezra reports about the return from exile. Together, these sources allow historians to say with confidence that Cyrus issued a decree freeing many groups, including the Jewish people.
ff02.happened: In 539 BC, a powerful king named Cyrus the Great led the Persian army to conquer the city of Babylon. This was an important moment because Babylon was one of the greatest cities in the world at that time. After he became ruler, Cyrus did something remarkable: instead of punishing the people he had defeated, he allowed groups who had been forced into exile to go back to their homelands. This included the Jewish people, who had been living far from Jerusalem for many years after being taken captive by the Babylonians. Cyrus gave a command, written down and later called the decree of Cyrus, that let them return to Jerusalem and rebuild their temple. This act of kindness and respect for different beliefs was rare for ancient rulers. The story was recorded by Cyrus’s own officials on a clay document called the Cyrus Cylinder, and also by the Jewish people in their scriptures. Cyrus’s decision helped many people feel hope again and started an era where more cultures and religions could live side by side in the great Persian Empire.
ff02.scripture: The scriptures speak directly about these events. Ezra 1 in the Old Testament records the decree Cyrus made, inviting the Jews to return and rebuild the temple in Jerusalem. Isaiah 44:28 and 45:1, written many years before Cyrus was born, mention him by name as the one who would help restore Jerusalem. The Book of Mormon and other Latter-day Saint scripture do not mention Cyrus directly, but teach about God’s ability to inspire rulers and bring about His purposes in unexpected ways (see 1 Nephi 3:7).
ff02.background: Before Cyrus and the Persians came to power, the region around Babylon was full of empires that ruled by force and fear, often taking people from their homes to work as servants or slaves in foreign lands. The Babylonians, who ruled before the Persians, destroyed Jerusalem’s temple and took many Jews far away from their homeland. Daily life for those in exile was difficult—they missed their homes and freedom to worship as they wished. Cyrus’s Persian Empire was different in that it allowed many groups to keep their own languages and beliefs, as long as they respected the laws of the empire. People lived in large cities and smaller villages, growing crops, herding animals, trading goods, and teaching their children stories and faith handed down from ancestors. Cyrus became known for a policy of kindness toward conquered peoples, which helped his large empire to stay together.

ff03.talk: Can you think of a time when someone believed something different than you? How did you treat them?
ff03.child: There was once a king named Ashoka who decided to stop fighting wars and instead ask everyone to be kind and fair to people of other religions. He wrote messages on stones, saying it’s good to respect how others worship. People still remember him as a peaceful ruler who helped his country get along.
ff03.learn: We can learn from Ashoka that even those with great power can choose peace, kindness, and respect for others. Sharing our belief lovingly invites others to see its goodness, but we must also honor their freedom to choose. When families and communities follow this path, they can grow strong and peaceful, no matter how different their beliefs may be.
ff03.matters: Ashoka’s edicts matter because they represent one of history’s earliest calls for religious tolerance and understanding, centuries before such ideas were common. For families of faith, his story is a gentle reminder that our Heavenly Father’s love and teachings can reach hearts without force or fear. It shows that faith can shape even powerful leaders to act with mercy and wisdom. Ashoka’s choices remind us that freedom to worship and respect for others’ beliefs are treasures that help build peaceful families and communities.

sources.name: Metropolitan Museum of Art: The Edicts of Ashoka
World History Encyclopedia: Ashoka’s Edicts
British Museum: Edicts of Ashoka

ff03.evidence: Much of what we know about Ashoka comes from the many stone pillars and rock faces carved with his words, which still stand across India, Nepal, and Pakistan. These inscriptions have been carefully studied, translated, and confirmed by archaeologists and historians. The words on these rocks match what ancient texts later wrote about Ashoka’s reign and beliefs. Recent archaeological surveys have helped confirm the locations and authenticity of the edicts, and show the spread of Ashoka’s message far beyond his own capital. Historians agree that Ashoka’s commitment to non-violence and respect for all faiths marked a real change in how empires could rule.
ff03.happened: Around 250 BC, the Mauryan emperor Ashoka made a momentous decision after witnessing the suffering caused by his own wars. Deeply troubled by the destruction and sorrow, especially after the conquest of Kalinga, Ashoka chose to follow the teachings of Buddhism. In a remarkable act for his time, he began to share these beliefs not through force, but with gentle words and official proclamations across his vast empire. Ashoka had his new ideals inscribed onto rock pillars and walls for all to see and ponder. Among these writings, called edicts, one stands out: Rock Edict XII. It teaches that everyone should honor the faiths of others. Ashoka warned that putting down another’s belief only harms one’s own, and true well-being comes when different faiths live in harmony. Instead of growing his empire with armies, Ashoka sent missionaries to share ideas peacefully. His example showed that a ruler with immense power could choose kindness and persuasion over violence and fear, making his realm known for its peace and prosperity.
ff03.scripture: While no specific scripture describes Ashoka or the edicts, the principle echoes the Savior’s teaching in Matthew 7:12—often called the Golden Rule: "Therefore all things whatsoever ye would that men should do to you, do ye even so to them." The Book of Mormon teaches in Alma 1:30 and 4:13 that believers were to look out for each other, showing love and not persecuting those who believed differently. Church leaders today, as found in Doctrine and Covenants 134:4, also uphold that religious freedom is sacred and “the right of all men.” These principles guide us to honor others’ beliefs, just as Ashoka’s edict suggests.
ff03.background: The Mauryan Empire, ruling from about 322 to 185 BC, was one of ancient India’s greatest empires, stretching across most of the subcontinent. Its people spoke many languages and followed differing ways of life, from farming to city trade. Daily life was shaped by religion—mostly Hinduism and older beliefs, until Ashoka’s conversion made Buddhism a guiding light in the court. Before Ashoka, rulers often believed that keeping power needed strict laws and sometimes warfare. Most people grew crops, raised cattle, or traded goods, and families lived in simple homes built from mud or wood. This was a time long before machines or modern comforts, but people valued family, honesty, and community.

ff04.talk: Why do you think people sometimes have to be brave to worship how they believe?
ff04.child: A king tried to stop the Jewish people from following their faith and made them choose between obeying him or God. Instead of giving up, they were brave and stayed true to what they believed. Their courage helped them win back their freedom and temple.
ff04.learn: Families today can learn from this moment in history that faith is precious and sometimes requires courage to keep. Technology and laws can be used for good or harm, depending on how people use them. When faith is threatened, standing together with kindness and hope can help a community stay strong. Even when things seem very hard, holding true to what is right can bring lasting blessings.
ff04.matters: This event is important because it shows what can happen when a government tries to control or erase people's beliefs. The attempt to suppress Judaism did not destroy it; instead, it led to the Maccabean revolt, where Jews fought for their freedom and faith. In family life, this history can teach us about the strength that comes from holding to beliefs, especially in hard times. It’s a reminder that faith can grow even stronger when it is challenged, and that respecting religious freedom is important for peace in any society.

sources.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica – Antiochus IV Epiphanes
Jewish Virtual Library – Hanukkah History
Bible Odyssey – Maccabean Revolt

ff04.evidence: Historians have reliable records about Antiochus IV and his decrees from ancient Jewish histories like 1 and 2 Maccabees, and from Greek historians of the time. Archaeologists have found remains of Greek altars in the area around Jerusalem and have uncovered coins and inscriptions from Antiochus’s reign. These findings support the written records that tell of Greek influence overtaking the region. The rededication of the Temple by the Maccabees, celebrated as Hanukkah, is still remembered in Jewish homes today. Scholars generally agree that these acts of persecution happened much as described, although exact details can be debated.
ff04.happened: In 167 BC, the ruler Antiochus IV, who was king of the Seleucid Empire, tried to make everyone in his kingdom follow Greek customs and religion. In Jerusalem, he made a harsh law that banned important parts of Jewish faith. People were forbidden from resting on the Sabbath, performing circumcision, or even owning a scroll of the Torah—their holy book. Anyone caught doing these things could be punished by death. Antiochus also sent his soldiers into the Temple in Jerusalem, the holiest place for the Jewish people, and set up altars to Greek gods inside. They offered sacrifices there that went against everything the Jewish people believed was holy. These actions were meant to erase the Jewish way of life and make everyone worship like the Greeks. Many Jews were forced to choose between their faith and their lives. However, instead of breaking their spirit, Antiochus’s harsh policies made many Jews even more determined to hold on to their faith.
ff04.scripture: The primary account of these events is found in the Apocrypha, specifically in 1 Maccabees and 2 Maccabees, which are not part of the standard Bible for most Latter-day Saints but are included in some other Christian Bibles. While the Book of Mormon, Doctrine and Covenants, and Pearl of Great Price do not describe this event, the principles found in Articles of Faith 11 (“We claim the privilege of worshiping Almighty God according to the dictates of our own conscience”) and stories of standing firm in faith under trial, like Daniel or Abinadi (Daniel 3; Mosiah 17), reflect similar themes of religious courage.
ff04.background: This event took place in Jerusalem, which at the time was under the control of the Hellenistic or Greek-influenced Seleucid Empire. The empire stretched from what is now Turkey all the way to parts of Iran. Jewish people in Judea had their own customs, laws, and worshipped the God of Israel. Their daily life centered around family, farming, and worship in the Temple. Before Antiochus’s rule, Jews and Greeks lived side by side, but tensions grew as new rulers tried to introduce more Greek customs. Antiochus IV, seeing religious differences as a source of trouble, wanted to make everyone the same in belief and practice. For many Jews, their faith was the heartbeat of their community, and the Temple was their spiritual center. The loss of their freedom to worship struck at the very core of daily life.

ff05.t: The Hasmoneans Force Conversion of the Idumeans
ff05.talk: Why do you think God wants us to let others choose what they believe?
ff05.child: A long time ago, some leaders made people join their faith or leave home. This was not the loving way God wants. We can learn to always treat others kindly, even if they are different.
ff05.learn: This story calls us to remember that faith must be offered with love, not forced on anyone. We each have the gift of agency to make our own choices, and others should have that same honor. Treating everyone's beliefs with respect—especially when we are strong or in charge—brings us closer to God's ways. Families can talk about the difference between sharing our faith and requiring it, and why kindness and patience are always in God's plan.
ff05.matters: This event is a reminder that even those who have suffered religious persecution may be tempted, once in power, to act harshly toward others. Families of faith can reflect on the importance of respecting freedom of belief, even when their own values feel strong or urgent. Recognizing both the strengths and the failings in our own traditions invites honesty and humility. John Hyrcanus' decision shows the lasting consequences of using force in matters of faith, impacting not only history but families for generations. How we treat others when we have the upper hand speaks deeply about our character and our trust in God's timing and mercy.

sources.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica – Hasmonean Dynasty
Jewish Virtual Library – John Hyrcanus
Metropolitan Museum of Art – Idumaea
Bible Odyssey – John Hyrcanus and the Hasmoneans

ff05.evidence: Most of what we know comes from the Jewish historian Josephus, who wrote centuries later in his book 'Antiquities of the Jews.' Other ancient writers, and later rabbis, also refer to this forced conversion, but sometimes with less detail. Archaeologists have found signs that Idumea as a population eventually blended with Judea, such as the appearance of Jewish customs and names among Idumeans. However, the exact details—like whether every person was forced or how many left—are less certain. Modern historians agree that some type of forced conversion took place, but debate the scale and methods involved. Josephus’ reliability is generally respected, but his writings are not free from bias or gaps.
ff05.happened: Around 125 BC, a difficult chapter unfolded after the Jewish people, led by the Hasmonean family, regained their independence from foreign rulers. John Hyrcanus, the high priest and ruler of the Jewish state, looked south to the land of Idumea—an area once known as Edom and inhabited by the Idumeans. According to the ancient historian Josephus, John Hyrcanus conquered Idumea and presented the people there with a hard choice: they could either accept the Jewish law, which included the practice of circumcision, or leave their land behind. Many Idumeans chose to stay and became part of the Jewish nation. This event is unique in Jewish history, as it involved requiring an entire people to join the faith not by personal choice, but by force or the threat of being driven from their homes. This episode would have lasting effects, as the Idumeans became integrated into Jewish society, sometimes even rising to powerful positions—most famously, Herod the Great, the ruler in the time of Jesus, was of Idumean descent.
ff05.scripture: There are no scriptures that directly reference the Hasmonean or Idumean episode. However, the Bible repeatedly teaches about agency and kindness. Joshua 24:15 declares, “Choose you this day whom ye will serve,” highlighting the importance of personal choice in faith. The Book of Mormon also warns against compulsion, as in Alma 30:7-9, which upholds religious freedom: “...there was no law against a man’s belief; for it was strictly contrary to the commands of God.” Doctrine and Covenants 121:41 reminds us: “No power or influence can or ought to be maintained by virtue of the priesthood, only by persuasion, by long-suffering, by gentleness and meekness, and by love unfeigned.”
ff05.background: Before the Hasmoneans gained independence, the Jewish people had endured decades of harsh Greek rule. Their culture and worship had been threatened, with their temple desecrated and laws against their faith enforced. The Maccabean revolt reclaimed religious freedom for the Jews, leading to a time of renewed Jewish rule over Judea and the surrounding regions. Idumea, to the south, had long been home to the Edomite people, who were related to the Israelites but often in conflict with them. In daily life, most people were farmers and shepherds, living in villages or small towns. Faith was tied closely to everyday traditions, and neighbors of different cultures mingled but did not always trust each other.

ff06.talk: What helps you stand up for what you believe, even if others don’t agree?
ff06.child: A long time ago, people who loved Jesus were treated very badly by leaders in Rome because they would not worship other gods. Even when it was scary, some Christians chose to follow Jesus, and their brave actions helped more people learn about Him. Their faith grew, even when it seemed very hard.
ff06.learn: We can learn from early Christians how important it is to be true to what we believe, even when it is hard or unpopular. Their example teaches us that the way we respond to challenges can inspire others and help our faith grow. Standing firm in kindness and hope, even under pressure, can help light the world and bring about change no person expects. We see that Heavenly Father watches over His children in every age, and nothing done in faith is wasted.
ff06.matters: This long season of persecution shows how faith can endure even when the strongest government tries to snuff it out. Instead of stamping out Christianity, the persecutions helped it grow and spread, as people were inspired by the courage of those who held to their beliefs even in the face of death. For families of faith, this history speaks to the importance of standing for our beliefs, with love and patience, even when it is hard. It also reminds us that the true source of freedom and faith is God, not any ruler or law. The story of the early Christians shows that God can bring good from suffering and that faith, built on Jesus Christ, can flourish even in hard places.

sources.name: Encyclopedia Britannica – Persecution of Christians
PBS – The Roman Empire in the First Century: Christians
National Geographic – Early Christian Martyrs

ff06.evidence: Many written records from Roman authors and Christian writers confirm the story of the persecutions. Roman historians like Tacitus and Suetonius mention Nero’s treatment of Christians. Letters, court records, and writings from Christian leaders like Tertullian, Ignatius, and Eusebius describe the sufferings, courage, and spread of the faith. Archaeologists have found catacombs and early Christian symbols that show how believers met in secret and honored those who died for their beliefs. While some early stories of martyrdom are dramatic and not all details can be checked, the reality of repeated, official persecution is very well supported from both Roman and Christian sources. The pattern of laws and punishments, especially under Diocletian, is described in many reliable records.
ff06.happened: From the year 64 AD, Christians in the Roman Empire faced government persecution that sometimes turned brutal. The first major crackdown started under Emperor Nero, who blamed Christians for the great fire that swept through Rome that year. He punished them harshly, sometimes in public spectacles. Later emperors, including Domitian, Decius, and Diocletian, enforced laws that required all citizens to offer sacrifices to the traditional Roman gods and to the emperor. Refusing was seen as both a religious offense and a crime against the unity of the empire. Christians believed in worshipping only one God, and many refused to take part in these sacrifices. As a result, they were arrested, imprisoned, forced into hard labor, or even killed. Some Christians hid their faith, while others stood firm, sometimes facing lions in the arena or painful execution. The harshest period came under Diocletian, starting in 303 AD, when he tried to erase Christianity completely by destroying scriptures, closing churches, and imprisoning leaders. Yet even while being treated so badly, many Christians remained faithful, and stories of their courage quickly spread.
ff06.scripture: Several scriptures speak to the courage and endurance shown by early Christians. In the New Testament, Acts 5:29 records Peter and the apostles saying, “We ought to obey God rather than men.” Paul’s words in Romans 8:35-39 remind us that nothing can separate us from the love of Christ, even tribulation, or persecution. In the Book of Mormon, Alma 1:19-20 speaks of believers enduring persecution patiently rather than returning evil for evil. Doctrine and Covenants 122:7-9 offers comfort to those suffering for their faith, affirming that all trials can be for our good, and that God will be with us. These passages help us remember that the Lord will support His people, even in difficult times.
ff06.background: The world of the Roman Empire was full of vibrant cities, temples, and traditions. Most people honored many gods and thought that the safety of their family and city depended on pleasing them. Loyalty to Rome also meant showing respect to the emperor, who was often considered divine. Daily life for most included work, family gatherings, and public festivals. Christians lived quietly within this world at first, meeting in homes, sharing meals, and serving the poor. Many Romans mistrusted Christians because they would not join in the usual sacrifices or festivals, thinking this put the city at risk. In this setting, the Roman leaders saw refusing sacrifice not just as a religious matter, but as a threat to public order and the empire's stability. The authorities acted out of fear of change and a desire to keep everyone under one set of beliefs, handled by law.

ff07.talk: Why is it important to let others believe and worship in their own way?
ff07.child: A long time ago, people weren't always allowed to pray the way they wanted. Then, two leaders decided everyone should be free to worship as they choose. This made many people happy and brought peace.
ff07.learn: From the Edict of Milan, we learn the value of religious tolerance and the positive impact it can have on society. It teaches us that allowing individuals the freedom to worship according to their beliefs can lead to greater peace and unity. This historical event also reminds us of the importance of standing firm in our faith, even in the face of adversity, trusting that righteousness will ultimately prevail.
ff07.matters: The Edict of Milan is significant because it established the principle of religious freedom within the Roman Empire, setting a precedent for future societies. For families of faith, it serves as a reminder of the importance of tolerance and the blessings that come from allowing individuals to worship according to their conscience. It also highlights how divine influence can guide leaders to enact policies that promote peace and unity among diverse populations.

sources.name: Edict of Milan - Wikipedia
The Edict of Milan – 313 AD – the “birth certificate for religious freedom” - International Center for Law and Religion
313 The Edict of Milan - Christianity Today

ff07.evidence: Historical records from early Christian writers such as Lactantius and Eusebius provide accounts of the Edict of Milan. Lactantius's "De Mortibus Persecutorum" and Eusebius's "Ecclesiastical History" both preserve versions of the edict, detailing its provisions for religious tolerance and the restoration of confiscated properties. While the original text of the edict has not survived, these accounts offer valuable insights into its content and the context in which it was issued.
ff07.happened: In February 313 AD, Roman Emperors Constantine I and Licinius met in Milan to discuss the future of the empire. They agreed to grant religious freedom to all individuals, allowing them to worship according to their own beliefs. This agreement, known as the Edict of Milan, specifically ended the persecution of Christians and restored confiscated church properties. The edict was later communicated through a letter from Licinius to provincial governors, emphasizing the importance of religious liberty for the stability and prosperity of the empire. This marked a significant shift from previous policies that had often targeted Christians for persecution.
ff07.scripture: The principle of religious freedom aligns with teachings found in the scriptures. In the Book of Mormon, 2 Nephi 2:27 states, "Wherefore, men are free according to the flesh; and all things are given them which are expedient unto man." This emphasizes the God-given agency to choose one's beliefs and actions. Additionally, Doctrine and Covenants 134:4 declares, "We believe that religion is instituted of God; and that men are amenable to him, and to him only, for the exercise of it." These passages underscore the importance of allowing individuals the freedom to worship as they choose.
ff07.background: Before the Edict of Milan, Christians in the Roman Empire faced periods of severe persecution, especially under emperors like Diocletian. The empire was vast and diverse, encompassing various cultures and religions. Daily life varied greatly depending on one's social status and location, but many citizens practiced polytheism, worshiping multiple gods. The rise of Christianity challenged traditional Roman religious practices, leading to tensions and, at times, violent suppression of Christian communities.

ff08.talk: Why do you think Heavenly Father wants us to choose to follow Him, instead of making us?
ff08.child: A long time ago, a ruler made a law that everyone had to be Christian the same way he believed. Anyone who wanted to keep old traditions was not allowed. When people are forced to believe, it can make hearts hard instead of kind.
ff08.learn: We can learn that faith is strongest when people are free to choose it. Using power or laws to make people believe in God does not lead to a strong, loving community. Families and children can talk about why it is important to respect what others believe, even if we don't agree. This event also helps us remember that Christ asks us to lead with kindness, honesty, and respect for agency—the same gifts Heavenly Father gives to all His children.
ff08.matters: This moment matters because it shows what can happen when faith is mixed with force. Earlier, Christianity grew stronger during times when it was gentle and could only be chosen. But once it became tied to political power, it sometimes lost the kindness and freedom that helped it grow. For families of faith, this story reminds us that God gives us the gift of choice. When belief becomes something people are forced to accept, it can lose its power to change hearts. This event is also important for understanding how faith traditions can be used to bring people together or to drive them apart.

sources.name: Edict of Thessalonica (Encyclopedia Britannica)
BBC History: Theodosius I and Christianity
Catholic Encyclopedia: Theodosius I
Church of Jesus Christ - Agency and Freedom

ff08.evidence: Historians have many records from this time, including the actual text of the Edict of Thessalonica and letters written by Theodosius and church leaders. Archaeologists have found closed or repurposed temples, and inscriptions that show the ending of many traditional sacrifices. Writers from the time, such as the church historian Theodoret, described these changes and their effects. There are many details known about how laws were enforced: for example, the closure or destruction of temples, and laws that punished those who held onto old traditions. The murder of Hypatia, a famous philosopher, is recorded by several ancient writers. Still, there are questions about how harshly the laws were enforced in every town, and how everyday people felt or responded. But that these laws were made and changed the empire is not in doubt.
ff08.happened: Between 380 and 392 AD, a major change took place in the Roman Empire. The emperor at the time, Theodosius I, decided that everyone in the empire must follow a specific form of Christianity, known today as Nicene Christianity. It began with the Edict of Thessalonica in 380, which declared this faith to be the only official religion. For those who practiced other religions—especially the old Roman ways where people worshipped many gods—life changed suddenly. Theodosius and his supporters closed temples, made sacrifices to the old gods illegal, and sometimes destroyed or took over places from other faiths. This even ended old traditions like the Olympic Games, which had been celebrated for centuries. People who clung to old beliefs risked losing their jobs, property, or worse. Even fellow Christians who disagreed with Nicene beliefs faced punishment. This shift meant that for the first time, the power of the empire was used to try to make everyone believe the same thing about God, and it started a pattern where rulers used faith as a way to bring people together—or to control them.
ff08.scripture: Scripture teaches about the importance of agency—the right to choose for ourselves. In the Book of Mormon, Alma 30:7–9 explains that 'there was no law against a man’s belief,' and that all people 'were free to believe whatsoever they pleased.' D&C 134:4–5 also teaches that religion is only to be governed by persuasion and love, not by force. The New Testament sometimes hints at these ideas, such as when Jesus teaches to love your neighbor (Matthew 22:39) and to treat others as you would be treated (Luke 6:31). There is no scripture that commands faith by force.
ff08.background: Before these changes, Rome was a place full of many gods, beliefs, and kinds of worship. For hundreds of years, people from many lands and traditions called the Roman Empire home, and nearly everyone honored the old gods in some way. Christians were a small group for a long time, often meeting in secret because they weren't allowed to worship openly. That changed in 313 with Emperor Constantine, who allowed Christianity to exist without fear of punishment. For decades after, Rome had both Christians and non-Christians living side by side, with religious differences managed by law rather than force. Daily life in cities like Constantinople or Rome was busy and colorful, with markets, public baths, plays, and big festivals. Families often held onto religious traditions for generations, finding meaning and comfort in old stories and rituals.

ff09.talk: What are some ways we can show kindness and respect to people who believe differently than we do?
ff09.child: Long ago in a city called Medina, people made an important promise to help and protect each other, even though they believed different things. They agreed everyone could worship in their own way. That made their city stronger and safer for everyone.
ff09.learn: We can learn that it is possible for people with very different beliefs to make promises, help each other, and live together in peace if they choose to. Respecting others’ rights to worship in their own way builds strong, trusting communities. Even if history sometimes goes differently later, this moment in Medina shows a way forward that can inspire our families and our world. Treating everyone fairly, as the Constitution of Medina tried to do, fits with what our faith teaches about kindness and freedom for all.
ff09.matters: The Constitution of Medina matters because it was one of the first times in recorded history that an agreement was created to protect religious minorities, help people live together, and work as one community, even with differences. For families of faith, it shows that respecting other people's beliefs and living peacefully with those who are different is possible—and important. The way the people of Medina made promises to protect each other's rights and safety reminds us that Heavenly Father wants us to treat everyone with kindness and fairness, no matter what they believe.

sources.name: The National Museum of Saudi Arabia
Encyclopaedia Britannica - Medina
World History Encyclopedia - Constitution of Medina
Church of Jesus Christ - Articles of Faith

ff09.evidence: The Constitution of Medina is referenced in early Islamic historical sources, such as the biography of Muhammad by Ibn Ishaq and later historians like al-Tabari. Though the actual document does not survive, these early accounts preserve its terms and describe how it was followed in Medina. Many scholars study these sources and generally agree that such a treaty existed and shaped early Islamic society. Archaeological work in Medina adds general context about life at the time but cannot directly verify the treaty’s text. Historians agree it marked a unique moment in religious and communal cooperation, though there is debate about the exact words and details since all we have are later written records, not the original.
ff09.happened: In the year 622 AD, something very important happened in the city of Medina, which is in present-day Saudi Arabia. The Prophet Muhammad and a group of his followers moved from Mecca to Medina to escape danger and build a new community. When they arrived, people in Medina were diverse—they included Muslims, several Jewish tribes, and other groups. To help everyone live together peacefully, the Prophet Muhammad created an agreement called the Constitution of Medina. This document set rules for how all these different groups would get along. It said that Muslims and Jewish tribes were part of one community, but each could follow their own religion. They promised to help each other if someone attacked the city and to stand up for fairness in disagreements between groups. This was new for the time because it meant that religious differences were respected, and everyone who agreed to the pact shared responsibilities for the safety and well-being of their city.
ff09.scripture: The Bible teaches us to 'love thy neighbour as thyself' (Luke 10:27). The Book of Mormon also tells us that 'all are alike unto God' (2 Nephi 26:33), showing He loves every person regardless of background or belief. While the scriptures do not speak about the Constitution of Medina, they encourage us to live peaceably with others, respect agency, and honor everyone’s freedom to choose their own beliefs. Doctrine and Covenants 134:4 and Articles of Faith 11 both speak plainly about letting men worship how, where, or what they may.
ff09.background: Before this event, Arabia was made up of many tribes, each often looking out just for its own people. Loyalty usually centered on clan and family. Mecca and Medina were trading cities where people from different tribes and backgrounds would meet, but tensions were common. Medina, called Yathrib back then, had both pagan Arab tribes and significant Jewish communities with their own customs, villages, and places of worship. People lived in simple homes and small villages. Life revolved around family, farming, and trading goods like dates and spices. Conflicts between tribes and families, however, often led to fighting. Into this world, the teachings of Islam began to spread with the message that all people could belong to one community based on belief and mutual respect.

ff10.t: Charlemagne Baptizes the Saxons by Force
ff10.talk: Why do you think God wants us to choose to follow Him instead of being forced?
ff10.child: A long time ago, a king wanted everyone in his land to be the same religion. He tried to make people join by making rules and punishments, but some people told him that faith must come from the heart. We can choose to follow Jesus because we want to, not because we have to.
ff10.learn: We can learn that following Jesus is a decision made in the heart, not by outward pressure or fear. Even in a time long ago, wise people could see that real faith must be freely chosen. Remembering this helps us respect the agency of others in their own journey to God and reminds us to share our beliefs with love, never force.
ff10.matters: This story matters because it shows how faith and freedom can come into conflict when one group tries to force its beliefs on another. Even during Charlemagne’s time, wise voices like Alcuin of York warned that faith cannot be compelled. For families who believe that faith should bring light and peace, this history asks us to remember that Heavenly Father invites, but does not coerce. It also reminds us that freedom to choose our faith is precious, and that the ways we share our beliefs matter as much as what we believe.

sources.name: Royal Frankish Annals (Internet Medieval Sourcebook, Fordham University)
Encyclopedia Britannica – Charlemagne: The Saxon Wars
BBC – Charlemagne and the Saxons

ff10.evidence: Our main evidence comes from the Royal Frankish Annals, which were written by people close to Charlemagne and aimed to record his reign. They tell of the events at Verden and the harsh laws placed on the Saxons. Scholars today debate the exact number of victims because copying errors or exaggerations were common in old records, but nearly all agree a large mass execution did occur. Archaeology shows the spread of Christian churches in Saxony soon after these events, but also hints that many Saxons continued their old customs in hiding for years. Letters from Alcuin, Charlemagne’s advisor, have been preserved and confirm the deep unease some Christians felt about the use of force.
ff10.happened: In the late 700s and early 800s, Charlemagne ruled over a growing Frankish kingdom in Western Europe. As part of his quest to unite and strengthen his lands, he wanted all his subjects to be Christians. The Saxons, a people who lived in what is now northern Germany, followed their own beliefs and often resisted his control. Charlemagne started a long campaign against them, marked not just by battles but also by harsh laws. In 782, the Royal Frankish Annals report that after a major uprising, Charlemagne ordered the execution of an enormous number of captured Saxon warriors—over 4,000 at a place called Verden. Alongside military force, he issued rules that demanded Saxons be baptized as Christians or face death; these rules also punished those who kept old customs, such as cremating the dead, or broke church rules during holy times. This period is remembered for the mixing of faith and force, with thousands converting under threat rather than through personal belief.
ff10.scripture: Scriptures from both the Bible and the Book of Mormon speak about agency—the power to choose. In the Book of Mormon, Helaman 14:30 teaches, 'Ye are free; ye are permitted to act for yourselves.' The New Testament contains the words of Jesus: 'If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me' (Matthew 16:24). This invitation implies choice, not compulsion. There are no scriptures that teach that faith should be forced by violence; on the contrary, agency is a central, sacred principle in God’s plan.
ff10.background: The world of Charlemagne was one of shifting kingdoms and frequent conflict. Christianity was spreading through Europe, but many people, like the Saxons, still followed older paths of worship and daily life rooted in nature and ancestors. Villages were small, and most people farmed or herded animals. Storytelling, ritual, and family ties shaped their identity. Charlemagne’s empire was growing fast—bringing new roads and monasteries, but also demands for loyalty to new rulers and religion. For the Saxons, keeping their customs meant honoring ages of tradition. For Charlemagne, unity in faith was seen as unity for his realm, even if it meant using force.

ff11.t: The Crusades and the Rhineland Massacres
ff11.talk: How can we show kindness to someone who believes differently than we do?
ff11.child: Long ago, some people hurt others because they believed differently. Jesus teaches us to love everyone, no matter what.
ff11.learn: From the Rhineland Massacres, we learn the dangers of allowing religious fervor to justify violence and persecution. It highlights the need for vigilance against intolerance and the importance of protecting vulnerable communities. As followers of Christ, we are called to be peacemakers, promoting understanding and love among all of God's children.
ff11.matters: The Rhineland Massacres of 1096 had profound and lasting impacts. They marked a significant escalation in antisemitic violence in Europe, setting a precedent for future persecutions. For families of faith, these events serve as a somber reminder of the consequences when religious zeal is misdirected into violence and intolerance. They underscore the importance of upholding Christ's teachings of love, compassion, and respect for all individuals, regardless of their beliefs. Reflecting on this history encourages us to promote understanding and peace in our communities today.

sources.name: Rhineland massacres
The Rhineland Massacres of the First Crusade - Medievalists.net
The Crusades and the Jews: Some Reflections on the 1096 Massacre - History Compass

ff11.evidence: Historical records from both Jewish and Christian sources document the events of the Rhineland Massacres. Jewish chronicles, such as those by Solomon bar Simson, provide detailed accounts of the attacks and their devastating effects on communities. Christian sources, including writings by Albert of Aachen, also acknowledge these events, though perspectives and details may vary. Archaeological evidence, such as remnants of destroyed synagogues and communal buildings, further corroborates these accounts. While exact numbers of those killed remain uncertain, estimates suggest that thousands of Jews perished during these attacks.
ff11.happened: In 1096, as the First Crusade was gathering momentum, bands of crusaders set out from Western Europe toward the Holy Land. Along their journey, particularly in the Rhineland region of present-day Germany, some of these groups turned their aggression toward local Jewish communities. In cities such as Speyer, Worms, Mainz, and Cologne, these crusaders attacked Jewish populations, leading to the deaths of thousands. The violence was fueled by a combination of religious fervor, economic motives, and deep-seated antisemitism. Some crusaders believed that before confronting non-Christians abroad, they should address those they considered infidels at home. Despite efforts by local bishops and authorities to protect Jewish residents, many communities faced devastation. These events are collectively known as the Rhineland Massacres and are among the earliest recorded large-scale persecutions of Jews in medieval Europe.
ff11.scripture: The scriptures consistently advocate for love and kindness toward others. In the New Testament, Jesus teaches, "Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself" (Matthew 22:39). The Book of Mormon echoes this sentiment, emphasizing that "all are alike unto God" (2 Nephi 26:33). These passages remind us that true discipleship involves treating all individuals with respect and compassion, irrespective of their background or beliefs.
ff11.background: The late 11th century was a time of significant religious and political upheaval in Europe. The Catholic Church, under Pope Urban II, called for the First Crusade in 1095, urging Christians to reclaim Jerusalem from Muslim control. This call ignited widespread enthusiasm, leading to the formation of various crusading groups. Among them were not only knights and nobles but also large bands of peasants and commoners, often referred to as the People's Crusade. These groups were less organized and lacked the discipline of the official crusading armies. The Jewish communities in the Rhineland had been established for centuries, living under the protection of local rulers and bishops. They were engaged in various trades, including moneylending, which was one of the few professions open to them due to restrictions on land ownership and other occupations. Despite their contributions to local economies, Jews often faced suspicion and resentment from their Christian neighbors.

ff12.t: The Almohads Force Conversion in Spain and North Africa
ff12.talk: What do you think would happen if someone told you that you had to believe exactly the same way they do?
ff12.child: A long time ago, a group called the Almohads made a rule that everyone had to join their religion or leave their homes. Many families had to move away or hide what they believed. This teaches us why it is important to let everyone choose their faith.
ff12.learn: We learn that laws and rulers, not just beliefs, shape how faith is lived. Even a place long known for its learning and tolerance can change quickly if power falls into the wrong hands. This teaches us to protect freedom of worship and to treat all people with respect, even if their beliefs are different from ours. When kindness is the standard, families, nations, and faith communities do better.
ff12.matters: This event matters because it reminds us that ideas and laws can quickly change the lives of whole communities. When beliefs are forced instead of offered with kindness, families can be hurt and cultures can be lost. The end of Jewish scholarship in Spain meant that much wisdom and learning was scattered or destroyed. For families of faith, it teaches humility—no tradition is always fair, and we should look for the best in every age while learning from mistakes. It also helps us to value religious freedom and the chance to teach our children their beliefs in peace.

sources.name: Encyclopedia Britannica: Almohads
United States Holocaust Memorial Museum: Maimonides
Jewish Virtual Library: Almohads

ff12.evidence: The history of the Almohads and their policies comes from Muslim, Christian, and Jewish sources from the period, as well as later scholars. Works like those of Maimonides mention fleeing the Almohads. Archaeological remains and documents show a flourishing Jewish and Christian life before the Almohad period, followed by a sudden disappearance or migration. There are records of exiles, forced conversions, and the destruction of synagogues and churches. Most historians accept that the Almohads changed the law, and that their rule saw these forced conversions and persecutions. Scholars can also see when learned families like Maimonides’ disappear from Spain and appear elsewhere, confirming the story through many records.
ff12.happened: In the year 1147, the Almohad dynasty, a new group of Muslim rulers from North Africa, conquered much of Spain and the Maghreb (Northwest Africa). They were different from the earlier Muslim dynasties in the region, such as the Almoravids and the Umayyads, who often allowed Jews and Christians to live as protected minorities, practicing their faiths and paying a special tax. The Almohads believed that their stricter view of Islam meant everyone under their rule needed to be Muslim. They passed harsh laws that forced Jews and Christians to either convert to Islam, leave their homes and lands, or face death. Many families were torn apart trying to decide what to do. Some converted outwardly but practiced their beliefs in secret; others fled to new lands, losing everything. These events were especially hard for the well-known Jewish community in Cordoba, which had been an important center of learning. The famous Jewish philosopher Moses Maimonides was a child during this time. His family chose to leave and later settled in Egypt, where he continued to write and teach. This period ended a long time of relative peace and cooperation where Muslims, Jews, and Christians had lived together in what is sometimes called convivencia.
ff12.scripture: Scriptures teach that forcing others in faith is not the Lord’s way. In Doctrine and Covenants 121:41–42, we learn that power and influence should be kept only by persuading, by long-suffering, by gentleness and meekness, and by love unfeigned. The Book of Mormon, in Alma 1:21, says that 'there was a strict law among the people of the church, that there should not any man, belonging to the church, arise and persecute those that did not belong to the church.' The Savior Himself taught love and respect for agency. These scriptures remind us of the importance of respecting others’ freedom to worship as they choose.
ff12.background: For several centuries before the Almohads, Spain, known as Al-Andalus, and parts of North Africa were places where people of different faiths—Muslims, Christians, and Jews—lived side by side. Earlier Muslim rulers usually allowed Jews and Christians to keep their faiths if they accepted a lower status and paid taxes. Cordoba became famous for its scholars, poets, doctors, and philosophers. Daily life for many families included study, trade, and worship, with streets that sometimes echoed with many languages. When the Almohads rose to power, they brought new religious ideas from North Africa believing that only Islam should be allowed and all must submit to their teachings.

ff13.talk: Why do you think it matters that people are free to choose what they believe about God?
ff13.child: A long time ago in Spain, people who followed different religions were forced to do things they didn’t choose. It made many families afraid and hurt the country for a long time. We can remember that a loving Heavenly Father wants us to choose faith for ourselves, not be forced.
ff13.learn: What we can learn is that using force to control beliefs can damage a nation and its people, harming not just those punished but everyone who depends on their talents and friendship. Faith given by God is meant to be chosen, not compelled. When families, towns, or even countries let people worship freely, they tend to thrive in peace, creativity, and kindness.
ff13.matters: The Spanish Inquisition matters because it shows us what can happen when faith is forced instead of freely chosen. Instead of building a community of trust, it led to fear, suspicion, and great loss. For families that value faith, it is a reminder that real faith grows best when people are free to choose it without any pressure or threat. Today, we can look back and see that the Inquisition pushed away many of Spain’s brightest and most creative people, which harmed the whole nation for many years. This history teaches us that protecting freedom of belief is a blessing to families, churches, and even countries.

sources.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica - Spanish Inquisition
BBC - The Spanish Inquisition
Jewish Virtual Library - The Spanish Inquisition

ff13.evidence: Historians have spent years studying records from the Spanish Inquisition. Early reports claimed far more deaths, sometimes tens of thousands, but careful modern scholarship by experts like Henry Kamen has found that the real number of executions is much lower—a maximum of about 3,000, and possibly up to 5,000 to 12,000 if poorly kept early records are included. Most punishments were actually forms of public confession, penance, or imprisonment, rather than execution. Nearly all evidence comes from the Inquisition’s own archives, which are detailed for later years but missing in places for the early decades. Economic and cultural records show that after the Jewish and Muslim communities were forced out, Spain began to fall behind other European countries in business and learning. This supports what many historians have written: that the drive for religious sameness hurt Spain’s prosperity for centuries.
ff13.happened: In 1478, King Ferdinand and Queen Isabella of Spain set up an organization called the Spanish Inquisition. Their goal was to make sure that everyone in Spain was following the Catholic faith as they understood it. This was a time when people thought that unity in religion was necessary for the strength of the country. The rulers asked permission from the Pope in Rome to begin, and he agreed. The main focus was on people who had recently changed from Judaism or Islam to Christianity. The Inquisition leaders believed that some might be hiding their real beliefs, so they began investigating anyone suspected of not being a true Catholic. People were called to testify, and many were punished if they were found guilty—sometimes through fines, imprisonment, public shame, or in the most serious cases, execution. Over hundreds of years, thousands lost their property and freedom, and modern research estimates that the Inquisition executed between 3,000 and 5,000 people, mostly in the early years. It was a dark period for Spain, as suspicion and fear touched many homes.
ff13.scripture: The scriptures teach that God gives people agency, the power to choose. In the Book of Mormon, 2 Nephi 2:27 says, "Wherefore, men are free according to the flesh; and all things are given them which are expedient unto man. And they are free to choose liberty and eternal life, ... or to choose captivity and death." The Bible teaches that faith must come from the heart (Romans 10:10). Nothing in the standard works supports using force to make someone believe in God; rather, the Lord invites all to come to Him and honors their choice.
ff13.background: Before the Inquisition, Spain was home to many Jewish and Muslim families who had lived in the region for centuries. They contributed to scholarship, business, and local communities. The late 1400s were a time of change: Spain had recently finished the Reconquista, a centuries-long campaign to reclaim the land from Muslim rule. Life for average people mostly revolved around farming, crafts, and family, but it was also a tense time, as the rulers worked to make everyone fit with their vision of a united, Christian land. Some Jewish and Muslim people converted to Christianity to stay safe, but many still faced mistrust. The idea of using force or fear to make people believe certain things about God was sadly common across Europe at this time, though not always with such intensity as in Spain.

ff14.talk: Why is it important to let people choose their own beliefs?
ff14.child: Long ago in Spain, the king and queen told all Jewish people they had to become Christians or leave the country. Many Jewish families had to move to new places far away. This teaches us how important it is to let everyone choose their own beliefs.
ff14.learn: From the Alhambra Decree, we learn the vital importance of religious freedom and the dangers of intolerance. Societies that respect and embrace diversity tend to flourish, while those that enforce uniformity through coercion often face decline. This history teaches us to value and protect the rights of all individuals to practice their faith freely.
ff14.matters: The Alhambra Decree is a stark reminder of the consequences of religious intolerance and the dangers of imposing faith by force. For families of faith, it underscores the importance of respecting religious freedom and the dignity of all individuals, regardless of their beliefs. The expulsion led to a significant loss of cultural and intellectual capital for Spain, while the regions that welcomed the exiles benefited from their contributions. This historical event teaches us that societies thrive when they embrace diversity and suffer when they enforce conformity through coercion.

sources.name: Alhambra Decree - Wikipedia
The 1492 Jewish Expulsion | Andalucía 365
Alhambra Decree - Conservapedia

ff14.evidence: Historical records, including the original text of the Alhambra Decree, provide clear evidence of the expulsion. Contemporary accounts describe the hardships faced by the Jewish community during this period. Archaeological findings, such as remnants of Jewish quarters in Spanish cities, attest to the once-thriving communities that were abruptly uprooted. Additionally, the cultural and economic contributions of Sephardic Jews in their new homelands further illustrate the impact of their forced migration. These pieces of evidence collectively confirm the occurrence and consequences of the Alhambra Decree.
ff14.happened: In 1492, King Ferdinand and Queen Isabella of Spain issued the Alhambra Decree, also known as the Edict of Expulsion. This decree mandated that all Jews in Spain either convert to Christianity or leave the country within four months. The primary aim was to eliminate Jewish influence on the large population of conversos—Jews who had previously converted to Christianity—amid fears that they might secretly practice Judaism. As a result, tens of thousands of Jews faced a harrowing choice: abandon their faith or their homeland. Many chose exile, leading to a significant diaspora. They sought refuge in various regions, including the Ottoman Empire, North Africa, and parts of Europe like the Netherlands. The Ottoman Sultan Bayezid II welcomed these exiles, reportedly remarking that Spain's loss was his gain. This mass expulsion not only disrupted countless lives but also had profound economic and cultural impacts on Spain and the regions that received the refugees.
ff14.scripture: The scriptures emphasize the importance of agency and the respect for individual choice in matters of faith. In the Book of Mormon, we read: 'Therefore, cheer up your hearts, and remember that ye are free to act for yourselves—to choose the way of everlasting death or the way of eternal life.' (2 Nephi 10:23) This principle highlights that faith cannot be compelled; it must be chosen freely. The Alhambra Decree serves as a historical example of the perils that arise when this divine principle is ignored.
ff14.background: Before 1492, Spain was a mosaic of cultures and religions, with Christians, Jews, and Muslims coexisting for centuries. The Jewish community, known as Sephardic Jews, had deep roots in the Iberian Peninsula, contributing significantly to the arts, sciences, and commerce. However, the late 15th century was marked by the Reconquista—the Christian reconquest of Spain from Muslim rule—which culminated in the fall of Granada in January 1492. This victory unified Spain under Christian rule. Amid this consolidation, there was a growing desire to enforce religious uniformity. The Spanish Inquisition, established in 1478, intensified efforts to identify and punish heresy, particularly focusing on conversos suspected of secretly practicing Judaism. This climate of suspicion and intolerance set the stage for the Alhambra Decree.

ff15.t: State Religion and Human Sacrifice in the Aztec Empire
ff15.talk: Why do you think Heavenly Father wants us to choose for ourselves instead of forcing us?
ff15.child: A long time ago, the Aztecs made people bring captives to their city for special ceremonies, thinking this made their gods happy. Many people did not want to do this, so when new people came, they joined together to change things. It's a story about what happens when people are not allowed to choose for themselves.
ff15.learn: We learn that forcing belief or demanding sacrifice through fear will not create strong, united communities. True faith grows best when people choose it freely and lovingly. This history reminds us to use the gifts of freedom and agency wisely, helping others with kindness and respecting their right to believe for themselves.
ff15.matters: This story matters because it shows how belief, power, and freedom can tangle together. When a government forces religious practice using fear or violence, it often sows anger and division among people, even if the rulers believe they are acting for a greater good. For families of faith, this history invites us to think about how Heavenly Father wants us to act: with real faith, love, and agency, not by force. Remembering the past helps us cherish the freedom to choose our beliefs and to invite others, rather than compel them.

sources.name: Smithsonian Magazine: Excavations reveal scale of Aztec sacrifices
Metropolitan Museum of Art: Aztec Human Sacrifice
British Museum: The Aztecs and Human Sacrifice

ff15.evidence: Archaeological digs at the site of the Templo Mayor in Mexico City have unearthed a massive skull rack, known as the 'tzompantli,' and evidence of thousands of human sacrifices, confirming that these acts occurred at large scale. Scholars still debate the exact numbers, as written Spanish accounts may exaggerate or misunderstand, but the evidence for regular, ritual human sacrifice under state direction is solid. The finding of the tzompantli and analysis of the site's layers give a credible record that the sacrifices happened and were part of the Aztec religious and political system.
ff15.happened: Between roughly 1428 and 1521, the Aztec Empire in what is now central Mexico grew into a large and powerful state, ruled from the grand city of Tenochtitlan. The Aztec rulers believed that their gods, especially the sun god Huitzilopochtli, required regular human sacrifices to ensure the world’s survival. The state religion wasn’t just a set of beliefs; it was enforced by law and backed by the government. Subject peoples and neighboring regions were required to supply tribute in goods, services, and, most famously, captives for ritual sacrifice. These sacrifices often took place at the Templo Mayor, a huge pyramid at the heart of Tenochtitlan, where thousands could be assembled. The sheer scale of the ceremonies was meant to show the power of the Aztecs and honor their gods. For the communities conquered by the Aztecs, the demand for captives and tribute was a heavy and constant burden. When the Spanish led by Hernán Cortés arrived in 1519, many of these peoples—such as the Tlaxcalans—chose to ally with them against the Aztecs, helping bring about the empire's fall in 1521. The resentment bred by forced tribute and sacrifice contributed greatly to the Aztec defeat.
ff15.scripture: The scriptures uphold the principle of agency and conversion by persuasion, not compulsion. In the Bible, Acts 8:36-38 describes conversion and baptism as a personal choice. The Book of Mormon speaks strongly in Alma 1:21-22 and 30:7-9 about religious freedom and the dangers of forcing belief. Article of Faith 11 from the Pearl of Great Price says, 'We claim the privilege of worshiping Almighty God according to the dictates of our own conscience, and allow all men the same privilege.'
ff15.background: The Aztecs were one of several peoples living in Mexico before the Spanish arrived. They founded Tenochtitlan in the early 1300s on an island in Lake Texcoco, building canals, temples, and markets. Society was complex; there were farmers, craftsmen, merchants, priests, and warriors. Religion was woven into daily life—not only believing in many gods, but also linking those beliefs to the cycles of farming, war, and leadership. The Triple Alliance of Tenochtitlan with Texcoco and Tlacopan formed the base of the Aztec Empire, which demanded tribute from all its territories. For most people, life meant daily work, trade in busy markets, and farmer’s chores. But the shadow of war and tribute was always present, especially for communities conquered by the empire.

ff16.talk: Why do you think it’s important for everyone to be able to choose their own beliefs?
ff16.child: A long time ago, rulers in Germany said everyone had to believe what their leader believed, or they could move away. This stopped a big fight, but it did not let each person choose their belief freely. Some people still could not worship how they wanted.
ff16.learn: From this event, we learn that giving people a choice—though imperfect—is better than forcing them to change their deepest beliefs. It reminds us that real religious freedom means everyone can worship, wherever they live, without needing to run away. We also see that, as people of faith, we may need to stand kindly for what we believe while recognizing the right of others to choose differently.
ff16.matters: The Peace of Augsburg matters because it was one of the first big attempts to solve the problem of different religions living side by side. For families of faith, it shows how people have tried to find ways to live together, even when they believe differently. It was a meaningful step towards freedom, but it did not allow everyone to choose their faith freely. True freedom of religion means a person can follow their heart and conscience wherever they live. This event still reminds us that moving to a new place is not the same as being free in your own home to believe and worship.

sources.name: Brittanica: Peace of Augsburg
Metropolitan Museum of Art: Reformation and the Arts
United States Holocaust Memorial Museum: Reformation

ff16.evidence: Historians use a rich collection of official records, letters, and treaties to show what happened before, during, and after the meeting in Augsburg. The document signed in 1555, called the Peace of Augsburg, still exists and has been carefully studied. Many personal stories have survived from people who had to move because of their beliefs, as well as reports from the rulers and church leaders at the time. Archaeologists and archivists have found evidence of changes in churches, villages, and even graveyards, reflecting shifts between Catholic and Lutheran control. None of these sources deny what happened, but they also show the sadness of those who were left out, like the Anabaptists and Reformed Christians, whose words and journeys have also been traced.
ff16.happened: In the year 1555, leaders from many areas of Germany came together in the city of Augsburg to end a long and bitter fight over religion. This event is called the Peace of Augsburg. At that time, most people in Europe followed either the Catholic Church or the new teachings of Martin Luther, known as Lutheranism. The two sides had fought wars, and people had suffered because rulers demanded everyone in their land share the same beliefs. The Peace of Augsburg tried to fix this. It created a rule called 'cuius regio, eius religio,' which is Latin for 'whose realm, his religion.' This meant that the ruler of each part of the Holy Roman Empire (a large group of smaller countries in what is today Germany and nearby areas) could decide if that area would be Catholic or Lutheran. If someone lived in a place and didn't agree with the religion chosen by the ruler, they were allowed to move to another area instead of being forced to join in. This law stopped a terrible civil war and helped keep peace for a time. But it only protected Catholics and Lutherans. Other groups, like Anabaptists and Reformed (Calvinist) Christians, were not allowed to worship freely and were still treated harshly.
ff16.scripture: While the scriptures do not discuss the Peace of Augsburg or this law directly, many teachings in the Bible and modern scripture honor the principle of religious freedom. In the Bible, Joshua 24:15 says, 'choose you this day whom ye will serve.' In Doctrine and Covenants 134:4, it says 'governments were instituted of God for the benefit of man... for the protection of the rights of all men.' These verses teach that God values agency—the right to choose—and that governments should protect people’s ability to follow God as they understand Him.
ff16.background: Europe in the 1500s was a place of big changes. A movement called the Reformation had begun when Martin Luther challenged some teachings and practices of the Catholic Church in 1517. Many people liked Luther's ideas, and new churches formed. This brought hope to some but caused worry for rulers who believed unity came from sharing the same religion. Life was hard for most families, who worked on farms or in small towns, and they looked to their faith for meaning and support. People usually practiced the religion of their ruler, and punishment for believing differently could be harsh—sometimes leading to loss of home, jail, or worse. Many wanted peace, but the question of faith kept causing arguments and even war.

ff17.talk: Why do you think it is important to let other people worship God in their own way?
ff17.child: A long time ago in Poland, leaders agreed that people should not be hurt because they believed differently about God. This helped many people live together in peace, even when things were hard in other places. Their choice teaches us that being kind to people of other faiths is very important.
ff17.learn: We can learn from the Warsaw Confederation that choosing kindness and tolerance, even when others don’t, can bring lasting peace. When we protect the freedom of others to worship as they wish, we also protect our own freedom. Remembering that God values agency helps us act with respect and understanding, even toward people who believe differently than ourselves. Just as the Polish-Lithuanian leaders showed, courage and faith can shape a society for good.
ff17.matters: The Warsaw Confederation matters because it showed the world that people from different faiths could choose to live together peacefully, even in a time when fear, violence, and suspicion were common across Europe. For families who value both faith and freedom, this event demonstrates that protecting another’s right to worship—even when beliefs differ—is a choice that can bless entire communities. It reminds us that agency, one of God’s great gifts, includes the freedom to seek, question, and follow faith. The story of the confederation encourages us to honor the rights of others and to recognize the blessings that come when people are not forced into belief.

sources.name: UNESCO Memory of the World Register – The Warsaw Confederation Act
Encyclopaedia Britannica – Warsaw Confederation
Norman Davies, God's Playground: A History of Poland
The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, D&C 134:4

ff17.evidence: The Warsaw Confederation is widely documented in both Polish and world history. The original parchment, covered in wax seals, is kept in the Central Archives of Historical Records in Warsaw and was entered into UNESCO’s Memory of the World Register in 2003 to mark its global importance. Historians agree about the details of the signing and the content of the act. Written records from the time, as well as later confirmations by kings, provide solid evidence that the Confederation was enforced for generations, especially among the noble class. While it’s clear that this was not universal freedom—peasants and some others were left out—there is no serious historical debate over the event’s main facts. Scholars use government and church records, diaries, and personal letters from people who lived at the time to help build the picture we have today.
ff17.happened: On January 28, 1573, leaders from the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth gathered in Warsaw because their king had died, leaving no one to rule. This time of waiting, called an interregnum, was tense because Europe was full of religious fighting, but the people of Poland and Lithuania chose a different path. The Sejm, their national parliament made up mostly of nobles, signed an important document called the Warsaw Confederation. This agreement said that no one should be harmed or killed because of their religion. To make their promise clear, 206 nobles pressed their personal wax seals onto the parchment. This act was unique in Europe at a time when people in many countries faced punishment, even death, for their religious beliefs. The Confederation didn’t give freedom to everyone—peasants and townspeople did not get these rights—but it did promise that the nobility and free persons could worship as they chose without fear. This agreement was accepted by every king crowned after that, who had to swear to uphold it. Over the next two centuries, as wars raged over religion in other parts of Europe, Poland-Lithuania became a safe place for Jews, Protestants, Eastern Orthodox Christians, and many others to live in peace. Some leaders elsewhere complained that the Commonwealth was too tolerant, but it stood as a place where different faiths could coexist without violence.
ff17.scripture: The scriptures do not speak directly about the Warsaw Confederation, but the principle of religious freedom appears many times. In the Bible, Paul teaches in Romans 14:5, “Let every man be fully persuaded in his own mind,” inviting respect for differences. The Doctrine and Covenants, in section 134:4, teaches, “We do not believe that human law has a right to interfere in prescribing rules of worship... but believe that every man should be protected in worshiping according to the dictates of his own conscience.” These passages support the idea that God values each person’s right to choose how to worship and expects us to respect that right in others.
ff17.background: Before this agreement, much of Europe was deeply divided by religion. After the Reformation began, many rulers tried to force everyone to follow their own faith, and wars broke out because of these differences. Poland-Lithuania, which included much of today’s Poland, Lithuania, Belarus, and Ukraine, was one of the largest and most diverse states in Europe. Its population was made up of people with many backgrounds and beliefs: Catholics, Orthodox Christians, Jews, Protestants, and others. Nobles had more power and freedom than most rulers allowed elsewhere. Ordinary life for most people, especially peasants, was hard: they worked the land, struggled through cold winters, and were expected to follow the religion of their local lord. But towns bustled with trade and crafts, and cities like Warsaw, Krakow, and Vilnius welcomed travelers, merchants, and scholars from afar. The need to keep peace among such a mixed population helped to make religious tolerance possible.

ff18.t: The Edict of Nantes and Its Revocation
ff18.talk: How do you feel when someone lets you make your own choices, even if they are different from theirs?
ff18.child: Long ago, in France, a king made a rule so that people could pray in their own way and live in peace. But later, another king took that rule away, and many families had to leave their homes. They still found ways to use their talents and bless new lands.
ff18.learn: This part of history shows us that real peace comes when people are allowed to worship freely, even when they choose different paths. It also warns of the harm that comes when fear and control are chosen instead of trust and respect. As families, we can remember how much good we do when we show kindness, make room for differences, and defend the right of all to seek God in their own way.
ff18.matters: The Edict of Nantes shows how powerful leaders' choices about freedom and faith can shape a country’s future. When families were allowed to worship in peace, France grew safer and richer. But when that freedom was taken away, fear returned, and France lost many people who made its society strong. For those who believe that every person is a child of God, this story reminds us how important it is to respect others’ beliefs. As families, we learn that freedom to worship can help a community become more peaceful and creative.

sources.name: Britannica – Edict of Nantes
History.com – Edict of Nantes
Encyclopedia.com – Huguenots
ChurchofJesusChrist.org – Religious Freedom: A Cherished Heritage

ff18.evidence: Historians widely agree on the main facts of the Edict of Nantes and its revocation. There are records of the edict itself, testimonies from people who lived through these events, and many official documents about the laws and their effects.
