Church records, city archives, and personal letters from the Huguenots and their neighbors reveal both the relief when the edict was signed and the hardship when it was revoked. Economic and migration records confirm that large numbers of Huguenots left France and that their skills helped the places they moved to. France’s loss in textile and silk industries, which were often run by Huguenots, is well documented. These sources give us a clear, reliable picture of what happened.
ff18.happened: In 1598, King Henry IV of France signed the Edict of Nantes, a special law that allowed French Protestants, called Huguenots, to worship openly. For a country that had been torn apart by religious fighting, this was a big step toward peace. The edict did not make everyone equal, but it let Protestants hold some jobs, build churches in certain places, and live without fear from the government. For nearly 90 years, this agreement brought stability. People with different beliefs learned to live side by side. But in 1685, King Louis XIV decided he wanted only the Catholic faith in his kingdom. He took away the Edict of Nantes and ordered Protestant churches destroyed. Huguenots were not allowed to leave, but many did anyway, running away to places like England, Prussia, and America. They brought valuable skills with them and helped other lands grow stronger, while France lost many talented people. The ending of the Edict not only broke families but also made France weaker in business and culture.
ff18.scripture: The Bible teaches the importance of loving one another and treating others as we want to be treated: Matthew 7:12, the 'Golden Rule.' The Book of Mormon in Mosiah 27:3 also teaches that 'there should be no persecutions among them, that there should be an equality among all men.' Doctrine and Covenants 134:4 states that religion is 'instituted of God; and men are amenable to him, and to him only, for the exercise of it,' which means that freedom in how we worship is a gift and a responsibility. These teachings underline the principle that faith should not be forced and that peace grows where respect is shown.
ff18.background: France in the 1500s and 1600s was a place where most people were Catholic, but a large group was Protestant. These Protestants, known as Huguenots, had started to grow in number after learning from reformers like John Calvin. At the time, people believed that a country needed one religion to stay united. Fighting between Catholics and Protestants turned into wars, causing suffering and death, like the Saint Bartholomew's Day Massacre in 1572, where thousands of Huguenots were killed in Paris and beyond. Life for most people was hard, with most families farming or working in crafts. Faith was central to daily life and decisions. King Henry IV himself was a former Protestant who turned Catholic to become king but wanted to stop the hurting and help every family live without fear.

ff19.talk: Why do you think Heavenly Father wants everyone to be free to choose how they worship?
ff19.child: Roger Williams wanted everyone to choose how to worship God. He made a town where people could be safe, even if they prayed differently or not at all. That helped make a place where all kinds of people could live together.
ff19.learn: We can learn from Roger Williams that standing up for what is right, even when it is unpopular, can bless many people. His example shows that protecting each person’s freedom to follow God, or not, makes a community stronger and brings peace. As families, we can talk about how we show respect for others’ beliefs, and how we want to be treated in return.
ff19.matters: Roger Williams’s founding of Rhode Island matters because it became the first place in America where people of different faiths could live together in peace, without fear of punishment for their beliefs. His ideas planted the seeds for religious liberty in the future United States and shaped how freedom of conscience is valued today. For families of faith, this reminds us that everyone’s journey to God is personal, and protecting the right to choose and worship is a sacred responsibility. Williams saw freedom of belief as a blessing from a loving Heavenly Father, meant to guide us as we help each other live in peace.

sources.name: Smithsonian Magazine: Roger Williams and the Creation of the American Soul
Rhode Island State Archives: Roger Williams
Encyclopaedia Britannica: Roger Williams

ff19.evidence: Historians agree that Roger Williams was forced to leave Massachusetts in 1636 and that he founded Providence on land given by the Narragansett people. His writings, including his book 'The Bloudy Tenent of Persecution,' clearly lay out his thoughts about religious freedom and the need to keep government and church separate. Documents from the time, like the Providence town compact and Rhode Island’s 1663 charter, survive and show Williams’s influence in creating space for people of different faiths. Many who fled religious persecution elsewhere found a safe home in Rhode Island, including the first Jewish community in North America. There is no serious doubt among historians about these events, which are also reflected in later American laws.
ff19.happened: In 1636, Roger Williams, a preacher from England, found himself at odds with the leaders of the Massachusetts Bay Colony. Williams believed strongly that no government should have power over a person's beliefs or worship. Because he spoke out about this, saying that everyone should be free to follow their conscience, the colony leaders decided he could not stay. Banished in the middle of winter, he walked through the snowy wilderness until he reached land the Narragansett tribe allowed him to settle. There, Williams founded a new community called Providence. He made a special promise: anyone, no matter their religion or if they had no religion at all, could live there and be free to worship as they chose. This idea, which was very unusual at the time, became the heart of Rhode Island, drawing not only Baptists and Quakers but also Jews, who faced persecution elsewhere. Williams wrote that the church and the state should be like two separate gardens, each with its own fence, protecting both from harm. This taught people that true faith and freedom must go together.
ff19.scripture: While no scripture describes Roger Williams or Rhode Island, the principle of religious liberty is rooted in many holy books. The Bible teaches that men and women are agents, free to choose (Joshua 24:15: 'choose you this day whom ye will serve'). The Book of Mormon teaches, 'it is not right that any man should be in bondage one to another' (Mosiah 23:13). Doctrine and Covenants 134:4 says that government should not control the soul, echoing Williams’ vision. These scriptures, across the standard works, show God values each person’s agency—the power to choose for themselves.
ff19.background: The early 1600s in New England was a time when church and government were closely mixed. Most settlements were ruled by Puritan leaders who expected everyone to live and worship the same way. People had to go to the official church, pay church taxes, and could be punished or thrown out if they disagreed. Roger Williams, himself a Puritan minister, saw the danger in forcing people to believe a certain way. Daily life involved hard work in a new land, with close-knit communities relying on one another just to survive. Yet, fear of difference led to suspicion and harsh measures against those who stood out. Into this world, Williams brought the radical idea that the soul’s freedom was a gift from God and could not be taken by any human law.

ff20.talk: What do you think could happen if people in our neighborhood started believing bad things about someone without proof?
ff20.child: A long time ago, in Salem, people were so afraid of witches that they blamed many innocent neighbors. Some people were hurt because others thought they were doing bad things. It is important to be kind and not judge others too quickly.
ff20.learn: We can learn from Salem that when a community uses fear or force to control belief, it often ends up hurting innocent people. Freedom of conscience—meaning the right to think and worship as you believe—is a gift that needs defending, even when people disagree. As families, we can teach each other not to judge without understanding, and to stand up quietly for the rights of others to choose.
ff20.matters: The Salem Witch Trials became one of America's most famous warnings about the dangers of letting fear control a community, especially when faith is backed by force rather than love or reason. For families who believe Jesus teaches kindness and freedom, this story is powerful. It reminds us that our Heavenly Father wants us to treat each person with fairness, not suspicion or anger, and to protect each other’s right to worship and think freely. The trials helped shape American ideas about justice—especially the need for real evidence in court and the importance of not judging others’ hearts or minds.

sources.name: Salem Witch Trials - Encyclopaedia Britannica
National Archives - Salem Witch Trials
The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints: Alma 30 Scripture Reference

ff20.evidence: Historians have many records from the Salem Witch Trials, including written testimonies, court records, and the names of those who were accused and executed. Most researchers agree that social tensions, religious fears, and even possible physical illnesses or local conflicts may have played roles in what happened. Scholars have also studied the events to understand why so many people accepted accusations with so little proof. There is no physical evidence of witchcraft, and the trials stand as a clear lesson in the dangers of unjust laws and misplaced faith. The colony’s own reversal and public repentance are well-documented, making this a strongly confirmed chapter in American history.
ff20.happened: In 1692, in the small town of Salem, Massachusetts, fear and suspicion swept through the community. Some young girls began behaving strangely, claiming they were being hurt by invisible forces and blaming certain neighbors for using witchcraft against them. The town leaders, deeply religious and wanting to keep their community safe from evil, started asking questions and holding trials. People accused each other of witchcraft, sometimes for reasons as simple as a quarrel or jealousy. The judges accepted a kind of evidence called “spectral evidence,” which meant believing that someone’s spirit or ghost had done harm, even if there was no physical proof. Over several months, twenty people—fifteen women and five men—were found guilty and executed, and about 150 others were put in jail. The trials finally stopped when more and more people began to doubt the accusations, seeing how easily anyone could be blamed. The colony later admitted the trials were a mistake, freed the survivors, reversed the guilty verdicts, and even set a day to pray and say sorry together as a community.
ff20.scripture: Scriptures teach that everyone is free to choose their beliefs; for example, in the Book of Mormon, Alma 30:7-9 speaks of "no law against a man’s belief" and the people having the power to choose. In the Bible, Matthew 7:1 warns, "Judge not, that ye be not judged." Doctrine and Covenants 134:4–5 also declares that government should not control or punish someone because of their beliefs. These verses remind us to be gentle, fair, and protective of others’ agency, trusting that only God can see the heart.
ff20.background: Salem in the late 1600s was a tough place to live, and most people there were Puritans, a group of Christians who wanted their community to strictly follow their beliefs. Their world was full of hard farm work, close families, and a deep sense of watching out for signs of good and evil. There were no modern comforts, and sickness, storms, and crop failures were often frightening and hard to explain. Because people believed evil could come into their lives through things like witchcraft, they were quick to worry when anything unusual happened. The Massachusetts Bay Colony had already shown itself ready to punish people with different beliefs, even banishing those who disagreed. The culture was close-knit but also tense, setting the stage for neighbors to turn against each other during the trials.

ff21.talk: Why do you think it is important for people to be able to choose how they worship?
ff21.child: A long time ago, leaders made a rule so nobody could be forced to join a church or stop worshiping in their own way. This rule helps everyone choose how to follow God or not, and helps many churches be safe here. We can thank God that we get to choose how to worship.
ff21.learn: From this moment, we learn the value of standing up for freedom and respecting others’ beliefs—even and especially when they differ from our own. Faith grows best when it is chosen, not forced, and when all voices can be heard. As families, teaching children to cherish and protect this freedom helps preserve it for the future and honors both God and country. We can also learn to support, not fear, those who worship differently, knowing that Heavenly Father loves all His children.
ff21.matters: The First Amendment matters deeply for families of faith. It created a place where faith can grow freely, not by force, but by choice. In the United States, believers from all over the world have come and found they could gather, worship, and teach as they felt was right. This freedom later made it possible for The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints to be restored and protected. Around the world, not every country has these freedoms. The First Amendment became a light to other nations, showing how faith and freedom can live together. For families, this means teaching and living the gospel is a right, not something to be hidden, as long as it respects the same right for others.

sources.name: National Archives – The Bill of Rights
Library of Congress – Religious Freedom
The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints – Religious Freedom
Encyclopaedia Britannica – First Amendment

ff21.evidence: Historians have studied the debates, letters, and published records from the Founding Fathers that show exactly how and why the First Amendment was written. Original documents, including drafts and the final Bill of Rights, survive in the National Archives and confirm the wording and purpose. Scholars agree that Jefferson, Madison, and others spoke often about religious liberty as essential for a just society. Over two centuries, the U.S. Supreme Court and historians have used these records to interpret what the First Amendment means. There is broad, well-preserved evidence supporting both the event and its significance, making this one of the best-documented moments in early American history.
ff21.happened: On December 15, 1791, the First Amendment became part of the United States Constitution when the Bill of Rights was adopted. This short sentence changed history: 'Congress shall make no law respecting an establishment of religion, or prohibiting the free exercise thereof.' For the first time, a nation promised in its highest law that it would not create an official church or force anyone to worship a certain way. This amendment grew out of deep discussions and worries among early Americans who remembered times—both in Europe and in America's own colonies—when governments tried to control religion or punished people for their faith. Lawmakers in Philadelphia, representing people from many backgrounds, debated and finally agreed on these new rules. The First Amendment made room for every person to follow their conscience and choose how, where, and if they would worship. This did not mean religion was unimportant; rather, it opened a door for many different faiths to thrive, side by side, each protected by the law.
ff21.scripture: Doctrine and Covenants 101:80 teaches that God 'established the Constitution of this land, by the hands of wise men whom I raised up.' The Lord said these laws were made for the good of everyone, to help all people seek the truth. The Book of Mormon shows how religious freedom brings peace (Alma 30:7–11), while the Bible encourages us to pray and worship without compulsion (Joshua 24:15, Revelation 3:20). The principle of agency—the right to choose—is central to God’s plan in the scriptures. The First Amendment embodies that same respect for choice in matters of faith.
ff21.background: Before the First Amendment, most countries in the world, including England, had a 'state church'—one faith supported by taxes and often enforced by law. Many early colonists in America had faced jail, fines, or even violence because of their beliefs. Even some of the colonies had official churches. The American Revolution helped spark new thinking about individual rights, especially the right to worship freely. Thomas Jefferson's 1786 Virginia Statute for Religious Freedom was an important step, declaring that no one should be forced to support or attend any religion. James Madison helped carry this idea into the Constitution. Daily life in 1791 was shaped by farms, small towns, and close-knit communities, with many churches at the heart of life—but now, for the first time, each person could worship as they chose, or not at all, without fear from the government.

ff22.talk: Why is it important to be kind to people who have different beliefs than we do?
ff22.child: A long time ago, people who believed in Jesus were told they couldn't live in their homes because others didn't like their beliefs. Some were hurt, and they had to find a new place to live. This teaches us to be kind to everyone, even if they believe differently.
ff22.learn: From this history, we learn the critical importance of protecting religious freedom and the dangers of allowing prejudice to dictate policy. It teaches us to be vigilant against intolerance and to advocate for the rights of all individuals to worship according to their conscience. For families, it serves as a lesson in resilience and the power of faith to overcome adversity.
ff22.matters: The events surrounding the Missouri Extermination Order and the Hawn's Mill Massacre highlight the challenges of religious freedom and the dangers of intolerance. For families of faith, this history serves as a reminder of the importance of standing firm in one's beliefs, even in the face of persecution. It also underscores the need for compassion and understanding toward those with differing views. Recognizing past injustices can inspire efforts to promote religious liberty and prevent similar occurrences in the future.

sources.name: Missouri Executive Order 44
Hawn's Mill Massacre
The Haun's Mill Massacre - BYU Studies

ff22.evidence: Historical records, including official documents and personal accounts, provide detailed evidence of the Missouri Extermination Order and the Hawn's Mill Massacre. Governor Boggs' Executive Order 44 is preserved in state archives, clearly stating the directive against the Mormons. Eyewitness testimonies from survivors of the massacre, such as those recorded by Joseph Young, offer vivid descriptions of the attack and its aftermath. Additionally, contemporary newspaper reports and later historical analyses corroborate these events, confirming the persecution faced by the Saints in Missouri during that period.
ff22.happened: In the autumn of 1838, tensions between members of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints and other Missouri settlers escalated into violent conflict. On October 27, 1838, Missouri Governor Lilburn Boggs issued Executive Order 44, declaring that Mormons must be treated as enemies and either exterminated or driven from the state. This directive led to increased aggression against the Saints. Three days later, on October 30, a militia force of approximately 240 men attacked the Mormon settlement at Hawn's Mill in Caldwell County. Despite attempts by the settlers to negotiate peace, the militia opened fire, killing 17 men and boys and wounding 15 others. Among the dead was a 10-year-old boy named Sardius Smith. The survivors, including women and children, fled into the surrounding woods to escape further violence. This tragic event became a defining moment in the history of the Church, symbolizing the severe persecution faced by its members during that period.
ff22.scripture: The scriptures teach the importance of enduring persecution with faith and patience. In the New Testament, Jesus counsels, "Blessed are they which are persecuted for righteousness' sake: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven" (Matthew 5:10). Similarly, in the Doctrine and Covenants, the Lord instructs, "Therefore, they must needs be chastened and tried, even as Abraham, who was commanded to offer up his only son" (Doctrine and Covenants 101:4). These passages remind believers that trials can strengthen faith and that enduring them faithfully brings eternal rewards.
ff22.background: In the early 19th century, the United States was expanding westward, and Missouri was a frontier state with a diverse population. Members of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, often referred to as Mormons, began settling in Missouri in the 1830s, believing it to be a place of gathering and refuge. However, their growing numbers and distinct religious practices led to suspicion and resentment among other settlers. Economic competition, cultural differences, and political tensions further strained relations. By 1838, these factors culminated in open hostility, with violent confrontations occurring between the Saints and local militias. The issuance of Governor Boggs' extermination order was a response to these escalating conflicts, reflecting the deep-seated animosity toward the Mormon community at that time.

ff23.talk: Why is it important to be kind to others, even when we're scared?
ff23.child: A long time ago, some people traveling through Utah were hurt by others who were scared and made a bad choice. We can learn to always be kind and make good choices, even when we're afraid.
ff23.learn: This event teaches us the dangers of allowing fear and prejudice to dictate actions. It highlights the necessity of adhering to moral principles, even in times of uncertainty. For families, it serves as a lesson in the importance of teaching empathy, understanding, and the courage to stand against wrongdoing.
ff23.matters: The Mountain Meadows Massacre stands as a somber reminder of the consequences of fear, misinformation, and unchecked authority. For families of faith, it underscores the importance of compassion, understanding, and the dangers of allowing fear to override moral principles. Acknowledging and learning from such events can help prevent future tragedies and promote a culture of empathy and accountability.

sources.name: The Mountain Meadows Massacre | American Experience | PBS
The real history of Utah’s Mountain Meadows Massacre | National Geographic
Mountain Meadows Massacre - World History Encyclopedia
How Juanita Brooks' history of the Mountain Meadows Massacre changed Mormon views of the past | Axios

ff23.evidence: Historical investigations have confirmed the involvement of local Mormon militia members in the massacre. Early reports attempted to place the blame solely on Native American tribes, but subsequent research, including the work of historian Juanita Brooks in 1950, provided compelling evidence of the militia's primary responsibility. In 2007, Elder Henry B. Eyring, representing The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, expressed profound regret for the massacre and acknowledged the church members' role in the tragedy.
ff23.happened: In September 1857, a wagon train known as the Baker-Fancher party, consisting of families from Arkansas, was traveling through Utah Territory on their way to California. As they reached Mountain Meadows, a lush valley in southern Utah, they were attacked by a group of local Mormon militia members, some of whom had disguised themselves as Native Americans. The emigrants defended themselves for several days but were ultimately deceived into surrendering under a false promise of safe passage. Once they laid down their arms, the militia, along with some Paiute participants, massacred approximately 120 men, women, and children. Seventeen children, all under the age of seven, were spared and taken into Mormon homes. This tragic event became known as the Mountain Meadows Massacre.
ff23.scripture: The scriptures teach the sanctity of life and the importance of loving one's neighbor. In the Book of Mormon, Alma 34:12 emphasizes the need for mercy and justice. The Doctrine and Covenants 98:16-17 counsels against retaliation and encourages seeking peace. These passages remind us of the divine command to treat all individuals with kindness and to seek peaceful resolutions to conflicts.
ff23.background: During the mid-19th century, tensions were high between the United States government and the Latter-day Saints in Utah Territory. The federal government had declared Utah in rebellion, and an army was marching west to assert control. This period, known as the Utah War, created an atmosphere of fear and suspicion among the Mormon settlers. The Baker-Fancher party arrived in Utah during this tumultuous time. They were primarily Methodists from Arkansas, seeking a new life in California. Their arrival coincided with the Mormons' preparations for potential conflict, leading to heightened distrust and hostility.

ff24.talk: Why do you think people kept believing in God even when it was dangerous or hard?
ff24.child: Long ago, people in Russia were not allowed to pray or go to church because the government said no one should believe in God. Some families still prayed quietly at home. When things changed, many people were happy to believe again out in the open.
ff24.learn: We can learn that faith often grows stronger when it is challenged. We also discover the importance of protecting the freedom of conscience for all people, no matter their beliefs. As members of families and communities, choosing kindness, tolerance, and courage when it comes to our beliefs can help us nurture our spiritual roots, even if the world around us changes.
ff24.matters: This long struggle matters because it shows that faith is deeply rooted in people's hearts, even when powerful leaders try to erase it. For families of faith, it offers a humbling lesson: beliefs may face opposition, but they can survive in quiet ways during difficult times. It also teaches us to value religious freedom, not only for ourselves but for everyone. History proved that faith, like a seed, can survive periods of darkness and come back to life when given sunlight again.

sources.name: The British Library: Religion under Communism
United States Holocaust Memorial Museum: Religion in the Soviet Union
Harvard Divinity School: Russian Orthodoxy under the Bolsheviks

ff24.evidence: Historical records from government archives, survivor accounts, and church documents all confirm the intense anti-religious campaigns carried out by the Soviet state. Photographs of destroyed churches and testimonies from those who worshipped in secret offer powerful evidence. Careful academic studies and state documents have counted tens of thousands of clergy executed or sent to the labor camps called gulags. By the end of World War II, almost all churches were closed. Yet, after 1991, the number of open and newly built churches—and the crowds attending them—show that belief endured. Recent histories continue to find more about underground networks where people kept their faith alive out of sight.
ff24.happened: Starting in 1917, when the Bolsheviks took power in Russia, the new Soviet government began a long and harsh campaign against religion. Churches and other places of worship were not just discouraged, but many were taken from their communities or destroyed. Priests and religious leaders from different faiths, like Orthodox Christianity, Catholicism, Judaism, Islam, and Buddhism, were arrested, sent to prisons and labor camps, or even killed. The Soviet state wanted everyone to believe in atheism, the idea that there is no God, and made this part of school lessons and daily life. Organizations like the League of the Militant Godless led public campaigns against belief in God. Families had to hide their faith, meeting in secret and passing down prayers quietly at home. Famous churches, like the great Christ the Saviour Cathedral in Moscow, were blown up to make a point that faith had no place in the Soviet future. Despite all these efforts, many people quietly kept their beliefs alive. When the Soviet Union ended in 1991, people were able to believe and worship openly again, with religion quickly returning to public life.
ff24.scripture: In 2 Nephi 2:27 and Joshua 24:15, scripture teaches the importance of agency—the God-given right to choose. The Doctrine and Covenants 134:4 says that governments should not prescribe laws interfering with conscience or religious practices. These verses remind us that everyone should have the freedom to worship, or not, as they choose. Even when agency was restricted by force, many held fast to their beliefs in quiet, determined ways.
ff24.background: Before the Soviet Union, Russia was a place where the Orthodox Christian Church was closely connected to daily life and the government, though Jews, Muslims, and others also lived across the vast land. Religion shaped holidays, family gatherings, and even school calendars. For many people, church was a place of comfort, learning, and music. After the chaos of World War I, revolution swept away the old rulers in 1917 and promised a new society built on equality, but also on strict control. The new leaders saw religion as an enemy of progress and unity and tried to erase it, forcing many families to make hard choices about what they taught and how openly they could worship.

ff25.t: The Saudi State and Enforced Religion
ff25.talk: Why do you think it's important for people to have the freedom to choose their own religion?
ff25.child: In Saudi Arabia, the government decided that everyone must follow the same religion, and people aren't allowed to practice other religions in public. This means that if someone wants to follow a different faith, they have to do it in secret.
ff25.learn: This history teaches us that while economic prosperity can bring modernization and development, it does not necessarily lead to greater personal freedoms. True progress includes respecting individual rights, including the freedom to practice one's religion. It also highlights the importance of separating religious authority from governmental power to ensure that faith is a personal choice rather than a state-imposed obligation.
ff25.matters: The establishment of Saudi Arabia as a state with enforced religious practices highlights the complex relationship between faith, governance, and individual freedoms. For the global community, it underscores the challenges of balancing religious authority with human rights. For families of faith, it serves as a reminder of the importance of religious freedom and the potential consequences when such freedoms are restricted. It also prompts reflection on how faith can be practiced in ways that respect both tradition and individual rights.

sources.name: 5 facts about religion in Saudi Arabia | Pew Research Center
Freedom of religion in Saudi Arabia - Wikipedia
2016 Report on International Religious Freedom: Saudi Arabia - U.S. Department of State

ff25.evidence: Historical records confirm the establishment of Saudi Arabia in 1932 through the alliance between the House of Saud and the Wahhabi movement. The country's legal framework is based on Sharia law, with strict regulations on religious practices. Reports from organizations like the Pew Research Center consistently rank Saudi Arabia among the most restrictive countries regarding religious freedom. For instance, a 2018 Pew report noted that the Saudi government follows an ultraconservative Wahhabi interpretation of the Quran, enforcing strict religious codes and practices. Despite some reforms in recent years, such as limiting the powers of the religious police, the core restrictions on religious freedom remain largely unchanged.
ff25.happened: In 1932, the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia was established through an alliance between the House of Saud and the Wahhabi religious movement. This partnership led to the creation of a state where Sunni Islam, particularly the Wahhabi interpretation, became the official religion. The government implemented strict laws based on Sharia, prohibiting the public practice of any religion other than Islam. Non-Muslim worship was confined to private spaces, and conversion from Islam to another faith was considered apostasy, punishable by death. The religious police, known as the Committee for the Promotion of Virtue and the Prevention of Vice, enforced these religious norms, ensuring public adherence to Islamic practices. Over the decades, Saudi Arabia's vast oil wealth enabled the country to fund the spread of Wahhabi institutions and teachings worldwide. Despite some reforms initiated in 2017, such as curbing the powers of the religious police and allowing women to drive, the core restrictions on religious freedom remain. Public non-Muslim worship is still prohibited, and apostasy continues to be a capital offense under the law.
ff25.scripture: The scriptures emphasize the importance of agency and the freedom to choose one's beliefs. In the Book of Mormon, 2 Nephi 2:27 states, "Wherefore, men are free according to the flesh; and all things are given them which are expedient unto man." This passage highlights the principle that individuals should have the freedom to choose their faith and actions. Additionally, Doctrine and Covenants 134:4 declares, "We believe that religion is instituted of God; and that men are amenable to him, and to him only, for the exercise of it." This suggests that religious practice is a personal matter between the individual and God, free from coercion by earthly authorities.
ff25.background: Before the establishment of Saudi Arabia, the Arabian Peninsula was a region of tribal societies with diverse religious practices, including Islam, Christianity, and indigenous beliefs. The early 18th century saw the rise of the Wahhabi movement, founded by Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab, who advocated for a return to what he considered the purest form of Islam. This movement aligned with the House of Saud, leading to the formation of a theocratic state. Daily life in the newly formed kingdom was deeply intertwined with Islamic principles, with strict adherence to religious practices enforced by the state. The discovery of vast oil reserves in the mid-20th century transformed the nation's economy, bringing rapid modernization in infrastructure and services. However, this economic development did not translate into greater religious freedom, as the government maintained strict control over religious expression and continued to enforce conservative Islamic practices.

ff26.talk: How can we help someone who is left out or treated unfairly?
ff26.child: Long ago, many people were hurt and killed just for being different. Some people bravely tried to help, even when it was dangerous. We remember so we can choose kindness and stand up for others.
ff26.learn: We learn from the Holocaust that kindness, truth, and courage matter—even when many others are silent or afraid. We are reminded that every person has a conscience, a sense of right and wrong, and that it is important to use our agency to help and protect others, not just ourselves. Remembering this history helps us recognize the warning signs if freedoms or lives are at risk again, and encourages us to speak up for those who cannot.
ff26.matters: The Holocaust matters deeply because it is a warning. It took place in a land known for its knowledge and achievement, showing us that education or technology alone do not stop evil if people ignore right and wrong. For families of faith, it draws attention to the importance of protecting agency—the God-given right to choose and act. We should remember those who suffered and those who helped, teaching our children that each person is precious, and that standing up for what is right, even when it is hard, is one way we serve God and our neighbors.

sources.name: United States Holocaust Memorial Museum: Introduction to the Holocaust
Yad Vashem: The World Holocaust Remembrance Center
BBC History: The Holocaust
The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints: Religious Freedom and Agency

ff26.evidence: Libraries, museums, and survivors hold millions of documents, photographs, and artifacts from the Holocaust. There are records from the Nazi government itself, with lists of people taken and orders given. After the war, survivors shared eyewitness accounts of the ghettos, camps, and rescue efforts. The sites of former camps, like Auschwitz, have been studied and preserved so that people can learn the truth about what happened. Historians have used this evidence to show not only the great numbers who were lost, but also the ways people tried to rescue others. The evidence is overwhelming and available to anyone who wishes to learn and remember.
ff26.happened: Between 1933 and 1945, a government in Germany called the Nazis came to power and used the tools of law and technology to persecute, harm, and finally try to erase entire groups of people. The largest group targeted were Jewish people. First, their rights and jobs were taken away, and they were blamed for problems they did not cause. Gradually, things became much worse: businesses and homes were attacked, families forced out of their neighborhoods, and special camps were built. In these camps, millions were murdered, not because of anything they did, but for who they were. The Nazis also killed Roma people, people with disabilities, Jehovah’s Witnesses, and others they labeled “unwanted.” Churches faced harsh pressure to support these wrongs or stay silent; a few, like Dietrich Bonhoeffer, bravely spoke out, even when it cost their lives. The death and cruelty shocked the world, and we now call these years the Holocaust.
ff26.scripture: The Book of Mormon teaches that all are alike unto God (2 Nephi 26:33), and that men are free to choose liberty and eternal life or captivity and death (2 Nephi 2:27). The Bible says to "love thy neighbor as thyself" (Leviticus 19:18; Matthew 22:39). Doctrine and Covenants 101:77-80 speaks of the importance of religious liberty. While these scriptures do not mention the Holocaust directly, they declare the worth of every soul and the principle that using force to crush faith or freedom is wrong before God.
ff26.background: Before the Nazis, Germany was a place with many great thinkers, artists, and inventors, but after losing World War I, times were hard. Money lost its value, and many people were afraid of the future. Some felt angry and looked for someone to blame. Adolf Hitler and the Nazi Party promised to fix things by uniting the nation, but they also used old lies and fears about the Jewish people and other minorities. At first, life for most families went on—school, work, church—but step by step, more rules and forced changes came. Most people were not directly involved, but many were silent as their neighbors were taken away. Others risked everything to help those in danger, showing that even in darkness, some people followed their conscience.

ff27.talk: Why do you think it is important for everyone to be able to choose what they believe?
ff27.child: A long time ago, leaders from many places wrote a promise that everyone should be able to choose what they believe about God. This helps all families be safe to pray, learn, and follow God together. That’s why it’s important today.
ff27.learn: We can learn how precious it is to have the freedom to think, worship, and believe as our hearts guide us. Article 18 helps remind us to protect the rights of others—even those who believe very differently than we do. Just as we wish to pray, change our hearts, or teach our children in our way, others must also be free to seek truth. As families study this moment, we can talk about helping everyone feel respected as God’s children, no matter what they believe.
ff27.matters: Article 18 matters because it marks a turning point in how the world sees religion and personal belief. For a family of faith, it means the right to teach children and worship together without fear. It stands as a reminder that true faith cannot be forced; it grows best where people are free to choose. For many Latter-day Saints, who have a long history of facing persecution for their beliefs, Article 18 feels like an answer to prayers for justice. Its promise helps protect families and communities who want to follow what they believe God teaches them, and it shows respect for the journey of every person seeking truth.

sources.name: United Nations: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights
Pew Research Center: Global Restrictions on Religion
History.com: Universal Declaration of Human Rights adopted

ff27.evidence: Historical records from the United Nations show how Article 18 was debated, written, and finally agreed upon. The final wording came after much discussion because different countries had different ideas about what freedom should look like. Some wanted to stop people from sharing new beliefs; others wanted total freedom. The records are clear: most nations in the UN agreed this article was needed to prevent the terrible things that had happened before. Since then, many groups, like Pew Research Center and the U.S. Commission on International Religious Freedom, use Article 18 as their measuring stick. Open records and court cases continue to show progress and setbacks in different countries, showing the struggle for real freedom is ongoing.
ff27.happened: On December 10, 1948, a group of people from many countries gathered in Paris, France, to agree on a set of rights that every person in the world should have, just because they are human. They called this important paper the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. One of its most powerful parts is Article 18. This short paragraph says that everyone—no matter where they live, which family they are born into, or what their leaders believe—has the right to think for themselves, believe what their heart tells them is true, and change their mind about their beliefs. They also have the right to share and practice their religion in public or private, alone or with others. This was the first time so many countries promised, together, that people should be free in what they believe. Article 18 set a clear standard for the world, because many places did not allow people to freely worship or choose their faith. Some changed their laws because they wanted to be part of this new promise, while others still struggle to let people choose their own beliefs. Over time, this article has become the test for whether a country is truly protecting the freedom of its people in matters of faith and conscience.
ff27.scripture: Scripture teaches that each person has the gift of agency—the power to choose for themselves. The Bible says, 'Choose you this day whom ye will serve' (Joshua 24:15), and Doctrine and Covenants 58:27 says, 'men should be anxiously engaged in a good cause, and do many things of their own free will.' The Book of Mormon also shows the importance of agency when Alma invites people to believe or not, without forcing them (Alma 30). None of these say exactly what Article 18 does, but all teach that freedom to choose and seek God comes from our Heavenly Father, and should be protected.
ff27.background: The world in 1948 was just waking up from the deep sorrow and pain of World War II. Millions had died, and many nations had seen terrible things happen to people just because of their race, religion, or beliefs. Families in Europe and beyond wanted to make sure such cruelty would never be allowed again. The United Nations, a group formed to help countries work together for peace, gathered leaders and thinkers from many places to find ways to protect people, especially those who were weak or easy to hurt. At that time, not everyone could say what they believed, and in some countries, believing the 'wrong' thing could lead to prison or worse. Ordinary daily life depended a lot on where you lived: in some homes, parents taught faith and children prayed freely, but in others, this was dangerous or forbidden.

ff28.talk: Why do you think it is important that no one is forced to believe a certain way about God?
ff28.child: The Catholic Church once said everyone should be free to choose their own religion and no one should be forced. This idea helps people be kinder to each other, even if they believe different things. God wants us to choose Him because we love Him, not because we have to.
ff28.learn: From this event, we learn that admitting past mistakes and choosing a better path is possible for anyone—even for institutions many centuries old. We see that God’s gifts, like the use of agency and the spreading of new ideas through technology, can be used to help all His children if guided by love and respect. As we make choices in our families and communities, we can remember the dignity of every person and seek to honor it, even if their beliefs are different from ours.
ff28.matters: This event matters deeply because it shows that even large and old institutions, such as the Catholic Church, can learn, change, and choose to repent. For families of faith, it gives hope that traditions can be improved and wrongs can be righted as understanding grows. Dignitatis Humanae helped shape later international agreements on human rights and encouraged more open and peaceful relations between people of different beliefs. It reminds us all that respect for conscience goes hand-in-hand with love for our neighbors, and that religious freedom is both a gift and a responsibility.

sources.name: Vatican Official Text: Dignitatis Humanae
Britannica: Dignitatis Humanae
U.S. Institute of Peace: Dignitatis Humanae and Religious Freedom

ff28.evidence: Dignitatis Humanae is a thoroughly documented event. The official text was published and is widely accessible. Historians have studied the council’s records, diaries, and speeches given by participants. The change in the Catholic Church’s teaching is plain to see when comparing earlier church laws and documents with Dignitatis Humanae itself. Pope John Paul II’s later public apologies are also a matter of public record, preserved in Vatican speeches and world news archives. Today, many scholars agree that the declaration marked a turning point not just for the Church, but for religious freedom movements worldwide.
ff28.happened: On December 7, 1965, leaders of the Roman Catholic Church gathered in Vatican City at the end of the Second Vatican Council and made a momentous declaration called 'Dignitatis Humanae.' This document stated clearly that every person has a right to religious freedom, meaning no one should be forced to act against their beliefs in matters of religion. For almost two thousand years, there were times when religious authorities, including the Catholic Church, supported or tolerated the use of force to keep people in line with religious teachings. But now, in this modern council, the Church declared that every person's freedom of conscience and belief must be respected. The declaration rooted this right in the dignity of each human being, which it said could be known both through faith and by using our own reason. This marked a major change for the Church and set an example for many people around the world. After this, the Church began to openly acknowledge mistakes in its own past, with future Popes like John Paul II making public apologies for wrongs done in the name of faith. From that point forward, the Catholic Church officially rejected religious coercion and affirmed that God wants people to seek Him freely, not under pressure.
ff28.scripture: In the Bible, Joshua 24:15 invites people to "choose you this day whom ye will serve," acknowledging personal agency. In the Doctrine and Covenants, section 134:4 teaches that "religion is instituted of God; and that men are answerable to him, and not to man, for the exercise of it." The Book of Mormon tells of Alma inviting people to faith without compulsion (Alma 5). These passages all support the principle that God values agency and invites, not forces, His children to follow Him, highlighting the scriptural foundation of religious freedom.
ff28.background: By the 1960s, the world was changing quickly. After two world wars and many struggles for civil rights, more people were asking hard questions about freedom, dignity, and the role of religion in society. Earlier, the Roman Catholic Church had, at times, played a role in laws or actions that limited religious freedom, such as the Inquisition. But the Second Vatican Council brought together bishops and leaders from all over the world to talk about how the Church should interact with the modern world. Many people wanted the Church to speak more clearly about human rights and freedom. For most families at the time, life was marked by both tradition and change. Radios and televisions were bringing new ideas into ordinary homes, and many countries were passing new laws to protect people's rights, including the right to worship as they chose.

ff29.t: The World's First Officially Atheist State
ff29.talk: Why do you think people kept believing in God, even when it was dangerous?
ff29.child: Long ago, a country told everyone they could not pray or go to church. Many people still believed in their hearts. When the rules changed, crowds came together to pray again.
ff29.learn: We learn that trying to erase faith through force does not truly remove it from people's hearts; it may even make it stronger once freedom returns. This story teaches that every family deserves the right to choose their beliefs, and that religious freedom is a blessing worth protecting. It also reminds us of the resilience and hope that faith can bring, even in times of great difficulty.
ff29.matters: This event highlights how important freedom of belief is, not only for society but for families and individuals. It shows that when the choice to believe is taken away, people do not simply stop believing; faith often remains quietly alive. For Latter-day Saint families, this story is a reminder that faith can endure in even the hardest times and that the right to worship freely is precious. The return of faith when freedom came back teaches that belief is deeply rooted in the human heart.

sources.name: Encyclopedia Britannica: Albania under Hoxha
Smithsonian Magazine: How Albania Became the World's First Atheist State
Human Rights Watch: Albania - Human Rights Developments

ff29.evidence: Records from the Albanian Institute of Political Studies and detailed historical research confirm the scope of Albania’s anti-religious campaign. Over 2,000 religious buildings were closed or repurposed, and reports from survivors, such as Father Simon Jubani, reveal the harsh punishments for clergy and believers. International observers from groups like Human Rights Watch documented the extreme isolation and poverty that followed state atheism. After religious freedoms were restored, the rapid return of open worship and large gatherings gave further evidence that faith had endured in private despite official suppression.
ff29.happened: In February 1967, Enver Hoxha, the leader of Albania, gave a powerful speech calling for the end of religious practice in his country. Soon after, Albania closed thousands of churches, mosques, and other religious buildings—many were destroyed or turned into places like sports halls or warehouses. The government declared the country officially atheist, meaning it did not allow anyone to openly believe in or practice any religion. Having written this into the constitution, Albania became the first nation in history to state, in law, that no religion would be permitted, and the government even ran campaigns teaching people not to believe in God. Religious leaders were sent to prison or even killed. Families had to hide their faith, and religious holidays and traditions disappeared from public life. This lasted for more than twenty years. When the government finally relaxed its grip in 1990, the first public religious service took place in a cemetery. Massive crowds soon gathered to worship in the open, showing how deeply faith had remained in the hearts of many, despite years of strict control.
ff29.scripture: The principle of agency—the gift to choose for ourselves—is taught throughout scripture. In the Book of Mormon, 2 Nephi 2:27 says, “Wherefore, men are free according to the flesh... to choose liberty and eternal life, through the great Mediator.” The Bible also teaches respect for others’ choices in Joshua 24:15: “Choose you this day whom ye will serve.” Doctrine and Covenants 134:4 upholds religious freedom by stating that "religion is instituted of God; and that men are amenable to him, and to him only, for the exercise of it."
ff29.background: After World War II, many Eastern European countries came under communist governments that restricted religion, believing it competed with loyalty to the state. Albania, a small country on the Balkan Peninsula, was among the poorest nations in Europe. Most Albanians identified as Muslim, Orthodox Christian, or Catholic, and religious life had been a part of their families for centuries. But under Enver Hoxha's strict rule, daily life grew harsh. The leaders thought that if they removed religion, people would become more loyal to the state and more united, but most ordinary Albanians quietly held onto their heritage and beliefs, even as jobs, food, and freedom became very scarce. Children grew up hearing little or nothing of faith, while parents worried about what would happen if their beliefs were discovered.

ff30.talk: Why do you think God wants us to choose for ourselves, instead of forcing us to believe?
ff30.child: A long time ago, leaders in Iran made a rule that everyone had to follow certain religious rules, even if they believed differently. Now, many young people in Iran don't want to follow that faith at all. It's important to let people choose for themselves.
ff30.learn: We can learn that faith cannot be forced. When religion is imposed by law, people may outwardly comply but inwardly drift away from true belief. Families might remember that the ability to choose for oneself is not only a right but a commandment, and that sincere faith flourishes when given space to grow. Teaching and trusting is always better than forcing.
ff30.matters: This event is important because it shows what can happen when faith and freedom are held in conflict. In Iran, the state chose to enforce faith by law—making everyone follow the same religious rules, even if their hearts or beliefs differed. For families of faith, this teaches how important it is to let belief be a matter of the heart. Freedom to choose faith, or not, is a principle many scriptures support. When freedom is taken away, faith often weakens instead of growing stronger. Around the world, Iran has become a symbol of what happens when government and religion are not kept in careful balance.

sources.name: Pew Research Center – Iran: Religious Restrictions
Encyclopedia Britannica – Iranian Revolution
Human Rights Watch – Iran: Baha’is Denied Higher Education

ff30.evidence: There is strong evidence from historians, government records, and human rights groups that after the Iranian Revolution, the state made Islamic law compulsory. Bahai people and other minorities have faced discrimination, with bans from government jobs and universities reported by organizations like Human Rights Watch. Surveys and reports by the Pew Research Center continue to rank Iran as one of the world’s most restrictive places for religious practice. More recently, Iranian and international surveys suggest that many young Iranians now identify as secular, a shift linked to exposure to compulsory religion, strict enforcement, and social controls.
ff30.happened: In 1979, Iran experienced dramatic change through what is called the Iranian Revolution. Before this, Iran was a monarchy ruled by the Shah, a king who tried to make the country more modern and closer to Western styles of life. Many Iranians, though, felt unhappy because they thought he ignored Islam, arrested those who spoke against him, and let outside influences take over their land. So, large numbers of people protested in the streets. This led to the Shah fleeing Iran, and the country soon came under the leadership of Ayatollah Khomeini, a powerful Shia Muslim religious leader. He and other clerics set up a new government where religious law would guide everything—from the courts to the way people dressed and behaved. All Iranians were required to follow Islamic rules, regardless of their own beliefs.
ff30.scripture: The scriptures teach about the value of agency and the dangers of compulsion. In the Bible, Joshua tells Israel, 'Choose you this day whom ye will serve' (Joshua 24:15), showing faith must be chosen. In 2 Nephi 2:27 in the Book of Mormon, we read, 'Wherefore, men are free... to choose liberty and eternal life, or to choose captivity and death.' Doctrine and Covenants 121:41-46 warns against unrighteous dominion, including the use of force in matters of belief. These verses do not mention Iran, but they teach that God honors the freedom to choose faith.
ff30.background: In the decades before 1979, Iran was known for being a place of old traditions changing quickly. Oil had brought money and foreign interest, especially from America and Britain. The Shah wanted Iran to be seen as strong and modern, so he let women study and work, invited foreign businesses, and angered many religious leaders by not giving their beliefs much say in laws. Most Iranians were Muslim, mainly following the Shia branch of Islam, but there were also Christians, Jews, Bahais, and others. Daily life for many people, especially in cities, started changing—fashions and music from the West became popular, but a growing part of the population felt this was disrespectful to their faith and identity.

ff31.t: The Taliban and the Bamiyan Buddhas
ff31.talk: Why do you think it is important for all children to be able to go to school?
ff31.child: The Taliban would not let girls go to school or people choose their own faith. They broke old statues that were special to many people. When people are not allowed to learn or choose, it hurts everyone.
ff31.learn: We can learn how important it is to allow every child to learn and to protect the choices others make about how they worship, dress, and live their lives. When freedom is lost, families and whole countries suffer. We also see how choices made by leaders can shape many lives for years to come. This is a reminder to value agency, education, and kindness toward all of God’s children.
ff31.matters: This story matters because it shows what can happen when power is used to take away the freedom to learn, worship, or live peacefully. For families of faith, we believe that agency—the ability to choose—is a sacred gift from God. When any society takes away education, especially from girls, it decides its own future. History shows that no country has prospered when it kept half its children from learning. Teaching, learning, and respecting others' beliefs are part of building Zion—a community where all can grow and share their talents. This story reminds us to value education for everyone and to protect religious freedom.

sources.name: UNESCO: The Destruction of the Bamiyan Buddhas
BBC: Afghanistan Profile - Timeline
Human Rights Watch: Afghanistan - Education

ff31.evidence: There is strong evidence for each part of this story. News reports, government documents, and images show the destruction of the Bamiyan Buddhas in March 2001. Academic studies and United Nations reports describe how education for girls was stopped and how the Hazara, a minority group, were persecuted, especially in the late 1990s and again after 2021. Surveys and world rankings after these bans consistently place Afghanistan near the lowest in literacy, life expectancy, and opportunity, confirming the deep effects of these decisions. Archaeologists continue to study what remains of the Bamiyan Buddhas and the valley. This is a well-documented period in modern history.
ff31.happened: Between 1996 and 2001, a group called the Taliban controlled most of Afghanistan. They followed a very strict form of Islamic law, which they enforced through severe rules. Girls were not allowed to go to school, and women were told what to wear and how to live. One of the most heartbreaking acts during this time happened in March 2001, when the Taliban destroyed two giant statues of Buddha that had stood in the Bamiyan Valley for over 1,400 years. These enormous statues were important not just to Buddhists, but to people all around the world because of their history and skill. Even when people from many countries, including other Muslim leaders, asked the Taliban to spare the statues, the Taliban went ahead and destroyed them with explosives. The Taliban also badly mistreated another group, the Shia Hazara, many of whom lived near the Buddhas and faced violence simply because they were a minority. In 2021, the Taliban regained power in Afghanistan, and once again banned secondary and higher education for girls. This kind of rule has left the country struggling with low literacy, poverty, and little hope for the future.
ff31.scripture: The scriptures teach the value of knowledge and the importance of agency. In Doctrine and Covenants 88:118 we read, “Seek ye out of the best books words of wisdom; seek learning, even by study and also by faith.” In the Book of Mormon, 2 Nephi 2:27 explains, “Wherefore, men are free according to the flesh... to choose liberty and eternal life... or to choose captivity and death.” These passages show God asks His children to learn and to choose. When others try to take away that chance, it is not following Heavenly Father's plan.
ff31.background: Afghanistan is a country with a long history, home to many groups of people and cultures. For centuries, it was a place where traders and travelers passed through along the Silk Road, and where Buddhism, Islam, and other faiths mixed. Most people in Afghanistan are Muslim, but there are different groups like the Sunni majority and the Shia Hazara minority. Before the Taliban, life in Afghanistan included more freedom for women and minorities in some areas, especially in the cities. But by the 1990s, years of war and hardship had made daily living dangerous and unstable. When the Taliban arrived, they promised order and peace, but soon ruled with fear and force, shaping every part of daily life to fit their strict rules, often at the expense of personal freedom and learning.

ff32.talk: Why is it important to respect and protect people who have different beliefs than ours?
ff32.child: A group called ISIS hurt many Yazidi people because of their beliefs. Many had to leave their homes to stay safe. It's important to be kind to everyone, no matter what they believe.
ff32.learn: The Yazidi genocide teaches us the critical importance of religious tolerance and the dangers of extremist ideologies. It reminds us to be vigilant in protecting the rights of all individuals to practice their faith freely. Supporting and standing in solidarity with persecuted communities is essential in fostering a world where diversity is embraced, and such atrocities are prevented in the future.
ff32.matters: The Yazidi genocide is a stark reminder of the devastating consequences of religious intolerance and extremism. For families of faith, it underscores the importance of protecting religious freedom and standing against persecution. The resilience of the Yazidi people in the face of such atrocities serves as an example of enduring faith and the human spirit's capacity to overcome immense suffering. Recognizing and remembering these events is crucial to prevent future genocides and to promote a world where diverse beliefs are respected and cherished.

sources.name: Yazidi genocide - Wikipedia
Yazda - Yazidi Global Organisation
Mortality and kidnapping estimates for the Yazidi population in the area of Mount Sinjar, Iraq, in August 2014: A retros
The Yazidi Genocide | Counter Extremism Project

ff32.evidence: Extensive documentation and survivor testimonies provide clear evidence of the Yazidi genocide. A study published in PLOS Medicine estimated that approximately 9,900 Yazidis were either killed or kidnapped during the initial ISIS assault in August 2014. The United Nations and various human rights organizations have conducted investigations, confirming the systematic nature of the atrocities committed against the Yazidis. Mass graves have been discovered in the Sinjar region, further substantiating reports of mass executions. The international recognition of these events as genocide reflects the overwhelming consensus on the severity and intent of ISIS's actions against the Yazidi people.
ff32.happened: In August 2014, the Islamic State (ISIS) launched a brutal assault on the Yazidi community in the Sinjar region of northern Iraq. Yazidis, a religious minority with ancient roots, were targeted in a campaign of mass executions, abductions, and forced conversions. Men and older women were often executed, while thousands of women and children were kidnapped. Many of these women and girls were subjected to sexual slavery, forced marriages, and other forms of abuse. Boys were taken from their families and coerced into military training. The United Nations estimated that approximately 5,000 Yazidis were killed during this period, and about 6,800 were kidnapped. This systematic persecution led to the displacement of over 400,000 Yazidis from their ancestral homeland. The international community, including the United Nations, the U.S. Congress, and the European Parliament, formally recognized these atrocities as genocide.
ff32.scripture: Scriptures teach the importance of compassion and standing against oppression. In the Book of Mormon, Alma 1:30 emphasizes caring for those in need: "And thus, in their prosperous circumstances, they did not send away any who were naked, or that were hungry, or that were athirst, or that were sick, or that had not been nourished." Similarly, Doctrine and Covenants 134:2 states: "We believe that no government can exist in peace, except such laws are framed and held inviolate as will secure to each individual the free exercise of conscience." These passages highlight the duty to support and protect those who are persecuted for their beliefs.
ff32.background: Before the ISIS assault, the Yazidis lived primarily in the Sinjar region of Iraq, practicing a monotheistic faith with elements from ancient Mesopotamian religions, Zoroastrianism, and Islam. Their unique beliefs and practices often led to misunderstandings and persecution. Daily life for the Yazidis involved farming, herding, and maintaining their cultural and religious traditions. The rise of ISIS in 2014, with its extremist ideology, posed a severe threat to all minority groups in the region, including the Yazidis. The group's rapid territorial expansion and violent tactics created an environment of fear and instability, disrupting the lives of countless individuals and communities.

ff33.talk: How can we show kindness to someone who is different from us?
ff33.child: Sometimes, people are treated unfairly because they are different. It's important to be kind and stand up for others, no matter who they are.
ff33.learn: This tragic event teaches us the dangers of intertwining religious identity with state power, leading to the persecution of minority groups. It reminds us of our responsibility to stand against injustice and to advocate for the rights and dignity of all individuals. As families of faith, we are called to embody principles of love, compassion, and justice, ensuring that our beliefs are never used to harm others.
ff33.matters: The plight of the Rohingya underscores the devastating consequences when religious and ethnic identities are manipulated to justify violence and exclusion. For families of faith, this tragedy serves as a reminder of the importance of compassion, justice, and the protection of the vulnerable. It challenges us to reflect on how faith can be misused to oppress others and calls for a commitment to uphold the dignity and rights of all individuals, regardless of their background.

sources.name: Human Rights Watch: Burma: Rohingya Recount Killings, Rape, and Arson
Human Rights Watch: 9 Years On: Accountability Needed for Myanmar Military Junta’s Atrocities Against the Rohingya

ff33.evidence: Extensive documentation by human rights organizations and the United Nations provides credible evidence of the atrocities committed against the Rohingya. Satellite imagery analyzed by Human Rights Watch revealed the widespread destruction of Rohingya villages. Eyewitness accounts detail systematic killings, sexual violence, and forced displacement. The UN Fact-Finding Mission on Myanmar concluded that the military's actions amounted to crimes against humanity and genocide. These findings have led to international legal actions, including proceedings at the International Court of Justice.
ff33.happened: In 2016, Myanmar's security forces initiated operations in Rakhine State, targeting the Rohingya Muslim minority. These actions included killings, sexual violence, and the burning of villages, leading to the displacement of tens of thousands. By December 2016, approximately 27,000 Rohingya had fled to Bangladesh, recounting harrowing experiences of violence and destruction. The United Nations and human rights organizations condemned these acts, with the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights highlighting the severity of the situation and the government's inadequate response. The crisis intensified in 2017, resulting in over 700,000 Rohingya seeking refuge in Bangladesh. The UN Fact-Finding Mission on Myanmar concluded that the military's actions carried genocidal intent, leading to international legal proceedings against Myanmar.
ff33.scripture: The scriptures teach us to love and care for all of God's children. In the Book of Mormon, we read: "When ye are in the service of your fellow beings ye are only in the service of your God" (Mosiah 2:17). This principle emphasizes the importance of serving and protecting others, especially those who are marginalized or persecuted. The Savior Himself taught, "Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you" (Matthew 5:44). These teachings remind us to extend love and compassion to all, regardless of differences.
ff33.background: The Rohingya are a Muslim ethnic group residing primarily in Myanmar's Rakhine State. Despite their long-standing presence, they have faced systemic discrimination, including denial of citizenship under Myanmar's 1982 Citizenship Law. This statelessness has led to severe restrictions on movement, access to healthcare, education, and employment. Tensions between the Rohingya and the Buddhist majority have been longstanding, with periodic outbreaks of violence. In 2012, communal clashes resulted in significant displacement and loss of life. The situation remained volatile, with the Rohingya living under oppressive conditions, making them vulnerable to further persecution.

ff34.t: The Uyghur Camps and the Sinicization of Religion
ff34.talk: Why is it important for everyone to have the freedom to practice their own religion?
ff34.child: In China, some people are not allowed to pray or go to their churches and mosques. The government is trying to make everyone follow the same rules and not let them practice their own beliefs. This is unfair because everyone should be able to believe and worship as they choose.
ff34.learn: This event teaches us the critical importance of safeguarding religious freedom and cultural identity. It reminds us that coercion and suppression are tools of power, not faith. As families, we can learn to cherish and protect our own freedoms while advocating for those who are denied such rights. It also highlights the resilience of the human spirit in the face of oppression, inspiring us to support and stand in solidarity with persecuted communities worldwide.
ff34.matters: The situation in Xinjiang is a stark reminder of how state power can be used to suppress religious freedom and cultural identity. For families of faith, it underscores the importance of protecting the right to worship and live according to one's beliefs without fear of persecution. It also highlights the resilience of communities who, despite severe oppression, strive to maintain their faith and traditions. This serves as a call to support and advocate for religious freedoms worldwide, recognizing that such liberties are fundamental to human dignity.

sources.name: China’s Repression of Uyghurs in Xinjiang | Council on Foreign Relations
Explained: China’s ‘ethnic unity and progress promotion’ law – Radio Free Asia
Governing Faith: The Sinicization of Islam in the Uyghur Region - Uyghur Rights Monitor
China: Decade of Impunity for Crimes Against Uyghurs | Human Rights Watch

ff34.evidence: Extensive documentation from human rights organizations, such as Human Rights Watch, provides evidence of the Chinese government's actions in Xinjiang. Reports detail mass detentions, forced labor, and systematic efforts to eradicate Uyghur cultural and religious practices. Satellite imagery has confirmed the destruction of mosques and religious sites. Testimonies from survivors and leaked government documents further corroborate these findings. The United Nations has acknowledged that these actions may constitute crimes against humanity, underscoring the severity of the situation.
ff34.happened: Since 2017, the Chinese government has detained over a million Uyghur Muslims and other ethnic minorities in Xinjiang, labeling these facilities as "reeducation camps." Detainees have faced forced labor, political indoctrination, and severe restrictions on religious practices. Beyond the camps, authorities have demolished mosques, banned religious attire, and criminalized everyday religious activities. The state has also implemented extensive surveillance, including facial recognition and smartphone tracking, to monitor and control the Uyghur population. In 2026, China enacted the "Law on Promoting Ethnic Unity and Progress," further codifying policies that suppress religious and cultural identities under the guise of national unity. This law extends the state's reach beyond its borders, threatening legal consequences for individuals abroad deemed to undermine ethnic unity.
ff34.scripture: The scriptures teach the importance of agency and the right to worship freely. In the Book of Mormon, Alma 30:7 states, "There was no law against a man's belief; for it was strictly contrary to the commands of God that there should be a law which should bring men on to unequal grounds." This passage emphasizes that coercion in matters of faith is contrary to divine principles. Similarly, Doctrine and Covenants 134:4 declares, "We believe that religion is instituted of God; and that men are amenable to him, and to him only, for the exercise of it." These teachings affirm the sacred right of individuals to worship according to their conscience.
ff34.background: The Uyghurs are a predominantly Muslim, Turkic-speaking ethnic group residing mainly in China's Xinjiang region. Historically, they have maintained a distinct cultural and religious identity. However, the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) has long viewed this distinctiveness as a challenge to national unity. Policies aimed at integrating Uyghurs into the broader Chinese society have intensified over the past decade, culminating in the current repressive measures. Daily life for Uyghurs has been profoundly affected, with traditional practices and religious observances being heavily monitored or outright banned. The state's emphasis on "Sinicization" seeks to align religious and cultural expressions with CCP ideology, effectively erasing unique ethnic identities.

ff35.talk: Why do you think it is important for everyone to be able to choose their own beliefs?
ff35.child: Some countries make it hard for people to pray or go to church the way they choose. In other places, people are free to believe and worship as they want. We can be thankful for our freedom and pray for others who need it.
ff35.learn: We can learn that freedom, including religious freedom, is precious and not something to take for granted. It is built on respect for others and a willingness to stand up for what is right—both by our personal example and in our communities. When we study these findings, we see the privilege it is to worship freely and the responsibility we have to support those who still face barriers. Our prayers, service, and kindness can help make the world a place where everyone can follow their faith in peace.
ff35.matters: This event matters because the freedom to believe, worship, and live according to one's conscience is a core human right and a principle taught in many faith traditions. For families who value both faith and freedom, these findings remind us that the two often go hand in hand. When religious freedom is protected, other rights and freedoms tend to be as well. When governments or societies limit religious practice, it can be a sign that other freedoms are also at risk. Understanding where the world stands on these issues helps families appreciate the blessings of liberty and encourages them to support and pray for those facing challenges elsewhere.

sources.name: Pew Research Center | Global Restrictions on Religion Rise Modestly in 2023
U.S. Department of State | 2023 Report on International Religious Freedom
Library of Congress | Freedom of Religion
Church of Jesus Christ | Religious Freedom and Fairness for All

ff35.evidence: Pew Research Center’s reports are widely respected for their careful methods, using public records, news sources, expert reports, and international groups to measure religious freedom around the world. Their Religion Restrictions project has been running for over a decade, making it one of the best ways to see long-term trends. The patterns they describe—high restrictions in authoritarian countries, low restrictions in established democracies—match findings from other research institutes and from reports by groups like Human Rights Watch and the United Nations. Pew’s indexes cover both laws (government restrictions) and everyday life (social hostilities), painting a fuller picture of how religion is experienced across cultures and borders.
ff35.happened: From 2023 to 2026, the Pew Research Center continued tracking how governments and societies across the world allow or restrict religious freedom. Their most recent findings showed that in 2023, out of 198 countries studied, 58 had high or very high restrictions on religion set by their governments. This number is nearly as high as the record set the year before. These government actions included laws or policies that made it difficult for people to practice their beliefs freely, such as strict rules, bans on certain groups, or support given to only one religion.
