Daily life was fraught with uncertainty, as political alliances shifted rapidly, and the threat of violence loomed large.

fp40.talk: What can we learn about being kind and fair from the story of Attila the Hun?
fp40.child: Attila the Hun was a powerful leader who led his people to conquer many lands. He fought against the Romans and was known for being very strong and fierce. After he died, his empire quickly fell apart.
fp40.learn: Attila's story teaches us about the impermanence of power and the consequences of unchecked aggression. It also highlights the resilience of societies that, despite facing formidable adversaries, can adapt and endure through faith and unity.
fp40.matters: Attila's campaigns significantly weakened the already fragile Western Roman Empire, contributing to its eventual fall in 476 AD. For families of faith, this period underscores the importance of resilience and faith during times of upheaval. The ensuing Dark Ages saw a decline in literacy and preservation of knowledge, highlighting the value of education and the transmission of faith and learning through generations.

sources.name: 8 Things You Might Not Know About Attila the Hun | HISTORY
Attila - Biography, Facts & Battles | HISTORY
Rome Halts the Huns | National Geographic
Who were the ruthless warriors behind Attila the Hun? | National Geographic

fp40.evidence: Historical records from Roman historians like Priscus provide detailed accounts of Attila's reign and interactions with the Roman Empire. Archaeological findings, such as Hunnic artifacts and burial sites, corroborate these accounts. However, some aspects, like the exact location of Attila's tomb, remain unknown, adding an element of mystery to his legacy.
fp40.happened: Attila the Hun, born around 406 AD, became the sole ruler of the Huns after the death of his brother Bleda in 445 AD. Under his leadership, the Huns expanded their territory across Central and Eastern Europe, launching devastating raids into both the Eastern and Western Roman Empires. In 451 AD, Attila invaded Gaul (modern-day France), but was halted at the Battle of the Catalaunian Plains by a coalition of Roman and Visigoth forces. The following year, he invaded Italy, sacking several cities, but withdrew before reaching Rome. Attila died suddenly in 453 AD on his wedding night, reportedly due to a severe nosebleed. His death led to the rapid decline of the Hunnic Empire.
fp40.scripture: While the scriptures do not directly mention Attila the Hun, they do speak to the principles of faith and endurance during times of trial. For instance, in the Book of Mormon, Alma 37:6 teaches that "by small and simple things are great things brought to pass." This reminds us that even in tumultuous times, small acts of faith and diligence can lead to significant outcomes.
fp40.background: In the 5th century AD, the Roman Empire was divided into Eastern and Western halves, both struggling with internal decay and external threats. The Huns, a nomadic people from Central Asia, had migrated into Europe, displacing other tribes and creating a ripple effect of migrations and conflicts. Daily life for many was marked by instability, as cities faced the constant threat of invasion, and rural areas were often left to fend for themselves. The Huns' arrival intensified these challenges, as their swift cavalry and brutal tactics overwhelmed many established defenses.

hl01.talk: Why do you think it’s important for doctors to promise to help people and never hurt them?
hl01.child: A long time ago, doctors promised to help sick people and never hurt anyone on purpose. This promise helps people trust their doctors. Even today, most doctors make a special promise like this before they start their work.
hl01.learn: We can learn from the Hippocratic Oath that choosing to do good—especially when it is not easy or popular—can change lives and even whole professions. It reminds us that the tools and knowledge Heavenly Father gives us are meant to be used to serve, bless, and protect others. In our own families, we can think about what promises we make to each other and to God, and how keeping those promises helps others feel safe and cared for.
hl01.matters: The Hippocratic Oath became the foundation for medical ethics—guidelines for how doctors should behave toward their patients. Its teachings remind us that medicine is about service, honesty, compassion, and responsibility. For families who believe in God, the Oath shows how caring for the sick is more than a job; it is a sacred trust. Even today, most doctors make a version of this promise when they begin their work. The Oath’s example helps us understand that true healing begins with a commitment to do good, just as we strive to follow Christ’s teachings in all we do.

sources.name: National Library of Medicine: The Hippocratic Oath Today
History.com: Hippocrates
Encyclopaedia Britannica: Hippocratic Oath

hl01.evidence: Historians have found copies of the Hippocratic Oath written in ancient Greek; the oldest fragments date back to the third century BC, while the ideas go back to Hippocrates’ lifetime. Many books written by Hippocrates and his students survive, collected under the name the 'Hippocratic Corpus.' Archaeologists have found evidence of healing temples from this period on Kos and elsewhere. Scholars agree Hippocrates was a real person, but the Oath we know today was likely refined by his followers. Its ideas, though, have guided doctors for over two thousand years and are considered a core part of medical history.
hl01.happened: Around the year 400 BC, on the Greek island of Kos, a group of physicians connected to Hippocrates began to change how people thought about sickness and healing. Before this time, many Greeks believed that diseases were punishments sent from the gods and could only be cured through prayers or special rituals. Hippocrates and those who worked with him started observing what happened to their patients very closely. They wrote down symptoms, tracked how different illnesses acted in different seasons, and paid attention to what helped people heal and what didn’t. Most importantly, these early doctors chose to make a special promise—an oath—to use their skills to help the sick, to never harm anyone on purpose, and to keep their patients’ secrets safe. This promise is known as the Hippocratic Oath. It helped set apart the work of medicine as a special calling to do good and created trust between healers and the families that turned to them for help.
hl01.scripture: Scripture teaches us about compassion and caring for those who are suffering. In the New Testament, Jesus Christ often healed the sick (Matthew 14:14). In Mosiah 2:17 from the Book of Mormon, we learn that when we serve others, we are serving God. While the scriptures do not mention the Hippocratic Oath, they do teach that kindness, integrity, and care for the vulnerable are pleasing to our Heavenly Father. These values line up closely with what Hippocrates wanted for those who would become healers.
hl01.background: Life in ancient Greece was filled with uncertainty. Everyday dangers like injury, illness, and famine were common, and medical knowledge was limited. The Greeks worshipped many gods, and religious practices shaped daily life. When someone was sick, families often prayed to the gods for healing, sometimes going to temples dedicated to Asclepius, the god of medicine. Most medical care happened at home or through local healers. Hippocrates was born into this world on the island of Kos, where his family had a long tradition of practicing medicine. He learned to use careful observation and reasoning instead of depending only on religious explanations. The Hippocratic Oath reflected this new way of thinking and treating people.

hl02.talk: Why do you think it’s important to help people who can’t give you anything back?
hl02.child: A long time ago, a kind man built a place where anyone who was sick or poor could be cared for, even if they couldn’t pay. This was the very first hospital. His idea was to love and help everyone, just like Jesus taught.
hl02.learn: We can learn that small acts of kindness can grow into something much bigger when many people work together with faith and love. The Basiliad shows us that caring for every person, especially those nobody else helps, is a powerful way to follow Heavenly Father’s will. Even one person’s dream, when inspired by true compassion, can change the world for generations.
hl02.matters: This moment matters because it changed the way people saw the sick and the poor. Before this, only families or the wealthy had help if they became ill—it was rare for strangers to be treated with dignity. Basil’s hospital inspired others. Soon, Christians all over the world built hospitals that cared for anyone, even those with no money or no hope of being cured. For families of faith, this stands as an example of Christlike love in action: seeing every person as a child of God, worthy of compassion. Many of today's hospitals trace their kindness back to this Christian beginning, even those that are not run by churches.

sources.name: Encyclopedia Britannica - Hospital: Historical Development
Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy - Basil of Caesarea
World History Encyclopedia - Basil of Caesarea
National Library of Medicine - The origins of the hospital in the ancient world

hl02.evidence: Historians have written much about Basil’s life and works, with several early sources describing the hospital complex he founded. Some writings from Basil himself mention the Basiliad and how it served the sick and needy. Archaeologists have found ruins in Caesarea that may be linked to this era. Documents from later Church councils show that hospitals quickly became important in the Christian world, and over time, the idea spread across Europe. While we do not have the whole hospital standing today, the records agree that Basil’s Basiliad led to the hospital becoming a central part of Christian life and caring for the vulnerable. Care for leprosy, so rare in other places, is especially well attested in accounts of the Basiliad.
hl02.happened: In the year 369 AD, a special place opened in Caesarea, a city in an area called Cappadocia (now in Turkey). St. Basil, a caring church leader, built what became the first real hospital, which people called the Basiliad. This was not just a building, but a whole center with places for the sick, poor, travelers, and those with leprosy—a terrible, contagious disease at that time. Basil brought together doctors and nurses who cared for everyone who came, no matter if they could pay or if their sickness could be cured. Money for the Basiliad came from generous gifts to the church, and people there believed that helping others was the same as serving God. In Roman society, temples were sometimes places for the sick, but these would turn away those who were dying or incurable, thinking it would make their temples unclean. The Basiliad was something completely new, putting compassion for every person before every other rule.
hl02.scripture: In the Gospel of Matthew, Jesus says, 'For I was an hungred, and ye gave me meat: I was thirsty, and ye gave me drink: I was a stranger, and ye took me in... Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me' (Matthew 25:35-40). The Book of Mormon teaches to 'succor those that stand in need of your succor' and to 'administer of your substance unto him that standeth in need' (Mosiah 4:16). While no scripture describes Basil or the Basiliad directly, these passages teach the principle of caring for the poor and suffering, showing that compassion is a holy work. Doctrine and Covenants 81:5 also commands to 'succor the weak, lift up the hands which hang down, and strengthen the feeble knees.'
hl02.background: Before Basil’s time, public healthcare the way we know it did not exist. The Roman Empire was filled with temples, markets, and busy towns. Doctors served mainly the rich, and caring for strangers or the poor was rarely anyone’s job. Most people lived simply, farming or working trades, and many faced hunger or illness with no help. Religious temples in the Roman world sometimes let people stay if they thought the gods could heal them, but if someone was too sick to get better, or might die, they were asked to leave. Christianity, still quite new and sometimes not trusted by rulers, taught its followers to care for everyone, including those most in need. Basil of Caesarea was moved by these teachings and dreamed of a place where everyone would be welcome, healed, and comforted, no matter their circumstances.

hl03.t: The Bimaristans of the Islamic World
hl03.talk: How can our family help someone who feels sick or alone this week?
hl03.child: A long time ago in Baghdad and Damascus, people made big hospitals to help anyone who was sick. They cared for everyone, no matter who they were, and tried to help with medicines and kindness. God wants us to help others, too.
hl03.learn: We can learn that caring for strangers and organizing our knowledge to help them can change many lives for years to come. If we choose to use the gifts of learning and technology with kindness and charity, we can bring hope and healing to others, just as these bimaristans did. It is a reminder that service, inspired by faith, often reaches far beyond what we can see at the moment.
hl03.matters: The story of the bimaristans shows how faith and charity can change a whole society. These hospitals introduced new ways of home and hospital care that shaped medical practice not just in the Islamic world, but across Europe later on. For families of faith, it is inspiring to see that both ancient Christians and Muslims, with no contact, felt called by God to heal strangers, and built lasting places to do so. This reminds us that technology and learning can be tools in the Lord's hands to bless His children, wherever they live, and calls us to look for ways we can serve others, no matter how different they are from us.

sources.name: Islamic Medical Manuscripts at the U.S. National Library of Medicine
Bimaristans – Science Museum, London
The Metropolitan Museum of Art – Science and Technology in the Medieval Islamic World

hl03.evidence: Historians have found many detailed records about bimaristans, from the writings of doctors and travelers of the time to remnants of the buildings in places like Damascus. Surviving documents show that these hospitals had administrators, kept patient logs, and followed procedures much like a modern institution. The Canon of Medicine by Ibn Sina and the medical encyclopedia by Al-Razi were preserved in Arabic and later Latin, used for hundreds of years across Europe. Archaeological remains, including old pharmacy equipment and wards in places like the Nur al-Din Bimaristan in Damascus, show the scale and care of these early hospitals. There is no real debate among scholars that these hospitals existed and that they provided care to all, supported by Islamic law and tradition.
hl03.happened: Around the year 805, in cities like Baghdad and Damascus, special hospitals called bimaristans began to appear, shaped by the faith and learning of the Islamic world. The word 'bimaristan' means 'house of the sick.' These were the first major hospitals that worked much as we imagine hospitals today. Anyone who came—whether rich or poor, whatever their faith or background—could receive care at no cost. Their support came from charitable endowments called waqf, funds given for the good of the community. Inside, medicines were prepared, patients had their own beds, and people with different illnesses were cared for in separate wards, much as in modern hospitals. Records were kept for each person, helping doctors understand what treatment worked. They even included some of the world’s first special places for those needing help with mental health. Over time, the work and writings of doctors in these bimaristans, like Al-Razi and Ibn Sina, became so respected that centuries later students in Europe were still learning from their books.
hl03.scripture: The scriptures encourage caring for the sick and needy. In the Bible, Jesus teaches, 'I was sick, and ye visited me' (Matthew 25:36). The Book of Mormon tells us to 'succor those that stand in need,' caring for their 'sicknesses and their infirmities' (Mosiah 4:16, Alma 1:30). Doctrine and Covenants 81:5 teaches: 'succor the weak, lift up the hands which hang down, and strengthen the feeble knees.' These passages invite us to see service to the suffering as a commandment from God and a way to become more like Christ.
hl03.background: Before these bimaristans, care for the sick mostly happened at home, in religious houses, or in small public clinics. The Islamic world of the early Middle Ages was a place of many bustling cities, famous for scholars, merchants, and travelers. Baghdad, founded just a few decades before 805, had grown into an intellectual center, where the works of Greece, Persia, and India met with Islamic learning. People there treasured knowledge, and their faith taught that caring for the sick and poor was a duty. Daily life was busy and the city was full of different faiths and backgrounds, trading goods and ideas along winding streets. The rulers and scholars wanted care that reached everyone, not just the wealthy, and that learning would be carefully preserved for future generations.

hl04.talk: Can you imagine what it would be like to have surgery without any medicine to stop the pain?
hl04.child: Long ago, doctors had to do surgeries while people were awake, which was very painful. Then, a doctor found a way to make people sleep during surgery so they wouldn't feel pain. This made surgeries much safer and less scary.
hl04.learn: The introduction of ether anesthesia teaches us the profound impact of innovation and the pursuit of knowledge in improving human life. It highlights the importance of compassion in medical practice and the relentless quest to alleviate suffering. This event also serves as a reminder that many of the comforts and advancements we enjoy today are the result of courage, curiosity, and dedication of those who came before us. Recognizing these contributions can inspire us to value and support ongoing efforts in medical research and innovation.
hl04.matters: The introduction of ether anesthesia was a monumental advancement in medicine, allowing surgeries to be performed with care and precision rather than haste. This innovation not only alleviated the immense suffering associated with surgical procedures but also paved the way for more complex and life-saving operations. For families of faith, this development can be seen as a manifestation of divine inspiration, providing humanity with tools to alleviate suffering and improve health. It underscores the belief that advancements in knowledge and technology can be blessings from a higher power, intended to enhance the well-being of His children.

sources.name: Massachusetts General Hospital - Ether Dome
Smithsonian Magazine - How Ether Went From a Recreational 'Frolic' Drug to the First Surgery Anesthetic
Wood Library-Museum of Anesthesiology - History of Anesthesia

hl04.evidence: Historical records and publications provide substantial evidence of the first public demonstration of ether anesthesia. Accounts from Massachusetts General Hospital detail the event, noting Dr. Warren's exclamation, "Gentlemen, this is no humbug," upon witnessing the procedure's success. Subsequent reports and studies document the rapid adoption of ether anesthesia in surgical practices worldwide. The Ether Dome remains preserved as a historical site, commemorating this groundbreaking moment in medical history. These records collectively affirm the authenticity and significance of the event.
hl04.happened: On October 16, 1846, in the operating theater of Massachusetts General Hospital, known today as the Ether Dome, a significant medical breakthrough occurred. William T. G. Morton, a Boston dentist, administered ether to Edward Gilbert Abbott, a printer suffering from a neck tumor. As Abbott inhaled the ether through a specially designed glass inhaler, he lost consciousness. Dr. John Collins Warren, a prominent surgeon, then proceeded to remove the tumor. Remarkably, Abbott remained insensible throughout the procedure and reported no pain upon regaining consciousness. This event marked the first public demonstration of surgical anesthesia, revolutionizing the practice of surgery by introducing a method to perform operations without causing pain to the patient.
hl04.scripture: While the scriptures do not directly address the advent of anesthesia, they do emphasize the importance of compassion and alleviating suffering. In the Book of Mormon, Mosiah 2:17 teaches, "When ye are in the service of your fellow beings ye are only in the service of your God." This principle aligns with the medical community's mission to serve and heal others. Additionally, Doctrine and Covenants 89, known as the Word of Wisdom, encourages practices that promote health and well-being, reflecting the value placed on caring for the physical body.
hl04.background: Before this pivotal demonstration, surgery was a harrowing experience. Patients underwent procedures fully conscious, enduring excruciating pain while being physically restrained. Surgeons prioritized speed over precision to minimize the patient's suffering. The concept of anesthesia was not entirely new; substances like opium and alcohol had been used to dull pain, but their effectiveness was limited. In the early 1840s, Dr. Crawford Long in Georgia had used ether for surgical procedures, but his work remained largely unrecognized at the time. The successful public demonstration in Boston brought the use of ether into the medical mainstream, transforming surgical practices worldwide.

hl05.talk: Why do you think it’s important to check if a story about the past is true or not?
hl05.child: Long ago, people started using medicine to help with the pain of having babies. Some people say that churches wanted to stop it, but that story is not really true. Most church leaders thought helping people hurt less was a good thing.
hl05.learn: This story teaches us to investigate before accepting popular claims, even if they seem widely believed. Sometimes stories get repeated so much that people stop checking the facts. We can also learn that faith and reason are not always in conflict, and that using our knowledge to lessen suffering is a good thing. When we hear something surprising about people of faith in history, it is wise to look for the truth in solid evidence.
hl05.matters: Understanding what really happened helps us know when to trust stories about the past. The tale that churches blocked medical advances often appears in books and movies, but this research shows that the real reasons for resistance were much more practical. For families of faith, this story encourages us to seek truth and not be quick to blame or believe negative stories about faith and science. It reminds parents and children that medicine and faith can work together and that careful thinking and compassion matter most.

sources.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: History of Anaesthesia
National Library of Medicine: Chloroform and Childbirth
Religion and Science: Beyond the Epistemological Conflict, Harvard University
PBS: Myth of Religion versus Science

hl05.evidence: Modern historians have reviewed newspapers, church bulletins, diaries, and other records from the 1800s and found little evidence of clergy-led protest against anaesthesia in childbirth. Instead, journals from doctors show they discussed the safety risks and possible effects of anaesthetics on labor. Some medical journals record early doctors worrying about new drugs slowing down childbirth or causing harm. Several well-known religious leaders of the time, like Rev. James Simpson in Britain, even recommended using anaesthesia. Scholar Ronald Numbers and others have carefully documented these findings, showing the myth of church opposition does not match the real records.
hl05.happened: In the mid-1800s, doctors in Britain and other parts of the world began using new medicines, such as ether and chloroform, to help people sleep through painful surgeries and childbirth. These medicines, called anaesthetics, changed the practice of medicine forever. As people looked back, a story grew that many churches and religious leaders had strongly opposed giving pain relief to women during childbirth. Some said they believed it went against the Bible, especially a verse in Genesis where it says women would have sorrow in childbirth. However, when historians looked carefully at journals, speeches, and church records from that time, they found almost no organized religious opposition. Instead, most of the worry came from doctors, not clergy. Physicians debated whether these drugs were safe for mothers and babies, and if they might slow or complicate childbirth. Surprisingly, some church leaders openly supported using anaesthetics, saying it could be a blessing to help ease suffering. The idea that churches were the biggest critics of anaesthesia during childbirth turned out to be more of a myth than a fact.
hl05.scripture: The Bible verse often mentioned in this story is Genesis 3:16, where God tells Eve, 'in sorrow thou shalt bring forth children.' However, the scriptures teach many principles about compassion and using knowledge for good. In the Book of Mormon, Mosiah 4:26 encourages us to 'succor those that stand in need of your succor.' Doctrine and Covenants 42:43-44 speaks about using the knowledge and skills we have to heal, with faith in the Lord. These suggest that relieving suffering is a good use of the talents and knowledge we are given, as long as we do so with faith and wisdom.
hl05.background: Before the 1840s, there was very little pain relief available for surgery or childbirth. Doctors, nurses, and families all managed pain as best they could, but operations were often terrifying and very risky. In Britain at this time, most people attended church regularly, and Christian faith shaped much of public life. Medicine was rapidly changing, with new discoveries but also strong debates about what was safe or right. There were also old beliefs about suffering being unavoidable or even necessary in life. Still, when ether and chloroform became available, many people welcomed them with hope. The first public demonstration of ether in surgery happened in 1846, and chloroform was used soon after, quickly becoming popular for childbirth.

hl06.talk: Why do you think it was important for Florence Nightingale to count and write down what happened in the hospital?
hl06.child: Florence Nightingale cleaned up a dirty hospital and kept careful notes so fewer soldiers would die. She knew God wanted her to help sick people. By counting what happened, she helped hospitals become safer for everyone.
hl06.learn: Florence Nightingale teaches us that caring for others is both a calling and a skill. Faith can inspire us to act with compassion, but doing good also means learning and applying the best knowledge we can find. Her example helps us see that keeping good records and being honest about what we find is essential to making real, lasting changes. As a family, we can remember that helping others well is something we do with both our hearts and our minds.
hl06.matters: Florence Nightingale’s story matters because it shows how one person’s faith and determination, combined with the careful use of knowledge, can change the world. She demonstrated that compassion needed to be guided by evidence – being kind was not enough without good practices. For families of faith, her example reminds us that God can inspire us to serve and to use all our talents, including our minds, to help others. The way she gathered and shared facts led to better care for everyone, showing that faith and reason can work hand in hand to bless lives.

sources.name: National Army Museum: Florence Nightingale
BBC History: Florence Nightingale
Florence Nightingale Museum: Scutari and the Crimean War

hl06.evidence: Historians and medical researchers have carefully studied Nightingale’s work at Scutari. Her records show dramatic drops in death rates once her sanitary reforms took hold, dropping from as high as 42% to less than 2% in some months. Her statistical diagrams, preserved in museums, are recognized as major contributions to public health and statistics. Later studies confirmed her claim that infection and poor sanitation were the biggest killers in military hospitals; today, infection control is standard practice worldwide. Her collected letters and diaries provide firsthand evidence of her faith and methods. All credible historical sources agree on these main points.
hl06.happened: In the year 1854, Florence Nightingale left her comfortable English home to serve as a nurse in Scutari, near the front lines of the Crimean War. Nightingale, who felt called by God to help others when she was just seventeen, was shocked by what she found. The hospital was filled with British soldiers, but most were not dying from their battle wounds – they were dying from infections caused by filthy conditions. There was little clean water, hardly any fresh air, and rats ran through the halls. Nightingale set out to change everything she could: she organized her team of nurses, started cleaning every part of the hospital, and made sure the men had better food and fresh air. She kept careful records of every death and disease, creating new types of charts that made it easy to see that most deaths were from preventable illnesses, not injuries. These charts, shaped like petals or fans, were new to Parliament and convinced them that things had to change. Nightingale’s work not only saved lives, but also made governments see the power of careful counting and honest reporting.
hl06.scripture: Florence Nightingale’s devotion to healing echoes the Savior’s care for the sick (Matthew 25:36: "I was sick, and ye visited me"). The Lord’s command to serve the least among us, without seeking reward, is found in Mosiah 2:17 in the Book of Mormon: "When ye are in the service of your fellow beings ye are only in the service of your God." Her method of recording and counting aligns with the scriptural principle of 'seeking out of the best books by study and by faith' (Doctrine and Covenants 88:118). While scripture does not mention modern nursing, it honors both faith-driven service and the wise use of knowledge to bless lives.
hl06.background: Before Florence Nightingale arrived, healthcare in military hospitals was terribly poor. Most nurses were untrained, and many people at the time did not see nursing as a respectable job. The Crimean War had brought thousands of wounded British soldiers to hospitals like the one in Scutari, but their care was often worse than the battlefields. Doctors did not understand germs, and so hygiene was not seen as important. In ordinary homes, families struggled through sickness with little more than folk remedies and prayer, and few people trusted hospitals. Florence Nightingale came from a wealthy family; her decision to become a nurse shocked many people, but her faith and determination pushed her forward.

hl07.talk: Why do you think it was hard for people to believe that tiny germs could make someone sick, when they couldn’t see them?
hl07.child: A doctor named Joseph Lister found that cleaning hands and tools with special soap helped stop people from getting sick after surgery. Before this, many people got very sick from germs they couldn’t see. His careful cleaning helped save many lives.
hl07.learn: We can learn that sometimes the best answers come from listening to new ideas and being willing to change old habits, even if it feels uncomfortable. Good ideas can be ignored if the world isn’t ready for them, but when people listen, miracles of healing can follow. Lister’s story also teaches us to value the work of those who quietly serve and seek better ways to care for others.
hl07.matters: Lister’s discovery matters because it saved countless lives and made surgery far safer. Before antiseptic treatment, even small surgeries could mean deadly infection. Lister’s work built the foundation for modern hospitals, where careful cleanliness and infection control are basic duties. For families of faith, this story shows how knowledge can bless many when it is received humbly and put to use. We are reminded that the Lord often gives answers and helps through wise people who seek truth and healing for others.

sources.name: Science Museum: Joseph Lister and Antisepsis
Royal College of Surgeons: Joseph Lister
National Library of Medicine: Joseph Lister

hl07.evidence: Historical records from Glasgow’s Royal Infirmary, where Joseph Lister worked, document the use of carbolic acid and the drop in post-surgery deaths. Medical journals from the 1860s and 1870s, as well as later accounts by doctors, tell about how controversial and then accepted Lister's methods became. The importance of Lister’s work is confirmed by the nearly universal practice of sterilizing surgical tools and hands today. Earlier efforts, such as Semmelweis’s hand washing, are also well documented, showing that both men were correct in seeing a link between cleanliness and survival, although Lister's work led to widespread change.
hl07.happened: In 1867 in Glasgow, Scotland, a surgeon named Joseph Lister made a discovery that changed the world of medicine. Lister knew about the new ideas of a scientist named Louis Pasteur, who found out that tiny invisible germs could cause sickness. Thinking about how many patients became very ill or died after surgeries, Lister wondered if these germs could be responsible. He decided to try using carbolic acid, a chemical for cleaning wounds and tools, to see if he could stop infections during surgery. He cleaned his hands, his instruments, and the area around wounds, and covered the wounds with cloths soaked in carbolic acid. The change was dramatic: the number of patients who died after surgery in his hospital dropped. This method of keeping things clean to kill germs, called antisepsis, soon spread to other hospitals. While it took some time for all doctors to accept these new ways, Lister’s work gave people hope that surgery could help more people, with less risk of deadly infections.
hl07.scripture: Scriptures speak of the need to serve and heal others, and to seek knowledge. In the Bible, the Savior healed the sick and taught compassion (Matthew 9:35). Doctrine and Covenants 42:43-44 encourages priesthood holders and families to use medicines and the wisdom of doctors along with faith and prayer. We are taught to "seek diligently and teach one another words of wisdom; yea, seek out of the best books words of wisdom" (Doctrine and Covenants 88:118), showing that all knowledge, including discoveries about health, are gifts to be used for good.
hl07.background: Before 1867, surgery was dangerous and often a last resort. Hospitals were crowded, and doctors did not know about germs—instead, they thought infections came from bad air, or were just unavoidable. Many patients died from fever and infection after simple operations. Doctors would move from patient to patient without washing their hands or their tools. Before Joseph Lister, another doctor named Ignaz Semmelweis had shown that cleaning hands could save lives, but few people listened to him, and he died without recognition. In the 19th century, most people lived without running water or strong medicines. Deaths from infection after surgery or childbirth were tragically common. Joseph Lister grew up in a Quaker family that valued learning and kindness, and he wanted to help suffering people.

hl08.talk: Why do you think it's important to help families who have lost someone they love?
hl08.child: Long ago, having a baby was very dangerous for mothers. Many mothers died when their babies were born because doctors didn't know how to keep them safe. Families often had to help each other when this happened.
hl08.learn: Reflecting on the high maternal mortality rates of the 19th century teaches us the value of medical advancements and the importance of community support. It reminds us to appreciate the progress made in maternal health and to continue advocating for safe childbirth practices worldwide. For families of faith, it reinforces the call to support those in need and to cherish the roles of mothers in nurturing and sustaining family life.
hl08.matters: The high maternal mortality rates of the 19th century had profound effects on families and societies. The loss of a mother disrupted family structures, often leading to economic hardship and emotional distress. For families of faith, these tragedies tested their resilience and trust in divine providence. The frequent occurrence of maternal deaths underscored the need for advancements in medical care and public health. It also highlighted the importance of community support and the role of extended families in providing care and stability in times of loss.

sources.name: The Decline in Maternal Mortality in Sweden: The Role of Community Midwifery
British Maternal Mortality in the 19th and Early 20th Centuries
Achievements in Public Health, 1900-1999: Healthier Mothers and Babies

hl08.evidence: Historical records from the 19th century provide detailed accounts of maternal mortality rates. In Sweden, data from seven parishes revealed a maternal mortality rate of 595 per 100,000 live births, with eclampsia, obstructed labor, and hemorrhage accounting for the majority of deaths. In England and Wales, records indicate that maternal mortality rates were around 5 per 1,000 live births between 1800 and 1850. These statistics are corroborated by studies from other countries, illustrating a global pattern of high maternal mortality during this period. The consistency of these records across different regions and populations underscores the widespread nature of the issue and the urgent need for medical and societal interventions.
hl08.happened: In the 19th century, childbirth was a perilous event for mothers worldwide. Maternal mortality rates were alarmingly high, with estimates ranging from 500 to 1,000 deaths per 100,000 live births. This means that for every 100 to 200 deliveries, one mother would not survive. The primary causes of these deaths included puerperal fever (a severe infection following childbirth), obstructed labor, and hemorrhage. In Sweden, for instance, maternal mortality declined from 900 per 100,000 live births in 1751 to 230 per 100,000 by 1900, yet the risk remained significant. In England and Wales, maternal mortality rates were around 5 per 1,000 live births between 1800 and 1850. Given that women often had multiple pregnancies, the cumulative risk over a lifetime was substantial. The loss of mothers during childbirth was so common that nearly every extended family experienced such a tragedy at some point. This frequent loss led to many children being raised by stepmothers or other relatives, and it influenced cultural narratives, including folklore about stepmothers, reflecting a society where remarriage after a mother's death was a norm.
hl08.scripture: The scriptures emphasize the sanctity of life and the importance of caring for the vulnerable. In the Bible, James 1:27 states, "Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction." This passage underscores the duty to support those who have lost loved ones, reflecting the communal responsibility to care for motherless children and widowed fathers. Additionally, in the Book of Mormon, Mosiah 18:9 teaches believers to "mourn with those that mourn; yea, and comfort those that stand in need of comfort," reinforcing the principle of compassion and support within the community.
hl08.background: During the 19th century, medical knowledge and practices were limited, especially concerning childbirth. The understanding of infection control was rudimentary, and antiseptic techniques were not widely adopted until the latter part of the century. In many regions, childbirth took place at home, attended by midwives or family members without formal medical training. Even in hospitals, the lack of sterile procedures led to high rates of puerperal fever. Societal norms placed women in the role of primary caregivers and childbearers, often resulting in large families. The combination of frequent pregnancies and inadequate medical care created a high-risk environment for mothers.

hl09.talk: Why do you think Heavenly Father wants us to use new knowledge and inventions to help and heal others?
hl09.child: Long ago, it was very dangerous for mothers to have babies, even in good hospitals. When new medicine was discovered, many more mothers were able to live and raise their children. Families were very thankful for this blessing, just like we can be today.
hl09.learn: We can learn that technology often comes as an answer to need, prayer, and effort. The sharp drop in mothers dying after new medicine and practices arrived shows how powerful good knowledge can be when used with wisdom, skill, and compassion. We should remember those who came before, honor their courage, and be grateful for the blessings we have, using them to lift and serve others as the Savior taught.
hl09.matters: This turning point matters deeply because it changed the lives of millions of families, making birth much safer for mothers everywhere those treatments and practices spread. For a family who believes that technology is a gift from God, it is a clear example of how inspired discovery and caring service can transform the world for good. The generations before us prayed for safety at birth, and many families grieved losses we can scarcely imagine today. Remembering this helps us be grateful for the blessings we enjoy now and consider how we can continue to use new knowledge to bless and heal, as the Lord would want us to.

sources.name: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention: 'Achievements in Public Health, 1900-1999: Healthier Mothers and Babies'
Wellcome Collection: 'How childbirth became safer in the 20th century'
Our World in Data: 'Maternal mortality'
National Institutes of Health: 'The History of Antibiotics'

hl09.evidence: Medical historians trace the dramatic fall in maternal deaths in high-income countries to the years following the introduction of sulfonamides and penicillin. Published studies show the maternal mortality rate dropping nearly ninety percent from levels before 1935 to the 1960s and even lower by the 1980s. Careful research confirms that these declines happened after these new medicines and procedures became common in obstetric care. No such sharp drop is seen before, even though other health improvements had been tried. Eventually, better training, hospital care, and early forms of intensive care also helped. These facts are well-documented in medical journals and public health records from that time.
hl09.happened: In the year 1935, something remarkable began to happen in the world of medicine that would transform childbirth forever. Sulfonamide antibiotics, the very first of their kind, appeared and were quickly used to treat infections. Not long after, penicillin arrived, joined by safer ways to give blood transfusions and much better training for doctors and nurses who cared for mothers during pregnancy and birth. For decades before this, even in the safest, richest countries, many mothers died from infections or complications after giving birth. Doctors had long tried to lower these numbers, but nothing worked very well until these new medicines and practices came. As hospitals used these discoveries more widely, the number of mothers dying in childbirth started to fall sharply after 1935. This life-saving change didn’t slow down after the first year; it kept going for decades. By the time most people’s grandmothers had children, dying in childbirth in high-income countries had become very rare compared to before. What once was a common and tragic part of family life quickly became unusual, bringing relief and longer life to families all over the world.
hl09.scripture: The scriptures do not tell this story directly, but the principle of healing and caring for others is found throughout. In Luke 10:34, the Savior told of the Good Samaritan who used oil and wine, the best medicines of his time, to help a suffering man. In the Doctrine and Covenants 42:43, the Lord says, 'And whosoever is sick among you, let them be nourished with all tenderness, with herbs and mild food, and that not by the hand of an enemy.' These verses remind us that using the best knowledge and skill available to help others, especially in times of illness or danger, is a holy and worthy endeavor.
hl09.background: Before 1935, even in countries with many doctors and hospitals, having a baby was dangerous. People often knew someone who had lost a mother, a daughter, or a friend to childbirth. Hospitals were learning and growing, but they didn’t yet have the tools to fight the bacteria that cause deadly infections, and blood transfusions were riskier. Families lived with the real fear that a mother might not survive giving birth, which made every birth a time of both hope and anxiety. The world was already changing in other ways: cars and radios were newer, and people had more ways to learn and connect, but medicine just hadn’t caught up yet in saving mothers’ lives. Most parents and doctors could only watch, hope, and pray.

hl10.talk: Why do you think Heavenly Father wants us to use both prayer and doctors when we're sick?
hl10.child: Some people believe that praying to Heavenly Father can heal them when they're sick. But it's also important to go to the doctor when we need help because Heavenly Father has given us doctors to take care of us.
hl10.learn: This event teaches the importance of integrating faith with practical knowledge and medical care. While trust in divine healing is a fundamental aspect of many religious beliefs, it should not exclude the use of medical resources that Heavenly Father has provided. Seeking medical care during pregnancy and childbirth is a responsible act that aligns with the principle of seeking wisdom and ensuring the well-being of oneself and one's family. It reminds us that faith and reason can coexist harmoniously, leading to healthier and more fulfilling lives.
hl10.matters: The Faith Assembly's experience highlights the critical importance of balancing faith with the use of available medical knowledge and resources. While faith and prayer are vital aspects of many individuals' lives, they should not replace essential medical care, especially during pregnancy and childbirth. This case serves as a cautionary tale, emphasizing that rejecting medical assistance can lead to preventable tragedies. For families of faith, it underscores the belief that Heavenly Father has provided both spiritual and medical means for healing, and utilizing both is a responsible and faithful approach to health and well-being.

sources.name: Perinatal and maternal mortality in a religious group avoiding obstetric care
Epidemiologic Notes and Reports Perinatal and Maternal Mortality in a Religious Group -- Indiana

hl10.evidence: Historical and medical studies have documented the outcomes of the Faith Assembly's practices. Research published in the American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology in 1984 investigated perinatal and maternal deaths among the group. The study found that members who avoided obstetric care had a perinatal mortality rate three times higher and a maternal mortality rate about 100 times higher than the statewide rates. These findings suggest that, even in the United States, women who avoid obstetric care have a greatly increased risk of perinatal and maternal death. This evidence highlights the dangers of refusing medical care during pregnancy and childbirth.
hl10.happened: Between 1975 and 1982, the Faith Assembly, a religious group in Indiana, adhered strictly to faith healing, rejecting all forms of medical care, including prenatal services and professional assistance during childbirth. Members believed that seeking medical help demonstrated a lack of faith in divine healing. Consequently, pregnant women received no prenatal care and delivered their babies at home, assisted only by family or friends without medical training. This practice led to significantly higher rates of maternal and perinatal mortality within the community. Studies revealed that the maternal mortality rate among Faith Assembly members was approximately 100 times higher than the statewide average, and their perinatal mortality rate was about three times higher. These findings underscore the severe health risks associated with the complete refusal of medical care during pregnancy and childbirth.
hl10.scripture: The scriptures teach the importance of seeking wisdom and knowledge. In Doctrine and Covenants 88:118, it states, "Seek ye out of the best books words of wisdom; seek learning, even by study and also by faith." This passage encourages the pursuit of knowledge through both spiritual and temporal means. Additionally, in 2 Nephi 2:25, it is written, "Adam fell that men might be; and men are, that they might have joy." Ensuring the health and safety of mothers and infants aligns with the divine desire for His children to experience joy and fulfillment in life.
hl10.background: In the mid-20th century, medical advancements had significantly improved maternal and infant health outcomes in the United States. Prenatal care, hospital deliveries, and professional medical assistance during childbirth became standard practices, leading to reduced mortality rates. However, some religious groups, like the Faith Assembly in Indiana, held beliefs that prioritized spiritual healing over medical intervention. Founded in 1973 by Rev. Hobart Freeman, the Faith Assembly emphasized reliance on faith for healing, viewing medical treatment as a lack of trust in divine power. This belief system led members to avoid medical care entirely, even during critical times such as pregnancy and childbirth.

hl11.talk: How do you think it feels to know you matter, even when you can't get better?
hl11.child: Cicely Saunders helped make a special place for people who were very sick to feel safe and cared for. She wanted everyone to know they matter, even when they are very old or very sick. Now, many people around the world are helped by hospices because of her idea.
hl11.learn: Families can learn from this story that caring for someone goes beyond finding cures. Offering kindness, listening, and giving comfort—especially when someone is suffering—can be as important a service as any medicine. It reminds us to value each moment and every person, all the way to the end. Heavenly Father cares about how we treat others, and sometimes, we bless others most when we help them feel loved, peaceful, and honored.
hl11.matters: What Cicely Saunders started still changes lives today. Her view that people at the end of life should be treated with respect and comfort has helped millions of families find peace. The hospice movement makes sure no one is forgotten or left in pain, and it supports families in difficult times. For families who see each soul as a child of God, this story reminds us of our sacred duty to care for others with patience and kindness, helping each person feel loved to the very end of their journey, just as we hope for ourselves.

sources.name: BBC History - Cicely Saunders and the Modern Hospice Movement
St Christopher's Hospice - About Our History
National Institutes of Health - A Historical Overview of Palliative Care

hl11.evidence: The founding of St Christopher’s Hospice is well documented in hospital and charity records, professional journals, and news articles from the time. Cicely Saunders wrote and lectured widely about her work, and her careful records showed how her approach relieved suffering and improved the final days of many people. Since her work, studies have confirmed that hospice and palliative care help people live more comfortably, reducing pain and stress for patients and families. The model she introduced is now recommended in medical guidelines worldwide and has become standard practice in many countries. Saunders’s words and actions are widely quoted and respected in medicine today.
hl11.happened: In 1967, Cicely Saunders, who had worked as a nurse, social worker, and doctor, opened St Christopher's Hospice in Sydenham, London. This was the first place designed especially to take care of people who were nearing the end of their lives from chronic or incurable illness. Before this, hospitals focused mainly on healing and trying to cure, but often had little to offer those whose diseases could not be stopped. Motivated by her Christian faith, Cicely Saunders believed deeply that every person matters, even in their final days. She felt that people who were dying deserved relief from pain, comfort, and dignity. Saunders developed the idea of "total pain," meaning that suffering is not just physical but can also be emotional, social, and spiritual. At St Christopher’s, doctors, nurses, and volunteers worked together not only to manage physical pain with medicines and new approaches, but also to offer support for worries, fears, family needs, and even spiritual questions. Families were welcomed and included, and the care did not stop with just the patient. This gentle, careful approach soon became a model around the world and started the modern hospice and palliative care movement.
hl11.scripture: Scriptures teach that every soul is precious in the sight of God. The Savior spent time with the sick and the suffering (see Matthew 25:34-40), teaching us to care for the least of these. The Book of Mormon teaches us to 'mourn with those that mourn; yea, and comfort those that stand in need of comfort' (Mosiah 18:9). While no scripture speaks of hospices directly, the principle of ministering and showing Christlike love, especially to those in need, is woven throughout all scripture and matches Sister Saunders’s example very well.
hl11.background: In the years before 1967, medicine had made great leaps forward—antibiotics and new treatments saved many lives that would once have been lost. Hospitals were busy, focused on cures and fast recovery, but people who could not be cured often ended up in crowded wards with little attention to their comfort. Pain relief was often not enough, and many people died feeling alone. Cicely Saunders had seen this in London hospitals herself, and it troubled her. The value of each life, right to the very end, was something that she accepted as a given because of her faith in God. Daily life in 1960s London was a mix of change and tradition, with modern medicine and new social ideas on the rise. Her idea that compassionate care for the dying should be as important as cures was new and often ignored.

hl12.talk: Why do you think it's important to help protect others from getting sick?
hl12.child: Long ago, many children got very sick from diseases like measles and polio. Doctors and helpers worked together to give shots to protect kids, and now many more children grow up healthy and strong.
hl12.learn: The success of the EPI teaches us the power of collective action and the importance of equitable access to healthcare. It reminds us that coordinated efforts can overcome significant challenges and save millions of lives. For families, it highlights the value of preventive care and the blessings that come from protecting our children and communities from preventable diseases.
hl12.matters: The EPI's success underscores the profound impact of immunization on global health. For families of faith, this achievement reflects the principle of stewardship—caring for the health and well-being of all God's children. The program's reach into remote and underserved areas exemplifies the importance of equitable access to life-saving interventions. It serves as a reminder of our collective responsibility to protect the vulnerable and to use the knowledge and resources we've been blessed with to alleviate suffering.

sources.name: WHO: Global immunization efforts have saved at least 154 million lives over the past 50 years
WHO: A Brief History of Vaccination
WHO: 50th anniversary of the Expanded Programme on Immunization (EPI)

hl12.evidence: Historical records and scientific studies provide robust evidence of the EPI's impact. A 2024 study published in The Lancet estimated that global immunization efforts have saved approximately 154 million lives over the past 50 years, with the majority being children under five. The study highlighted that measles vaccination alone accounted for 60% of the lives saved due to immunization. Additionally, the WHO reported that global coverage with the third dose of the DTP vaccine increased from less than 5% in 1974 to 84% by 2024, demonstrating significant progress in immunization coverage worldwide.
hl12.happened: In 1974, the World Health Organization (WHO) launched the Expanded Programme on Immunization (EPI) to ensure that children worldwide received vaccines against six major diseases: tuberculosis, diphtheria, tetanus, pertussis (whooping cough), polio, and measles. At that time, less than 5% of infants globally had access to routine immunization. Over the following decades, the EPI expanded its reach and the number of diseases it targeted. By 2024, the program had contributed to vaccinating 84% of infants with three doses of the diphtheria, tetanus, and pertussis (DTP) vaccine, a key indicator of immunization coverage. This massive global effort has been credited with saving approximately 154 million lives over 50 years, with 146 million of those being children under the age of five. Measles vaccination alone accounted for 60% of the lives saved due to immunization efforts.
hl12.scripture: The scriptures teach us to care for the health and well-being of others. In the Doctrine and Covenants 89:4, the Lord warns of "evils and designs which do and will exist in the hearts of conspiring men in the last days," and provides the Word of Wisdom as guidance for health. While this passage doesn't directly address immunization, it emphasizes the importance of seeking and following divine counsel for physical well-being. Additionally, Mosiah 2:17 reminds us that "when ye are in the service of your fellow beings ye are only in the service of your God," encouraging us to support efforts that promote health and save lives.
hl12.background: In the early 1970s, many countries faced high child mortality rates due to infectious diseases. Vaccines existed for several of these illnesses, but access was limited, especially in low-income regions. The success of the smallpox eradication campaign demonstrated the potential of coordinated vaccination efforts. Inspired by this, the WHO initiated the EPI to extend the benefits of immunization to all children, regardless of their geographic or economic circumstances. Daily life in many parts of the world was marked by the constant threat of outbreaks of preventable diseases, leading to significant loss of life and economic hardship for families and communities.

hl13.t: Clean Water and the Quiet Victory
hl13.talk: What would it be like if we had to bring all our water from a river every day?
hl13.child: Clean water helps keep children healthy so they can grow, play, and learn. Getting water from a safe pipe means fewer kids get sick. Helping with simple things, like water, can save lives.
hl13.learn: We learn that some of the biggest blessings come from steady, humble efforts that are not always in the spotlight. When families, communities, and leaders work together to solve real problems, miracles happen over time. We also learn that technology, when used wisely and kindly, becomes a tool in Heavenly Father’s hands to answer prayers and help His children. We can remember the value of simple yet powerful solutions and the loving service behind them.
hl13.matters: This matters because clean water and sanitation are among the most important ways to keep people healthy—much more than medicine can do alone. For families of faith, it is a gentle reminder that simple, unseen service can bring great blessings. Just as the Savior served quietly, often unnoticed, making sure everyone had what they needed, so too is bringing clean water a way to love and care for others. Having safe water means more children live to grow and learn, parents can work instead of worrying, and everyone can better serve and lift each other. Trust in steady, humble solutions often saves more lives than dramatic miracles.

sources.name: World Health Organization: Drinking-water
UNICEF: Progress on household drinking water, sanitation and hygiene 2000-2022
Our World in Data: Clean Water and Sanitation

hl13.evidence: Multiple studies and world health reports confirm the facts about clean water’s impact. The United Nations and the World Health Organization track access to safe water and sanitation. Since 1990, the global population with access to safely managed drinking water services rose from about 76% to over 90%, and improved sanitation coverage has expanded similarly. Researchers consistently find that improvements in water and sanitation have been a main driver in declining child death rates worldwide, outpacing most modern drugs or vaccines in lives saved. Diarrhoeal diseases, which killed millions of young children every year, now cause far fewer deaths, mainly due to cleaner water and better hygiene. These results show up in health records, reports from hospitals, and international surveys.
hl13.happened: Since 1990, the world has quietly changed for the better in a way that is rarely celebrated, but has saved millions of lives. Governments, communities, and organizations worked together to bring clean water and safe toilets to places that had little or none. This meant running pipes to towns and villages, building wells, teaching about hygiene, and building sewers where people once had to use unsafe open latrines or rivers. Because of these efforts, over two billion more people now have safe water to drink and better ways to get rid of waste. These changes may not sound exciting, but they have given children a better chance to grow up healthy. One of the most important results has been a huge drop—more than two-thirds—in deaths from diarrhoeal diseases, which used to be one of the main threats to young children, especially in poorer countries. These victories did not come quickly or easily. Each new well or water tap was a step against sickness and loss, often requiring teamwork, wise use of money, and steady faith from those who believed things could improve. Little by little, the quiet work of bringing water in and carrying waste away has made the world kinder and safer for everyone, especially children.
hl13.scripture: Scriptures teach us about caring for the basic needs of others and protecting health. In Matthew 25:35, Jesus says, "I was thirsty, and ye gave me drink," showing kindness by meeting simple needs. In Mosiah 2:17, we read, "when ye are in the service of your fellow beings ye are only in the service of your God." The Law of Moses (Deuteronomy 23:12-14) gives guidance for keeping camps clean, which helped prevent disease. While the scriptures do not mention plumbing, they show that caring for bodies and health is holy work. Clean water and sanitation are ways to show Christlike love, serving quietly but blessing lives deeply.
hl13.background: Before these improvements, life in many parts of the world was much harder and more dangerous for families, especially for children. In 1990, over a third of the world’s population had to drink unclean water or shared water sources with animals, and many used simple pit toilets or open fields. Sickness from dirty water was common; diarrhoeal disease often struck the youngest children, and many did not survive. For families, daily life could mean long walks to fetch water, careful rationing of every drop, and worry each time someone became ill. Most parents could do little when sickness came again and again. The people living through this were regular mothers, fathers, and children, just wanting a safe life. When improvements started, they often came through small local projects, with neighbors helping each other. Over time, bigger projects from governments and international groups reached more people.

hl14.talk: What could we do to help mothers and babies be safer, even if they live far away?
hl14.child: Many mothers in some places do not have enough help when they have a baby, and that can be very dangerous for them. If we share what we have and help care for each other, more moms and babies can be safe and healthy. Helping one another is something Heavenly Father wants us to do.
hl14.learn: We can learn that with better planning, caring, and sharing of resources, many lives can be saved. Simple solutions, like clean birthing spaces, trained midwives, and reliable ways to get emergency help, make a big difference. Families, communities, and leaders who remember each mother and child as precious can inspire and support real change. Knowing about this kind of suffering helps us see what kind of work matters most in the world and how we might be part of making it better, even from far away.
hl14.matters: This matters deeply because every mother is precious, and each loss leaves behind grieving families and children. For families of faith, believing life is sacred means seeing these deaths not as numbers, but as real heartbreaks that can be eased. Across the world, when we use our knowledge and means to help heal and save lives, we honor the gift of life and the tools Heavenly Father has allowed us to learn. It also reminds us that caring for one another, especially the vulnerable, is part of building a just and loving society.

sources.name: World Health Organization Maternal Mortality Fact Sheet
UNICEF Maternal Mortality Data
The Lancet: Global progress on maternal health has stalled

hl14.evidence: The numbers used today come from worldwide health organizations, such as the World Health Organization (WHO), which collects careful medical records and surveys from almost every country. These numbers are reviewed and compared each year to measure progress and find places where help is needed most. Studies confirm that most maternal deaths in the poorest regions could be prevented if simple care were available: basic medicines, clean places to give birth, good roads to get there, and people trained to help. The large differences between countries mostly track not disease, but access to resources and trained help. This is supported by decades of careful study, including WHO, UNICEF, and joint reports from global health experts.
hl14.happened: In the year 2023, the world saw about 260,000 women lose their lives because of problems during pregnancy and childbirth. This means that, each day, almost 712 mothers died—one almost every two minutes. Most of these deaths happened in countries where hospitals are scarce, there are few trained doctors and nurses, and basic medicines and safe roads are limited. Sub-Saharan Africa was the region hit hardest, accounting for about 70 percent of all these deaths. When a woman there tries to bring a new baby into the world, she faces dangers that women in wealthier places rarely see anymore. These risks aren’t tied to being from a certain place or people, but to whether the help she needs is nearby—like blood for transfusions, skilled workers, or just a clinic she can reach. Compared with a mother in Australia or New Zealand, a mother in sub-Saharan Africa is about 150 times more likely to die giving birth. While the world made good progress lowering these deaths from 2000 to 2016, getting even better has been hard since then, leaving many families still hoping and working for change.
hl14.scripture: The scriptures teach strongly about caring for the vulnerable. In Mosiah 4:26, King Benjamin teaches that we should "succor those that stand in need of your succor." In Matthew 25:40, the Savior says, "Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me." While no passage names maternal health directly, the principle of compassion and responsibility toward mothers and children shines throughout both the Bible and Book of Mormon. Doctrine and Covenants 81:5 also speaks of supporting the weak and lifting the hands which hang down. We are asked to love and serve one another whenever and wherever we can.
hl14.background: This happened in a world where medical knowledge has grown, but its blessings are unevenly shared. In most big cities in wealthier countries, mothers who give birth are surrounded by trained staff, clean facilities, and medicine. But in much of sub-Saharan Africa, villages are often far from clinics, roads can be rough, and there may be very few trained midwives. Life is shaped by the closeness of family, hard work, and sometimes waiting long hours or days to get help. Most people in these areas do not have the resources or the health systems that people in places like Australia or the United States may expect. These differences shape how safe and joyful an ordinary day can be for a family, especially when welcoming a new life.

hl15.t: What Happens to Children Under Stress
hl15.talk: Can you think of a time when you felt safe and loved at home? What was happening?
hl15.child: When children have hard things happen to them, it can make them feel sad or sick even after they grow up. But if someone in the family shows love and is always there, that helps them a lot. Kindness at home can help keep our hearts and bodies strong.
hl15.learn: We learn from this history that church, community, and especially family can be places of deep healing and protection. Even one steady, loving adult can tilt the balance for a child who faces difficulty. This asks every parent, teacher, and leader to strive for warmth and gentleness in their care. It also reassures families that the small acts of kindness in daily parenting are as powerful for a child's future as any great event or milestone.
hl15.matters: This study matters deeply because it shows that families do far more than shape how children learn or behave — they help build the foundation for lifelong health. For people of faith, it underlines the importance of loving, mindful homes where children feel safe and cherished. It also assures parents and leaders that, even when children face hard times, consistent kindness and presence can make a lasting difference. The ACE study gave the world new understanding of how the day-to-day decisions made around the kitchen table can change generations, physically and emotionally.

sources.name: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention - Violence Prevention: ACEs
Kaiser Permanente: About the ACE Study
Harvard University Center on the Developing Child: ACEs and Resilience
Church of Jesus Christ - Gospel Topics: Parenting

hl15.evidence: The ACE study is now one of the most cited works in public health, with its findings repeated in new research across many countries and populations. Follow-up studies strongly confirm its main results: adverse childhood experiences predict higher rates of diseases, mental illness, and early death, while positive relationships buffer these effects. The original data are well-documented, and thousands of scientists and doctors have reviewed and built upon them. Current research continues to show that the presence of a caring adult can greatly reduce the long-term health impacts of stress or trauma in childhood.
hl15.happened: In 1998, a groundbreaking study called the Adverse Childhood Experiences (ACE) study was published by researchers from Kaiser Permanente and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) in San Diego, California. More than 17,000 adults who were seeking regular healthcare filled out surveys about difficult things they might have gone through as children, such as physical or emotional abuse, neglect, or living in a home where parents struggled with addiction, mental illness, or separation. The researchers then linked those answers to the individuals’ medical records to see how those early-life hardships affected later health. The results revealed something powerful: the more types of adversity a person experienced as a child, the higher their risks were for serious health problems as adults. These included heart disease, cancer, depression, addiction, and even a shorter life. But the study also found hope — stable, nurturing relationships with at least one caring adult could protect children from many of these effects. What happened in the safety or hardship of home childhood years later appeared in the hospital charts of grown men and women.
hl15.scripture: Scripture teaches that every soul is precious and that 'no power or influence can or ought to be maintained... only by persuasion, by long-suffering, by gentleness and meekness, and by love unfeigned' (Doctrine and Covenants 121:41). The Savior Himself said, 'Suffer the little children to come unto me, and forbid them not: for of such is the kingdom of God' (Mark 10:14). Although the scriptures do not speak directly about scientific studies, these verses remind us how vital it is to care for and shield children with love, patience, and constancy. Such gentle watchfulness can ease the burdens that young hearts may carry.
hl15.background: Before this study, doctors and scientists knew that severe events in childhood could cause stress or sadness, but most believed these effects would fade with time. The 1990s was a period when most American families were busy balancing work and home, and healthcare focused mainly on treating illness, not investigating the causes rooted so far in the past. The people involved in the study were patients at a large health clinic in San Diego. Many led everyday lives—going to work, raising families, and managing normal stresses. Few realized that events from their earlier years, even if long hidden or unspoken, could still be shaping their bodies and minds decades later. This study invited thousands to look back and remember, offering insights into how the stories of their childhood might still be quietly unfolding within them.

hl16.talk: What are some simple ways we can help others stay healthy and safe?
hl16.child: Long ago, many children and mothers got very sick and died because they didn't have clean water or doctors to help them. People worked hard to bring clean water, food, and medicine to these families, and now many more children and mothers are healthy and happy.
hl16.learn: This history teaches us that significant progress often comes from consistent, humble efforts rather than grand gestures. By focusing on fundamental needs—clean water, proper nutrition, basic medical care—we can achieve profound outcomes. It encourages us to value and support the essential, everyday work that contributes to the well-being of our communities, recognizing that faithfulness in small things can lead to great blessings.
hl16.matters: This remarkable reduction in mortality rates underscores the profound impact of simple, accessible health interventions. For families of faith, it serves as a testament to the power of collective effort and the importance of caring for the most vulnerable among us. It reminds us that through dedicated service and stewardship of the resources provided by Heavenly Father, we can make a significant difference in the lives of others, embodying the principle of loving our neighbors as ourselves.

sources.name: World Health Organization: Child Mortality (Under 5 Years)
World Health Organization: Maternal Mortality
UNICEF: Maternal, Newborn and Child Survival
Global Analysis Shows Maternal Mortality Fell 41% Since 2000

hl16.evidence: Historical and scientific data confirm the effectiveness of these interventions. The World Health Organization reports that between 2000 and 2024, the global under-five mortality rate declined by approximately 60%, largely due to expanded access to immunization, improved nutrition, better management of childhood illnesses, and wider availability of skilled health personnel at birth. Additionally, a study published in 2025 found that improved maternity care accounted for 61.2% of the overall decline in maternal mortality during this period, highlighting the critical role of accessible and quality healthcare services.
hl16.happened: Between 2000 and 2024, the world witnessed a significant decline in child and maternal mortality rates. The number of children under five who died each year dropped from over 9.9 million in 2000 to 4.9 million in 2024. Similarly, maternal deaths decreased by about 40% during this period. This progress was largely due to simple, cost-effective interventions: providing clean water and sanitation, expanding vaccination programs, administering antibiotics, promoting oral rehydration therapy, improving nutrition, and ensuring skilled health personnel attended births. These measures, though unglamorous, saved millions of lives worldwide.
hl16.scripture: The scriptures teach us the value of caring for others. In Matthew 25:40, Jesus says, 'Verily I say unto you, Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me.' This passage emphasizes that serving those in need is akin to serving the Lord Himself. Similarly, Mosiah 2:17 in the Book of Mormon states, 'When ye are in the service of your fellow beings ye are only in the service of your God.' These teachings inspire us to engage in acts of compassion and service, reflecting the love of Christ in our daily lives.
hl16.background: At the turn of the 21st century, many regions, especially in sub-Saharan Africa and Southern Asia, faced high rates of child and maternal deaths. Health systems were often under-resourced, and access to basic medical care was limited. Common causes of death included preventable diseases like pneumonia, diarrhea, and malaria, as well as complications during childbirth. Daily life in these areas was marked by challenges such as inadequate sanitation, limited access to clean water, and insufficient nutrition, all contributing to the high mortality rates among mothers and children.

lg01.talk: Why do you think it is important to write things down, like in your journal or the scriptures?
lg01.child: Long ago, people in Sumer started writing by pressing funny marks into clay with sticks. This helped them remember things and tell stories that would last a long time. Because of their writing, we can still read their stories today.
lg01.learn: From the story of Sumerian writing, we learn that Heavenly Father can use even the smallest inventions to help His children. Writing began as a simple way to count grain, but soon carried words that spoke of faith, hope, and courage—and even stories like the flood, echoing truths found in scripture. When we honor and keep records in our own lives, whether that’s a journal, a letter, or family scripture study, we’re continuing an important tradition that stretches back to the world’s first writers.
lg01.matters: The beginning of writing matters deeply for families of faith. Before words could be saved on a page, God’s messages depended on memory and retelling; they might be changed or forgotten.
