The spread of Greek culture and language across the Mediterranean, especially after Alexander the Great’s conquests, further amplified these ideas. Scholars agree that Greek philosophical concepts directly influenced early Christian writings, especially in how they described Christ and His divine nature.
sd08.happened: Around 500 years before Jesus was born, Greek thinkers began asking deep questions about the world around them. Among these thinkers were philosophers like Heraclitus, Plato, and Stoics, who all discussed something called the 'Logos.' Logos is a Greek word that means 'word,' 'reason,' or 'order.' These Greeks taught that there was a guiding principle of reason in the universe—a force that makes sense of what we see and keeps everything ordered. Plato, a famous philosopher, also taught that beyond the things we see—like trees, rocks, and people—there are perfect, unchanging ideals called Forms, like perfect truth, beauty, and goodness. He believed these Forms were more real than anything in the world and that our souls could know them. As time went on, these ideas became very important in Greek culture and helped set the stage for new ways of thinking about life, God, and the world.
sd08.scripture: The Gospel of John begins, 'In the beginning was the Word (Logos), and the Word was with God, and the Word was God' (John 1:1). This passage uses the Greek term Logos to name Jesus Christ as the divine, guiding force in creation. Modern scripture teaches that God is a God of order (Doctrine and Covenants 88:34–40), and His creations are governed by laws and reason. These ideas echo the ancient Greek search for order and truth beyond what we can see.
sd08.background: At this time, Greece was not a single country but a collection of city-states like Athens, Sparta, and Corinth, spread around the Mediterranean Sea. People lived in small towns with lively markets and spent time discussing big questions in public spaces. Religion was a part of daily life, but the Greeks also loved to debate and wonder about the gods, nature, and the meaning of life. Travel and trade brought them into contact with other cultures, sharing ideas and goods. Before the great philosophers, stories about gods explained almost everything, but now, some Greeks wanted logical answers, using their minds to understand the world instead of just relying on old myths.

sd09.talk: How can we show that everyone is our brother or sister, no matter where they come from?
sd09.child: A long time ago, some people called Stoics taught that being good is what really matters. They believed everyone is important and should be treated like family. Their ideas helped people understand the gospel of Jesus when it was shared later.
sd09.learn: We learn that honest and kind ideas can prepare people’s hearts for greater truth that comes later. Stoicism teaches that everyone is worthy of respect because we all share something deep within. It reminds us to look for truth wherever it is found, and to treat everyone as brothers and sisters, even if they seem different from us. Like the Stoics, we can try to live with courage and kindness each day.
sd09.matters: The Stoic teaching that everyone shares the same inner worth helped prepare people to hear the gospel that Paul and other apostles shared years later. When Paul wrote that in Christ ‘there is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither bond nor free’ (Galatians 3:28), he was sharing radical good news in words people could understand. For families who believe each person is a child of Heavenly Father, this story shows that truth can be prepared across cultures and centuries. Stoicism’s sense of brotherhood and personal virtue helped make the world ready to hear the idea that all are equal before God and deserve kindness.

sources.name: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Stoicism
Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Stoicism
BBC History: The ancient philosophy of Stoicism
ChurchofJesusChrist.org: All Are Alike unto God (2 Nephi 26:33)

sd09.evidence: We know about Stoicism from many surviving writings by Stoic teachers like Seneca, Epictetus, and Marcus Aurelius. Ancient histories and Roman letters mention public lectures and discussions of Stoicism in Rome and other cities from the second century BCE onward. Evidence from ancient inscriptions and documents shows that Roman society began to use Stoic ideas to discuss law and fairness, though the world was still far from equal. Modern historians see the influence of Stoic vocabulary and ideas in early Christian writings, including Paul’s letters, showing that these ancient teachings were well known and discussed at the time. Archaeologists have found statues and household items featuring Stoic maxims, showing how widely respected the school was.
sd09.happened: Around 100 years before Jesus was born, the Stoic philosophers were teaching in Rome and throughout the Mediterranean. Their main idea was that virtue, or good character, was the only thing that truly mattered and could make someone happy. To the Stoics, things like wealth, health, or honor were not real goods; they could come and go, but virtue stays with you always. One of their most surprising ideas for their time was that all human beings, not just Romans or Greeks, share a common rational nature—meaning everyone can think, choose, and do good. This meant everyone was like a brother or sister, no matter where they were born, what language they spoke, or if they were free or enslaved. The Stoics believed that external troubles like sickness, poverty, or other people's actions can't take away your inner peace if you live by reason and try to be good. They often gathered in public places, like porches (‘stoa’ in Greek), to teach and discuss these ideas, inviting anyone to listen. Their teachings made such an impact that even people who weren't philosophers picked up the ideas in their daily lives, and later Christian teachers like Paul would use similar words to explain the gospel.
sd09.scripture: Paul’s letters reflect Stoic ideas when he says that nothing can separate us from God’s love (Romans 8:38-39), and when he teaches about spiritual gifts given to everyone (1 Corinthians 12). The Book of Mormon teaches that God ‘inviteth them all to come unto him and partake of his goodness; and he denieth none that come unto him, black and white, bond and free, male and female’ (2 Nephi 26:33). While Stoicism is not scripture, its principle—that each person has value and should be treated as a brother or sister—echoes plainly in these sacred texts.
sd09.background: By the time Stoicism was spreading, Rome ruled much of the known world. People in the Roman Empire spoke many languages and came from different cultures. The city of Rome was crowded and busy, with senators, merchants, soldiers, slaves, and freedmen from many nations. Most people believed some were born better than others, and slavery was very common: slaves were often seen as property, not people. Earlier, Greek philosophers had searched for wisdom about how to live well, but few had said that everyone was truly equal. Stoic teachers took ideas from thinkers before them and brought them to the heart of Roman life, making them something “for everyone,” not just a few scholars. Ordinary people might not have become Stoics, but they could hear and share the Stoic ideals. Their attitude towards others—slaves, women, foreigners—was more respectful than was usual at the time, even if not every Stoic lived up to their own teachings.

sd10.talk: How can we show respect for the world Heavenly Father created for us?
sd10.child: Long ago, people in places like Ireland and Scotland believed that the world around them was very special and close to heaven. They thought that trees, rivers, and mountains were gifts from God and should be treated with care. They also believed that being kind and welcoming to others was very important.
sd10.learn: From Celtic Christianity, we learn the importance of seeing the divine in the world around us. Recognizing the sacredness of creation can inspire us to be better stewards of the environment and to appreciate the beauty and wonder of nature. It also teaches us the value of community and hospitality, encouraging us to build strong, supportive relationships with others and to serve those in need.
sd10.matters: Celtic Christianity's emphasis on the sacredness of creation offers a perspective that aligns with the gospel's teachings about the earth as a divine gift. This tradition reminds us to see the world around us as a reflection of God's handiwork and to treat it with respect and care. For families of faith, embracing this view can deepen our appreciation for nature and encourage us to be stewards of the environment. It also highlights the importance of community and hospitality, values that strengthen family bonds and foster a sense of belonging and service to others.

sources.name: Celtic Christianity
Ancient Celtic religion
Celtic Animism

sd10.evidence: Historical records and archaeological findings provide insights into Celtic Christianity. Writings from the early medieval period, such as the works of Saint Patrick and Saint Columba, reveal a faith deeply connected to nature and community. Artifacts like the intricately decorated Celtic crosses and illuminated manuscripts, such as the Book of Kells, reflect a fusion of Christian symbolism with traditional Celtic art, emphasizing the sacredness of creation. These sources collectively illustrate a tradition that honored both the Creator and His creation.
sd10.happened: In the early 5th century, as the Roman Empire's influence waned in the British Isles, a distinctive form of Christianity emerged among the Celtic peoples of Ireland, Scotland, Wales, and Brittany. This tradition, known as Celtic Christianity, integrated Christian teachings with the Celts' deep reverence for nature. They viewed creation as sacred, believing that the divine permeated the natural world, making every place a 'thin place' where heaven and earth were closely connected. This perspective led them to see every person as bearing the image of God, and they considered creation itself a form of revelation. Community and hospitality were central to their faith, reflecting their belief in the interconnectedness of all life. Monastic communities flourished, with figures like Saint Patrick in Ireland and Saint Columba in Scotland leading missionary efforts that preserved and spread Christianity during a time of significant upheaval.
sd10.scripture: The scriptures teach that the earth and all things in it were created by God and are good. In Genesis 1:31, it states, 'And God saw every thing that he had made, and, behold, it was very good.' The Doctrine and Covenants also emphasizes the sacredness of creation, instructing us to 'behold the glory of the Lord, and the riches of eternity' in the things He has made (D&C 88:47). These passages encourage us to recognize the divine in the natural world and to treat it with reverence.
sd10.background: Before the arrival of Christianity, the Celtic peoples practiced a polytheistic religion deeply intertwined with nature. They believed that spirits inhabited natural features like rivers, mountains, and trees, and they held rituals to honor these spirits. Daily life was closely connected to the land, with communities relying on agriculture and livestock. The transition to Christianity began in the 4th and 5th centuries, as missionaries introduced the new faith. Rather than completely abandoning their previous beliefs, the Celts integrated Christian teachings with their existing reverence for nature, leading to a unique expression of Christianity that honored both the Creator and His creation.

sd11.talk: Why do you think people from different places have stories about gods who come to visit them?
sd11.child: Long ago, people in places like Mexico and Guatemala believed in a special god called the Feathered Serpent. This god was part bird and part snake, showing how the sky and earth are connected. They built big temples to honor him, and during certain times of the year, shadows would make it look like a snake was moving down the temple steps.
sd11.learn: The story of the Feathered Serpent teaches us about the deep spiritual connections ancient cultures sought with the divine. It reminds us that across different societies, there is a common yearning to understand our origins and purpose. Recognizing these shared narratives can foster greater appreciation for the diverse ways humanity seeks and experiences the divine.
sd11.matters: The enduring presence of the Feathered Serpent across Mesoamerican cultures highlights a shared spiritual framework and the importance of deities that bridge the earthly and the divine. For families of faith, this underscores the universal human desire to understand and connect with higher powers. The narratives of a divine figure arriving from the east and promising to return resonate with themes of prophecy and fulfillment found in various religious traditions, including Christianity. Such parallels invite reflection on the ways different cultures perceive and anticipate divine intervention.

sources.name: Kukulkan - World History Encyclopedia
Kukulkan: The Legend of the Feathered Serpent | Mayan.org
Kukulkan - Mesoamerican Pantheon Deity | Mythos Atlas

sd11.evidence: Archaeological findings, such as the Temple of the Feathered Serpent in Teotihuacan and the Temple of Kukulkan in Chichen Itza, provide tangible evidence of the widespread veneration of this deity. Iconography depicting a feathered serpent appears in various artifacts, murals, and sculptures across Mesoamerica, indicating its significance. Historical records from Spanish chroniclers and indigenous codices also reference the Feathered Serpent, though interpretations vary. Some scholars suggest that the legends of a light-skinned deity arriving from the east may have been influenced by post-conquest narratives, making it challenging to separate pre-Columbian beliefs from later interpretations.
sd11.happened: In ancient Mesoamerica, the Feathered Serpent, known as Quetzalcoatl to the Aztecs and Kukulkan to the Maya, was a revered deity symbolizing the union of earth and sky. This god was associated with creation, wind, rain, and the morning star. The earliest depictions of the Feathered Serpent appear in Teotihuacan around 200 AD, but the concept likely originated earlier with the Olmec civilization. Over time, the worship of this deity spread across various cultures, including the Maya and Aztecs. In Maya tradition, Kukulkan was both a god and a cultural hero who brought knowledge and civilization. The Temple of Kukulkan at Chichen Itza is a testament to his significance, where during the equinoxes, a shadow resembling a serpent descends the pyramid's staircase, symbolizing the god's arrival. Some legends describe the Feathered Serpent as a light-skinned figure who arrived from the east and promised to return, a narrative that has intrigued scholars and believers alike.
sd11.scripture: While the scriptures do not directly mention the Feathered Serpent, the Book of Mormon records Christ's appearance to the Nephites in 3 Nephi 11. This event shares thematic similarities with Mesoamerican legends of a divine teacher who came from the east. Additionally, the Bible speaks of God's outreach to all nations, as in Acts 17:26-27, emphasizing that He 'hath made of one blood all nations of men... that they should seek the Lord.' These passages suggest that divine manifestations are not limited to a single people or region but are part of a broader, universal plan.
sd11.background: Mesoamerica, encompassing regions of present-day Mexico, Guatemala, and Honduras, was home to advanced civilizations like the Olmec, Maya, and Aztec. These societies developed complex social structures, impressive architectural feats, and rich mythologies. Daily life was deeply intertwined with religious beliefs, with deities governing aspects like agriculture, weather, and celestial events. The Feathered Serpent emerged as a central figure in this spiritual landscape, embodying the connection between the earthly and the divine. The Olmecs, often considered the 'mother culture' of Mesoamerica, laid the foundation for many religious concepts, including the Feathered Serpent, which subsequent cultures adapted and integrated into their own belief systems.

sd12.talk: Why do you think people in different places all believe in a loving Creator?
sd12.child: Long ago, Native American people believed in a loving Great Spirit who made everything. They prayed to thank Him and tried to live in harmony with the earth. This helps us remember that Heavenly Father loves all His children, all around the world.
sd12.learn: We can learn that Heavenly Father’s truth and love are not bound by time or place. He has always reached out to His children, giving them ways to know Him even if they never had the Bible or the Book of Mormon. Learning about others’ faith traditions can help us be more humble, more appreciative, and more willing to see God’s hand everywhere. It also teaches us that gratitude and respect for creation are holy habits.
sd12.matters: This belief in a Great Spirit matters because it shows how God’s light can reach every heart, no matter when or where they are born. For families of faith, it is a gentle reminder that Heavenly Father’s love and truth can be found everywhere—a lesson of respect for all His children. When later missionaries taught Native Americans about God the Father, many already understood Him as a loving, all-powerful Creator. This shows that seeds of truth had already been planted. Respecting this heritage can help us see God’s hand moving in every nation.

sources.name: Smithsonian National Museum of the American Indian: Native American Religions
Encyclopedia Britannica: Native American religions
Purdue University: Native American Spirituality

sd12.evidence: Historians and anthropologists who have studied Native American beliefs find strong evidence that many Indigenous North American communities held a foundational belief in a supreme Creator or Great Spirit. While every tribe had unique names, stories, and traditions, the similarity of a single, loving, creative force is widely noted in oral histories and traditional practices. Early Jesuit missionaries in the 1600s wrote about meeting people who already believed in a single Creator. Today, records and oral histories shared by Native elders, as well as studies from university and museum programs, confirm that this tradition was embedded in society long before Europeans arrived. Artifacts, stories, and ceremonies reflect these deep beliefs, even as details varied by region and tribe.
sd12.happened: Long before European explorers ever set foot in North America, hundreds of Native American nations lived across forests, plains, deserts, and mountains. Though each nation had its own traditions, languages, and stories, many shared a gentle and deep belief in what they called the Great Spirit. This Great Spirit was seen as the Creator of all things—the earth, the sky, people, and animals—and was understood as a good and loving power. When people wanted to show gratitude for a good harvest, a child’s healing, or the beauty of nature, they offered prayers or ceremonies to the Great Spirit. These ceremonies often focused on harmony: being in balance with each other, with the land, and with the animals. Every year, families gathered in circles, listened to elders tell of the Great Spirit, and gave thanks for life and the world they were given. This sense of a loving, watchful Creator runs like a strong, quiet river through the history and memory of many Indigenous peoples.
sd12.scripture: In Acts 17:22-28, Paul teaches that God ‘is not far from every one of us’ and that He gives ‘life, and breath, and all things’ to all people. The Book of Mormon confirms that the Lord speaks to all nations (2 Nephi 29:7) and that ‘all are alike unto God’ (2 Nephi 26:33). These passages support the idea that Heavenly Father has given light and witness to all His children, reaching across languages and cultures—even before the fullness of the gospel was shared with them.
sd12.background: Around 2,500 years ago, the land we now call North America was home to many different societies. These peoples farmed, hunted, and fished. They built villages, traded, and cared for each other. Children learned from their elders not just how to survive, but how to live in a way that respected all living things. Religion and daily life were closely joined. The world was seen as full—every stream, stone, and star had meaning. Most nations honored those who had come before and felt responsible to those who would follow after. Even though languages and customs were different from place to place, the idea of a great Creator or Great Spirit was a thread tying many together. In this way, Indigenous religious life was both practical and uplifting, touching every part of a person’s day.

sd13.talk: Can you think of a time when you felt sad because someone you love was making a bad choice?
sd13.child: Long ago, the people of the Andes believed in a kind creator named Viracocha, who made the sun, moon, stars, and people. They said he loved his children so much that he cried when they were sad or did wrong things.
sd13.learn: The story of Viracocha teaches us that the concept of a compassionate and sorrowful creator is not unique to one culture or religion. It reminds us that Heavenly Father has revealed His nature to various peoples in ways they could understand. This understanding encourages us to respect and learn from the spiritual insights of different cultures, recognizing the universal truths that connect us all as children of God.
sd13.matters: The story of Viracocha is significant because it illustrates a universal theme: a creator who loves and feels sorrow for his children. This resonates with the scriptural account in Moses 7:28-29, where God weeps for the wickedness of the earth. For families of faith, this parallel underscores the idea that Heavenly Father has revealed aspects of His loving nature to all His children, regardless of time or place. Recognizing these shared truths can deepen our appreciation for the diverse ways in which God's love has been manifested throughout history.

sources.name: Viracocha - World History Encyclopedia
Viracocha - Wikipedia
Viracocha: The Nature and Antiquity of the Andean High God | Peabody Museum of Archaeology & Ethnology

sd13.evidence: Archaeological findings, such as the monumental structures at Tiwanaku near Lake Titicaca, provide insights into the religious practices of pre-Inca cultures. The Gateway of the Sun, a significant artifact at Tiwanaku, features a central figure that some scholars associate with Viracocha, depicted with a crown and holding staffs. However, interpretations vary, and some argue that this identification may be influenced by later Inca traditions. Additionally, Spanish chroniclers recorded accounts of Viracocha, describing him as a bearded man who traveled among the people, teaching and performing miracles. While these accounts offer valuable information, they were documented after the Spanish conquest and may reflect a blend of indigenous beliefs and European interpretations.
sd13.happened: Long ago, in the Andean regions of present-day Peru, Bolivia, and Ecuador, the people revered Viracocha as their supreme creator deity. According to their beliefs, Viracocha emerged from the waters of Lake Titicaca and brought forth the sun, moon, stars, and humanity. He was often depicted wearing the sun as a crown, holding thunderbolts, and with tears streaming from his eyes, symbolizing rain. After creating the world, Viracocha traveled across the lands, teaching people the arts of civilization and imparting wisdom. Once his work was complete, he departed across the sea, promising to return one day. This narrative highlights a creator who not only formed the world but also deeply cared for his creation, expressing sorrow and compassion for humanity.
sd13.scripture: In Moses 7:28-29, we read of Enoch witnessing God weeping over the wickedness of His children: 'And it came to pass that the God of heaven looked upon the residue of the people, and he wept.' This passage reveals a God who is deeply compassionate and sorrowful over the choices of His children. Similarly, the Andean depiction of Viracocha as a weeping creator reflects this profound truth—that our Creator is not distant or indifferent but is intimately concerned with our well-being and choices.
sd13.background: Before the rise of the Inca Empire, the Andean region was home to various cultures, each with its own traditions and beliefs. The people lived in close harmony with nature, relying on agriculture, particularly the cultivation of maize and potatoes, and domesticated animals like llamas and alpacas. They built impressive structures and developed complex societies. The concept of a creator god like Viracocha was central to their worldview, reflecting their understanding of the universe and their place within it. This belief system provided a foundation for the later Inca civilization, which integrated and expanded upon these earlier traditions.

sd14.talk: Why do you think some people kept the idea of a loving, great God a special secret?
sd14.child: Many, many years ago, the Maori people had a special name for God: Io. They believed He was the father of everything and the source of all light. Only special leaders knew this name and taught about Him very carefully.
sd14.learn: From the story of Io, we learn that truth can be found in many places, prepared by God in ways that fit different people and their needs. It teaches us to be humble and curious about how others have experienced the divine, and to honor the quiet faith that often grows in unexpected places. It also helps us see that our Heavenly Father is loving and aware of all His children around the world.
sd14.matters: For families of faith today, stories like that of Io remind us that Heavenly Father’s truth is sown in many places, often long before missionaries or scriptures reach a land. It matters to our world because it shows respect for the faith and searching hearts of all peoples. In the case of the Maori, their belief in a supreme and loving Father God helped prepare the way for the restored gospel when missionaries finally arrived. For families, it’s a gentle witness that God knows His children across the earth and prepares them in ways that are right for them.

sources.name: Te Ara - The Encyclopedia of New Zealand: Io – supreme being
Encyclopædia Britannica: Maori
Church News: Maori and the Book of Mormon

sd14.evidence: Historians and anthropologists have found that the tradition of Io was recorded in Maori oral histories and first written down by Maori elders in the nineteenth century, especially as Christian missionaries arrived and asked more about traditional beliefs. Some scholars debate whether the concept of Io was as ancient as claimed or whether it was shaped partly by contact with Christian ideas, as Io was not publicly spoken of before the 1800s. However, respected Maori sources and cultural leaders have maintained that the tradition of Io was kept sacred and secret for many centuries. Modern scholarship affirms that knowledge about Io existed among Maori priests before widespread European contact, though exactly how far back it goes is still studied and discussed.
sd14.happened: Around 1000 BCE, deep in the Pacific, the Maori and other Polynesian peoples carried with them a sacred tradition of a supreme being named Io. Unlike the gods commonly spoken of in day-to-day stories—gods who governed the winds, seas, or forests—Io was different. Io was seen as above all others, eternal and uncreated, the father and source of all life. This knowledge was so sacred that only the highest priests, the tohunga, were taught of Him, and then only after a long and careful preparation. These teachings were passed on quietly from one generation to the next, held close and respected as the deepest spiritual truth. Io was described as the God of light and truth, dwelling in the highest heaven, and seen as the source of wisdom, order, and all that was good. This belief guided the priests in their prayers, rituals, and understanding of life itself, giving a foundation of faith that something above and loving watched over them, even if ordinary people did not always hear the name Io in their everyday lives.
sd14.scripture: While the Bible teaches plainly of one God, the Father of all, such as in Malachi 2:10 (“Have we not all one father?”), and the Book of Mormon testifies that God is “the same yesterday, today, and forever” (Mormon 9:9), there is no direct mention of Io or Polynesian beliefs. However, the principle in Alma 29:8 speaks to this: the Lord “doth grant unto all nations, of their own nation and tongue, to teach his word.” Doctrine and Covenants 1:2 also assures us that God speaks to all “the nations of the earth.”
sd14.background: The people living in the Pacific islands at this time were master navigators, traveling across vast stretches of ocean in great double-hulled canoes. They settled islands from Hawai’i in the north, to Easter Island in the east, and New Zealand in the south. Their days were shaped by fishing, farming, and caring for their families, but also by a deep trust in the unseen world of spirits and ancestors. Religion was at the heart of community life, guiding decisions, ceremonies, and connections to the land. Among the Maori and other Polynesian groups, stories of the gods were passed in chants and songs, but the special knowledge of Io was kept in sacred trust by the chosen few. Life was not easy, but it was rich in meaning and ties to each other and to the divine.

sd15.t: Universal: The Flood in Every Culture
sd15.talk: Why do you think so many different cultures have stories about a big flood?
sd15.child: Long ago, many people told stories about a big flood that covered the world. In these tales, a good person built a big boat to save their family and animals. After the flood, they started life anew.
sd15.learn: These flood stories teach us about the resilience of the human spirit and the importance of preparedness and faith in the face of adversity. They remind us that while challenges and disasters may arise, hope and renewal are always possible. For families, these narratives can serve as lessons in morality, obedience, and the consequences of actions, emphasizing the importance of living righteously and being mindful stewards of the earth.
sd15.matters: The widespread presence of flood stories across various cultures highlights a shared human experience and the importance of water in shaping civilizations. For families of faith, these narratives can be seen as evidence of a common ancestry and shared history, reinforcing the belief that humanity is interconnected. Recognizing these shared stories can foster a sense of unity and understanding among diverse peoples, emphasizing the universal themes of survival, renewal, and divine intervention.

sources.name: List of flood myths
Evidence for a Flood
Is There Proof of Noah's Flood?

sd15.evidence: While many cultures have flood myths, scientific evidence for a global flood covering the entire earth is lacking. Geological studies indicate that sedimentary layers and fossil records were formed over millions of years through various processes, not a single catastrophic event. However, there is evidence of significant regional floods in history. For instance, research suggests that around 7,500 years ago, the Mediterranean Sea breached a natural dam, leading to the rapid flooding of the Black Sea basin. Such events could have inspired local flood legends, which over time, may have been adapted into the broader narratives found in various cultures.
sd15.happened: Long ago, many cultures around the world told stories about a massive flood that covered the earth. These tales often describe a divine being who, displeased with humanity, sent a great deluge to cleanse the world. In these narratives, a righteous person or family is warned in advance, builds a vessel, and saves themselves along with various animals. After the waters recede, they repopulate the earth. For example, the Mesopotamian "Epic of Gilgamesh" tells of Utnapishtim, who was instructed by the gods to build a boat to survive a flood meant to destroy humanity. Similarly, in Hindu tradition, the story of Manu describes a man who is forewarned by a fish about an impending flood and builds a boat to save himself and the seven sages. These stories, though differing in details, share a common theme of a catastrophic flood and a chosen survivor, suggesting a shared memory or experience among diverse peoples.
sd15.scripture: The Bible recounts the story of Noah's Ark in Genesis 6-9, where God, seeing the wickedness of humanity, decides to bring a flood to cleanse the earth. Noah, a righteous man, is instructed to build an ark to save his family and pairs of every animal species. After the floodwaters recede, God establishes a covenant with Noah, symbolized by a rainbow, promising never to destroy the earth by flood again. This narrative underscores themes of obedience, faith, and God's mercy.
sd15.background: In ancient times, civilizations often settled near rivers and bodies of water, which were vital for agriculture, transportation, and sustenance. However, these areas were also prone to flooding. Such natural disasters could be devastating, destroying homes, crops, and lives. The unpredictability and magnitude of these floods left a significant impact on these societies, leading them to incorporate such events into their oral traditions and myths. Over generations, these stories evolved, reflecting each culture's values, beliefs, and experiences, but the core narrative of a great flood remained consistent.

sd16.talk: Can you think of a time today when someone treated you with kindness, or when you did that for someone else?
sd16.child: Everywhere people have lived, they've learned to be kind to others because they wanted kindness too. Treating others how you want to be treated makes the world a better place.
sd16.learn: We can learn that every person, no matter when or where they lived, has been given a sense of right and wrong by Heavenly Father. The Golden Rule reminds us to pause and consider the feelings and needs of those around us. When we live by this principle, we carry forward an ancient truth that binds communities and families together in safety and peace.
sd16.matters: The Golden Rule matters because it teaches us that kindness and respect are not only good but essential for all to flourish. For a family of faith, it is a sign that Heavenly Father cares for all His children, planting in every heart the desire to treat others fairly. This principle builds trust in homes, schools, and nations, and helps us see others as He sees them, no matter where they live or what they believe. Teaching our children the Golden Rule helps them become peacemakers and good friends, both in our families and in the world beyond.

sources.name: BBC Ethics - The Golden Rule
Encyclopaedia Britannica - Golden Rule
The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints - Bible Dictionary: Golden Rule

sd16.evidence: Scholars have collected versions of the Golden Rule from every major civilization with written records, including ancient Egypt, Greece, China, India, and the Americas. Although these cultures were often separated by great distances and had no contact, their core teaching to treat others with fairness and kindness appears independently. Historians believe this reflects a shared human capacity for empathy, which psychologists have observed even in young children. Although some details differ, the core message is the same. Archaeological evidence, such as ancient texts, scrolls, and inscriptions, confirms that kindness and fairness were taught long before the modern era. This widespread presence suggests that the Golden Rule is one of humanity’s earliest and most lasting moral ideas.
sd16.happened: Long before there were cities, countries, or even written language, people all around the world began thinking about how to treat one another. In every major culture, from ancient Egypt and China, to the first people of India and Greece, something wonderful happened: each community found their own way to say that we should treat others as we hope to be treated. This simple idea became known as the Golden Rule. Some taught it in wise sayings passed from parents to children; others wrote it in sacred books or shared it as stories and parables. In China, Confucius shared it around 500 BC. Buddhists and Hindus taught their own versions about the same time. A bit later, it is found in Jewish teachings, and then in the teachings of Jesus Christ, who said, 'All things whatsoever ye would that men should do to you, do ye even so to them.' Later, Islam and many other faiths passed on this same wisdom. These people lived in different places and times, often without knowing of each other's existence, yet they discovered this golden truth on their own.
sd16.scripture: In the Bible, Jesus teaches the Golden Rule in Matthew 7:12, 'Therefore all things whatsoever ye would that men should do to you, do ye even so to them: for this is the law and the prophets.' The Book of Mormon shares related counsel, such as in Mosiah 2:17, where King Benjamin says, 'when ye are in the service of your fellow beings ye are only in the service of your God.' Doctrine and Covenants 59:6, about loving one another, and Moses 7:18 in the Pearl of Great Price, where the people of Zion are described as being 'of one heart and one mind,' also touch on this principle.
sd16.background: Early humanity lived in small villages or tribes, working together to gather food, care for animals, and find shelter. Life was often uncertain, so people depended on one another for survival. Most did not have writing or schools, but they learned by watching, listening, and sharing stories around their fires. As families grew into larger communities, rules for living together became more important. Spiritual leaders, wise elders, and parents tried to help everyone get along and be safe. Their advice was shaped by their experiences and their desire to make life better for everyone. In time, their simple rules of kindness, fairness, and respect became core teachings passed down through generations.

sf01.t: Honour Thy Father and Thy Mother
sf01.talk: Why do you think it's important to honor your parents?
sf01.child: Long ago, God gave Moses ten special rules called the Ten Commandments. One of them tells us to honor our parents so we can have a happy and long life. This means listening to them, helping them, and showing them love.
sf01.learn: This event teaches us the enduring value of family and the importance of honoring our parents. It reminds us that strong family relationships are foundational to a stable and prosperous society. By respecting and caring for our parents, we not only fulfill a divine commandment but also set an example for future generations, fostering a culture of love, respect, and mutual support.
sf01.matters: The commandment to honor one's parents underscored the importance of family as the cornerstone of society. It established a moral framework that emphasized respect, responsibility, and care within the family unit. For families of faith today, this principle reinforces the belief that strong familial bonds are vital for personal growth and societal stability. It teaches that honoring parents is not just a duty but a path to receiving God's blessings and ensuring the well-being of future generations.

sources.name: Ten Commandments - World History Encyclopedia
Commandments, the Ten - The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints
Ten Commandments - Encyclopedia of The Bible - Bible Gateway
Ten Commandments | Encyclopedia.com

sf01.evidence: The historical accuracy of the Israelites' exodus from Egypt and the events at Mount Sinai has been a subject of scholarly debate. While definitive archaeological evidence directly confirming these events is limited, some scholars point to ancient inscriptions and cultural parallels that suggest a historical basis for the narratives. For instance, the discovery of proto-Sinaitic inscriptions in the Sinai Peninsula indicates early forms of writing that could align with the period traditionally associated with the Exodus. However, the exact dating and interpretation of these findings remain topics of ongoing research and discussion.
sf01.happened: Around 1450 BC, the Israelites, having been freed from Egyptian slavery, camped at Mount Sinai. There, Moses ascended the mountain and received the Ten Commandments directly from God. These commandments were inscribed on two stone tablets and served as the foundation for Israelite law and covenant with God. Among them, the fifth commandment stood out: "Honor thy father and thy mother, that thy days may be long upon the land which the Lord thy God giveth thee." This commandment uniquely included a promise of longevity and prosperity for those who honored their parents. The Israelites committed to these laws, establishing a society where family was central, and responsibilities toward parents were deeply valued.
sf01.scripture: The fifth commandment is explicitly stated in Exodus 20:12: "Honor thy father and thy mother: that thy days may be long upon the land which the Lord thy God giveth thee." This directive is reiterated in Deuteronomy 5:16. In the New Testament, the Apostle Paul references this commandment in Ephesians 6:2-3, emphasizing its significance and the promise attached to it. Additionally, the Book of Mormon echoes the importance of honoring parents in Mosiah 13:20.
sf01.background: The Israelites had endured centuries of slavery in Egypt, where they were subjected to harsh labor and oppression. Their deliverance, led by Moses, was marked by miraculous events, including the parting of the Red Sea. Upon reaching Mount Sinai, they were in a transitional phase, moving from a life of bondage to forming their own identity as a free nation under God's guidance. Daily life was communal, with a strong emphasis on obedience to God's laws, which were seen as essential for their survival and prosperity in the promised land.

sf02.talk: Why do you think it's important for families to spend time together and support each other?
sf02.child: Long ago in Sparta, boys had to leave their families at age seven to live and train together to become strong soldiers. They learned to be tough and to work as a team, but they didn't get to see their families much. This shows us how important it is to spend time with our families and take care of each other.
sf02.learn: The Spartan experience teaches us the importance of maintaining a balance between communal obligations and family responsibilities. While dedication to a larger cause is commendable, it should not come at the expense of family bonds and individual well-being. For families today, this serves as a reminder to prioritize nurturing relationships within the home and to be cautious of external influences that may seek to diminish the role of the family in society.
sf02.matters: The Spartan model offers a historical example of a society that prioritized the state over the family unit, leading to significant consequences. While it produced highly disciplined soldiers, this system also resulted in a decline in population, as the emphasis on communal living and military service overshadowed family life and reproduction. For families of faith, this serves as a reminder of the importance of balancing communal responsibilities with the nurturing and preservation of family bonds. It highlights the potential risks of allowing external institutions to overshadow the fundamental role of the family in society.

sources.name: Agoge - Spartan Library
How Ancient Sparta's Harsh Military System Trained Boys Into Fierce Warriors - HISTORY
Agoge, the Spartan Education Program - World History Encyclopedia

sf02.evidence: Historical accounts, particularly from ancient historians like Plutarch and Xenophon, provide detailed descriptions of the Spartan agoge and its practices. Plutarch notes that Spartan boys were taken from their families at age seven to begin their training, which included physical endurance tests and survival skills. Archaeological evidence supports the existence of communal barracks and training grounds that align with these descriptions. However, some aspects, such as the practice of exposing weak infants, are debated among scholars. While Plutarch describes infants being left to die if deemed unfit, modern archaeology has not found conclusive evidence to confirm systematic infanticide. This suggests that while the Spartan emphasis on strength and fitness is well-documented, some of the more extreme practices may have been exaggerated or misinterpreted over time.
sf02.happened: In ancient Sparta, beginning around the 7th century BC, the state implemented a rigorous education and training system known as the agoge. At the age of seven, boys were removed from their family homes and placed into communal groups under the supervision of state-appointed officials. This program aimed to cultivate discipline, endurance, and loyalty to Sparta. The boys underwent intense physical training, learned survival skills, and were encouraged to steal food to develop cunning, though they were punished if caught. They endured minimal clothing and slept on makeshift beds of reeds. This harsh regimen continued until they reached adulthood, preparing them to become the formidable warriors Sparta was renowned for. Marriage was permitted, but men often lived apart from their wives until the age of thirty, prioritizing their commitment to the state over family life. This societal structure emphasized the collective over the individual, with the state's needs taking precedence over personal and familial bonds.
sf02.scripture: The scriptures emphasize the importance of family and the responsibilities of parents toward their children. In the Book of Mormon, Enos reflects on the teachings of his father, stating, "I, Enos, knowing my father that he was a just man—for he taught me in his language, and also in the nurture and admonition of the Lord" (Enos 1:1). This passage underscores the role of parents in guiding and nurturing their children within the family unit. Additionally, in the Doctrine and Covenants, the Lord instructs parents to teach their children to understand the principles of the gospel (D&C 68:25). These teachings highlight the divine mandate for parents to be the primary educators and nurturers of their children, emphasizing the central role of the family in spiritual and moral development.
sf02.background: Sparta was a prominent city-state in ancient Greece, known for its military prowess and austere lifestyle. Unlike other Greek city-states that valued art and philosophy, Sparta focused on creating a society centered around warfare and discipline. The Spartan social system was built upon a class of free citizens who were full-time soldiers, supported by a larger population of non-citizens and enslaved people who handled agriculture and other necessary tasks. Daily life in Sparta was communal and regimented, with citizens expected to prioritize the needs of the state above personal desires. This environment fostered a culture where strength, obedience, and loyalty were paramount, and individual freedoms were often sacrificed for the greater good of the community.

sf03.talk: Why do you think Heavenly Father wants us to honor our parents and grandparents?
sf03.child: Confucius taught people to honor their parents and grandparents, and that families matter most. When families are strong and loving, everyone is happier and safer. This has helped people care for each other for thousands of years.
sf03.learn: We learn that a loving family is the beginning of a good society, and that showing respect for parents and grandparents can change not only homes, but whole communities and nations. The same principle is found both in the words of prophets and in the teachings of wise people all over the world. When we honor our families, we are part of something much bigger and older than ourselves, carrying forward a pattern that Heavenly Father wants for all His children.
sf03.matters: The teachings of Confucius still affect millions of families today. His focus on respecting parents and caring for elders has helped whole cultures value family ties and support systems, something many families of faith strive for too. These lessons remind us that God’s commandment to honor our parents is not just for one group of people or one time, but is a truth that blesses all of God’s children. In our families, when we show love and care for parents and grandparents, we’re building something strong and lasting—just like families have done in Asia for thousands of years.

sources.name: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Confucius
The British Museum: Who Was Confucius?
BBC: Confucianism and Family Values

sf03.evidence: Many historical records and ancient texts, such as the Analects, preserve Confucius’s teachings about family and social harmony. Archaeologists have found writings and ritual objects from his era that support his importance in shaping Chinese thought. Genetic and demographic studies show that East Asian societies have maintained long-lasting family structures and patterns of caring for elders across centuries. Even today, public ceremonies and holidays honoring ancestors remain important in East Asia. Western historians such as those from Stanford University agree that Confucius’s vision of filial piety has deeply influenced the culture, laws, and social policies of China and neighboring countries, outlasting many political systems.
sf03.happened: Confucius was a wise teacher who lived in China about 2,500 years ago, in a small town called Qufu. He taught his students about xiao, which means honoring and respecting parents and ancestors. Confucius believed this was the starting point for all good character. He said that if children learn to care for their parents, families will be peaceful and strong. And if all families are strong, then the whole country will be stable and fair. To Confucius, the way a parent cares for a child, and a child honors a parent, shapes every part of life—from family meals to how a king should act. His lessons about family relationships became so important that they spread from China to Korea, Japan, and Vietnam. Even governments were compared to families, with rulers expected to act like good fathers to their people. These ideas didn’t just stay in books or classrooms: they shaped laws, ceremonies, and everyday life for millions over thousands of years. People gathered on special days to honor ancestors, cared for elderly parents at home, and spoke kindly to elders. Through all sorts of battles and changing rulers, these family values have endured, showing the lasting mark of Confucius on East Asian societies.
sf03.scripture: The Bible teaches, 'Honour thy father and thy mother' (Exodus 20:12), which is the fifth of the Ten Commandments, and is echoed in Ephesians 6:1-3. The Book of Mormon encourages caring for families, such as in Mosiah 4:14-15, where parents are taught to raise their children in love and truth. Modern scripture in Doctrine and Covenants 68:25-28 calls parents to teach and care for their children. These verses show that respect and care within families is a principle taught across all scripture, fitting closely with what Confucius taught in his time.
sf03.background: Confucius lived during a time of great change and trouble in China, known as the Spring and Autumn period. There were many small kingdoms fighting and breaking old traditions. Most people were farmers, living in small villages with large families. Life could be hard, with little safety from war or hunger. In this world, the family was a person’s main source of strength and belonging. Families cared for each other and survived together. Confucius was one of many teachers traveling from court to court, sharing ideas about how to make society better. But unlike others, he believed good government began at home, with each person learning kindness and respect in their family first.

sf04.t: Rome Tries to Legislate Marriage Back
sf04.talk: Why do you think people need to want to be a family, not just be told to be a family?
sf04.child: A long time ago in Rome, leaders made strict rules to try to make people get married and have more children, but most people did not listen. Real families grow strong when we choose to love and help each other, not just because someone tells us to.
sf04.learn: We can learn that good laws can help, but they cannot replace the hearts and choices of people. Building strong families takes love, trust, and true commitment, not just rewards or penalties from outside. For us, it is a reminder to treasure our homes and relationships, and to teach our children the value of family with kindness and example, relying on Heavenly Father to help us do what is right.
sf04.matters: This event matters because it shows that laws alone cannot make people choose to marry or have children. True desire for family grows inside people’s hearts and is nurtured by love, faith, and trust, not by fear of punishment or hope of a reward. For families of faith, this reminds us that the family is a gift from Heavenly Father, and strong families need real care and teaching, not just rules. In any society, leaders may try to encourage marriage and children, but the real work happens at home, in the way we value and support each other.

sources.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Augustus - The Establishment of the Principate
Metropolitan Museum of Art - Daily Life in Ancient Rome
British Museum - Ancient Rome Family Life

sf04.evidence: Historians have found records of these laws and how they worked. Inscriptions, writings, and letters from Roman times describe how people tried to avoid the rules. Roman historian Tacitus, writing about 100 years later, said these laws had little real effect, and the elite were still not having many children. Other evidence from tombstones and family records confirms that the birth rate remained low. Archaeologists see no sudden change in family size after these laws passed. Scholars today agree that, while the laws were meant to help, they did not succeed in restoring large families among the Roman upper class.
sf04.happened: Around the year 18 BC, the leader of Rome, Caesar Augustus, grew worried because many wealthy Romans were not marrying or having children. Instead of big families, people were getting divorced and staying single, especially among the rich and powerful. Augustus believed this was bad for Rome's future, so he created strict new laws, called the Lex Julia and later the Lex Papia Poppaea. These laws made it harder for people to stay unmarried or without children by making them pay more taxes or miss out on inheritances. Married couples with three or more children were given rewards, and serious punishments were given to those caught in adultery. Augustus hoped that by making these rules, more Romans would choose to get married, stay faithful, and raise children for the good of the city and the empire. However, the people often found clever ways to avoid these laws or made excuses, and many did not change their behavior. The laws were unpopular and, over time, did little to solve the problems Augustus hoped they would fix. Even after these rules, the birth rate stayed low, and Rome’s leaders kept trying new laws but saw little improvement.
sf04.scripture: The scriptures teach much about the family. In Genesis 2:24, the Bible says, “Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh.” The Book of Mormon also praises the love within families, such as in 1 Nephi 1:1, where Nephi talks about being “born of goodly parents.” Doctrine and Covenants 68:25-28 gives parents the duty to teach their children faith, repentance, and the commandments. While no scripture commands government to make marriage laws like Augustus did, the principle of building family by love, teaching, and example, rather than compulsion, is clear.
sf04.background: Rome at this time was the center of a huge empire stretching across Europe, the Middle East, and North Africa. The richest Romans lived in big houses, enjoyed lots of parties and entertainments, but also faced pressures to keep family honor and wealth. Marriage was often arranged for money or alliances more than love. Divorce was common, and children were sometimes seen as a burden among the elite. Most ordinary Romans worked hard as farmers, soldiers, or traders, and their family life was simpler but also faced challenges. Augustus wanted Rome to be strong and last forever, and he thought traditional family life was important for that. But in his world, people’s habits were changing, and some did not want big families like before.

sf05.talk: Why do you think the early Christians chose to save and care for abandoned babies?
sf05.child: Long ago, in the Roman Empire, some families left unwanted babies outside to die. Early Christians believed every life was precious, so they saved these babies and raised them as their own.
sf05.learn: The actions of early Christians in rescuing and adopting abandoned infants teach us the profound impact of living according to compassionate and moral principles. By valuing and protecting the most vulnerable, they not only saved lives but also influenced societal norms and laws. This historical example reminds us that upholding the sanctity of life and the importance of the family can lead to meaningful change in society. It encourages us to be proactive in caring for those in need and to recognize the family as a vital institution for nurturing values and fostering growth.
sf05.matters: The early Christians' rejection of infant exposure and their proactive efforts to rescue and adopt abandoned children had profound implications. Their actions not only saved countless lives but also set a moral precedent that challenged and eventually influenced broader societal norms. By valuing and protecting the most vulnerable, Christians demonstrated a commitment to the sanctity of life and the importance of the family unit. This compassionate approach contributed to the growth and stability of Christian communities, as they maintained more balanced sex ratios and higher natural growth rates compared to the surrounding population. For families of faith today, this historical example underscores the significance of upholding moral principles, caring for the vulnerable, and recognizing the family as a cornerstone for transmitting values and fostering societal change.

sources.name: Exposure (infant) - Wikipedia
Early Christian Teaching on Abandoning Infants - The Historic Faith
Infant Exposure and Infanticide - The Oxford Handbook of Childhood and Education in the Classical World
The Exposed Child: Transplanting Roman Law into Late Antique Jewish and Christian Legal Discourse - American Journal of

sf05.evidence: Historical records and archaeological findings provide evidence of the early Christians' opposition to infant exposure and their efforts to rescue abandoned children. Writings from early Christian leaders, such as Justin Martyr and Tertullian, explicitly condemn the practice of exposing infants and advocate for their protection. Archaeological discoveries, including inscriptions and burial sites, indicate that Christians took in exposed children, sometimes only to provide them with a proper burial. Additionally, legal reforms initiated by Christian emperors in the 4th century, such as those by Constantine the Great, began to address and discourage the practice of infant exposure, reflecting the influence of Christian values on Roman law.
sf05.happened: In the Roman Empire, from the 1st to the 4th century AD, it was common for families to abandon unwanted newborns, a practice known as infant exposure. Fathers, under the legal authority called 'patria potestas,' had the right to decide the fate of their children, including the option to leave them exposed to the elements. This often led to the death of the infants or their survival as slaves if taken by others. Early Christians, however, stood in stark contrast to this societal norm. They condemned the practice of exposing infants, as evidenced in early Christian writings like the Didache, which explicitly forbade such actions. Christian communities actively rescued and adopted these abandoned children, providing them with care and integrating them into their families. This compassionate approach not only saved many lives but also demonstrated the Christians' commitment to the sanctity of life and the family unit.
sf05.scripture: The scriptures emphasize the value of every individual and the responsibility to care for the vulnerable. In the Bible, Psalm 127:3 states, 'Lo, children are an heritage of the Lord: and the fruit of the womb is his reward.' Similarly, in the Book of Mormon, Mosiah 4:14-15 instructs parents to teach their children to love and serve one another, highlighting the importance of nurturing and protecting the young. These passages reflect the divine mandate to cherish and care for all children, aligning with the early Christians' actions in rescuing and adopting abandoned infants.
sf05.background: During the early centuries AD, the Roman Empire was a vast and diverse society with complex social structures. Families were patriarchal, with the father holding significant authority over household decisions, including the fate of newborns. Economic hardships, social status, and personal preferences often influenced the decision to expose infants, particularly females and those with disabilities. This practice was legally and socially accepted, reflecting the broader Roman attitudes toward life and family. In contrast, the emerging Christian communities, guided by teachings that emphasized love, compassion, and the inherent value of every individual, rejected such practices. They viewed every life as precious and took active steps to protect and nurture the most vulnerable members of society.

sf06.talk: Why do you think it’s important for both people to want to get married?
sf06.child: A long time ago, people didn’t always get to choose whom they married. The Church helped make a rule that both people have to say yes for a marriage to be real. This helps everyone have a say in their own family.
sf06.learn: We can learn that even in times and places when the powerful could control almost everything, faith and law together helped build respect for individual agency. It reminds us that every person is precious to God, and that the choices we make, especially about making promises, shape our lives and families. It also teaches that big changes often start in small ways, through people who stand up for what is right.
sf06.matters: This principle is important because it put agency at the heart of marriage, recognizing that both men and women should have a voice in their own lives. For families of faith, the idea that a sacred promise like marriage must be chosen freely fits with the belief that Heavenly Father wants us to use our agency to choose good, including our closest relationships. Even today, laws and customs about marriage in many places go back to this idea that two people must both want to be married for it to be true. It lifts up respect and mutual consent as the foundation of a family.

sources.name: Encyclopedia Britannica, 'Western European Marriage: Canon Law and Consent'
Medievalists.net, 'Medieval Marriage: Consent and Coercion'
Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Marriage and Consent in Western Thought'

sf06.evidence: Historians study Gratian’s Decretum, which survives in many old manuscripts and was well-known in church courts. We know that church leaders wrote letters and held councils that discussed and confirmed the rule of consent. After this time, legal cases began to appear about whether true consent had taken place. Archaeologists have found documents, sometimes marriage contracts or legal disputes, that show how slowly this idea was accepted in different regions. Scholars agree that while it took centuries for these changes to affect all of society and later state law, the church’s teaching about consent started spreading from the mid-1100s onward. Most major histories of Western marriage point to the Decretum as the moment this vital principle became law.
sf06.happened: Around the year 1140 in Bologna, Italy, an important change happened in the laws of the Christian church about marriage. A scholar named Gratian collected and organized many church rules and wrote them into a great book called the Decretum. In this book, he taught that marriage was not just about families or rulers making deals, but about the man and the woman freely promising themselves to each other. Over the next seventy years, church leaders across Europe studied and agreed with Gratian’s teaching. They decided that if a marriage happened without both people saying yes of their own free will, that marriage wasn’t real in the eyes of God or the law. Fathers, mothers, or even kings could no longer force someone to marry against their wishes. This new rule slowly spread through all the lands where the Church had influence. It changed the way people thought about marriage, putting the power to choose in the hands of the couple themselves, not their families or superiors.
sf06.scripture: There is no passage in the Bible or other scriptures that sets out civil marriage law in these words, but the principle of agency runs through all of scripture. In Joshua 24:15, Joshua calls the people to "choose you this day whom ye will serve." Doctrine and Covenants 101:78 says, "every man may act in doctrine and principle... according to the moral agency which I have given unto him." Marriage as a covenant is also spoken of by Christ in Matthew 19:4-6. These all support the idea that to be real and lasting, covenants must be entered into freely, not forced.
sf06.background: Before Gratian’s time, families, especially powerful ones, often arranged marriages to build alliances, gain wealth, or settle disputes. A father or lord might decide who his daughter or servant would marry, sometimes without even asking her. Daily life for most people in medieval Europe was hard, with few rights, especially for women and the poor. Life was centered around the farm, the church, and the local lord’s manor. The Church itself was a strong voice in everyone’s life, guiding not only worship but also the rules about families and society. Most people could not read or write, but they trusted priests to teach them right from wrong. Gratian’s Decretum gave new guidance that slowly began to shape the world’s view of personal freedom within the family.

sf07.talk: What is one way we can help each other in our family that shows love to Heavenly Father?
sf07.child: Martin Luther married Katharina, and they made their home full of love and learning. They showed that helping your family and caring for each other is very important to God. Even little things you do at home can be very special.
sf07.learn: From Luther and Katharina’s story, we learn that everyday family life matters deeply to God. We see that caring for others—whether it is helping with chores, teaching, or sharing meals—can be holy work. Their example invites us to see our homes as places where faith grows and to remember that small, loving acts can be some of the most important work we do in our lives.
sf07.matters: Luther and Katharina’s marriage matters because it showed that family life—raising children, running a household, and serving neighbors—could be just as holy as any life devoted to religious vows. For the first time in generations, church leaders, especially in Protestant communities, began to see marriage and family as central to Christian living. This change encouraged more learning, as pastors’ homes became places where boys and girls studied and talked about faith together. Today, churches like ours still teach that family is at the heart of Heavenly Father’s plan, and that ordinary work done in love can draw us close to Him.

sources.name: Lutheran World Federation: Martin Luther and Katharina von Bora
British Library: Marriage of Martin Luther
Encyclopedia Britannica: Martin Luther

sf07.evidence: History gives us clear evidence of Luther and Katharina’s marriage, including letters, records from the city of Wittenberg, and reports from guests who visited their home. Luther often wrote about his family and household in his many letters and sermons. Scholars have also found official papers recording their marriage. The couple’s home, the Black Cloister, still stands today as a museum, where visitors read about their daily life and the impact it had on the Reformation. These sources show that the home they built together influenced not just their own children, but many others, as their household model spread across Protestant Europe.
sf07.happened: On June 13, 1525, Martin Luther, a former Catholic monk, married Katharina von Bora, who had herself been a nun. Their wedding in Wittenberg, Germany was not just a personal matter—it was a public declaration challenging the old belief that God is best served by people living apart from family in monasteries or convents. Luther and Katharina began their life together in the Black Cloister, once a monastery but now their lively home. Their household quickly grew to include not only their six children but also orphans, relatives, and young students whom they taught and cared for. Katharina became known for her skill in managing their busy house, farm, brewery, and a boarding house for university students. In their home, the daily joys and chores of family life were woven into their faith, showing that serving each other in simple ways was as sacred as any religious duty in a monastery. Their marriage set an example for pastors and believers across Europe, helping to shape what many came to see as the ideal Christian home.
sf07.scripture: The Bible teaches that marriage and family are honored by God. In Genesis 2:24, we read that "a man shall leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife." Paul, in 1 Corinthians 7, speaks of marriage as a good and honorable choice. Modern scripture adds to this: The Family: A Proclamation to the World (from The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints) declares that "marriage between a man and a woman is ordained of God" and that "family is central to the Creator's plan." These teachings affirm that the work of caring for and teaching families is sacred and valued by God.
sf07.background: Europe in 1525 was changing quickly. For centuries, the Catholic Church had taught that monks, nuns, and priests showed the highest devotion to God by living separate from family in religious communities. Martin Luther, once an Augustinian monk, became known for his challenges to these ideas. Katharina von Bora was one of many women who left the convent after hearing Luther’s teachings. Together, they lived in a time when most people worked hard on farms or in small towns, sharing homes with many relatives, and only a few could read or write. Luther and Katharina’s marriage and active household offered a new picture of how faith and family could fit together.

sf08.talk: Why do you think it's important for big promises, like marriage, to be made in front of others and written down?
sf08.child: A long time ago, people could get married in secret, but sometimes that caused problems. Church leaders made a rule that marriages had to be done in public with a priest and written down. Now, thanks to that, we can find out who our great-great-grandparents were!
sf08.learn: We can learn how wise it can be to make important promises in front of others who will remember and record them. When families and leaders work together to protect and record marriages, trust grows and the family line can be remembered for generations. Heavenly Father wants us to be honest and careful with each other, especially with promises like marriage. By making these promises openly, before God and others, we honor each other and our ancestors.
sf08.matters: This change at Trent mattered for everyone. Public marriages protected women and families from secret promises and abandonment, making them safer in society. For families of faith today, especially those who use FamilySearch or do temple work, this rule still blesses lives. The written marriage records that began because of Tametsi are the very ones we use to find our ancestors and turn our hearts to them, just as Malachi and the Doctrine and Covenants promise will happen in the last days. Public, recorded marriages help families stay safe and connected through time, just as Heavenly Father wants.

sources.name: Encyclopedia Britannica: Council of Trent
FamilySearch: Why We Need Marriage Records
BBC: The Council of Trent

sf08.evidence: There is strong historical evidence that this event happened. The decree Tametsi was recorded as part of the Council of Trent's documents and is discussed by historians, church scholars, and legal experts today. Parish registers still exist in old Catholic countries, and researchers have found marriage entries dating from the late 1500s onward. Before this decree, very few birth, marriage, or death records survive except from a few wealthy families. After Tametsi, systematic records began, providing proof that this change really happened and changed the lives of millions. These historic records are now digitized and indexed by genealogy volunteers and used by people all over the world to trace their families.
sf08.happened: On November 11, 1563, something important happened at the Council of Trent, a major meeting of Catholic Church leaders held in Trent, Italy. They made a rule called the decree Tametsi. This new rule said that people who wanted to get married in the Catholic Church had to do it in front of a priest and two witnesses, and their names and the details had to be written down in a parish register. Before this rule, couples could secretly promise to marry each other, often with no one else around and no written proof. While some couples really did love each other, others especially men, used these secret marriages to trick or even abandon women, since there was no way to prove the marriage had ever happened. With Trent's new law, marriage in Catholic Europe became something that everyone could see, with records kept safely by the church. Over time, this meant that almost every marriage was written down, and these records became some of the first detailed family lists in Europe that we still use for family history today.
sf08.scripture: Though the scriptures do not mention the Council of Trent, the Bible teaches that marriage is honorable (Hebrews 13:4) and should not be entered into secretly or lightly. Doctrine and Covenants 132:7 teaches that covenants made before God and proper authority are recognized by Him. The principle of doing important things by witnesses is also found in Doctrine and Covenants 6:28, which says, "in the mouth of two or three witnesses, shall every word be established." This matches well with what Tametsi required: marriages to be witnessed, recorded, and public, so all could know and remember the promises made.
sf08.background: The world in 1563 was very different from today. Europe was mostly Christian, and life was shaped by church teachings and village customs. Most people could not read or write, and births, marriages, and deaths were not officially recorded unless churches kept track. In those days, family honor and a woman's good name were very important, but the rules for getting married were not always clear. A couple could promise in private to marry and, for hundreds of years, that private promise was seen as real marriage. This led to confusion, broken promises, and sometimes real heartache, especially for women who found themselves abandoned and with no proof they were once married. The Council of Trent was trying to bring order to church practices during a time of religious argument and reform.

sf09.t: The Slave Trade Breaks Families by Law
sf09.talk: What do you think makes family so important, even when it is hard to be together?
sf09.child: Long ago, some people were made slaves, and the law said they couldn’t keep their families together. Still, they did everything they could to find and care for each other. They never stopped loving or hoping to be together again.
sf09.learn: We can learn from this history that family bonds matter deeply, even when the world tries to break them. The people who kept looking for one another, even after many years, remind us to never give up on those we love. Every family faces challenges, but caring for each member and holding tightly to hope is always worth it. We also learn to stand against anything that tries to harm families, and to help others whose families have been hurt.
sf09.matters: This part of history matters so much because it shows the deep strength of human love and family, given by our Heavenly Father and precious to every culture. Even when everything seemed against them, people held onto each other. Their struggle teaches us that the bond between parent and child or spouses is not just something societies invent. Instead, it is something that survives even the hardest trials. For families of faith, it reminds us to value, defend, and cherish our own connections, and to recognize the ongoing pain that injustice causes, which still echoes in families and communities today.

sources.name: Smithsonian National Museum of African American History and Culture: Enslaved Family Life
Library of Congress: Information Wanted Ads
PBS: Slavery and the Making of America - Family

sf09.evidence: Historical evidence from court records, letters, slave narratives, and advertisements shows that enslaved people’s marriages were not legally recognized. Scholars have found thousands of 'Information Wanted' ads, placed by formerly enslaved people seeking loved ones after emancipation. First-person accounts, such as those recorded in the Federal Writers’ Project Slave Narratives, describe families torn apart by sale and the never-ending hope to find one another again. Archaeological studies of slave quarters reveal how people adapted daily life to care for one another. These sources confirm that, despite the laws, the desire to hold families together was powerful and persistent.
sf09.happened: Between the 1500s and 1865, the transatlantic slave trade and the laws it created deeply hurt families. In this system, people from Africa were taken by force and sold across the Atlantic world—places like the Americas and the Caribbean. The law did not recognize marriages or family ties between enslaved people. A husband and wife or parents and children could be separated at any moment, depending only on the owner’s decision. This often happened when people were sold to different plantations or countries. Enslaved people still chose each other and made families quietly, holding onto promises to love each other as long as they could—sometimes saying, 'until death or distance do us part.'
