Building trustworthy bonds in families, congregations, and neighborhoods is part of how people of faith contribute to the greater good.
so02.matters: Tocqueville’s discovery—that faith and liberty can support one another—challenges the idea that religion is always in conflict with free society. For families of faith, it’s reassuring to know that past generations found ways to let belief shape a strong and free community. Tocqueville’s work teaches that involving ourselves in church, community service, and honest discussion can strengthen both our faith and our freedom. His book still speaks to how we build trust, handle differences, and seek the good of our neighbors, whether we’re leading a congregation or simply helping in our town or school.

sources.name: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy – Tocqueville on Democracy and Religion
Library of Congress – Democracy in America: Alexis de Tocqueville
National Endowment for the Humanities – Lessons from Tocqueville

so02.evidence: Tocqueville’s journey is well documented through his own journals, letters, and especially his published volumes of "Democracy in America." Historians widely regard his account as a careful, thoughtful reflection of what he saw, even as they note that his outsider’s view shaped what he understood. American historians point to the wide growth of voluntary associations in the 1800s as further evidence that Tocqueville’s observations were accurate. His writing has been cited for nearly two centuries as a key source for understanding early American society, and there’s abundant historical confirmation—both by records from the time and through later scholarship—that faith and voluntary organizations played a central part in American life.
so02.happened: In 1831, a young French nobleman named Alexis de Tocqueville traveled across the United States, hoping to understand what made American society unique. With his friend Gustave de Beaumont, he visited cities and small towns, courts and churches, and spoke to people from many different backgrounds. Tocqueville expected to find that American liberty would clash with religion, much as he’d seen in post-revolutionary France, where church and state were often in conflict. Instead, what Tocqueville discovered surprised him: in America, the spirit of religion and the spirit of freedom were not enemies but friends. Americans seemed to hold strong religious beliefs while also valuing their civil liberties. He was impressed by the way Americans formed all sorts of voluntary groups—churches, clubs, charities, and town meetings—that helped people work together for the common good. In his book, "Democracy in America," published in two parts (1835 and 1840), Tocqueville wrote that religion in America supported freedom and helped people care for each other. His careful observations became one of the most influential studies of society ever written, shaping how we understand democracy and the role of faith in public life.
so02.scripture: The scriptures teach principles that Tocqueville observed: loving your neighbor and seeking each other’s welfare. In the Bible, Jesus teaches, “Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself” (Matthew 22:39). The Book of Mormon shows King Benjamin teaching his people to serve one another (Mosiah 2:17). Doctrine and Covenants 58:26–27 encourages people not to wait to be commanded in all things, but to be “anxiously engaged in a good cause.” While the scriptures do not directly describe what Tocqueville saw, they do teach that faith, service, and community go together and bless all.
so02.background: When Tocqueville visited, America was still a young country, less than 60 years old. People were spreading out westward, building new towns and communities. Most Americans lived in small, rural settings, relied on close ties with neighbors, and attended local churches. Unlike in Europe, there was no official state church in the United States, and different religious groups coexisted peacefully in most places. Tocqueville himself had seen the results of the French Revolution back home, where religion and political freedom had often been set against each other. For many in Europe, faith seemed like something from the past, but in America, it was woven into everyday life and democratic participation.

so03.talk: Why do people need both answers and hope, not just facts?
so03.child: A man in France named Comte gave us the word 'sociology' and thought science would take the place of religion. But even he saw people still needed love, hope, and belonging. Today, we use both science and faith to help us live better lives.
so03.learn: We can learn from Comte’s life that while technology and scientific knowledge are blessings, people’s need for connection and spiritual purpose remains strong. Faith traditions answer questions and give comfort that facts alone cannot. As we learn and grow, it is wise to honor both our minds and our spirits, recognizing that both are gifts. Families can talk about how to use science and faith together to solve problems and love others.
so03.matters: Comte’s story matters because it shows how people search for meaning and order, especially when the world is changing quickly. For families of faith, it reminds us that knowledge and science are gifts but do not replace our spiritual needs. Even a great champion of science found people still longed for the sense of hope, purpose, and belonging that faith and worship provide. Today, sociology helps us understand communities, traditions, and how we can serve one another, but it cannot fully replace the deeper questions answered by faith and revelation.

sources.name: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Auguste Comte
Britannica: Auguste Comte
Scientific American: Religion of Humanity
Encyclopedia.com: Religion of Humanity

so03.evidence: Historians have well documented Comte's life and work. His books, especially 'Course in Positive Philosophy,' show how he developed the idea of sociology and argued for his three-stage model of human thought. Scholars agree that his later effort to create a secular religion was real, if small and short-lived, and was discussed by critics such as Thomas Huxley. The failure of Comte's 'Religion of Humanity' is noted in history books as a unique, but not lasting, attempt to create meaning by human design alone. However, his invention of sociology gave rise to an important field that continues today, and his writings are preserved and studied in universities around the world.
so03.happened: In 1838, a French thinker named Auguste Comte gave a name to a new way of studying people and their societies—he called it sociology. Comte believed that human thinking goes through three great stages: first, people explain the world through religion (the theological stage), then through abstract ideas and philosophy (the metaphysical stage), and finally, he said, humanity would reach the 'positive' or scientific stage, where everything is understood through observation and reason. Comte imagined that science would become the main guide for societies, replacing religion's place at the center. He thought that, as science grew stronger, people would trust facts and evidence more than faith or tradition, and that this would bring social progress and peace. However, as Comte grew older, he noticed that people deeply needed meaning, ritual, and community—things religion gave them. So, he tried to create a 'Religion of Humanity,' with new rituals, temples, and saints. Despite his effort, this movement attracted only a few and faded away. Comte's bold prediction—that science alone could organize human life as religion once did—did not come true, but his work began the field of sociology, changing how people study and understand society.
so03.scripture: The scriptures do not speak directly about sociology or Auguste Comte, but they teach that both faith and learning are important. Doctrine and Covenants 88:118 encourages us to seek learning, 'by study and also by faith.' The Bible, especially in Proverbs 4:7, says, 'Wisdom is the principal thing; therefore get wisdom: and with all thy getting get understanding.' These teachings remind us to value both knowledge and the spiritual gifts that connect us to God and to each other.
so03.background: Comte lived in Paris during a time of great change. France had just gone through its Revolution and struggled with what would come next. Old political and religious powers were being questioned, and many thinkers were trying to find better ways for society to work. Daily life in the early 1800s was full of uncertainty—there were advances in science and industry, but also poverty, disease, and unrest. Comte himself was shaped by these experiences and by the thinkers before him, such as Enlightenment philosophers who believed in reason and progress. The people around him were hungry for answers about how societies could improve and how people could live well together. His ideas about 'social physics,' later known as sociology, reflected this search for new principles to hold society together.

so04.talk: Why do you think it’s important to ask who benefits when we see a rule or idea?
so04.child: Karl Marx thought a lot about why some people have more stuff and power than others. He wanted to help people see if things were fair or not. We can ask good questions to help everyone be treated kindly and fairly.
so04.learn: We can learn to ask good questions when we see an idea, a rule, or even a tradition. Who does this help most? Who might it leave out? This helps us care for others and notice what needs changing. At the same time, it is helpful to remember that every tool, even a powerful idea like Marx’s, can be used for good or harm, depending on the heart and wisdom of those who use it. As families, we can use the gospel as our first guide for fairness, compassion, and love.
so04.matters: These ideas matter because they introduced a way to look behind the scenes at society and question who really benefits from how things are done. For a family of faith, it helps us remember that Heavenly Father cares deeply about how we treat one another; fairness, compassion, and concern for those in need are connected to the gospel. Conflict theory doesn’t have to lead to division—it can help us notice when someone is being left out or when unfairness is hiding in plain sight, and inspire us to lift up the downtrodden, as Jesus did.

sources.name: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Karl Marx
British Library: Karl Marx
BBC History: Karl Marx
The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints: Scriptures Topic - Equality

so04.evidence: The historical record about Marx’s life and writings is strong and confirmed through published books, letters, and firsthand accounts from people who knew him. His influence on political movements and academic thought is openly documented. Modern scholars widely agree about the facts of his life and what he wrote, though they debate how well his ideas match reality and what should be done with them. Archaeological findings from London and other major cities help us understand how industrialization changed living conditions and sharpened class divides at the time Marx was writing. Today, social scientists use his tools—like asking who benefits from a rule or belief—even if they draw different conclusions.
so04.happened: Between 1848 and 1867, in London, England, Karl Marx wrote some of the most influential works in the study of society. Most famously, he co-authored the Communist Manifesto in 1848 and, years later, published the first volume of Das Kapital in 1867. Marx argued that the best way to understand society is by looking at how people get their needs met—mainly through work, ownership, and the rules about who gets what. He believed that throughout history, people have often been divided into groups, or "classes," who have different amounts of power and wealth. According to Marx, these classes compete and even struggle with each other over resources and rights. He wrote that in every age, the group with more power shapes the big ideas and rules of society, while the experiences and beliefs of those with less power are often overlooked or called less important. One of his most famous lines claimed that religion can help hurting people cope, but might also keep them from seeing unfairness—he called it "the sigh of the oppressed creature" and "the opium of the people." These ideas started what is now called conflict theory in sociology, which studies how struggles between groups shape laws, ideas, and lives.
so04.scripture: While the scriptures do not speak directly about Karl Marx or his theories, many passages address fairness, justice, and caring for the poor. The Book of Mormon teaches, "...they had all things common among them; therefore there were not rich and poor" (4 Nephi 1:3). The Bible says, "He that hath two coats, let him impart to him that hath none" (Luke 3:11). Doctrine and Covenants 104:16 reminds us that "the poor shall be exalted, in that the rich are made low." These verses teach us about Heavenly Father’s desire for His children to help each other and address needs without pride or greed.
so04.background: These writings came at a time when Europe was changing quickly. The Industrial Revolution had filled cities like London with factories and workers, but also with crowded neighborhoods and real poverty. A growing number of people had to work long hours for little pay, often while a much smaller group owned most of the businesses and land. There were protests and debates about how to make things fairer. Karl Marx came from Germany but spent much of his life in exile in places like England with his friend Friedrich Engels, discussing and writing about how these conflicts between workers and owners might change society. For many, daily life meant hard labor and uncertainty, and the old rules seemed less and less fair.

so05.talk: Can you think of a time when you felt really close to your family or church, like everyone wanted to help each other?
so05.child: Long ago, a wise man noticed that some people live close like a family and help each other, while others just work together because they have to. He taught that it's special to be part of groups where people care for each other deeply. Family and church should feel like that kind of group.
so05.learn: We can learn that strong, loving communities are built on more than just rules—they need trust, shared values, and caring hearts. Even in our busy, modern world, families and congregations can protect and strengthen these close ties by making time for each other and serving together. We can use technology to help us connect, but we should remember to nurture the warmth of real belonging that Heavenly Father wants us to have.
so05.matters: Tönnies' ideas matter because they give us words to notice what kind of ties we want and need in our own lives. For families of faith, understanding the difference between community and society can help us treasure the trust and warmth of close relationships. It also gives us a way to think about how technology and modern life can make some ties weaker, but also help us create new communities, even across great distances. His work invites us to ask ourselves: Are we building relationships of love and support, or just crossing paths because it’s needed for work or convenience? This question remains important for families, congregations, and even the world.

sources.name: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Ferdinand Tönnies
Encyclopedia Britannica: Ferdinand Tönnies
Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Community and Society

so05.evidence: Historians have closely studied Tönnies' writings through his original book, 'Gemeinschaft und Gesellschaft,' first published in 1887. Scholars have found that his distinction is helpful for understanding many societies, both past and present. Archaeological and social science research shows that small communities throughout history, like ancient villages, relied on shared beliefs and cooperation rather than contracts or laws. Modern sociology continues to use Tönnies’ ideas to examine how our ways of living are changing, such as in internet communities or city neighborhoods. There is clear evidence that relationships have shifted in many places from close-knit trust to more formal, rule-based interactions, just as Tönnies described.
so05.happened: In 1887, a thoughtful German scholar named Ferdinand Tönnies wrote about two very different ways people come together and live with each other. He called them Gemeinschaft and Gesellschaft. Gemeinschaft describes groups where people are closely tied to each other, like families, neighborhoods, or congregations. In these groups, people care for each other because of what they share: kinship, tradition, faith, and a sense of belonging. You help and trust people not because there’s a written rule, but because you feel connected at heart. Gesellschaft, on the other hand, describes the kinds of relationships that grew more common as towns turned into cities during the Industrial Revolution. Here, people interact mostly for practical reasons: they follow contracts, laws, or self-interest rather than deep bonds. You work with others or do business not because you know them, but because it’s required. Tönnies saw that as cities and industries grew, more and more relationships became like these contracts. His idea helped people understand why life in a small village felt so different from life in a big, modern city, and why some people missed the closeness of older ways of living.
so05.scripture: Scripture teaches the value of belonging and loving care within a community. In the Bible, Acts 2:44-47 describes early Christians living in unity, sharing what they had, and meeting daily with one accord. Mosiah 18:21 in the Book of Mormon urges the Saints to have 'their hearts knit together in unity and in love one towards another.' Doctrine and Covenants 38:27 reminds, 'Be one; and if ye are not one ye are not mine.' These passages all speak to the principle that true community—Gemeinschaft—comes from shared belief, kindness, and service, not just formal rules.
so05.background: Before Tönnies wrote his book, Germany and much of Europe were changing rapidly. The 1800s were a time when many people left farms and small villages to work in noisy, crowded factories in big cities. New technology, like trains and electric light, sped up daily life. Old traditions sometimes faded, and families were often separated by work. Most people in Germany were still deeply shaped by their local villages and churches, but the Industrial Revolution brought new ways of working and living that felt unfamiliar. Ferdinand Tönnies grew up in northern Germany, in Kiel, which was a small city but felt these changes, too. He watched as the simple ties of family and neighborly trust were replaced by agreements and contracts, and began to ask what this shift meant for people's lives and happiness.

so06.talk: Why do you think having friends and family around us makes us feel better?
so06.child: When people feel alone or disconnected, they might feel very sad. Being part of a family and having friends can help us feel happy and safe.
so06.learn: Durkheim's study teaches us that our connections to family, community, and faith are not just beneficial but essential for our well-being. It reminds us that fostering strong, supportive relationships can provide resilience against life's challenges. For families of faith, it reinforces the value of nurturing these bonds and participating actively in community life as a means of promoting both individual and collective health.
so06.matters: Durkheim's study is foundational in sociology, illustrating how individual behaviors are influenced by societal factors. For families of faith, his findings underscore the protective role of strong social bonds, such as those found in religious communities and family units. The study suggests that belonging to a faith community and maintaining close family relationships can provide a buffer against despair and isolation. This aligns with the belief that human connections and shared values are vital for emotional and spiritual well-being.

sources.name: Suicide (1897) by Émile Durkheim
Books Reconsidered: Suicide, A Study in Sociology: Emile Durkheim
The Social Roots of Suicide: Theorizing How the External Social World Matters to Suicide and Suicide Prevention

so06.evidence: Durkheim's work has been both influential and subject to critique. While his identification of social factors influencing suicide has been supported by subsequent research, some scholars have pointed out limitations in his methodology, such as the reliance on official statistics that may not capture all cases and the challenge of inferring individual behavior from group data. Despite these critiques, the core association between social integration and lower suicide rates has been repeatedly confirmed in modern studies. For instance, research continues to show that individuals with strong social ties, whether through family, community, or religious affiliation, tend to have lower rates of suicide and better mental health outcomes.
so06.happened: In 1897, Émile Durkheim, a French sociologist, published "Suicide: A Study in Sociology," a groundbreaking work that examined suicide not as an individual act but as a social phenomenon. Durkheim analyzed extensive data from various European countries, focusing on factors such as religion, marital status, and family life. He discovered that suicide rates were consistently higher among Protestants compared to Catholics and Jews, higher among unmarried individuals than those married, and lower among those with children. Durkheim introduced the concept of "anomie" to describe a state of normlessness, where individuals feel disconnected from the collective conscience of society. He identified different types of suicide: egoistic (resulting from insufficient social integration), altruistic (from excessive integration), and anomic (from a lack of social regulation). This study was pioneering in demonstrating that even deeply personal decisions like suicide could be influenced by societal structures and norms.
so06.scripture: The scriptures emphasize the importance of community and mutual support. In Ecclesiastes 4:9-10, it is written: "Two are better than one... For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow." Similarly, in Mosiah 18:21 from the Book of Mormon, believers are encouraged to "look forward with one eye, having one faith and one baptism, having their hearts knit together in unity and in love one towards another." These passages highlight the strength and protection found in unity and shared faith, resonating with Durkheim's findings on social integration.
so06.background: In the late 19th century, Europe was undergoing significant social changes due to industrialization and urbanization. Traditional social structures were being challenged, leading to shifts in family dynamics, religious practices, and community ties. During this period, sociology was emerging as a distinct academic discipline, with scholars like Durkheim seeking to apply scientific methods to understand social phenomena. Durkheim, born in 1858 in Épinal, France, was deeply influenced by the political and social upheavals of his time. He aimed to establish sociology as a rigorous science, distinct from psychology and philosophy, by focusing on social facts—patterns of behavior that exist outside the individual but exert control over them.

so07.talk: Why do you think it’s important to listen to people’s real stories before making up our minds about them?
so07.child: Du Bois wanted to know how people in Philadelphia were really living, so he asked them directly and listened closely. He learned that they faced unfair treatment not because of who they were, but because of how the city worked. His careful work helps us understand how to treat others more kindly and fairly.
so07.learn: We can learn that truly understanding another person—or a whole community—takes careful listening, honest questions, and respect. Du Bois teaches us that evidence and loving curiosity help us discover the truth about others’ lives. Parents and children can remember that it’s not enough to accept old ideas or stories. We can seek out the real experiences of people around us, recognizing their struggles and strengths, and choosing to show Christlike compassion and fairness.
so07.matters: Du Bois’s work matters to the world because he showed that careful, honest study can reveal truth even when others prefer easy answers. He refused to blame individuals for problems that society itself caused. For families of faith, his example helps us see each person’s worth and reminds us not to judge others without knowing their story. His careful listening and gathering of facts invite us to treat everyone as a child of God, deserving understanding and fair treatment. Today, his work still teaches us the value of wise, loving observation before making decisions about others.

sources.name: Encyclopedia of Greater Philadelphia: Du Bois, W. E. B. and The Philadelphia Negro
Smithsonian Magazine: W.E.B. Du Bois’ Data Portraits
University of Pennsylvania: The Philadelphia Negro by W.E.B. Du Bois

so07.evidence: Historians have confirmed that Du Bois visited and interviewed thousands of families in Philadelphia over a span of about 15 months. His notebooks, letters, and published book—The Philadelphia Negro—exist in archives and are widely cited by today’s scholars as pioneering social research. His maps and charts helped people see patterns of work, health, and housing that no one had put together before. For many decades, his findings were left out of textbooks, but today, universities and museums recognize his contributions as foundational to sociology. Modern research often builds on his honest methods and findings.
so07.happened: In 1899, a man named W. E. B. Du Bois set out to understand how people lived, worked, and felt in a big city—Philadelphia. Rather than guessing what life was like for Black people there, he went door to door, gently talking with over 5,000 Black households. He asked questions about family, work, money, health, and daily problems. Du Bois carefully wrote down what each family shared, creating a clear map of their lives. He did something unusual for his time: he looked at real evidence instead of simply believing what others assumed or said. When he gathered all his notes, he found that Black Philadelphians faced unfair treatment not because of something wrong within themselves, but because of big barriers—like employers refusing to hire them or landlords not renting decent homes. He showed that the difficulties these families faced were built into the way society worked, not just personal mistakes. His book, The Philadelphia Negro, was the first big study of its kind in the United States, leading the way for a whole field called urban sociology, even though it was ignored by most scholars for many years.
so07.scripture: Scripture asks us to treat all people as our neighbors and to be fair in judgment. In the Book of Mormon, Alma counsels his people to "judge righteously" and to "impart of your substance to the poor," reminding us to help and understand those in need (Alma 34:28-29). The Savior also taught us to "judge not according to the appearance, but judge righteous judgment" (John 7:24). While no scripture mentions research studies, these passages encourage us to look deeper than the surface and seek true understanding, just as Du Bois did.
so07.background: At the end of the 1800s, America was changing fast. Many people were moving to cities, looking for jobs in factories, shops, and railroads. Philadelphia was one of the country’s largest cities and had a strong Black community, some of whom had come for freedom and safety from the South. But even in Philadelphia, Black families faced prejudice. They often had trouble finding good work, were kept out of certain neighborhoods, and didn't always feel included in city life. Most people didn’t know what daily life was really like for these families—there were a lot of rumors and unfair guesses instead of real facts. Du Bois, a well-educated Black scholar, was invited by a group trying to help the city to find out what was really happening, hoping that kind, honest facts could help.

so08.talk: How do you think our beliefs about work and helping others affect the way we live our lives?
so08.child: Long ago, a man named Max Weber thought about why some people worked very hard and became successful. He believed that certain religious ideas made people feel that working hard was a way to show they were good. This idea helped people build businesses and make the world more modern.
so08.learn: We can learn that religious beliefs and practices can have profound effects on economic and social development. However, it's essential to consider multiple factors, such as education and cultural values, when examining these relationships. This understanding encourages us to reflect on how our own beliefs influence our daily lives and societal contributions.
so08.matters: Weber's analysis offers insight into how religious beliefs can influence economic systems and societal structures. For families of faith, it underscores the importance of understanding how spiritual values can shape daily work and ethical choices. It also serves as a reminder to balance material pursuits with spiritual well-being, ensuring that economic success does not lead to a loss of deeper meaning and purpose in life.

sources.name: The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism by Max Weber Plot Summary | LitCharts
Was Weber Wrong? A Human Capital Theory of Protestant Economic History | University of Stirling
Max Weber - Wikipedia

so08.evidence: Weber's thesis has been the subject of extensive debate. In 2009, economists Sascha Becker and Ludger Woessmann analyzed data from 19th-century Prussia and found that Protestant regions were indeed more prosperous. However, they attributed this prosperity to higher literacy rates resulting from the emphasis on reading the Bible, rather than solely to a unique work ethic. Their study suggests that education played a significant role in economic development, challenging the idea that religious beliefs alone were responsible for the rise of capitalism.
so08.happened: In 1905, German sociologist Max Weber published "The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism," a work that explored the relationship between Protestantism and the development of modern capitalism. Weber observed that in countries with both Protestant and Catholic populations, Protestants often held leadership roles in business and skilled labor, while Catholics were more frequently found in less economically advanced positions. He proposed that certain Protestant beliefs, especially those of Calvinism, fostered a disciplined work ethic and a focus on worldly success as a sign of divine favor. This, he argued, contributed to the rise of capitalism. Weber also cautioned that this rational, methodical approach to work could lead to a dehumanizing "iron cage" of bureaucracy and a loss of spiritual meaning in modern life.
so08.scripture: The scriptures teach the value of diligent work and the importance of balancing material and spiritual pursuits. In the Doctrine and Covenants, the Lord instructs, "Thou shalt not be idle; for he that is idle shall not eat the bread nor wear the garments of the laborer" (D&C 42:42). This emphasizes the virtue of industriousness. However, the Savior also cautioned against placing material wealth above spiritual treasures, teaching, "Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth... But lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven" (Matthew 6:19-20). These teachings encourage a balanced approach to work and material success, ensuring that spiritual priorities remain foremost.
so08.background: At the turn of the 20th century, Europe was undergoing significant social and economic transformations. The Industrial Revolution had reshaped economies, leading to urbanization and new social structures. In this context, scholars like Weber sought to understand the cultural and religious factors influencing these changes. Weber, born in 1864 in Germany, was deeply interested in the interplay between religion and society. His work aimed to explain why certain societies embraced capitalism more readily than others, focusing on the role of religious beliefs in shaping economic behavior.

so09.talk: How do you think Jane Addams’ life would have been different if she had tried to help people without ever talking to them or living with them?
so09.child: Jane Addams moved to a busy part of the city to help people who needed it. She lived with them, asked good questions, and wrote down what she saw so others would know how to help too.
so09.learn: Jane Addams teaches us that if we want to help, we need to listen and learn from others close up—not just guess from far away. Sometimes, new ways of caring for people get overlooked, but faithfully serving, learning, and sharing truth can shape a better community. Her life lets us see how quietly loving and careful work can change a city and even a country.
so09.matters: Hull House and Jane Addams changed how people thought about helping others. Instead of studying problems from far away or guessing what people needed, she and her team lived among the people and learned from them directly. Their careful records made it impossible for city officials to ignore conditions like child labor and unsafe housing. This led to laws that protected children and improved neighborhoods. For families of faith, this example shows God’s way: to love our neighbors not just in word, but in deed, and to meet them where they are as Christ did.

sources.name: Encyclopædia Britannica: Jane Addams
Library of Congress: Hull House Maps and Papers
National Women's History Museum: Jane Addams and Hull House

so09.evidence: Much historical evidence supports the story of Hull House. Photographs from the time show the building, the families who lived nearby, and some of the first playgrounds and kindergartens offered there. Hull-House Maps and Papers remains a clear record of the surveys and findings compiled by Addams and her team. Historians have noted that their work was important in shaping early laws about child labor and housing standards. Jane Addams’ influence is confirmed by the recognition she received, including the Nobel Peace Prize in 1931, and her writings continue to be studied in universities today.
so09.happened: In 1889, a woman named Jane Addams, along with her friend Ellen Gates Starr, opened Hull House in Chicago. They chose a neighborhood where many immigrant families lived, people who had come from other countries hoping to find better lives but often facing hard work and poor living conditions. Jane and her fellow residents did not just give out food or clothing—they made Hull House a place where people could learn English, join clubs, or take music and art classes. One thing made Hull House special: the people who worked there lived right in the neighborhood. They paid attention to what was happening around them. They carefully wrote down facts about jobs, wages, where people came from, what kinds of homes they lived in, and even how the garbage was collected. They published these findings in a book called Hull-House Maps and Papers in 1895. This was one of the first times anyone had studied how people really lived in those city blocks and shared exact numbers with leaders and lawmakers.
so09.scripture: The principle shown at Hull House is closely tied to the commandment to love our neighbors as ourselves, found in Matthew 22:39. The Book of Mormon also teaches that when we are in the service of our fellow beings, we are only in the service of God (Mosiah 2:17). Doctrine and Covenants 81:5 tells us to “succor the weak, lift up the hands which hang down, and strengthen the feeble knees.” Jane Addams’ approach of serving directly and carefully seeing the needs connects to each of these teachings.
so09.background: When Jane Addams founded Hull House, big American cities were growing fast as immigrants arrived from Europe and other countries. Chicago, in particular, was crowded, noisy, and not always a safe or clean place for new families. Many immigrants found work in factories or as laborers, with little pay and long hours, and children often worked too. There were very few rules to protect workers or keep neighborhoods healthy and clean. Most people worked hard just to have enough to eat, and few city leaders really knew how hard life was for the poor. Jane herself was from a well-off family, but she felt a calling to help others, wanting to do more than simply give charity from afar.

so10.talk: Why do you think people continue to believe in God even when the world changes?
so10.child: Even when people thought religion would disappear as the world changed, it didn't. Instead, many more people around the world kept believing in God and practicing their faith.
so10.learn: We learn that human societies are complex, and predictions about cultural shifts can be uncertain. The resilience of faith traditions suggests that spiritual needs persist regardless of technological or social advancements. This teaches us to approach societal trends with humility and to recognize the enduring importance of faith in people's lives.
so10.matters: The secularization thesis matters because it reflects on how we understand the role of faith in a changing world. For families of faith, it underscores the resilience and adaptability of religious belief amidst societal transformations. The unexpected growth of religion globally suggests that faith continues to provide meaning and community, even in modern contexts. This challenges assumptions that modernization inevitably leads to secularism and invites a reevaluation of how faith and progress coexist.

sources.name: Pew Research Center: Islam was the world’s fastest-growing religion from 2010 to 2020
Pew Research Center: How the Global Religious Landscape Changed From 2010 to 2020

so10.evidence: Historical and demographic studies provide evidence against the secularization thesis. Pew Research Center's analysis from 2010 to 2020 shows that Muslims were the fastest-growing religious group, increasing by 347 million people. Christianity remained the largest religion, with 2.3 billion adherents, though its growth did not keep pace with global population increases. The religiously unaffiliated also grew, but their share of the global population rose by only 1 percentage point. These trends indicate that, contrary to earlier predictions, religion continues to play a significant role worldwide.
so10.happened: In the mid-20th century, sociologists like Peter Berger, Thomas Luckmann, and David Martin proposed the secularization thesis. They believed that as societies modernized—embracing industrialization, urbanization, and scientific advancements—religion would decline, becoming a private matter before fading away. Berger, in a 1968 interview with The New York Times, suggested that by the 21st century, religious believers would be small, isolated groups. However, this prediction did not materialize. Instead, religion experienced significant growth, especially in the global South. Pentecostalism expanded rapidly, attracting hundreds of millions of followers. Islam also saw substantial growth, becoming the world's fastest-growing religion between 2010 and 2020. Religion reasserted itself in public life across many nations, with Western Europe being the notable exception. This unexpected resurgence challenged the secularization thesis, highlighting the complex relationship between modernization and religious belief.
so10.scripture: Scriptures emphasize the enduring nature of faith. In the Bible, Matthew 16:18 records Jesus saying, "Upon this rock I will build my church; and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it," highlighting the resilience of the Church. The Book of Mormon in 2 Nephi 2:11 discusses the necessity of opposition in all things, suggesting that challenges, including societal changes, are part of God's plan. Doctrine and Covenants 1:30 declares that the Church will remain steadfast, emphasizing its enduring presence despite worldly shifts.
so10.background: During the 1950s and 1960s, the world was undergoing rapid modernization. Western societies were experiencing economic growth, scientific breakthroughs, and increased urbanization. This period also saw the rise of secular ideologies and a decline in traditional religious practices in some regions. Sociologists observed these trends and theorized that as societies advanced, religion would become less central to public and private life. Peter Berger, Thomas Luckmann, and David Martin were prominent figures in this discourse, analyzing the interplay between societal development and religious adherence. Daily life in many Western countries was marked by a shift towards secular values, with religion increasingly viewed as a personal choice rather than a societal cornerstone.

so11.talk: How do you think your family and your friends help you learn new things?
so11.child: A big study found that how well kids do in school depends a lot on their families and friends, not just the school itself. This means our home and the people around us help us learn.
so11.learn: We can learn that education is not just about buildings and books; it is about people and relationships. Strong families, supportive teachers, and good friends all help children learn and grow. As families, we can work together to create homes and communities where all children can thrive, and we can recognize that every child’s success starts before they ever walk into a classroom.
so11.matters: The Coleman Report matters because it shifted the national conversation from just looking at school budgets to recognizing the powerful role families and communities play in a child’s education. For people of faith, this is a reminder of the sacred duty of parents to nurture their children and the blessings that strong families and healthy communities bring. The report’s message is that every child’s learning is deeply connected to home life, and that working together as families and neighbors can be as important as any school reform.

sources.name: Encyclopedia Britannica - Coleman Report
National Center for Education Statistics - The Condition of Education
National Academy of Education - Revisiting the Coleman Report

so11.evidence: The findings of the Coleman Report have been supported, challenged, and expanded upon by decades of follow-up research. Most agree with the central idea that family background and social environment have a major impact on student achievement. Later research has also shown that effective schools and teachers can make a big difference, especially for children facing disadvantages. School resources matter, but the original study’s emphasis on family and peer influences has stood the test of time and still shapes conversations about education policy.
so11.happened: In 1966, James Coleman, a respected sociologist, led a massive study that changed the way Americans think about schools and learning. Congress asked him and his team to find out if differences in how much money each school received were causing big gaps in how well students learned. Coleman’s team worked very hard, visiting schools all over the United States and asking questions of about 600,000 students, teachers, and principals. They gathered an incredible amount of data and expected to show that schools with more money and better facilities would always produce better results. However, what they discovered surprised almost everyone. The study found that things outside the school building—especially the family backgrounds of students and the kinds of friends and classmates they had—were much stronger predictors of how well children did in school. This finding did not ignore the importance of good teachers or safe buildings, but it suggested that even the best schools might not overcome the challenges many children faced if their home lives were difficult or their school communities were struggling. The findings sparked debate and became a turning point in how researchers, educators, and lawmakers thought about education and equality.
so11.scripture: Several scriptures teach the importance of home and parents in nurturing children. In the Bible, Proverbs 22:6 says, 'Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it.' The Book of Mormon counsels parents as well (Mosiah 4:14-15), urging them to teach their children to walk in truth and love. Doctrine and Covenants 93:40 reminds that parents are commanded to bring up their children in light and truth. While nothing in scripture discusses school funding, the principle the scriptures teach is clear: the family’s role in learning and character is foundational.
so11.background: The 1960s in America were a time of enormous social change. The country was working through the Civil Rights Movement, and one major concern was whether all children—no matter their background or the color of their skin—had the same chance to succeed in school. Many schools were still deeply unequal because of patterns of segregation and funding tied to local taxes, so poorer areas had less money for their schools. James Coleman was asked to look hard at these issues. At that time, families often lived near people who were like themselves, and schools were mostly attended by children from those neighborhoods. Many believed that if the government could just make funding equal, children would all have equal opportunities to learn.

so12.talk: Why do you think it's important to understand the history of others when we try to help them?
so12.child: A long time ago, a man named Mr. Moynihan wrote about how some families were having a hard time because of unfair treatment in the past. He wanted to help people understand so they could make things better.
so12.learn: The Moynihan Report teaches us the importance of addressing social issues with a comprehensive understanding of historical and structural contexts. It reminds us that well-intentioned analyses can be misinterpreted if not communicated sensitively. For families, it underscores the value of strong familial relationships and community support in overcoming societal challenges. It also highlights the need for ongoing dialogue and research to effectively address complex social issues.
so12.matters: The Moynihan Report remains a pivotal document in understanding the complexities of race, family, and policy in America. It underscores the importance of considering historical and structural factors when addressing social issues. For families of faith, the report serves as a reminder of the significance of strong family bonds and the need for community support in overcoming adversity. It also highlights the potential consequences of miscommunication and the importance of framing discussions about sensitive topics with care and empathy.

sources.name: The Negro Family: The Case for National Action | U.S. Department of Labor
Explaining the 'Moynihan Report' | American Masters | PBS
Four decades later, scholars re-examine 'Moynihan Report' — Harvard Gazette

so12.evidence: Historical analyses confirm that the Moynihan Report accurately highlighted the economic and social challenges faced by Black families in the 1960s. Data from that era showed higher rates of unemployment and poverty among Black communities compared to their white counterparts. Subsequent research has supported Moynihan's assertion that systemic racism and historical injustices contributed significantly to these disparities. However, the report's focus on family structure was criticized for not fully accounting for the broader socio-economic factors at play. Over time, scholars have recognized the need to address both structural inequalities and family dynamics to foster social progress.
so12.happened: In March 1965, Daniel Patrick Moynihan, serving as Assistant Secretary of Labor, authored an internal report titled "The Negro Family: The Case for National Action." This document examined the challenges faced by Black families in the United States, highlighting issues such as high rates of unemployment, poverty, and family instability. Moynihan argued that these challenges were deeply rooted in the historical injustices of slavery and systemic discrimination, leading to a cycle of poverty and social disintegration. He emphasized that legal advancements in civil rights, while crucial, would not suffice to address these entrenched issues without targeted social policies aimed at strengthening Black family structures. Although intended for internal use, the report was leaked to the public, sparking intense debate. Critics accused Moynihan of blaming Black families for their struggles, while supporters contended that he was shedding light on the structural barriers imposed by racism. The controversy surrounding the report led to a reluctance among researchers to study family structures in Black communities for many years.
so12.scripture: The scriptures emphasize the importance of family unity and support. In the Book of Mormon, Mosiah 4:14-15 instructs parents to teach their children to walk in the ways of truth and soberness, highlighting the role of family in moral and spiritual development. Similarly, in the Bible, Proverbs 22:6 advises to "Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it," underscoring the lasting impact of early family guidance. These passages reflect the belief that strong family foundations are essential for individual and communal well-being.
so12.background: The mid-1960s were a period of significant social change in the United States. The Civil Rights Movement had achieved landmark victories, including the Civil Rights Act of 1964, which aimed to end segregation and discrimination. However, despite these legal gains, many Black Americans continued to face economic hardships and social inequalities. Urban areas experienced rising unemployment rates among Black men, and there was growing concern about the stability of Black family units. Daniel Patrick Moynihan, a sociologist and policy analyst, was deeply involved in these issues, working within the Department of Labor to address employment and social welfare challenges. His report emerged from a context where policymakers were grappling with how to translate civil rights victories into tangible improvements in the daily lives of Black citizens.

so13.talk: Can you think of a time when you learned something new that changed what you believed before?
so13.child: A man who once thought people would stop believing in God changed his mind when he saw so many still loved their faith. He bravely told everyone he was mistaken and shared what he had learned. It showed how important it is to look for truth, even when it surprises us.
so13.learn: We learn from Peter Berger’s example that it is good to ask questions and brave to admit when we were wrong. Families of faith can take comfort in knowing that faith is not old-fashioned or disappearing, but instead, can be strong and renewing in every age. By trusting in God and seeking knowledge honestly, we help make a home where truth and love can grow together.
so13.matters: Berger’s public reversal matters because it reminds us that even the best experts can be mistaken when evidence changes. For families of faith, it is a gentle sign that believing in God is not simply something people grow out of as they become more educated or progress in society. Instead, faith can adapt and even grow stronger in response to new challenges. Berger’s honesty also encourages all of us, including parents and children, to seek truth and be willing to change our mind when we learn more – a virtue that brings people closer to both knowledge and each other.

sources.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica – Peter L. Berger
Pew Research Center – The Future of World Religions
Harvard University – Peter Berger and The Desecularization of the World

so13.evidence: The evidence leading Berger to recant his theory was visible both in numbers and in personal stories. Across the globe, religious movements were growing in Africa, Asia, and the Americas as the twentieth century ended. Data from the Pew Research Center and other reputable sources tracked significant increases in religious practice outside of Western Europe, where secularization was stronger. Berger himself noted that only a small, fairly isolated group—university-educated people in very wealthy nations—seemed to fit the secularization pattern. Surveys and studies consistently showed that, even in “modern” societies, people continued to find meaning, community, and hope in faith. These findings became widely accepted and led other sociologists to rethink secularization as a rule, recognizing it as only one possible path among many.
so13.happened: In 1999, a respected scholar named Peter Berger, who had spent much of his career promoting a certain idea about religion and society, openly changed his mind. Berger was known for the 'secularization thesis.' This was the belief that as societies became more modern through science, education, and economic growth, religious belief and practice would fade away. For decades, many people, especially those studying society, took this idea almost as a fact. But Berger saw something different happening. Instead of religion disappearing, he noticed it was growing or changing in many parts of the world. Major faiths were strong and even getting stronger outside of certain European countries. This led Berger to write a book, The Desecularization of the World, where he declared that his old theory had been proven wrong. He honestly admitted that most people, including himself, had not predicted how powerful and resilient faith would be for so many. He even pointed out that the only people who truly lived in a mostly non-religious world were a small, international group—mainly those who worked in universities or similar places, often far from everyday believers. Berger’s willingness to state his mistake in public and explain what the evidence showed was seen as unusually brave and honest for a scholar.
so13.scripture: Many scriptures teach about humility, seeking truth, and the lasting power of faith even as times change. In the Bible, James 1:5 invites anyone lacking wisdom to ask God, who gives freely. The Book of Mormon, Moroni 10:5, says "by the power of the Holy Ghost ye may know the truth of all things." Doctrine and Covenants 88:118 encourages us to “seek learning, even by study and also by faith.” These verses remind us that true knowledge often comes when we are humble enough to learn from both faith and evidence, willing to be corrected when necessary.
so13.background: Peter Berger lived and worked in a time when many experts believed the world was moving away from old traditions, including religion. In the last half of the twentieth century, countries like the United States, much of Europe, and other developed places were growing quickly in technology, science, and education. There was hope and prediction that this progress would make people less religious, as new answers seemed to come from science instead of faith. People like Berger worked in big cities and taught at universities, often surrounded by others who saw little need for religion. Daily life in cities like Boston, where Berger worked, involved busy routines, new inventions, and wide access to knowledge. But even as these cities changed, much of the wider world saw faith remain deeply important in family and community life.

so14.talk: Why do you think being part of a group, like our church or a team, makes us want to help others more?
so14.child: When people spend time together in groups, like at church or community events, they are more likely to help others and be kind. Being part of a group makes us feel connected and encourages us to do good things for our community.
so14.learn: These studies teach us that the mechanisms fostering generosity and civic engagement are deeply rooted in community participation and personal relationships. It is not merely abstract beliefs that encourage individuals to contribute to society, but the experience of belonging to a community and engaging in shared activities. For families of faith, this underscores the importance of active involvement in congregational life and community service, as these experiences cultivate a spirit of generosity and mutual support.
so14.matters: The decline in social capital has profound implications for both society and families of faith. For society, reduced civic engagement can lead to weaker communities, diminished trust among citizens, and challenges in addressing collective problems. For families of faith, the findings underscore the importance of active participation in religious and community organizations. Such involvement not only strengthens individual faith but also fosters a sense of belonging and mutual support. The research suggests that the benefits of religious participation are closely tied to the communal aspects of faith, highlighting the value of congregational friendships and shared activities in promoting civic virtues and social cohesion.

sources.name: Bowling Alone: The Collapse and Revival of American Community
American Grace: How Religion Divides and Unites Us
Summary of 'Bowling Alone: The Collapse and Revival of American Community'
American Grace: How Religion Divides and Unites Us | Harvard Kennedy School

so14.evidence: Empirical studies support the conclusions drawn by Putnam and Campbell. Data from the General Social Survey indicate a decline in membership and participation in traditional civic organizations over the latter half of the 20th century. For example, while the number of people who bowled increased, participation in bowling leagues declined, illustrating a shift from communal to individual activities. Further research has shown that individuals who are actively involved in religious congregations are more likely to engage in volunteer work and charitable giving, not only within their religious communities but also in secular contexts. This suggests that the social networks and sense of belonging fostered by religious participation play a significant role in promoting civic engagement and social responsibility.
so14.happened: In 2000, Robert D. Putnam, a political scientist at Harvard University, published "Bowling Alone: The Collapse and Revival of American Community." In this influential work, Putnam analyzed data from nearly 500,000 interviews conducted over the previous 25 years to demonstrate a significant decline in social capital in the United States. He observed that Americans were participating less in community activities such as voting, attending public meetings, and engaging in civic organizations. Even leisure activities reflected this trend; for instance, while more people were bowling, they were increasingly doing so alone rather than in leagues. Putnam attributed this decline to various factors, including the rise of television and the internet, suburbanization, and changes in work and family structures. He emphasized that this erosion of social connections had measurable civic costs, affecting everything from public health to the functioning of democracy. A decade later, in 2010, Putnam, along with David E. Campbell, published "American Grace: How Religion Divides and Unites Us." This book examined the role of religion in American civic life, revealing that religiously observant individuals were more likely to volunteer, donate to charity, and participate in civic activities, even for secular causes. The authors found that the key factor was not religious doctrine but the sense of community and belonging fostered by congregational friendships.
so14.scripture: The scriptures emphasize the importance of community and collective worship. In Hebrews 10:24-25, it is written: "And let us consider one another to provoke unto love and to good works: Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as the manner of some is; but exhorting one another." Similarly, in Mosiah 18:8-9, the Book of Mormon describes the covenant of baptism as a commitment to "bear one another's burdens, that they may be light;... and to mourn with those that mourn; yea, and comfort those that stand in need of comfort." These passages highlight the scriptural principle that gathering together and supporting one another are essential aspects of faith and community life.
so14.background: In the mid-20th century, American society was characterized by a strong sense of community and civic engagement. People regularly participated in local organizations, attended religious services, and engaged in social activities with neighbors and friends. This period saw high levels of trust and cooperation among citizens, contributing to a robust democratic society. However, by the late 20th century, significant societal changes began to emerge. Technological advancements like television and the internet altered how people spent their leisure time, often leading to more solitary activities. Urbanization and suburbanization changed the physical and social landscapes, making it more challenging for individuals to maintain close community ties. Additionally, shifts in work and family dynamics, including increased work hours and dual-income households, left less time for community involvement. These changes contributed to a gradual decline in traditional forms of social interaction and civic participation.

so15.talk: Can you think of a time when you learned something new and then checked if it was really true?
so15.child: Some science studies about people’s thoughts and feelings did not work again when others tried them. This taught scientists to check their work more carefully. Now, we know it’s wise to ask if something has been tested more than once.
so15.learn: From this event, we learn that real knowledge is built patiently, step by step. It reminds us to check whether a truth has stood the test of time and careful study, not just impressive headlines. In families, this means talking together about where information comes from and not being afraid to ask questions. By doing so, we can gather wisdom, help each other learn, and honor both faith and reason in our search for truth.
so15.matters: This crisis matters because it teaches us to be humble about scientific knowledge, especially when it comes to understanding people and society. It shows the importance of checking, double-checking, and sharing honest results. For families of faith, it is a gentle reminder that all truth belongs to God, but even sincere seekers can make mistakes. Learning to ask good questions and to look for repeated, careful evidence can help us wisely use what is true and set aside what is not. This habit helps keep our minds and decisions open to learning, correction, and greater light.

sources.name: American Psychological Association: Replicability and Reproducibility
Center for Open Science: Reproducibility Project: Psychology
NPR: Many Psychology Findings Not as Strong as Claimed, Study Says

so15.evidence: Researchers now use stronger practices to make their work more trustworthy. This includes sharing their data openly, deciding ahead of time how they will test a question (preregistration), and using bigger groups of people in studies. Efforts like the Reproducibility Project in 2015 highlighted how often scientific studies in psychology could not be repeated successfully. New tools, like 'registered replication reports,' allow many scientists to work together to check if results hold up. Today, studies that pass these tests are valued more highly, and unreliable ones are slowly being removed from textbooks and advice. All of this is steadily making science stronger, safer, and more honest.
so15.happened: Around the year 2011, scientists who study people and how we act—such as psychologists and other social scientists—noticed a growing problem. Many important studies, which had been taught in schools and cited in textbooks, could not be repeated with the same results. When new groups of researchers tried to follow the same steps in these famous experiments, they often found very different answers. In 2015, one major project tried to repeat 100 well-known psychology studies, but only about a third to half showed the same results again. Some studies that were believed for years were questioned, revised, or even found to be wrong. A few researchers were discovered to have made up data or taken shortcuts that made their findings unreliable. This led to a wide conversation about how we know what we know, and how we can be sure that the science we trust is true.
so15.scripture: The principle of seeking truth with patience and careful testing is taught in scripture. In Doctrine and Covenants 9:8-9, we are invited to study things out in our mind and then seek confirmation. Alma 32:27-43 describes how faith and knowledge grow by testing, nurturing, and seeing if the results are good over time, like a seed. These passages remind us that discovering truth is usually a process, not a single moment, and that both faith and reason work together for learning.
so15.background: Before this crisis, many people trusted the findings of social science, especially studies on how people think, feel, and behave. Scientists worked in universities and labs, publishing their results in respected journals. Everyday life saw these findings used in schools, businesses, and counseling offices. But even with good intentions, science faced pressures to make exciting discoveries quickly, which sometimes led researchers to skip careful steps. Studies with smaller groups or striking headlines often got more attention, even if the results could not be repeated by others. As everyday people, many trusted these findings without knowing to check how strong or well-tested the evidence really was.

so16.talk: Who are some people in our family or ward that help you feel like you belong?
so16.child: People are happiest and strongest when they belong to each other, not just because they have to, but because they care. Even scientists found that family, friends, and helping others make life better. That’s why families and church matter so much.
so16.learn: We can learn that giving time and care to family, friends, and even neighbors we barely know, does real good. Strong, loving bonds are not only taught in scripture as part of God’s way, but also repeatedly found to be good for us by people who studied societies. Whether or not someone shares our faith, all people need to belong, feel needed, and be part of something bigger than themselves. These ties strengthen hearts, families, and the whole world.
so16.matters: This matters because it shows something about how people, through time and across the world, are built for community. For families who believe in God and the gospel of Jesus Christ, it's reassuring to know that strong, loving bonds are not just nice to have—they're essential for well-being. Science has found that belonging, shared meaning, and commitments to others help people lead happier and healthier lives. These discoveries remind us that investing in family and congregation isn't just a spiritual task but a practical way to bless each other in this life.

sources.name: Harvard Study of Adult Development (Harvard Gazette)
Britannica - Sociology
Robert Putnam, Bowling Alone (The Atlantic)

so16.evidence: Many major, long-term studies have shown that people with close social connections are healthier and happier. Robert Putnam's famous studies on "social capital" showed that communities with more trust and involvement had less crime and better overall well-being. Other researchers, like James Coleman, found that family bonds and ties to community make a real difference in education and safety. These patterns appear across cultures—even when the studies do not mention religion. For example, a massive Harvard study following people over decades found those who felt connected to others lived longer and healthier lives. The evidence is very strong that humans need more than contracts and casual ties; they need belonging, meaning, and responsibilities to others. These findings are widely confirmed in the scientific community today.
so16.happened: Over the past several centuries, scholars have asked a big question: what keeps a society strong and together when people no longer share the same old traditions or beliefs? Thinkers from different cultures and times, like Ibn Khaldun, Emile Durkheim, Ferdinand Tönnies, James Coleman, and Robert Putnam, each studied what binds people. Some saw social life in grand communities, while others noticed close family bonds or a sense of belonging. Again and again, their research showed that people flourish when they are connected—not just through business or agreements, but also through deeper ties of loyalty, care, and shared meaning. Even when new ways of work or life made old village life impossible, people needed something more than contracts. Across generations and worldwide, sociologists—many of whom had no personal interest in defending religion—found something surprising: the very sorts of belonging, shared purposes, and care for others that religions help create are crucial for societies to thrive.
so16.scripture: Scriptures speak often about caring for one another and being united. Jesus teaches, "A new commandment I give unto you, That ye love one another; as I have loved you, that ye also love one another. By this shall all men know that ye are my disciples, if ye have love one to another" (John 13:34–35). Paul describes the Church as a body with many members, each needing the others (1 Corinthians 12:12–27). The Book of Mormon shows both the strength and the suffering that come with unity or the lack of it (see 4 Nephi 1:15–18). These passages answer that strong, caring ties are part of God’s plan for His children.
so16.background: The world where these findings first appeared was changing fast. Cities were growing, old villages breaking apart, and new kinds of work meant people moved around more. Families were sometimes separated by distance or circumstance, and many scholars wondered if society could keep working without the familiar bonds of common faith, family, or community. Those who studied these changes wanted to understand what happened when neighbors were strangers and when people depended more on rules and contracts. Their studies reflected real questions families faced about friendship, trust, and where they belonged. Everyday life for many became less about inherited customs and more about making choices, yet the human need for connection remained.

sv01.talk: Why do you think it took so long for people to see that owning others was wrong?
sv01.child: Long ago, people in almost every place on earth kept slaves. They thought it was normal, even though it was not fair. We can remember how wrong it was, and try to be kinder and more fair to everyone.
sv01.learn: One of the most important lessons is that it is possible for societies to change, even when a wrong seems permanent. It can help us develop more patience and understanding, recognizing that what we see as common sense today took a long, difficult journey to become widely held. Remembering this history helps families talk openly about fairness, responsibility, and how all people deserve to be treated.
sv01.matters: Understanding that slavery existed almost everywhere—and for so long—helps us recognize both the deep roots of injustice and the incredible change that has happened in human hearts over time. For a family of faith, it’s a reminder that the tools and ideas people have today to fight injustice are blessings from God, not something our ancestors always had. Instead of seeing slavery’s story as only about one nation or group, we see it as a shared human burden, showing us how much we all need guidance from our Heavenly Father to become truly just and kind.

sources.name: Metropolitan Museum of Art – Slavery in Ancient Civilizations
British Museum – Hammurabi’s Law Code
World History Encyclopedia – Slavery in Antiquity

sv01.evidence: Excavations and written records from places like Sumer, Egypt, Babylon, and China show that systems of slavery shaped early societies. Documents like Hammurabi’s Code clearly mention the sale of human beings. Ancient graves often reveal the remains of people who may have lived as slaves, based on their poor health or their location in burial grounds. In Mesoamerica, archaeological finds support the existence of forced labor and captive-taking. Recent historical research shows that every major ancient civilization practiced some form of slavery, whether for debt, punishment, or conquest. Museums and history books across the world agree on this point: slavery was part of nearly every early organized society whose records we can read.
sv01.happened: Slavery has been a part of human life for as long as there have been cities and written history. Thousands of years ago, in places like Sumer, Babylon, Egypt, China, India, Greece, and Rome, people were often forced to work as slaves. Some were captured in wars; others became slaves because they could not pay their debts. Ancient laws, like Hammurabi’s Code in Babylon (around 1750 BC), even had rules about how to buy and sell slaves and what rights, if any, they had. Slaves helped build temples and pyramids, worked in fields, or served in homes. The same pattern showed up far from the Middle East, too—in the ancient Americas, much of Africa, and the Pacific Islands. While the way slavery looked and worked was different in each place, what did not change was that almost no one doubted whether slavery was right. The big question was more about who it was acceptable to enslave—foreigners, criminals, the poor—but not whether the practice itself should exist.
sv01.scripture: Scripture speaks to the worth of every soul and to the principle of loving one another as ourselves. In the Old Testament, laws in Exodus 21 and Leviticus 25 outline rules about slavery, but those rules reflect the world as it was, not as God ultimately wants it. In the New Testament, Paul teaches in Galatians 3:28 that “there is neither bond nor free: for ye are all one in Christ Jesus.” The Book of Mormon, especially Mosiah 2:17 and Mosiah 27:4, also teaches against oppressing others and calls for service and compassion. While scripture records slavery, its deeper call is always toward treating others as children of God.
sv01.background: Life in early civilizations like Sumer, Egypt, China, and Greece was both impressive and very hard. Most people lived in small villages, raised crops or animals, and worked from sunup to sundown. Powerful kings, priests, and a few rich families controlled much of the wealth and land. Writing and laws had only just begun to develop, and physical strength often determined who held power. Capturing slaves during wars was common and seen as a normal part of victory. Debt and poverty also drove many families to sell a child or themselves into slavery simply to survive. Because survival was so uncertain, and counts of people or ideas about rights were different from today, nobody spoke out against slavery as something wrong in itself.

sv02.talk: Can you think of a time when you felt helped or protected during a difficult situation?
sv02.child: A long time ago, God's people were slaves in Egypt. God helped them escape and led them to a new land where they could be free. This story shows us that God cares for His children and helps them when they are in trouble.
sv02.learn: The story of the Exodus teaches us about the importance of faith, perseverance, and the belief in divine deliverance. It reminds us that, even in the face of great adversity, trust in God's promises can lead to liberation and new beginnings. The narrative also emphasizes the significance of remembering past struggles to inform and guide present and future actions.
sv02.matters: The Exodus is a foundational event in the history of the Israelites, symbolizing liberation and the establishment of a covenantal relationship with God. For families of faith, it underscores themes of deliverance, faith, and obedience. The story has resonated through millennia, inspiring movements for freedom and justice, including the American abolitionist and civil rights movements. Spirituals like "Go Down Moses" reflect this enduring legacy, drawing parallels between the Israelites' journey and the struggles against oppression.

sources.name: Is there evidence of the Exodus from Egypt?
Is There Evidence That the Exodus From Egypt Happened as Depicted in the Bible?
Is the Bible's story of the Jewish exodus from Egypt accurate?
The Exodus

sv02.evidence: The historicity of the Exodus is a subject of ongoing debate among scholars. There is no direct Egyptian record of a mass departure of Israelite slaves. However, some scholars point to indirect evidence, such as the presence of Semitic peoples in Egypt during the relevant period and Egyptian texts that mention groups like the "Shasu of Yahweh," which some interpret as references to early Israelites. Archaeological findings in the Nile Delta, particularly at sites like Avaris (modern Tell el-Dab'a), indicate the presence of Semitic populations, which some associate with the Israelites. The Merneptah Stele, dating to the late 13th century BC, contains the earliest known reference to "Israel" outside the Bible, suggesting the existence of a people by that name in Canaan at that time. Despite these findings, the lack of direct evidence has led many scholars to view the Exodus narrative as a theological and cultural foundation rather than a precise historical account.
sv02.happened: The Exodus is the biblical account of the Israelites' departure from slavery in Egypt, led by Moses. According to the Book of Exodus, the Israelites had been enslaved in Egypt for generations. God called upon Moses to confront Pharaoh and demand the release of His people. When Pharaoh refused, Egypt was struck by a series of ten plagues, culminating in the death of the firstborn in every Egyptian household. Following this devastation, Pharaoh permitted the Israelites to leave. They journeyed toward the Red Sea, where, as the narrative describes, God parted the waters to allow them to cross on dry ground. When the Egyptian army pursued them, the waters returned, drowning the soldiers. The Israelites then traveled through the wilderness to Mount Sinai, where they received the Ten Commandments and entered into a covenant with God.
sv02.scripture: The Book of Exodus (chapters 1–14) provides the primary account of the Israelites' departure from Egypt. Deuteronomy 5:15 reminds the Israelites to remember their slavery and deliverance: "Remember that you were slaves in Egypt and that the Lord your God brought you out of there with a mighty hand and an outstretched arm." In the Book of Mormon, 1 Nephi 17:23–25 references the Exodus as a demonstration of God's power and faithfulness.
sv02.background: The setting of the Exodus is ancient Egypt, a powerful civilization along the Nile River known for its monumental architecture, advanced agriculture, and complex society. The Israelites, according to the Bible, were descendants of Jacob who had migrated to Egypt during a famine and eventually became enslaved.
