Daily life for the Israelites in Egypt would have involved labor-intensive tasks, particularly in construction and agriculture, under harsh conditions. Egyptian society was hierarchical, with Pharaoh at the top, considered a god-king, and a vast population of workers and slaves at the bottom. Religious practices were polytheistic, with numerous deities associated with natural and societal elements.

sv03.t: Slave Societies of Greece and Rome
sv03.talk: Why do you think Jesus would want us to help people who are not free or are treated unfairly?
sv03.child: A long time ago in Greece and Rome, many people were forced to be slaves. They had to work hard without a choice and were not treated kindly. Today, we know it is important to treat everyone with love and respect, because everyone is special to Heavenly Father.
sv03.learn: We learn that great civilizations can miss basic truths about kindness and justice. Intelligence and high achievement are no guarantee of goodness. When we read about slavery in history, we are reminded to look at our own lives and how we treat others. We are called to stand up for freedom and treat every person—no matter their background or situation—as a beloved child of God.
sv03.matters: Studying slavery in Greece and Rome matters because it helps us see that even societies famed for their wisdom and accomplishments sometimes failed to see the dignity of every person. It reminds us that clever laws and grand achievements do not always guide people to do what is right. For families of faith, it is a lesson in using our knowledge and gifts from God to lift others and defend their freedom, not to exploit them. Compassion, not just intelligence, is what brings us closer to the Savior’s way.

sources.name: British Museum: Slavery in the Roman World
Stanford University: Slavery in Ancient Rome
National Geographic: Slavery in Ancient Rome
Church of Jesus Christ: Scripture References on Bondage

sv03.evidence: Historians have found records on stone, papyrus, and in books that describe slavery in Greece and Rome. Archaeologists have uncovered slave quarters, tools, and even chains. Ancient writers such as Cicero and Seneca discuss daily life, laws, and the treatment of slaves. The grave markers and household ruins bear silent witness to the millions who lived and labored in bondage. Roman legal documents plainly show slaves were considered property, and census documents reveal just how common slavery was. These sources agree on the scale and reality of slavery in the ancient Mediterranean.
sv03.happened: Between about 500 BC and 500 AD, the civilizations of Greece and Rome built their societies using the labor of enslaved people. In these ancient lands around the Mediterranean Sea, many people were forced to live as slaves. Slaves did almost every kind of work: they worked on large farms, dug in dangerous mines, cooked and cleaned in wealthy homes, and even fought as gladiators for crowds in arenas. Some educated slaves served as teachers or accountants. In Roman Italy, at its height, possibly one out of every three people was a slave. Roman law did not protect slaves much—they were seen as the property of their owners, not as people with rights. Owners could punish, sell, or even kill slaves without penalty. Some slaves gained freedom, but most lived and died without hope of changing their status. This system kept going for centuries, supported by wars that brought in new captives from places like Gaul, Britain, Greece, and North Africa. Over time, as the Roman Empire weakened, the institution of slavery changed. While the old system of owning people slowly faded away, it was replaced by serfdom, where poor workers were still not truly free, but tied to the land.
sv03.scripture: The Bible recognizes slavery as a part of the world it was written in, with passages about masters and servants in both the Old and New Testaments (see Ephesians 6:5-9 or Colossians 4:1). The Book of Mormon also mentions bondage, such as Alma 27:8-9, where the Nephites help free the people of Ammon. Doctrine and Covenants 101:79 teaches the importance of freedom by saying, 'it is not right that any man should be in bondage one to another.' While scripture sometimes describes the world as it was, it points us to a higher law: to love our neighbor and protect each person's dignity.
sv03.background: The ancient Greeks and Romans lived in busy cities and villages along the Mediterranean. Wealth and power often concentrated in the hands of a few, while most people were either small farmers, tradespeople, or slaves. Daily life in Athens or Rome meant seeing slaves everywhere—from bustling markets to grand villas. Slavery had already existed in the ancient world long before Greece and Rome, going back to Egypt and Mesopotamia. In Greece and Rome, however, the scale was much larger. Slaves could be born into slavery, captured in war, or even abandoned children sold by desperate parents. Most people, enslaved or not, lived in close quarters, working hard just to survive. Religion, philosophy, and law all coexisted with the practice, and few questioned the system directly.

sv04.talk: How can we show love and kindness to others, even when it's difficult?
sv04.child: Paul wrote a letter to Philemon, asking him to welcome back Onesimus, not just as a servant, but as a dear brother in Christ. This teaches us to treat everyone with kindness and see them as part of our family in faith.
sv04.learn: From Paul's letter to Philemon, we learn the power of the gospel to transform relationships and challenge societal norms. It teaches us the importance of forgiveness, reconciliation, and viewing others as equals in Christ. This message encourages us to treat everyone with love and respect, recognizing the inherent worth and dignity of every individual.
sv04.matters: Paul's letter to Philemon is significant because it addresses the complex issue of slavery within the context of Christian faith. By urging Philemon to accept Onesimus as a brother, Paul introduced a radical idea that transcended societal norms. This message planted a seed that would eventually contribute to the questioning and abolition of slavery among Christian communities. For families of faith, this letter underscores the importance of viewing all individuals as equals before God and treating each other with love and respect, regardless of social or economic differences.

sources.name: Introduction to Philemon | ESV.org
The Epistle of Paul to Philemon | churchofjesuschrist.org
Epistle to Philemon | Wikipedia
Bible Study Guide: Philemon | American Bible Society

sv04.evidence: The authenticity of Paul's letter to Philemon is widely accepted among scholars, with its personal tone and specific details supporting Pauline authorship. The letter's references to individuals and its alignment with other Pauline epistles, such as Colossians, provide historical context. Archaeological findings in Colossae, including inscriptions and artifacts, offer insights into the city's social structure and the prevalence of slavery during that period. These pieces of evidence collectively support the historical credibility of the events described in the letter.
sv04.happened: Around 60 AD, the Apostle Paul, while imprisoned, wrote a personal letter to Philemon, a Christian in Colossae. Philemon owned a slave named Onesimus, who had left him and met Paul. During their time together, Paul converted Onesimus to Christianity. In his letter, Paul appealed to Philemon to welcome Onesimus back, not merely as a slave, but as a beloved brother in Christ. Paul emphasized the transformation Onesimus had undergone and suggested that their relationship should now be based on Christian love and fellowship. He also offered to repay any debt or wrongdoing Onesimus might have caused, highlighting the importance of reconciliation and forgiveness within the Christian community.
sv04.scripture: The Epistle to Philemon is the primary scriptural text addressing this event. In Philemon 1:16, Paul writes, "Not now as a servant, but above a servant, a brother beloved." Additionally, in Galatians 3:28, Paul states, "There is neither bond nor free... for ye are all one in Christ Jesus," emphasizing the equality of all believers. These passages highlight the Christian principle of unity and the breaking down of social barriers within the faith community.
sv04.background: In the first-century Roman Empire, slavery was a common and accepted institution, with slaves making up a significant portion of the population. Slaves were considered property and had limited rights. Colossae, located in Asia Minor (modern-day Turkey), was a city with a diverse population and a mix of cultural influences. Philemon was a wealthy Christian who hosted a church in his home, indicating his prominent status in the community. The early Christian movement emphasized unity and equality among believers, challenging existing social hierarchies and promoting a sense of brotherhood among all members, regardless of their social status.

sv05.t: The Trans-Saharan and Indian Ocean Trades
sv05.talk: Why is it important to treat everyone with kindness and respect, no matter where they come from?
sv05.child: Long ago, people were taken from their homes in Africa and forced to work in faraway places. This was very unfair and hurt many families. We should always treat others with kindness and respect.
sv05.learn: Studying the trans-Saharan and Indian Ocean slave trades teaches us about the complexities of human history and the consequences of exploiting others for economic gain. It reminds us of the resilience of the human spirit and the importance of advocating for justice and equality. By learning about these histories, we can better understand the roots of present-day social and cultural dynamics and work towards a more compassionate and just society.
sv05.matters: Understanding the trans-Saharan and Indian Ocean slave trades is crucial for acknowledging the full scope of human history and the pervasive nature of slavery across different cultures and continents. For families of faith, this history serves as a reminder of the importance of recognizing the dignity and worth of every individual, as all are children of God. It also underscores the need for compassion, justice, and the pursuit of righteousness in our interactions with others. Reflecting on this history can inspire us to advocate for the oppressed and to work towards a world where freedom and equality are upheld for all.

sources.name: Indian Ocean slave trade
Trans-Saharan slave trade
Understanding the long-run effects of Africa’s slave trades

sv05.evidence: Historical evidence of the trans-Saharan and Indian Ocean slave trades comes from various sources, including historical texts, travelers' accounts, and archaeological findings. For instance, the 14th-century traveler Ibn Battuta documented the presence of slaves in various regions he visited, noting their roles in society and the markets where they were traded. Archaeological excavations in coastal regions of East Africa have uncovered artifacts indicating trade connections with the Middle East and Asia, suggesting the movement of goods and people across these routes. Despite the challenges in quantifying the exact numbers involved due to limited records, the widespread impact of these trades is evident in the cultural and demographic influences observed in the regions affected.
sv05.happened: From around 650 AD to the early 20th century, extensive slave trades operated across the Sahara Desert and the Indian Ocean. These trades involved the capture and transportation of millions of individuals from sub-Saharan Africa to various regions, including North Africa, the Middle East, the Indian subcontinent, and islands in the Indian Ocean. The trans-Saharan trade routes facilitated the movement of slaves northward, where they were often sold in markets across the Maghreb and the Levant. Similarly, the Indian Ocean trade routes enabled the shipment of slaves to destinations such as Arabia, Persia, India, and Southeast Asia. The demand for slaves in these regions was driven by needs for domestic servants, laborers, soldiers, and concubines. Unlike the trans-Atlantic slave trade, which predominantly transported men for labor-intensive plantation work, the trans-Saharan and Indian Ocean trades often involved a higher proportion of women and children, reflecting the different societal roles they were expected to fulfill in the destination regions. The scale of these trades is difficult to quantify precisely due to sparse records, but historians estimate that the numbers are broadly comparable to those of the Atlantic slave trade, with figures ranging from 6 to 10 million individuals over the centuries.
sv05.scripture: The scriptures teach us about the inherent worth of every individual and the importance of treating others with kindness and respect. In the Book of Mormon, King Benjamin reminds us that when we are in the service of our fellow beings, we are in the service of our God (Mosiah 2:17). Additionally, the Doctrine and Covenants instructs us to remember the poor and the needy, and to administer to their relief (D&C 44:6). These teachings emphasize the responsibility to care for and uplift those who are suffering or in bondage.
sv05.background: In the centuries leading up to the 7th century, various forms of slavery existed across Africa, the Middle East, and Asia. The rise of Islam in the 7th century and the expansion of Muslim empires facilitated increased trade and cultural exchanges across these regions. The establishment of extensive trade networks allowed for the movement of goods, ideas, and people. The demand for labor in growing urban centers and agricultural estates, as well as the need for soldiers and domestic servants, contributed to the expansion of the slave trade. Societies in North Africa, the Middle East, and parts of Asia developed complex economies that relied on both free and enslaved labor. Daily life in these regions varied, but for many, it involved agricultural work, artisanal crafts, and trade. The integration of enslaved individuals into households and economies was a common practice, reflecting the social and economic structures of the time.

sv06.talk: What would you do if someone was being treated unfairly or left out?
sv06.child: A long time ago, people were taken from Africa on ships and forced to be slaves far away. Many families were hurt and people were very sad. We remember them because everyone is special to God.
sv06.learn: We can learn to see the cost of forgetting that every person has divine worth, and how important it is to stand against any form of injustice or cruelty. The history of the Atlantic slave trade shows the deep harm caused when families are torn apart and people are treated as property. By remembering these stories, we can teach compassion and remember our duty to love and protect one another.
sv06.matters: This matters because it changed the course of millions of lives and shaped whole societies. For families of faith, knowing what happened helps us see the suffering caused when people forget that all are children of Heavenly Father. The forced separation of families and the lasting scars—emotional, social, and spiritual—remind us of the need for kindness, justice, and healing. When we learn about this history, we can better keep the commandments to love our neighbors and remember the worth of every soul.

sources.name: Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade Database - Emory University
Smithsonian National Museum of African American History and Culture: Slavery in America
Britannica: Transatlantic slave trade

sv06.evidence: Historical evidence for the Atlantic slave trade is extensive. Researchers have studied ship logs, port records, firsthand accounts, and even the physical remains of ships to document the number of voyages, the conditions aboard slave ships, and the fates of those transported. The Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade Database is a major scholarly effort that brings together thousands of documents to trace who was taken, where they came from, and what happened. Archaeologists have uncovered wrecked slave ships and items left by enslaved people, adding details to written records. The numbers are staggering, but the stories uncovered by historians and archaeologists help us remember these were individual people, not just statistics.
sv06.happened: In 1444, Portuguese sailors took their ships to the coast of West Africa and, for the first time in European history, brought enslaved Africans back to Europe. This act marked the beginning of what became known as the Atlantic slave trade, a massive movement of people against their will across the ocean. Over the next 400 years, ships from Portugal, Britain, France, Spain, the Netherlands, and later the United States, captured or bought men, women, and children from African kingdoms and transported them—under terrible conditions—to work as slaves in the Americas. These voyages were brutally difficult: people were packed into ship holds with barely enough room to move, suffering from hunger, sickness, abuse, and grief. Many died before ever reaching land. The largest database built by historians estimates about 12.5 million Africans were forced onto these ships, but only about 10.7 million survived the ordeal of the ocean crossing. The impact was devastating, not only for those taken, but for the families, villages, and cultures left behind, many of them depopulated or disrupted for generations.
sv06.scripture: The Bible teaches that all people are children of God and worthy of love. In Acts 17:26, Paul writes that God "hath made of one blood all nations of men for to dwell on all the face of the earth." The Book of Mormon echoes this in 2 Nephi 26:33, saying the Lord "inviteth them all to come unto him... and he denieth none that come unto him, black and white." While the scriptures do not describe the Atlantic slave trade specifically, they teach the principle of honoring freedom, agency, and the value of every person.
sv06.background: Before 1444, slavery existed in many parts of the world, but nowhere on such a large scale as what soon followed across the Atlantic. West Africa at the time was home to many kingdoms and peoples, each with its own ways of life, markets, and traditions. Some African rulers grew powerful through trade, including in gold, ivory, and, sadly, people. In Europe, Portugal was eager to find new trade routes and became the first major power to explore by sea along Africa’s coast. Life in West Africa before the slave trade included farming, herding, fishing, building families, and passing on traditions; people lived in towns and cities and traveled for trade. Few could have imagined how much their world was about to change as Europeans sought profit far across the sea.

sv07.talk: Why do you think it is important to treat everyone with kindness, even if they look or live differently than us?
sv07.child: Four friends wrote a letter saying everyone should be treated like they want to be treated, no matter who they are. At first, nobody listened, but what they wrote helped change minds many years later. Even a small good thing can grow bigger than we can see.
sv07.learn: We can learn from the Germantown Quakers that even a quiet, ignored act can have great meaning. When people stick to what is right, even if others are not ready, they help shape a better future. Speaking up kindly and clearly matters, even when it seems no one is listening. God can work through small beginnings to bring about wonderful changes. Our choices and our courage may matter more, and for longer, than we can see today.
sv07.matters: This event shows the power that simple acts of faith and courage can have over time. The Germantown Protest did not end slavery right away or even change many minds at first. Still, by putting their beliefs into writing in peaceful, clear words, four ordinary men planted a seed. The change started silently, spread quietly, and eventually shifted an entire faith community—and much later, the world. For families who treasure both faith and freedom, this story reminds us that sometimes standing up for what is right may not be popular or rewarded quickly, but it can start a chain of good that reaches far beyond our lifetimes.

sources.name: National Park Service – Germantown Quaker Petition Against Slavery
Friends Journal – The 1688 Germantown Protest Against Slavery
Encyclopedia Britannica – Germantown Protest

sv07.evidence: Historians have carefully preserved the text of the Germantown Protest, and the original document still exists in the Friends Historical Library at Swarthmore College. The handwriting, signatures, and the names of the men—Francis Daniel Pastorius, Garret Hendericks, Derick up de Graeff, and Abraham up de Graeff—have been checked and confirmed as residents of Germantown in 1688. Written records from the time show how the petition was passed through the Quaker meeting system and finally archived without a ruling, matching reports from later Quaker leaders. Books, articles, and museum exhibits today verify the protest’s timing and its unique status as America’s first written stand against slavery.
sv07.happened: On February 18, 1688, four Quaker men living in Germantown, Pennsylvania, wrote and signed a document that would become the first formal protest against slavery in the American colonies. Their message was clear and heartfelt: if you want to be treated kindly and fairly, you should treat others the same, no matter what they look like or where they come from. This protest was written in a spirit of Christian faith. The men shared the paper with their local Quaker congregation, hoping their words would encourage all Quakers to reject slavery. The leaders took the petition and passed it up their church system, but, uncertain and not ready for such a strong stand, the issue was quietly put aside. Even though this first effort was ignored, the message did not vanish. Over the next decades, many Quakers continued to speak against slavery. By 1776, their persistence paid off: the Society of Friends (Quakers) officially barred its members from holding slaves, making them the first group in America to take such a firm stance.
sv07.scripture: The principle of the Golden Rule, 'therefore all things whatsoever ye would that men should do to you, do ye even so to them,' taught by Jesus in Matthew 7:12, stands at the core of the Germantown Protest. Similarly, the Book of Mormon teaches in Mosiah 2:17 that 'when ye are in the service of your fellow beings ye are only in the service of your God.' There is also the simple reminder in Doctrine and Covenants 101:79 that every person has the right to be free, as taught by the Lord to modern prophets. These passages all teach the dignity of each child of God and remind us to treat others with love and respect, no matter their background or color.
sv07.background: Life in 1688 Pennsylvania was rough and new for settlers. Germantown was a small community, part of the larger Pennsylvania colony, which was a place of many faiths but also a place where enslaved Africans were forced to work. Quakers, also known as the Society of Friends, were a Christian group known for their plain dress, simple living, and belief in peace and equality. While some Quakers owned slaves then, others began to see a conflict between their belief in the worth of every soul and the practice of slavery. These early Quakers faced the daily challenge of surviving in a new land, growing crops, and building homes, while also building their religious communities and wrestling with hard questions about right and wrong.

sv08.talk: How do you think Granville Sharp felt when he decided to help someone he didn’t even know?
sv08.child: A man named Granville Sharp helped James Somerset, who was a slave, get his freedom in England. Because of this, a judge said people could not keep slaves in England anymore. Doing the right thing helped set someone free.
sv08.learn: Somerset’s Case shows that one person’s compassion and courage, guided by faith, can open the door to greater freedom for many. When we see something wrong, we may not always change the whole world, but we can bring hope to someone and plant a seed for bigger change. It teaches us that laws and hearts can change, especially when people act with love and stand up for others’ rights, following the example of Jesus Christ.
sv08.matters: The Somerset case is important because it set a turning point for how slavery was seen in England and gave hope to enslaved people everywhere. For families of faith, this story is a reminder that standing up for what’s right, even for one stranger, can change the hearts and laws of nations. Granville Sharp’s courage grew from his faith that every soul matters to Heavenly Father. The case gave strength to the abolition movement and showed that laws can be changed when faith and justice come together.

sources.name: BBC History - The Somerset Case and Abolition
The National Archives (UK) - James Somerset's Case
Encyclopedia Britannica - Somerset Case

sv08.evidence: Court records, letters, and newspaper articles from 1772 carefully document what happened in Somerset’s Case. The decision by Lord Mansfield is still studied by legal scholars today. Somerset's release was widely reported in period newspapers, and writings from Granville Sharp and others involved have survived, letting us know their thoughts and motivations. Many historians agree that the ruling was a key legal blow to slavery in England, even though it did not free enslaved people across the whole British Empire at once. Later abolitionists quoted this case as proof that freedom could be defended in court.
sv08.happened: On June 22, 1772, in London, England, a court case changed the meaning of freedom for many people. James Somerset was an enslaved man brought from America to England by his owner, Charles Stewart. Somerset escaped for a time but was found and put on a ship to be sent to Jamaica, where he would likely be sold again. Granville Sharp, a deeply religious man who had helped others in similar bondage before, was moved by Somerset’s situation and used his own money to challenge this in court. The case came before Lord Mansfield, the most senior judge in England. After hearing arguments, Lord Mansfield declared that English law did not support slavery and that no person could be forcibly removed from England as a slave unless there was a specific law allowing it. Somerset was released, and people across Britain and America paid close attention.
sv08.scripture: The Bible teaches us to love our neighbor as ourselves (Matthew 22:39) and not to oppress the stranger (Exodus 22:21). The Book of Mormon reminds us that all are alike unto God (2 Nephi 26:33), while modern revelation reaffirms the freedom and dignity of each child of God (Doctrine and Covenants 98:8). Though the scriptures do not speak directly of this court case, they teach the principle that every person is precious in the Lord’s sight and that justice requires us to protect the rights of others.
sv08.background: At the time of Somerset’s case, Britain was a powerful country with a large empire, and slavery was legal in many of its colonies and common in parts of its trade. London itself had several thousand enslaved people living in homes, often without rights or protections. Laws about slavery were unclear in England, even though it was a central part of the empire's economy elsewhere. Granville Sharp was an evangelical Christian who believed all people were equal before God, and Lord Mansfield was known for careful, cautious decisions. Daily life for most people in England was shaped by strict social classes, faith, and growing debates about what freedom and personhood meant.

sv09.talk: Why do you think it's important to stand up for what's right, even when it's hard?
sv09.child: A long time ago, some people believed it was okay to make others work without pay and treat them badly. But a man named William Wilberforce and his friends thought this was wrong. They worked very hard for many years to change the rules so everyone could be free.
sv09.learn: The story of Wilberforce and the Clapham Sect teaches us that steadfast faith and persistent effort can overcome even the most entrenched injustices. It reminds us that aligning our actions with our moral and spiritual convictions can lead to meaningful change. This history encourages us to stand firm in our beliefs and to work diligently toward a more just and compassionate world.
sv09.matters: The abolition of the slave trade and slavery itself stands as a testament to the power of faith-driven activism against entrenched economic interests. For families of faith, this history underscores the importance of perseverance, moral conviction, and the belief that societal change is possible through dedicated effort. It serves as a reminder that aligning actions with spiritual beliefs can lead to profound transformations in society, even when the odds seem insurmountable.

sources.name: Clapham Sect
William Wilberforce
The Clapham Sect and the abolition of the slave trade
William Wilberforce & The Clapham Sect

sv09.evidence: Historical records, including parliamentary debates, personal letters, and contemporary publications, provide extensive evidence of the Clapham Sect's activities and their impact on the abolition of the slave trade. The Slave Trade Act of 1807 and the Slavery Abolition Act of 1833 are well-documented legislative milestones. Personal accounts, such as Olaudah Equiano's autobiography, offer firsthand perspectives on the horrors of slavery and the moral imperative for its abolition. These documents collectively affirm the historical accuracy of the events and the pivotal role played by the Clapham Sect and William Wilberforce.
sv09.happened: In 1787, William Wilberforce, a Member of Parliament and devout evangelical Christian, felt a divine calling to end the transatlantic slave trade and reform societal morals. He joined forces with the Clapham Sect, a group of like-minded evangelical Anglicans, including Granville Sharp, Thomas Clarkson, Hannah More, and Olaudah Equiano, a former enslaved man whose autobiography deeply moved the British public. Together, they campaigned tirelessly against the slave trade. Wilberforce introduced numerous abolition bills in Parliament, facing defeat for eighteen years. Their persistent efforts bore fruit when the Slave Trade Act was passed in 1807, abolishing the trade within the British Empire. The struggle continued until the Slavery Abolition Act of 1833, which freed approximately 800,000 enslaved people across the British Caribbean by 1838. Wilberforce passed away just three days after the act's passage, witnessing the culmination of his lifelong mission.
sv09.scripture: The scriptures teach the inherent worth of every individual. In the Bible, Galatians 3:28 states, "There is neither Jew nor Greek, slave nor free, male nor female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus." Similarly, the Book of Mormon emphasizes the equality of all people before God. These passages affirm the principle that all humans are equal in the eyes of God, providing a spiritual foundation for the abolitionist cause.
sv09.background: In the late 18th century, the British economy heavily depended on the transatlantic slave trade, with enslaved Africans being transported to work on plantations in the Americas. This period was marked by a growing evangelical movement within the Church of England, emphasizing personal faith and social reform. The Clapham Sect, named after the London village where many members resided, emerged from this movement. They were wealthy and influential individuals who believed their Christian faith compelled them to address social injustices, including slavery. Daily life in Britain was characterized by stark social inequalities, and the moral fabric of society was a concern for many reformers. The Clapham Sect's commitment to ending slavery was rooted in their belief in the inherent dignity of all humans as creations of God.

sv10.talk: Why is it important to help others who are being treated unfairly?
sv10.child: A long time ago, some people were taken from their homes and made to work for others without pay. The British Navy sent ships to stop this and help free those people. They worked hard for many years to make sure everyone could be free.
sv10.learn: The story of the West Africa Squadron teaches us that confronting and rectifying past wrongs is both necessary and demanding. It illustrates that meaningful change often requires sustained effort, resources, and, at times, personal sacrifice. This history encourages us to be vigilant against injustices in our own time and to take proactive steps to promote freedom and dignity for all people. It also serves as a reminder that while we cannot undo the past, we can work diligently to create a more just and compassionate future.
sv10.matters: The West Africa Squadron's mission underscores the profound impact that dedicated efforts can have in combating systemic injustices. For families of faith, this historical episode serves as a testament to the importance of standing against wrongdoing, even when it requires significant sacrifice. The squadron's actions demonstrate that repentance and restitution are possible on a national scale, though they come at a considerable cost. This history encourages us to reflect on our responsibilities to advocate for justice and to support efforts that promote the well-being and freedom of all individuals.

sources.name: West Africa Squadron - Wikipedia
Blockade of Africa - Wikipedia
West Africa Squadron Memorial Fund

sv10.evidence: Historical records provide substantial evidence of the West Africa Squadron's operations and impact. Official Royal Navy logs document the capture of approximately 1,600 slave ships and the liberation of around 150,000 Africans between 1808 and 1860. These records also detail the significant human cost to British sailors, with nearly 1,600 deaths from disease between 1830 and 1865. The squadron's efforts are further corroborated by treaties and agreements made with other nations to allow the interception and inspection of ships suspected of engaging in the slave trade. While some historians debate the overall effectiveness of the squadron, the documented actions and outcomes highlight its significant role in suppressing the transatlantic slave trade.
sv10.happened: In 1808, following the British Parliament's passage of the Slave Trade Act in 1807, the Royal Navy established the West Africa Squadron to suppress the transatlantic slave trade. Initially, the squadron comprised two ships, HMS Solebay and HMS Derwent, tasked with patrolling the West African coast to intercept vessels engaged in illegal slave trading. Over time, the squadron expanded significantly, at its peak deploying up to 25 ships and 2,000 naval officers. Between 1808 and 1860, the squadron captured approximately 1,600 slave ships and freed around 150,000 Africans who were destined for slavery. The mission was perilous; sailors faced not only the dangers of combat but also the high risk of tropical diseases. Between 1830 and 1865, nearly 1,600 British sailors died, primarily from disease. Despite these challenges, the squadron's persistent efforts played a crucial role in diminishing the transatlantic slave trade.
sv10.scripture: The scriptures teach us about the value of each soul and the importance of seeking justice. In the Book of Mormon, we read, 'But behold, the Lord hath redeemed my soul from hell; I have beheld his glory, and I am encircled about eternally in the arms of his love.' (2 Nephi 1:15) This passage reminds us of the Lord's love for all His children and the importance of working to free others from bondage, both physical and spiritual. Additionally, Doctrine and Covenants 101:79 states, 'Therefore, it is not right that any man should be in bondage one to another.' These scriptures emphasize the divine mandate to seek freedom and justice for all.
sv10.background: The early 19th century was a period of significant change regarding the institution of slavery. While the transatlantic slave trade had been a lucrative enterprise for many European nations, growing abolitionist movements, particularly in Britain, began to challenge its morality and legality. The British Parliament's passage of the Slave Trade Act in 1807 marked a pivotal shift, making it illegal for British ships to engage in the slave trade. However, the trade persisted under other flags, prompting Britain to take active measures to enforce the ban. The establishment of the West Africa Squadron was a direct response to this ongoing illicit activity. The squadron's operations were part of a broader humanitarian effort to end the suffering caused by the slave trade, reflecting a national commitment to uphold the principles of freedom and human dignity.

sv11.talk: Why do you think it's important to treat everyone fairly, especially when trying to fix past mistakes?
sv11.child: A long time ago, people in Britain decided to stop owning other people as slaves. They paid the former owners money for losing their workers, but the people who had been slaves didn't get anything. This reminds us to always be fair and kind to everyone.
sv11.learn: This history teaches us that while taking steps toward justice is essential, the methods we choose matter greatly. Compensating those who benefited from injustice, while neglecting the victims, can perpetuate feelings of inequality and resentment. It underscores the need for thoughtful, equitable solutions when addressing past wrongs, ensuring that all individuals are treated with the dignity and respect they deserve.
sv11.matters: The passage of the Slavery Abolition Act was a significant step toward ending the inhumane practice of slavery within the British Empire. However, the manner in which it was implemented—compensating slave owners while providing nothing to the formerly enslaved—highlights the complexities and injustices involved in societal transitions. For families of faith, this history serves as a reminder of the importance of advocating for true justice and equality, ensuring that efforts to right wrongs do not perpetuate further injustices.

sources.name: The 1833 Abolition of Slavery Act and compensation claims - The National Archives
Slavery Abolition Act 1833 - Wikipedia
The Scandal of the British Slavery Abolition Act Loan - Social and Economic Studies

sv11.evidence: Historical records, including parliamentary documents and financial accounts, confirm the details of the Slavery Abolition Act and its compensation scheme. The National Archives of the UK provide extensive documentation on the Act and the compensation claims submitted by slave owners. Additionally, financial records from the Bank of England detail the loan taken to fund the compensation and its final repayment in 2015. These sources provide clear evidence of the events and decisions made during this period.
sv11.happened: In 1833, the British Parliament passed the Slavery Abolition Act, which aimed to end slavery throughout most of the British Empire. This legislation declared that enslaved individuals in British colonies were to be freed. However, the Act introduced a system called 'apprenticeship,' requiring the newly freed people to continue working without pay for their former owners for a period of up to six years, ostensibly to ease the transition to freedom. This system was widely abused, leading to its early termination in 1838. Notably, the Act allocated £20 million—a substantial sum at the time, representing about 40% of the government's annual expenditure—to compensate slave owners for the loss of their 'property.' The enslaved individuals received no compensation for their years of forced labor. To fund this compensation, the British government took out a significant loan, which was not fully repaid until 2015, meaning that taxpayers, including descendants of enslaved people, were servicing this debt for 182 years.
sv11.scripture: The scriptures teach us about the inherent worth of every individual. In the Book of Mormon, we read: 'But the laborer in Zion shall labor for Zion; for if they labor for money they shall perish.' (2 Nephi 26:31) This passage reminds us that our efforts should be for the betterment of all, not for personal gain at the expense of others. Additionally, the Doctrine and Covenants instructs: 'Remember the worth of souls is great in the sight of God.' (Doctrine and Covenants 18:10) These teachings emphasize the importance of valuing each person and working toward their freedom and well-being.
sv11.background: Before the 1833 Act, Britain had a long history of involvement in the transatlantic slave trade, which was abolished in 1807. Despite this, slavery itself continued in British colonies, particularly in the Caribbean, where economies heavily depended on enslaved labor for sugar production. Enslaved individuals endured harsh conditions, with limited rights and freedoms. The abolitionist movement, comprising individuals and groups advocating for the end of slavery, gained momentum in the early 19th century, leading to increased public pressure on Parliament to act against the institution of slavery.

sv12.talk: How can we make sure we're using the scriptures to help us be kind and fair to everyone?
sv12.child: A long time ago, some churches argued about whether it was okay to have slaves. Some people used the Bible to say it was right, while others used the Bible to say it was wrong. This teaches us to always use God's teachings to do what's kind and fair.
sv12.learn: This history teaches us the importance of aligning our actions with the core principles of our faith, such as love, justice, and equality. It reminds us to be vigilant against using scripture to justify personal or societal wrongs and to seek divine guidance in interpreting sacred texts. Acknowledging past mistakes and striving for repentance and reconciliation are essential steps in living a Christ-centered life.
sv12.matters: The schism among American churches over slavery underscores the profound impact of societal issues on religious institutions. It serves as a reminder that interpretations of scripture can be influenced by personal interests and societal norms. For families of faith, this history highlights the importance of seeking divine guidance and striving for moral clarity, especially when societal pressures challenge ethical principles. It also emphasizes the need for humility and repentance when past actions or beliefs are found to be in conflict with the core teachings of love and justice.

sources.name: Southern Baptist Convention
Frederick Douglass
May 8, 1845: Formation of the Southern Baptist Convention
7 facts about Southern Baptists

sv12.evidence: Historical records confirm that the Southern Baptist Convention was founded in 1845 due to disagreements over the eligibility of slaveholders to serve as missionaries. The Triennial Convention and the Home Mission Society had adopted a neutral stance on slavery, but when they refused to appoint a slaveholder as a missionary, Southern Baptists viewed this as a violation of their rights and formed their own convention. Prominent figures like Frederick Douglass documented the use of scripture by both pro-slavery advocates and abolitionists, highlighting the moral and theological conflicts of the time. Douglass's writings, such as his autobiography, provide firsthand accounts of these debates and the hypocrisy he observed among Christian slaveholders.
sv12.happened: In the mid-19th century, the United States grappled with deep divisions over slavery, a conflict that extended into religious communities. In 1845, this tension led to a significant schism among American Baptists. The national Baptist mission boards had decided that individuals who owned slaves could not serve as missionaries. This decision was unacceptable to many Southern Baptists, who believed that slaveholders should be eligible for missionary work. As a result, representatives from Southern Baptist churches convened in Augusta, Georgia, and established the Southern Baptist Convention (SBC) to support missions that included slaveholders. This division was not unique to Baptists; other denominations, such as Methodists and Presbyterians, also split along similar lines over the issue of slavery. Southern clergy often cited scripture to defend the institution of slavery, while Northern abolitionists used the same scriptures to argue for its abolition. Prominent abolitionist Frederick Douglass highlighted this contradiction by distinguishing between the "Christianity of Christ" and the "slaveholding religion of this land," emphasizing the moral chasm between true Christian teachings and the practices of those who used religion to justify slavery.
sv12.scripture: The scriptures provide clear guidance on the treatment of others. In the Bible, the Apostle Paul teaches, "There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither bond nor free, there is neither male nor female: for ye are all one in Christ Jesus" (Galatians 3:28). This passage emphasizes the equality of all individuals before God. Similarly, the Book of Mormon teaches, "...he denieth none that come unto him, black and white, bond and free, male and female..." (2 Nephi 26:33), reinforcing the principle that all are alike unto God. These teachings remind us that true discipleship involves recognizing and honoring the inherent worth of every individual.
sv12.background: During the early 19th century, the United States was a nation deeply divided over the issue of slavery. The Southern economy heavily depended on agriculture, particularly cotton, which relied on the labor of enslaved African Americans. In contrast, the Northern states were becoming more industrialized and had largely abolished slavery. This economic and moral divide permeated all aspects of society, including religious institutions. Churches were central to community life, and their teachings influenced public opinion and policy. As the abolitionist movement gained momentum in the North, Southern churches faced increasing pressure to justify the continuation of slavery. This period also saw the rise of the Second Great Awakening, a religious revival that emphasized personal salvation and moral reform, further intensifying debates over the morality of slavery within Christian communities.

sv13.t: Harriet Tubman and the Underground Railroad
sv13.talk: Why do you think Harriet Tubman risked her life over and over to help people she didn’t know?
sv13.child: Harriet Tubman was brave and helped many people escape from slavery. She listened to God and went back to help others, even when it was very dangerous. She wanted everyone to be free.
sv13.learn: We learn from Harriet Tubman that it is not enough to be safe ourselves when others are still in danger. Faith can give us the courage to act for others, even when doing so means real risk. Her story reminds us that answers to prayer often call us to work hard and help rescue those Heavenly Father loves, wherever and whoever they are.
sv13.matters: Harriet Tubman’s story shows that faith can inspire people to risk great danger for others, even after they themselves are safe. Her actions helped weaken slavery by proving that freedom was worth fighting for, and by offering hope to those still enslaved. For a family of faith, Tubman’s life teaches that the answer to prayer can sometimes call us to help those who are in danger or suffering, using our gifts and courage to bless others as God wants.

sources.name: National Park Service – Harriet Tubman and the Underground Railroad
Smithsonian National Museum of African American History & Culture – Harriet Tubman
Library of Congress – Harriet Tubman: A Resource Guide
Encyclopedia Britannica – Harriet Tubman

sv13.evidence: Historians agree on the main facts of Tubman’s life. There are official records, testimonies, and newspapers from the time describing her escapes and work. Tubman herself could not write, but left behind interviews and stories told to others, and many people she helped later confirmed her bravery. Details like the exact number of trips and how many people she led to freedom have been studied, with most historians agreeing she made about thirteen trips and freed about seventy herself. The wider Underground Railroad likely helped tens of thousands escape before the Civil War. The evidence matches what is widely written and taught in museums and by experts.
sv13.happened: In 1849, Harriet Tubman made a brave decision—she escaped from slavery in Maryland by herself. But she did not stop there. Instead of staying safe in the North, she risked her life over and over again. Over the next eleven years, she went back to the South about thirteen different times, helping her family and many others escape as well. Tubman led about seventy people to safety herself, and always said she was guided by answers to prayer. She never lost a single passenger. The secret system she worked with was called the Underground Railroad—a network of safe houses and helpers who guided people to freedom. Tubman was known to be strong, wise, and deeply faithful. She often said it was the Lord who told her where to go and kept her safe. Her work and courage helped inspire others to join in: the Underground Railroad, which included Black families, Quakers, and people from many churches, eventually helped tens of thousands be free.
sv13.scripture: Scriptures teach about setting captives free and loving our neighbors. In the Bible, Isaiah 61:1 speaks of proclaiming liberty to captives. In the Book of Mormon, Mosiah 18:9 asks us to mourn with those who mourn and comfort those in need. Doctrine and Covenants 101:79 says that God wants all people to be free. Tubman’s story reflects these teachings: she listened for God’s voice and worked so others could be free too.
sv13.background: At this time in America, slavery was still the law in many southern states. People were owned as property, forced to work on plantations, and had few rights, even over their own families. Maryland was one of these states. African American families lived under harsh rules; it was very dangerous to run away. The Underground Railroad was not a real railroad, but a hidden network run by free Black communities, Quakers, and others who believed slavery was wrong. They helped enslaved people escape north to free states or Canada. Daily life for an enslaved person was full of work from dawn to dark, always facing the fear of being separated from loved ones.

sv14.talk: Why do you think families are so important that people risked everything to find each other again?
sv14.child: A long time ago, some people were forced to work and not allowed to be with their families. A new law ended this and let families try to find each other and be free. God wants us all to be free and with those we love.
sv14.learn: We can learn from the Thirteenth Amendment that changing the law can help heal deep wrongs, but it also takes courage and kindness to finish the work. Families can learn that God treasures freedom and that, even after pain or hurt, love binds people back together. Seeing what once was, we can be more grateful for our freedom and more willing to help others who suffer or are alone.
sv14.matters: The Thirteenth Amendment matters greatly because it marked the beginning of true freedom for millions and ended a cruel practice. For families, especially those who follow Christ, it reminds us of the deep value of each person and the sacredness of families. The sacrifices made for this change show how precious freedom is. It also serves as a reminder that while laws can change, the work of healing, forgiving, and helping others is ongoing. God gave us all the ability to choose and to care for one another, and this history calls us to use our freedom to help those still struggling today.

sources.name: National Archives - The 13th Amendment of the U.S. Constitution
Smithsonian National Museum of American History - Slavery and Freedom
Church of Jesus Christ - The Worth of Souls and Equality before God

sv14.evidence: The historical record is strong and detailed for this event. The text of the Thirteenth Amendment, the dates when states ratified it, and accounts from people freed by it are all preserved in government documents, letters, and newspapers from the time. Census records and testimonies from formerly enslaved people show how families searched for each other, placed newspaper ads, and built schools and churches. Historians have traced how the exception in the amendment (punishment for crime) led to later abuses, such as convict leasing, confirming both the progress the amendment brought and the work still left to do. Modern scholarship and primary sources agree on the core facts.
sv14.happened: On December 6, 1865, the United States took a huge step to end a terrible part of its history by passing the Thirteenth Amendment to the Constitution. This new law said that slavery and forced work, called involuntary servitude, would no longer be allowed in America—except as punishment for people convicted of a crime. This change happened after the country fought a long and bloody Civil War, where the question of slavery was a central cause. The amendment’s words meant that nearly four million people—men, women, and children—as soon as it was ratified, were declared legally free, no longer considered the property of others. This freedom was more than just a legal change; it meant families that had been ripped apart by being sold could try to find each other again. Many rushed to reunite, marry legally, and start new lives by creating schools and churches. Yet, the part about punishing criminals left room for new, unfair systems to develop, such as making some prisoners work against their will, often targeting those newly freed. Still, this amendment changed the nation and gave hope to millions, showing the high price America paid to protect freedom for all people.
sv14.scripture: Scripture teaches the worth of all souls and the command to love our neighbor. In the Bible, Galatians 3:28 says, 'There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither bond nor free... for ye are all one in Christ Jesus.' The Book of Mormon often teaches that all are alike unto God (2 Nephi 26:33). Doctrine and Covenants 101:79 directly states, 'Therefore, it is not right that any man should be in bondage one to another.' These teachings remind us that God wants all His children to be free and to treat each other as brothers and sisters.
sv14.background: Slavery had been a part of American life since before the nation was founded. People kidnapped from Africa, along with their children after them, were forced to work for no pay, mainly on farms and plantations in the South. White families benefited from their labor, while enslaved people lived with few rights, harsh punishments, and constant threat of being separated from loved ones. Many enslaved families never had legal marriages or certainties that their children would stay with them. There had always been voices against slavery, from some church groups to individuals who believed all people were equal in God’s sight. Tensions between free states and slave states grew, leading to the Civil War from 1861 to 1865, which left deep scars but ended with a promise of freedom for all.

sv15.t: Brazil, the Last in the Americas
sv15.talk: Why do you think it's important to treat everyone fairly and with kindness?
sv15.child: A long time ago in Brazil, many people were forced to work without pay, which was very unfair. One day, a princess named Isabel signed a special paper that said everyone should be free. This made many people happy because they could finally live their lives freely.
sv15.learn: The abolition of slavery in Brazil teaches us the importance of perseverance in the fight for justice. It reminds us that societal change often requires both grassroots activism and legislative action. Additionally, it highlights the need for comprehensive support systems to assist those transitioning from oppression to freedom, ensuring that liberation leads to true equality and opportunity.
sv15.matters: The abolition of slavery in Brazil marked the end of over 300 years of forced labor and human suffering. It serves as a poignant reminder of the resilience of the human spirit and the importance of advocating for justice and equality. For families of faith, this event underscores the belief that all individuals are children of God, deserving of dignity and freedom. It also highlights the responsibility to stand against oppression and to support those who are marginalized. The aftermath of abolition, however, reminds us that ending an unjust system is only the beginning; true healing and equality require ongoing effort and commitment.

sources.name: The Abolition of Slavery and the Aftermath of Emancipation in Brazil
Golden Law
The Abolition of Brazilian Slavery, 1864–1888
Lei Áurea

sv15.evidence: Historical records, including the original manuscript of the Lei Áurea housed in the Brazilian National Archives, provide clear evidence of the abolition of slavery in Brazil. Contemporary newspaper articles and personal accounts document the immediate effects of the law, including the joy of freed individuals and the economic concerns of former slave owners. Scholarly analyses, such as those found in the Oxford Research Encyclopedia of Latin American History, offer detailed examinations of the political, social, and economic factors leading to abolition. These sources collectively confirm the events of May 13, 1888, and provide insight into the complexities of this pivotal moment in Brazilian history.
sv15.happened: On May 13, 1888, Brazil took a monumental step by abolishing slavery through the Lei Áurea, or Golden Law. Princess Isabel, acting as regent for her father, Emperor Pedro II, signed this brief yet powerful law, which declared, "From this date, slavery is declared extinct in Brazil." This act immediately freed approximately 600,000 enslaved individuals, making Brazil the last country in the Western Hemisphere to end the institution of slavery. The law did not provide compensation to slave owners, reflecting a decisive break from the past. The abolition was met with widespread celebration among abolitionists and the newly freed population. However, it also intensified tensions with plantation owners, who felt betrayed by the lack of compensation and support. This discontent contributed to the fall of the Brazilian monarchy the following year, leading to the establishment of a republic in 1889.
sv15.scripture: The scriptures teach us about the inherent worth of every individual. In the Bible, Galatians 3:28 states, "There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither bond nor free, there is neither male nor female: for ye are all one in Christ Jesus." Similarly, in the Book of Mormon, Mosiah 2:17 reminds us that "when ye are in the service of your fellow beings ye are only in the service of your God." These passages emphasize the importance of treating all individuals with love, respect, and equality, principles that are directly opposed to the practice of slavery.
sv15.background: In the 19th century, Brazil's economy heavily depended on slave labor, particularly in the coffee, sugar, and cotton industries. The country had received nearly 40% of all Africans brought to the Americas, amounting to about 5.5 million people. Daily life for enslaved individuals was marked by grueling labor, harsh punishments, and a lack of basic rights. Over time, internal and external pressures mounted against the institution of slavery. Internationally, countries like Great Britain, which had abolished slavery in its own colonies, exerted diplomatic pressure on Brazil to follow suit. Domestically, abolitionist movements gained momentum, advocating for the end of slavery and the humane treatment of all individuals. Prior to the Lei Áurea, Brazil had enacted gradual measures such as the Law of the Free Womb in 1871, which declared that children born to enslaved mothers would be free, and the Sexagenarian Law in 1885, which freed slaves over the age of 60. Despite these laws, the institution of slavery remained deeply entrenched until the decisive action in 1888.

sv16.talk: Why do you think it is important that no one should ever be a slave?
sv16.child: A long time ago, not everyone agreed that people should be free. In 1948, many leaders decided together that nobody should ever be a slave again, anywhere in the world. Now, we remember how important it is to treat everyone fairly.
sv16.learn: We learn that it can take a very long time for people to agree on what is right, and even longer to make it happen everywhere. Laws like Article 4 remind us why it is important to keep working for freedom and fairness. Families can help by standing up for those who are mistreated and by teaching children to see every person as a child of God. Change starts with kindness and grows when we act on what we know is true.
sv16.matters: Article 4 matters because it marked the moment when freedom from slavery became a right for every person, not just a privilege for a few. For families who believe that God loves all His children, this is a powerful reminder that each soul has great worth. No law can make people perfect, but a law that protects freedom helps us build a world where faith can grow and kindness can flourish. This lesson invites children and adults to see others as equals and remember that every person deserves to be free.

sources.name: United Nations: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights
British Library: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights
United States Holocaust Memorial Museum: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights

sv16.evidence: There are many records and historical documents from 1948 showing how the Universal Declaration of Human Rights was agreed upon. You can find transcripts of the meetings, the signed Declaration itself, and testimonies from people who were present. The United Nations keeps records of how the Declaration was written and voted on. Over time, almost every country has accepted these rights, including the ban on slavery, although sadly, some forms of slavery and exploitation still exist in secret. Making the promise on paper was an important step; making it real for everyone is a work that continues.
sv16.happened: On December 10, 1948, leaders and representatives from many countries met in Paris, France, and agreed on something very important: a document called the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. For the first time in history, Article 4 of this document clearly stated that no one, anywhere in the world, should ever be held in slavery or servitude. It also said that all forms of slavery and the slave trade should be completely forbidden. This was different from older laws, which had only tried to stop slavery in individual countries. Now, the nations wanted to show the whole world that treating people as property was wrong—no matter where they lived. The meetings were hard and included people who had just come through the pain of World War II. By signing the Declaration, these leaders agreed that freedom from slavery is a right every person is born with. This helped set a moral standard for the world, even though not every country was ready to enforce it right away.
sv16.scripture: The scriptures teach that all men are alike unto God (2 Nephi 26:33, Book of Mormon) and that we should love our neighbors as ourselves (Matthew 22:39, Bible). The Doctrine and Covenants also says, 'It is not right that any man should be in bondage to another' (D&C 101:79). These verses remind us that God wants all His children to be free to choose and to act for themselves, respecting the dignity He gives each person.
sv16.background: Before Article 4, slavery had existed for thousands of years in almost every part of the world. Some nations had already banned slavery, while in others it was still a painful part of life. In 1948, the world was just starting to recover from World War II, a conflict that had shown how cruelly people could treat one another. Many families had lost loved ones, and countries were rebuilding. People from different backgrounds—men and women, those who had suffered in war or grown up in peace—came together to write the Declaration. Their goal was to create a future where everyone could live in dignity and freedom, no matter their race, background, or beliefs.

sv17.talk: What can we do to help people who are being treated unfairly or forced to do things against their will?
sv17.child: Even though slavery was made illegal long ago, many people are still forced to work without pay or are made to marry against their will. It's important to learn about this so we can help stop it and make the world a better place for everyone.
sv17.learn: Understanding that modern slavery still exists today teaches us the importance of vigilance and compassion. It calls us to be aware of the origins of the products we consume and to support ethical practices. By educating ourselves and others, advocating for stronger laws, and supporting organizations fighting against modern slavery, we can contribute to ending this grave injustice.
sv17.matters: The persistence of modern slavery is a profound moral and social issue. It violates fundamental human rights and undermines the dignity of millions. For families of faith, it serves as a stark reminder of the importance of compassion, justice, and the responsibility to protect the vulnerable. Recognizing that modern slavery exists even today calls for collective action to raise awareness, support victims, and advocate for stronger laws and enforcement to eradicate this inhumane practice.

sources.name: Global Slavery Index 2023
International Labour Organization: Global Estimates of Modern Slavery

sv17.evidence: The Global Slavery Index, produced by Walk Free, provides comprehensive data on modern slavery. The 2023 report estimates that 50 million people are living in modern slavery, marking a 25% increase over five years. The report highlights that modern slavery is hidden in plain sight and is deeply intertwined with life in every corner of the world. It also points out that G20 countries collectively import billions of dollars worth of goods at risk of being produced by forced labor every year. This evidence underscores the widespread nature of modern slavery and the urgent need for global action to address it.
sv17.happened: In 2023, the Global Slavery Index reported that approximately 50 million people were living in modern slavery worldwide. This figure includes 28 million individuals subjected to forced labor and 22 million in forced marriages. Modern slavery manifests in various forms, such as debt bondage in South Asian brick kilns and agriculture, forced labor in fishing and manufacturing supply chains, state-imposed labor, and sex trafficking. Alarmingly, about one in four victims is a child. This data underscores that modern slavery is a pervasive issue affecting every region, including affluent nations. The increase of 10 million people in modern slavery since 2016 highlights the growing severity of this global crisis.
sv17.scripture: The scriptures emphasize the inherent worth of every individual and the call to love and serve one another. In the Bible, Galatians 5:13 states, 'By love serve one another.' The Book of Mormon teaches, 'When ye are in the service of your fellow beings ye are only in the service of your God' (Mosiah 2:17). These passages remind us of our duty to help those in bondage and to work towards their freedom and well-being.
sv17.background: Historically, slavery was a legally sanctioned system where individuals were owned and forced to work without pay. Over time, global movements led to the abolition of legal slavery, with many countries enacting laws to prohibit it. Despite these legal advancements, modern slavery persists in clandestine forms. Factors such as poverty, lack of education, political instability, and weak governance contribute to individuals becoming vulnerable to exploitation. In today's interconnected world, complex supply chains and global demand for cheap labor have further exacerbated the problem, allowing modern slavery to thrive in various industries.

sv18.talk: Can you think of a time when someone stood up for what was right, even when it was hard or unpopular?
sv18.child: Long ago, most people thought slavery was okay. But then, many followers of Jesus worked together to help everyone see that it wasn't right, and they helped the world change. They believed everyone is a child of Heavenly Father and should be free.
sv18.learn: From this great change, we learn that belief can move people to stand up for what’s right, sometimes against long-standing wrongs. The work of ending slavery took time, help from many, and faith that all people are God's children. We also learn that what becomes normal can change, and we have a part to play in making our world kinder and fairer. Even when history took a long time to change, conviction and effort eventually made the difference.
sv18.matters: This turning point matters because it shows that real change is possible, even when something has always been done a certain way. For families of faith, it’s important to see that good people—acting on their beliefs about God's love for every soul—can shape whole societies for the better. The abolition of legal slavery teaches us about conscience, courage, and the power of a community standing up against what is wrong, even when it takes time and sacrifice. It also reminds us that change often comes from both inner conviction and public action, working together.

sources.name: Smithsonian National Museum of African American History & Culture - Slavery and Freedom
Encyclopedia Britannica - Abolitionism
Church of Jesus Christ - What Does the Book of Mormon Teach About Equality?

sv18.evidence: Historians have found abundant evidence that the major abolitionist movements in Britain and America were led by people of faith, especially Quakers, evangelical Christians, and members of Black churches. Letters, meeting notes, and church records show these groups organizing campaigns, helping people escape slavery, and influencing laws. Economic changes and Enlightenment ideas also played roles, but primary documents reveal that the language of human equality and dignity often came right from religious convictions. Scholars still debate how much weight to give each cause, but most agree that faith-inspired groups were at the forefront and made lasting impact. Comprehensive research at museums like the Smithsonian and published work by universities have confirmed the main story and details.
sv18.happened: Between the late 1700s and the early 1900s, the world saw a change no one had truly expected: people across nations began to see slavery itself as something deeply wrong. Until then, for nearly all of remembered history, most communities normalised slavery, thinking of it as an ordinary part of life. But over about 120 years, groups of men and women—many moved by faith—gathered to argue, pray, write, and work for its end. In Britain and the United States, especially, the movement to abolish slavery was powered by churches, religious groups, and believers who taught that every person mattered to God. It was not a sudden or easy victory. Laws had to change, wars were fought, and many people suffered for pushing against the old way. Yet by the early 1900s, keeping people as slaves became not just illegal but almost unthinkable in many countries. The world didn’t become perfect, but it did change its mind, and slavery was no longer seen by most as a normal or respectable institution.
sv18.scripture: The scriptures teach that every person is precious to God. The Bible states in Acts 17:26 that God "hath made of one blood all nations of men for to dwell on all the face of the earth." In the Book of Mormon, 2 Nephi 26:33 teaches that the Lord invites all to come to Him, and "he denieth none that come unto him, black and white, bond and free, male and female." Doctrine and Covenants 101:79 also states, emphasizing the value of agency: "Therefore, it is not right that any man should be in bondage one to another." While scriptures reflect the world they were written in, these passages have been powerful principles for those who worked to end slavery.
sv18.background: Before this time, slavery existed on nearly every continent, shaping daily life for both the powerful and the powerless. In most cities and villages, it was common for people to own, sell, or inherit human beings, and most grew up not questioning it. Slaves could be captured in war, born to enslaved mothers, or sold in times of hardship. Life for many enslaved people was harsh, with few rights and little hope. Enslaved men, women, and children often worked on farms, built roads, or cleaned homes. While some faith groups quietly questioned slavery for centuries, there was little open challenge until the late 1700s, when religious thinkers and activists began public campaigns for abolition, especially in Britain and America. This world was changing fast with new ideas about rights and humanity.

w001.talk: Why do you think it's important to stand up for what you believe in, even when it's hard?
w001.child: A long time ago, the Greeks fought to keep their homes safe from a big empire called Persia. They worked together and won, which helped keep their way of life and language alive. Later, this language was used to write about Jesus, so many people could learn about Him.
w001.learn: The Greco-Persian Wars teach us the value of courage, unity, and the defense of one's principles against formidable challenges. They remind us that the preservation of culture and language can have far-reaching impacts, influencing future generations and the spread of transformative ideas, such as the teachings of Christ.
w001.matters: The Greek victories in the Greco-Persian Wars were pivotal in preserving their unique culture, political structures, and philosophies. This cultural preservation had profound implications for the development of Western civilization. For families of faith, these events underscore the importance of resilience and unity in the face of overwhelming challenges. The survival of Greek language and thought provided a foundation for the dissemination of the gospel centuries later, as the New Testament was written in Koine Greek, making it accessible to a broad audience across the Mediterranean world.

sources.name: Greco-Persian Wars
New Testament
Koine Greek

w001.evidence: Historical records from both Greek and Persian sources, including Herodotus's 'Histories,' provide detailed accounts of the Greco-Persian Wars. Archaeological findings, such as weaponry and fortifications, corroborate these narratives. The widespread use of Koine Greek in the Eastern Mediterranean during the first century AD is well-documented, with numerous manuscripts of the New Testament written in this dialect, indicating its role as the lingua franca of the time.
w001.happened: The Greco-Persian Wars were a series of conflicts between the Persian Empire and Greek city-states, occurring from 499 to 449 BC. The initial spark was the Ionian Revolt (499–493 BC), where Greek cities in Asia Minor rebelled against Persian rule. Athens and Eretria supported this revolt, leading to Persian King Darius I's desire for retribution. In 490 BC, Darius launched the first Persian invasion of Greece, culminating in the Battle of Marathon, where the Athenians achieved a surprising victory. A decade later, Darius's son, Xerxes I, led a massive invasion. The Greeks, under Spartan King Leonidas, made a legendary stand at Thermopylae but were ultimately overcome. However, the Greek navy, commanded by Themistocles, secured a decisive victory at the Battle of Salamis in 480 BC. The following year, Greek forces triumphed at the Battle of Plataea, effectively ending Persian ambitions in Greece. These victories ensured the survival and flourishing of Greek civilization.
w001.scripture: While the Bible does not directly reference the Greco-Persian Wars, the principle of God's providence in guiding nations and events is evident throughout scripture. In Acts 17:26, Paul speaks of God determining the times and boundaries of nations, suggesting a divine hand in historical events. This aligns with the belief that the preservation of Greek culture and language was instrumental in the spread of the gospel, as the New Testament was written in Koine Greek, facilitating its reach across diverse populations.
w001.background: In the late 6th century BC, the Persian Empire, under Cyrus the Great and later Darius I, expanded its vast territories, encompassing diverse cultures and regions, including the Greek-inhabited areas of Ionia. The Greeks, organized into independent city-states like Athens and Sparta, valued their autonomy and democratic practices. Daily life in these city-states revolved around agriculture, trade, and civic participation. The Persian approach of appointing local tyrants to govern the Greek cities in Ionia led to unrest, as the Greeks resisted external control and sought to preserve their way of life.

w002.talk: How do you think something that looks like a problem, like a war, could ever help something good happen later?
w002.child: A long time ago, Rome and Carthage fought three big wars. Rome won, built strong roads, and later those roads helped Paul and other early Christians tell people about Jesus. God used things from those wars to help His work later.
w002.learn: From the Punic Wars, we learn that the choices of nations and leaders can shape history for centuries. We also see that Heavenly Father can use even the tools and plans of powerful empires to prepare for His messengers and His teachings. As families, we can trust that the Lord sees the bigger picture and can use even hard times for His good purposes.
w002.matters: The Punic Wars matter because their outcome shaped the world that Jesus and His apostles entered. They helped Rome become the greatest power in the region, making the Pax Romana, a long period of peace and stability. The Romans built safe roads across their empire for soldiers, but later these roads helped missionaries like the Apostle Paul travel and share the gospel. For families of faith, it reminds us that even big, difficult events in history can play a part in God’s work and in preparing the world for His message.

sources.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Punic Wars
BBC History: The Punic Wars
Smithsonian Magazine: How Rome Destroyed Carthage
Church of Jesus Christ: Paul's Journeys

w002.evidence: Archaeologists have uncovered the ruins of Carthage in modern-day Tunisia, showing a city with strong walls and busy marketplaces. Roman records and writings tell us about the wars, the leaders, and the battles, especially about Hannibal’s daring march with elephants into Italy. Ancient coins and weapons have been found, confirming much of the story. Some details—like the numbers involved—are still debated, but the main facts are well-supported by both Roman and Carthaginian sources from the time and confirmed with physical evidence dug from the ground.
w002.happened: The Punic Wars were a series of three major wars fought between Rome and Carthage over a period of more than 100 years, from 264 to 146 BC.
