Thousands were deported to remote areas, imprisoned, or executed. The state imposed unrealistic grain quotas on these collective farms. When the quotas weren't met, authorities confiscated not only grain but all available food, leaving families with nothing to eat. To prevent people from seeking food elsewhere, the government restricted movement, effectively trapping them in famine-stricken areas. This deliberate policy led to a catastrophic famine, known as the Holodomor, in Ukraine during 1932-1933, resulting in the deaths of millions.
wk08.scripture: The scriptures emphasize the importance of agency and the stewardship of one's own labor. In the Doctrine and Covenants, the Lord instructs, "It is not meet that I should command in all things; for he that is compelled in all things... the same is slothful and not a wise servant" (D&C 58:26). This teaches that individuals should have the freedom to act and make choices, including how they work and provide for their families. Additionally, the Bible warns against oppressing the poor and needy: "He that oppresseth the poor reproacheth his Maker" (Proverbs 14:31). These passages remind us of the divine principle that each person should have the opportunity to work, make choices, and be treated with dignity and respect.
wk08.background: In the late 1920s, the Soviet Union was undergoing rapid changes under Stalin's leadership. The government aimed to transform the country from a primarily agrarian society into an industrial powerhouse. To achieve this, they believed that collectivizing agriculture would produce enough surplus grain to export and fund industrial projects. Ukraine, often referred to as the "breadbasket of Europe" due to its fertile soil, was central to this plan. Before collectivization, Ukrainian farmers, or peasants, worked their own land, growing crops and raising livestock to feed their families and sell at local markets. Life was challenging but manageable, with communities built around shared traditions and mutual support. The sudden shift to collectivization disrupted this way of life, stripping individuals of their property and autonomy, and replacing traditional farming practices with state-controlled methods.

wk09.talk: Why is it important to tell the truth, even when it's hard?
wk09.child: Long ago in China, leaders tried to make the country grow very fast by changing how people lived and worked. They made everyone share farms and cook together. But this plan didn't work, and many people didn't have enough food, leading to a lot of sadness and loss.
wk09.learn: The Great Leap Forward teaches the critical importance of informed decision-making, the dangers of suppressing dissent, and the necessity of aligning policies with the well-being of individuals. It reminds us that economic and social initiatives should be implemented with careful consideration of their impact on people's lives and that transparency and accountability are essential in governance.
wk09.matters: The Great Leap Forward serves as a stark reminder of the dangers of implementing large-scale economic and social policies without adequate planning and consideration of human costs. For families of faith, it underscores the importance of stewardship, the value of individual agency, and the need for compassionate leadership. The tragedy highlights how the suppression of truth and the absence of accountability can lead to devastating consequences, emphasizing the necessity of honesty and integrity in both personal and communal endeavors.

sources.name: Great Leap Forward
Great Chinese Famine
Great Leap Forward famine | History | Research Starters | EBSCOhost
China's forbidden memory of the greatest famine in history

wk09.evidence: Historical records, survivor testimonies, and demographic studies provide substantial evidence of the events and consequences of the Great Leap Forward. Scholars such as Frank Dikötter and Yang Jisheng have conducted extensive research using Chinese archival materials, estimating death tolls ranging from 36 to 45 million. These studies highlight the role of policy decisions, such as forced collectivization and unrealistic production targets, in exacerbating the famine. The lack of accurate data due to government censorship has made precise figures challenging to determine, but the consensus acknowledges the immense human cost of the campaign.
wk09.happened: In 1958, China's leader, Mao Zedong, launched the Great Leap Forward, aiming to rapidly transform the country from an agrarian society into an industrialized socialist nation. This campaign involved merging individual farms into large communes, abolishing private land ownership, and promoting communal living and dining. Peasants were encouraged to produce steel in backyard furnaces, diverting labor from agriculture. Local officials, under pressure to meet unrealistic production targets, often reported exaggerated harvest figures. Consequently, the government requisitioned grain based on these inflated numbers, leaving insufficient food for the rural population. Combined with flawed agricultural techniques and adverse weather conditions, this led to a catastrophic famine between 1959 and 1961, resulting in the deaths of an estimated 15 to 45 million people.
wk09.scripture: The scriptures teach the importance of truth and accountability. In Doctrine and Covenants 93:24, it states, "And truth is knowledge of things as they are, and as they were, and as they are to come." This emphasizes the need for honesty and transparency. Additionally, in Mosiah 29:26-27, it warns against the dangers of unrighteous leadership and the consequences of collective iniquity, highlighting the responsibility of both leaders and citizens to uphold righteousness.
wk09.background: Prior to the Great Leap Forward, China was primarily an agrarian society with a vast rural population engaged in subsistence farming. The Chinese Communist Party, under Mao Zedong, had established control in 1949 and sought to rapidly modernize the nation. Inspired by the Soviet model of industrialization, Mao aimed to surpass Western economies by mobilizing the masses. The late 1950s were marked by political campaigns to consolidate power and suppress dissent, creating an environment where ambitious policies could be implemented without significant opposition. Daily life for many Chinese involved traditional farming practices, and the sudden shift to collectivization and industrialization disrupted established routines and social structures.

wk10.talk: Why do you think people in East Germany wanted to move to West Germany?
wk10.child: After World War II, Germany was split into two parts: West Germany, where people could own businesses and make choices, and East Germany, where the government controlled everything. Many people in East Germany wanted to move to the West for a better life.
wk10.learn: The division of Germany teaches us that economic systems profoundly affect individual freedoms and national prosperity. Systems that respect personal agency and encourage innovation tend to foster greater well-being. It also reminds us of the resilience of the human spirit in seeking freedom and better opportunities.
wk10.matters: The division of Germany serves as a profound lesson on the impact of economic systems on national prosperity and individual freedoms. For families of faith, it underscores the importance of agency and the ability to make choices that align with one's values. The stark differences between East and West Germany highlight how systems that respect individual rights and encourage personal responsibility can lead to greater well-being and societal progress.

sources.name: How Germany Was Divided After World War II | HISTORY
East Germany has narrowed economic gap with West Germany since fall of communism, but still lags | Pew Research Center
Economy of East Germany - Wikipedia

wk10.evidence: Historical data reveals significant economic disparities between East and West Germany. In 1989, West Germany's GDP was approximately ten times that of East Germany. Additionally, the standard of living, access to consumer goods, and personal freedoms were markedly higher in the West. The construction of the Berlin Wall in 1961 was a direct response to the mass exodus of East Germans seeking better opportunities in the West, highlighting the failures of the centrally planned economy.
wk10.happened: After World War II, Germany was divided into four occupation zones controlled by the United States, the United Kingdom, France, and the Soviet Union. In 1949, the zones controlled by the Western Allies merged to form the Federal Republic of Germany (West Germany), adopting a market-based economy. The Soviet-controlled zone became the German Democratic Republic (East Germany), implementing a centrally planned economy. This division led to significant economic disparities. By 1989, West Germany's GDP per capita was approximately double that of East Germany. The Berlin Wall, erected in 1961, aimed to prevent East Germans from fleeing to the West, as about 2.7 million had already done so. The Wall became a symbol of the stark differences between the two systems.
wk10.scripture: The principle of agency is central to the gospel. In the Book of Mormon, Lehi teaches that "men are free according to the flesh... to choose liberty and eternal life... or to choose captivity and death" (2 Nephi 2:27). This underscores the importance of the freedom to choose, which was severely restricted in East Germany's centrally planned system.
wk10.background: Post-World War II Europe was marked by the ideological struggle between capitalism and communism. Germany, at the heart of this divide, became a focal point. The Western Allies introduced the Marshall Plan to rebuild economies, fostering rapid growth in West Germany. In contrast, East Germany's economy was centrally planned, with the state controlling production and distribution. Daily life in East Germany was characterized by limited consumer goods and restricted freedoms, leading many to seek better opportunities in the West.

wk11.talk: What do you think happens when families and people can own things and choose their own work?
wk11.child: Long ago, one country, Korea, was split in two. One side let people own things and run businesses, and the other side kept almost everything owned by the government. After many years, the side that let people work and trade freely became much richer and happier.
wk11.learn: One key lesson is that systems that respect ownership, allow people to trade and work freely, and encourage invention and learning tend to lead to greater peace and prosperity over time. But we also learn how divisions can last for generations, causing pain and loss for countless families. In our own homes and communities, we can remember to respect others’ property, use our gifts wisely, and look for ways to help all people prosper together.
wk11.matters: The story of North and South Korea matters because it offers a rare example in history: the same people, divided by an idea and by systems of property and work, whose outcomes could be compared. For families who believe God gives us tools, talents, and agency, the Korean case invites us to notice what happens when people are free to use property, trade, and labor in different ways. It also reminds us of the pain caused by division and the importance of seeking peace and prosperity for all, wherever we live.

sources.name: Britannica: Korea Division and War
World Bank: South Korea Data
Heritage Index of Economic Freedom: North Korea vs. South Korea
NASA Earth Observatory: Korea at Night

wk11.evidence: Historical and economic evidence clearly show the differences between North and South Korea’s outcomes since the divide. According to studies from the World Bank and United Nations, South Korea transformed from deep poverty in the 1950s to become one of the world's leading economies, with strong exports and advanced education. North Korea, by contrast, remains one of the least developed and most closed economies on earth. Satellite photos from NASA show the stark difference at night: South Korea is bright and bustling, while North Korea is nearly dark. Economic indexes like the Heritage Foundation’s Index of Economic Freedom regularly rank North Korea last in the world for property rights and business freedom. Experts widely agree that these differences are a result of the economic and property systems each country chose after the war.
wk11.happened: In 1953, after three years of brutal fighting during the Korean War, the land of Korea was split in two right at the 38th parallel—a line drawn almost straight across the middle of the country. Families were suddenly separated, sometimes with family members trapped on opposite sides. The north became the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea (North Korea) under a communist government backed by the Soviet Union and China. The south became the Republic of Korea (South Korea) with a government influenced more by Western countries like the United States. Over the next seventy years, these two Koreas took very different paths. North Korea’s leaders chose a system where almost all property, businesses, and farmland belonged to the state. South Korea, meanwhile, encouraged private ownership, running businesses for profit, and trading with other countries. As years passed, these decisions deeply shaped the lives of their people. South Korea emerged as a country known for its technology, education, and international business, while North Korea became one of the poorest and most isolated places on earth. Even today, the difference is so dramatic you can see it from space: at night, South Korea glows with bright city lights, while North Korea remains almost completely dark.
wk11.scripture: No single scripture speaks directly about modern Korea, but many teach about the principles involved. In Genesis 1:28, God gives Adam and Eve stewardship over the earth, inviting responsible use of its resources. The parable of the talents (Matthew 25:14-30) shows the importance of working, multiplying what we are given, and accountability. In Doctrine and Covenants 134:2, we read that governments were instituted for the benefit of man, and individuals should be protected in their rights of property and labor. These principles suggest that the way we use resources and organize work truly matters to the Lord.
wk11.background: Koreans share a rich history going back thousands of years, with a common language, traditions, and family-centered culture. Before the split, daily life in Korea was tough—most people were poor farmers working the land, and very few owned much more than the basics. In the early 1900s, Japan ruled Korea as a colony, forcing many harsh changes and taking much of what people produced. When World War II ended in 1945, Korea was finally freed from Japanese control. However, almost immediately, Soviet forces occupied the north and Americans took the south, leading to new foreign influences and the start of tension about how Korea should be governed. Families hoped for peace but lived with uncertainty, not knowing the deep divide that would soon come.

wk12.t: Eighteen Farmers Sign a Secret Contract
wk12.talk: Why do you think people work harder when they know they can keep some of what they earn?
wk12.child: A long time ago, some farmers in China made a secret promise so their families could keep and eat the food they grew. Because they worked so hard and shared, their village grew more food than ever and helped change the country.
wk12.learn: We can learn that when people are trusted and allowed to care for their own families, they often work harder and come up with wise solutions. Heavenly Father values honest work and letting people grow through their efforts. Sometimes, brave choices—made quietly and kindly—can bring blessings to many others, both now and far into the future.
wk12.matters: This event matters because it shows the deep connection between work and the right to enjoy its fruits. When families had a chance to benefit from their own labor, they worked harder and produced more food, not only helping themselves but eventually helping their entire country. For families of faith, this story reminds us that sharing the blessings of work, stewardship, and caring for each other’s children are holy principles. God gives us the tools to solve problems together and expects us to care for our neighbors, especially in hard times.

sources.name: World Bank: Understanding China’s Poverty Reduction Success
PBS: The Xiaogang Village Story
National Geographic: A Decisive Harvest

wk12.evidence: The story of the Xiaogang agreement has been widely documented in Chinese government records, news reports, and scholarly studies. The original contract itself, with fingerprints from all eighteen farmers, is on display at a museum in Xiaogang. Interviews with the farmers and their families have confirmed many details, and the dramatic growth in Xiaogang’s harvest is supported by official crop records. Economic analyses have shown that after this system was adopted nationwide, over 800 million people in China escaped extreme poverty, an achievement recognized by the World Bank and other international organizations.
wk12.happened: In December 1978, in the tiny village of Xiaogang in Anhui, China, eighteen farmers were hungry and desperate. Their families faced not just hunger, but real fear for their lives, as years of poor crops and strict government rules meant they did not have enough to eat. One cold night, these men gathered in secret to write out an agreement. They decided to divide the commune’s farmland into small family plots. Each family would grow crops on its own piece of land, still giving the required share to the government. Anything they grew beyond the quota, they could keep for themselves or sell. They each pressed their thumbprints to the paper, knowing this could cost them their lives. At the bottom, they wrote a promise that if anyone was caught and killed, the others would raise their children. The next year, Xiaogang’s harvest was larger than the five years before put together. Soon, China’s leaders learned about the village’s success. Instead of punishing them, the government decided to make this idea legal across the country. This change helped millions of families work their way out of poverty.
wk12.scripture: The principle of reaping the rewards of one’s own labor is found throughout scripture. In the Bible, Paul wrote, 'And that ye study to be quiet, and to do your own business, and to work with your own hands' (1 Thessalonians 4:11). In the Book of Mormon, Alma teaches that 'every man should have an equal chance...to reap and to eat the fruit of his labors' (Alma 30:32). The Doctrine and Covenants also counsels, 'Thou shalt not idle away thy time, neither shalt thou bury thy talent' (D&C 60:13). These verses affirm the dignity of honest work and the blessings of self-reliance.
wk12.background: At that time in China, all farmland was owned by the government and managed through what was called ‘communal farming.’ Everyone worked together, and no one got to keep what they grew—everything went into one big pot, and the harvest was shared out by officials. This system was part of the larger policies under Chairman Mao Zedong, whose leadership had brought many years of hardship. People were told what to plant and when to harvest, whether it worked or not. During the years before the Xiaogang contract, there were severe food shortages. Many families had lost loved ones to famine. The people in Xiaogang were poor farmers—most did not read or write—simply trying to find a way to feed their families.

wk13.talk: Why do you think it is important for people to have the chance to work and try new things?
wk13.child: India used to have many rules that made it hard to open a shop or grow a business. When they took away those extra rules, many people were able to get new jobs and take better care of their families. This helped millions of families have better lives.
wk13.learn: We can learn that sometimes, giving people more freedom to use their talents and work hard brings wonderful results. When leaders trust their people and invite new ideas, whole communities can grow and improve. As families, we can think about how encouraging effort and wise choices in our own homes and neighborhoods can help everyone succeed and serve one another.
wk13.matters: This event teaches us that sometimes, the rules we live by can make a big difference in people’s lives. India’s decision to let people build businesses more freely helped millions of families find work and hope. For families of faith, this reminds us that agency, or the right to choose and act, is an important principle. When people are trusted to use their gifts and work hard, they can make a real difference in their lives and communities. It also shows that change does not always mean giving up what is important in our beliefs and culture. Sometimes, it is just about letting good people try new things.

sources.name: World Bank – India’s Economic Reforms
Britannica – India Since 1947
BBC – How 1991 changed Indian economy

wk13.evidence: Researchers and economists have closely studied India’s reforms in 1991. Historical records, government data, and international reports show that after these changes, India’s economy grew much faster. The rate of poverty decreased dramatically, especially extreme poverty, which fell from about half the population in 1991 to less than 10 percent in recent years. Studies from groups like the World Bank confirm these results. While not all problems were solved, and challenges remain, most experts agree that opening up the economy and reducing unnecessary rules led to much better opportunities for many families in India.
wk13.happened: In July 1991, India faced a very tough situation with its economy. The government was almost out of money and could not pay for necessary things from other countries. To solve this, India made a big change. For many years, to start or run a business in India, people needed to get lots of permissions from the government. This was called the Licence Raj. It made opening or growing a business slow and hard, as officials had to approve almost every step. In 1991, India's leaders decided to remove many of those rules. They made it much easier for people to start businesses and open shops, and they also lowered the taxes that made foreign goods very expensive. India began welcoming foreign companies and investment, allowing more ideas, jobs, and products into the country. These changes allowed businesses to grow much faster and helped families find more jobs and better opportunities. Over the next decades, these steps led to stronger growth for the whole country and lifted hundreds of millions of people out of extreme poverty.
wk13.scripture: Scriptures teach about the blessings of working diligently and using our agency wisely. In the Bible, Proverbs 10:4 says, 'He becometh poor that dealeth with a slack hand: but the hand of the diligent maketh rich.' The Book of Mormon often encourages us to be wise stewards and help each other prosper, such as in Mosiah 4:26, which speaks of sharing and serving one another. Doctrine and Covenants 58:27-28 encourages each person to 'be anxiously engaged in a good cause' and use their own talents and initiative for good. These scriptures underline that hard work, service, and wise use of our freedoms can bless many lives.
wk13.background: Before 1991, India’s economy was very controlled by the government. Many rules protected local businesses, but also kept many people very poor. The government wanted to keep control so that people would not be taken advantage of by big companies from other countries. Life was often hard for ordinary families. Jobs were hard to find, and most people lived in rural areas and worked on farms. Starting any new business meant going through many government offices, filling out forms, and waiting a long time for permission. Daily life for most families meant worrying about money, finding work, and making do with less, even though India had many bright people and good ideas.

wk14.talk: Why is it important for families to have official papers that show they own their homes?
wk14.child: When families have papers that prove they own their homes, they can use them to get loans to start businesses or fix their houses. This helps them have better lives.
wk14.learn: Recognizing and formalizing property rights can empower individuals and families to fully utilize their assets, leading to economic growth and self-reliance. Simplifying legal processes and reducing bureaucratic barriers are crucial steps in enabling this transformation.
wk14.matters: De Soto's work underscores the importance of property rights in economic development. For families of faith, it highlights the principle of stewardship—responsibly managing and utilizing resources. Recognizing and formalizing what families already possess can lead to self-reliance and prosperity, aligning with the belief that all individuals should have the opportunity to improve their circumstances through honest efforts.

sources.name: Hernando De Soto: Integrating the poor into official legal system can unleash their economic potential
The Mystery of Capital | Environment & Urbanization
Formalisation of land rights in the South: An overview - ScienceDirect

wk14.evidence: Studies following land titling programs in countries like Peru, Thailand, and Rwanda have generally found positive outcomes. These include increased investment in properties, greater access to credit, and enhanced household labor supply. However, some critiques suggest that merely providing titles doesn't automatically lead to economic benefits without supportive policies and infrastructure. The effectiveness of such programs often depends on the broader economic and legal context.
wk14.happened: In 2000, Peruvian economist Hernando de Soto published "The Mystery of Capital," highlighting how the poor possess assets that remain economically inactive due to lack of formal property rights. He termed these unrecognized assets "dead capital," estimating their global value at approximately $9.3 trillion. De Soto's research revealed that in Peru, registering a small business could take up to 300 days of full-time effort, deterring many from entering the formal economy. This bureaucratic complexity left many unable to leverage their assets for economic advancement. De Soto advocated for integrating informal property into the legal system to unlock this potential.
wk14.scripture: The principle of stewardship is emphasized in Doctrine and Covenants 104:11, where the Lord instructs, "It is expedient that I, the Lord, should make every man accountable, as a steward over earthly blessings." This teaches that individuals are entrusted with resources and are accountable for their use, aligning with the idea that formalizing property rights enables better stewardship and utilization of assets.
wk14.background: During the late 20th century, many developing countries, including Peru, experienced rapid urbanization. This led to the proliferation of informal settlements where residents lacked legal property titles. Without formal recognition, these individuals couldn't access credit or fully participate in the formal economy. De Soto, through his Institute for Liberty and Democracy, studied these challenges, emphasizing the need for legal reforms to empower the poor by formalizing their property rights.

wk15.talk: What do you think would happen if someone took away your favorite toy, even if they said it was to share with everyone?
wk15.child: In Venezuela, the government took many people’s businesses and farms because they wanted to share better. But it made things worse, and lots of people had to leave their homes. It teaches us that being able to work and own things helps families stay strong and safe.
wk15.learn: We learn that a country’s greatest treasure is not just in its soil or oil, but in its people having the freedom and trust to work, provide, and care for their families. When property rights are not protected, it can become difficult to bless others or plan for the future. As a family, we can remember that stewardship is both a gift and a responsibility — and to pray for those who are suffering far from home, hoping for better laws and leaders.
wk15.matters: This event matters because it shows that even a country with great natural wealth can struggle if the rules of property and ownership change suddenly or unfairly. For a family of faith, it reminds us that agency and stewardship come with responsibility. When people do not feel safe in what they own, they may lose the ability to provide for their loved ones or help their neighbor. Families everywhere can see from Venezuela that stable laws and trust in fair dealings are part of what help communities prosper and care for each other. It also teaches us the importance of wise leaders who protect both the poor and the freedoms family life needs.

sources.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Venezuela
United Nations Refugee Agency: Venezuela Situation
BBC News: Why is Venezuela in crisis?
International Monetary Fund: The Collapse of Venezuela’s Economy

wk15.evidence: Historical records, news reports, and studies by groups like the United Nations and International Monetary Fund confirm this story. Beginning in 1999, Venezuela’s government nationalized large sectors of its economy, taking property from private owners and imposing strict controls. Reports show that these actions led to reduced production, higher unemployment, shortages in basic goods, and one of the world’s worst cases of hyperinflation. By 2023, millions had migrated to other countries, making Venezuela one of the largest current sources of displaced people. Economic research clearly connects the loss of private property rights and the crisis that followed. These findings are open, widely reported, and not seriously debated among historians or economists today.
wk15.happened: In 1999, Venezuela began a dramatic change in how property and businesses were owned and controlled. Led by President Hugo Chávez, the government decided that industries like oil, steel, cement, phone companies, and farms should belong to everyone, not just private owners or foreign companies. This process, called nationalization and expropriation, meant the government took over thousands of businesses. They believed this would help share the country's wealth more fairly, especially since Venezuela has the largest oil reserves in the world. The government also set limits on what things could cost, trying to make essentials like food and medicine affordable. Over the years though, these new rules made many businesses close or shrink because they could not survive without fair prices or private investment. By the 2010s, Venezuela’s economy had collapsed. There was not enough food or medicine, money lost its value, and millions could not find work or support their families. The crisis grew so severe that about 7.7 million Venezuelans left their homes — one of the largest refugee crises today. Families had to separate, and life for many became about survival.
wk15.scripture: Laws about property and honest work are mentioned throughout scripture. In the Bible, Exodus 20:15 commands, “Thou shalt not steal.” In the Book of Mormon, Mosiah 2 and Alma 1 praise honest labor and generosity, but warn against compulsion and forced sharing. Doctrine and Covenants 134:2-3 teaches that governments should secure the right to own and control property. This principle echoes through scripture: the Lord values both caring for the needy and respecting our ability to choose and steward our resources wisely, without force or fear.
wk15.background: Before these changes, Venezuela was rich in oil and had strong trading ties with other countries. Many families worked in oil fields, factories, farms, and businesses, enjoying a middle-class life for much of the twentieth century. However, inequality and wealth gaps still existed. Some Venezuelans were very rich, while others lived in poverty. Politics in Latin America were shifting in the late 20th century, with some leaders trying big new ways to help poor families, including nationalizing industries. When Hugo Chávez was elected in 1998, many people hoped his ideas would bring more fairness and dignity. Daily life for most people changed as the government took over more of the economy: new rules came, prices were controlled, and some lost family businesses.

wk16.t: Married Women Gain the Right to Own
wk16.talk: Why do you think it's important for both parents to be able to own things and make decisions for the family?
wk16.child: A long time ago, when a woman got married, she couldn't own things or keep the money she earned; it all belonged to her husband. Then, people worked hard to change the laws so that married women could have their own things and money. This helped families because moms could help take care of their children better.
wk16.learn: From this history, we learn the importance of recognizing and respecting the agency of all individuals, regardless of gender. Legal systems that acknowledge and protect individual rights contribute to the well-being of families and society. For families of faith, this underscores the value of partnership and equality in marriage, where both spouses have the opportunity to contribute fully to the family's success and spiritual growth.
wk16.matters: These legal changes were pivotal in recognizing women as individuals with their own rights and responsibilities. For families of faith, this shift underscores the importance of agency and stewardship. When women gained the ability to own property and manage their earnings, they could better contribute to their families' well-being and make decisions that aligned with their values. This empowerment allowed for a more balanced partnership in marriage, reflecting the principle that both husband and wife are equal partners in the family unit.

sources.name: Married Women's Property Act 1870
Married Women's Property Act 1882
Married Women's Property Acts in the United States

wk16.evidence: Historical records show a clear progression of legal reforms granting property rights to married women. The Married Women's Property Act of 1870 in Britain allowed women to keep earnings and inheritances as their separate property. The 1882 Act expanded these rights to all property, regardless of its source. In the United States, Mississippi's 1839 law was the first of its kind, and by 1900, most states had enacted similar legislation. These reforms were the result of persistent advocacy by women's rights activists and marked a significant shift in the legal recognition of women's rights.
wk16.happened: In the 19th century, laws in Britain and the United States began to change, allowing married women to own property and control their earnings. Before these changes, under a legal principle called coverture, a married woman's identity was legally merged with her husband's. This meant she couldn't own property, sign contracts, or keep her own wages; everything she had became her husband's upon marriage. The shift began in 1839 when Mississippi passed the first Married Women's Property Act, granting married women the right to own property separately from their husbands. This movement gained momentum, and by 1870, Britain enacted its own Married Women's Property Act, allowing women to keep earnings and inheritances as their separate property. Further progress was made with the 1882 Act, which extended these rights to all property, regardless of its source. By 1900, most American states had passed similar laws, marking a significant step toward legal equality for women.
wk16.scripture: The scriptures teach the principle of agency and the importance of stewardship. In the Doctrine and Covenants, it is stated that "it is not meet that I should command in all things; for he that is compelled in all things, the same is a slothful and not a wise servant" (D&C 58:26). This emphasizes the importance of individuals making their own choices and being accountable for them. The changes in property laws for married women align with this principle, as they allowed women to exercise agency over their own property and earnings.
wk16.background: Before these reforms, society operated under the doctrine of coverture, where a married woman's legal rights were subsumed by her husband's. This system left women financially dependent and without legal autonomy. Daily life for women was largely confined to domestic roles, with limited opportunities for education or employment. The push for change was driven by women's rights activists who argued for legal recognition of women's individuality and economic independence. Their efforts were part of a broader movement toward gender equality, challenging longstanding societal norms and advocating for women's rights in various spheres of life.

wk17.talk: How can we make sure we help others but also remember people who might be hurt by our choices?
wk17.child: A long time ago, people could get land if they promised to live on it and take care of it. Many families worked hard to make new farms, but the land was taken from people who lived there first. We learn from both the good and the hard parts of this story.
wk17.learn: The story of the Homestead Act teaches that even good ideas, like helping families get land, can have serious costs if not done carefully. It reminds us to look at history honestly, see both the blessings and the harms, and strive for fairness. Today, we can learn to be grateful for opportunities to work and build, while also remembering and respecting those whose lives were changed or hurt. By teaching children about this, we can help them become wise and caring stewards in their own time.
wk17.matters: The Homestead Act matters because it made it possible for millions of ordinary families to own land and work for themselves, building new communities across the middle of America. For many, it meant a chance to provide for their children and have a place to call their own. At the same time, it reminds us that laws can bless some while hurting others. For families of faith, it shows that the ability to work and steward land is a gift from God, but our choices should always consider justice and kindness for everyone, especially those who are displaced or vulnerable. The story of land and work is never just about what is gained, but also about who loses and how they are treated.

sources.name: National Park Service: Homestead Act
Smithsonian Magazine: How the Homestead Act Transformed America
Library of Congress: Primary Documents in American History - Homestead Act

wk17.evidence: Historical documents record how the Homestead Act was passed, who signed up, and where they settled. Millions of homestead records are still kept in archives, showing names, dates, and the land claimed. Archaeological remains of old homesteads, tools, and household items have helped us learn how these families lived and farmed. Census records show how quickly the American interior filled with new settlers. Scholars also study broken treaties with Native nations, examining government records and first-hand accounts to understand how Native families were affected, and how much land was lost. The stories from both homesteaders and Native Americans give a fuller picture of what really happened during this period.
wk17.happened: On May 20, 1862, President Abraham Lincoln signed the Homestead Act into law. This new law promised that any adult citizen, or anyone intending to become one, could have 160 acres of land from the public domain, as long as they lived on it and improved it for five years. Improvement could mean building a house, farming the land, or making a garden. This opportunity was open not just to men, but also to single women and, after the Civil War, freed slaves. People from many different backgrounds and places streamed west to try to find a new start. Families traveled by wagon or train, carried all their belongings, and began the hard work of turning empty fields into homes. Over the years, about 1.6 million claims were made, eventually covering about one in ten acres of land in the United States. This law helped many people become landowners, but the land itself had first belonged to Native American tribes, who were often forced to leave and whose ways of life were disrupted, sometimes through broken treaties or by later laws that divided their lands as well. The Homestead Act changed the shape of the country, filling it with small farms and new towns—but also left a legacy that is both hopeful and painful.
wk17.scripture: Scriptures often speak of the blessings and responsibilities of working the land. In Genesis 2:15, Adam is placed in the Garden of Eden "to dress it and to keep it," showing that caring for the earth is a sacred trust. Doctrine and Covenants 104:17 reminds us, “the earth is full, and there is enough and to spare; yea, I prepared all things, and have given unto the children of men to be agents unto themselves.” These verses teach that land and resources are gifts from God, and how we use them matters, especially in how we treat others in the process.
wk17.background: The United States in the 1860s was a nation in the middle of major change. Big cities were growing in the East, while the West seemed wide open to people looking for land and opportunity. Before the Homestead Act, much of America was frontier, and most land in the interior belonged to Native American nations whose families had lived there for centuries. Life was hard for most families: they grew or made nearly everything they needed, and homes were far apart. The coming of railroads and new tools made moving west easier, and the country was full of people hoping for a better future. This era saw both great hope and deep injustice as the US government pushed for settlement and expansion, promising free land but also taking land from others.

wk18.talk: Why do you think it's important for people to have the freedom to make their own choices about work and property?
wk18.child: When people are free to make choices about their work and property, they often do better and live happier lives. But it's also important to be honest and kind to others.
wk18.learn: The 2026 Index of Economic Freedom teaches us that while economic freedom is a vital component of prosperity, it is not the sole determinant. Societal values, cultural norms, and individual behaviors also play significant roles. Therefore, fostering an environment that promotes both economic freedom and strong moral principles is essential for holistic and sustainable development.
wk18.matters: Understanding the relationship between economic freedom and prosperity is crucial for families and societies. Higher economic freedom often leads to better job opportunities, higher incomes, and improved living standards. For families of faith, this underscores the importance of stewardship and the responsible use of resources, aligning with principles of self-reliance and community support.

sources.name: Index of Economic Freedom: About the Index | The Heritage Foundation
Heritage 2026 Index of Economic Freedom: United States Recorded “Greatest Improvement Amongst Advanced Economies”; Pro-G

wk18.evidence: Historical and economic studies consistently show a strong correlation between economic freedom and various measures of prosperity. Countries with higher economic freedom scores tend to have higher GDP per capita, longer life expectancy, and lower poverty rates. For example, the 2026 Index of Economic Freedom reports that countries in the top quartile of economic freedom have an average GDP per capita more than double that of those in the bottom quartile. This evidence suggests that policies promoting economic freedom can lead to significant improvements in economic and social outcomes.
wk18.happened: In 2026, the Heritage Foundation released its 32nd annual Index of Economic Freedom, evaluating 184 countries on factors like property rights, government size, regulatory efficiency, and market openness. Singapore topped the list with a score of 84.4, followed by Switzerland, Ireland, Taiwan, and Luxembourg. Notably, the United States saw significant improvement, reversing previous declines and achieving its highest score since 2001. Conversely, China remained classified as "repressed" with a score of 48.2, ranking 154th. The Index highlighted a strong correlation between economic freedom and prosperity, with countries scoring higher experiencing greater economic dynamism and overall well-being.
wk18.scripture: The scriptures emphasize principles that align with economic freedom, such as honesty, integrity, and the fair treatment of others. For instance, in the Doctrine and Covenants 134:2, it states, "We believe that no government can exist in peace, except such laws are framed and held inviolate as will secure to each individual the free exercise of conscience, the right and control of property, and the protection of life." This highlights the importance of protecting individual rights, including property rights, which are fundamental to economic freedom.
wk18.background: The Index of Economic Freedom has been published annually since 1995, aiming to measure the degree of economic freedom in countries worldwide. Over the years, it has become a valuable tool for policymakers, economists, and researchers to assess the impact of economic policies on prosperity and growth. The 2026 edition continues this tradition, providing updated scores and analyses based on data from the preceding years.

fam01.talk: What is your favorite story from the scriptures, and how would you like to hear it at bedtime?
fam01.child: A dad named Levi made bedtime stories from the scriptures for his daughters. These stories became so special that families all over the world started listening to them too. Now, many children enjoy learning about the scriptures before they go to sleep.
fam01.learn: From 'Little Scripture Travelers,' we learn that integrating faith into daily family routines can be both engaging and impactful. It shows that with creativity and dedication, parents can find innovative ways to teach their children about their beliefs, making spiritual education a cherished part of everyday life.
fam01.matters: 'Little Scripture Travelers' matters because it bridges the gap between ancient scripture and modern family life, making spiritual teachings accessible and engaging for children. For families of faith, it offers a tool to instill religious values in a way that resonates with young minds, fostering a love for scripture from an early age. By transforming bedtime into a time of spiritual exploration, it strengthens family bonds and supports the passing down of faith traditions to the next generation.

sources.name: Monticello Utah Temple
Monticello, Utah: The High Town in the Canyon Country

fam01.evidence: The success of 'Little Scripture Travelers' is evident in its widespread adoption by families seeking faith-based educational materials. While specific data on the brand's reach may not be publicly available, the growing demand for children's religious content indicates a positive reception. Additionally, the initiative reflects a broader trend of integrating technology and media into religious education, demonstrating how modern tools can be used to enhance spiritual learning.
fam01.happened: In 2025, in the small town of Monticello, Utah, a father named Levi found inspiration in the bedtime routines he shared with his daughters. Wanting to make scripture stories more engaging for children, he created 'Little Scripture Travelers,' a faith-based children's media brand. This initiative transformed traditional scripture narratives into captivating bedtime tales, aiming to bring families closer together through shared spiritual experiences. The brand quickly gained popularity, reaching families worldwide and offering resources that turned scripture reading into a delightful and meaningful part of daily life.
fam01.scripture: The scriptures emphasize the importance of teaching children about faith. In Deuteronomy 6:6-7, it is written: 'And these words, which I command thee this day, shall be in thine heart: And thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children.' Similarly, in the Book of Mormon, Mosiah 4:15 advises: 'But ye will teach them to walk in the ways of truth and soberness; ye will teach them to love one another.' These passages highlight the responsibility of parents to impart spiritual knowledge to their children, aligning with the mission of 'Little Scripture Travelers.'
fam01.background: Monticello, Utah, is a close-knit community nestled at an elevation of about 7,000 feet, serving as the county seat of San Juan County. With a population of approximately 1,740 people, the town is known for its strong community ties and rich cultural heritage. The presence of the Monticello Utah Temple underscores the town's deep-rooted faith traditions. In this environment, families often seek meaningful ways to incorporate their beliefs into daily routines, making it fertile ground for initiatives like 'Little Scripture Travelers.'

ch_a01.talk: Why do you think it's important for children to have their own rights and be treated with kindness?
ch_a01.child: Long ago in Rome, fathers had all the power in their families. They could decide everything, even if a new baby would live or not. Children had to work hard and had no rights of their own.
ch_a01.learn: Reflecting on the concept of patria potestas teaches us the importance of recognizing and valuing the individuality and rights of each child. It reminds us that the compassionate treatment of children is a relatively recent development in human history, achieved through persistent advocacy and societal change. This awareness encourages us to continue fostering environments where children are nurtured, protected, and respected as individuals with their own divine potential.
ch_a01.matters: Understanding the historical context of patria potestas highlights the profound evolution in societal attitudes toward children and family dynamics. For families of faith, recognizing this shift underscores the importance of viewing children as individuals with inherent worth and divine potential. It serves as a reminder of the blessings that come from nurturing and protecting the vulnerable, aligning with the belief that every child is a gift from Heavenly Father. This historical perspective encourages gratitude for modern legal and social structures that prioritize the well-being and rights of children, reflecting a more compassionate and just society.

sources.name: Patria Potestas: Meaning, Scope, and Modern Legacy - LegalClarity
Childhood in Ancient Rome - World History Encyclopedia
Patria Potestas: The Father's Absolute Power | Ancient Rome

ch_a01.evidence: Historical records, legal texts, and archaeological findings provide substantial evidence of the practices associated with patria potestas in ancient Rome. Legal documents, such as the Twelve Tables, codified the father's authority over his family, including the right to expose unwanted infants. Archaeological discoveries, like the remains of infants in refuse sites, corroborate accounts of infant exposure. Additionally, skewed sex ratios in certain Roman populations suggest a higher rate of female infant exposure. These findings collectively affirm the historical reality of these practices and offer insight into the societal norms and values of ancient Rome.
ch_a01.happened: In ancient Rome, the head of the household, known as the pater familias, held a legal authority called patria potestas, granting him absolute control over his family members, including children, grandchildren, and even adopted individuals. This authority encompassed the power to make all decisions regarding the family's property, arrange marriages, and enforce discipline. One of the most severe aspects of this power was the ius vitae necisque—the right to decide life or death over his children. This meant a father could legally expose a newborn he did not wish to raise, leaving the infant in a public place to die or be taken by others. This practice was often influenced by economic hardship, physical deformities in the child, or the desire to limit family size. Daughters were more frequently exposed than sons, leading to imbalanced sex ratios in certain regions. Children were also expected to contribute to the household from a young age, engaging in labor as soon as they were physically capable. They had no legal standing independent of their father and could be subjected to severe punishment or even sold into slavery. The concept of childhood as a protected and distinct stage of life was virtually nonexistent; children were viewed primarily as small workers and legal possessions of their fathers.
ch_a01.scripture: While ancient Roman practices like patria potestas are not directly addressed in scripture, the Bible emphasizes the value and importance of children. In the New Testament, Jesus Christ teaches, "Suffer the little children to come unto me, and forbid them not: for of such is the kingdom of God" (Mark 10:14). This passage highlights the inherent worth of children and the necessity of treating them with love and respect. Additionally, the Book of Mormon underscores the significance of teaching and nurturing children in righteousness, as seen in Mosiah 4:14-15, which instructs parents to teach their children to walk in the ways of truth and soberness. These scriptures advocate for a view of children as precious individuals to be cherished and guided, contrasting sharply with the ancient Roman perception of children as property.
ch_a01.background: The world of ancient Rome was structured around a patriarchal family system where the father held ultimate authority. Society valued discipline, hierarchy, and tradition, with the family unit serving as the fundamental building block. The economy was largely agrarian, and families relied on the labor of all members, including children, to sustain themselves. High infant mortality rates and limited medical knowledge contributed to the normalization of practices like infant exposure. Additionally, the legal system reinforced the father's dominance, with laws codifying his extensive rights over family members. This environment fostered a view of children as economic assets and extensions of the father's will, rather than individuals with their own rights or identities.

ch_a02.talk: Why do you think Jesus said we should be like little children to enter the kingdom of heaven?
ch_a02.child: Jesus loves children and wants them to come to Him. He teaches us to be kind and humble, just like little children.
ch_a02.learn: This event teaches us to value and respect children, recognizing their inherent worth and the lessons they offer about humility and trust. It encourages us to approach our faith with the openness and sincerity characteristic of a child, fostering a deeper connection with the divine.
ch_a02.matters: Jesus' welcoming of children and His declaration that the kingdom of God belongs to such as these was revolutionary. It elevated the status of children, emphasizing their inherent worth and purity. For families of faith, this teaches the importance of nurturing and valuing children, recognizing their unique perspectives and the lessons they offer about humility and trust. It also serves as a reminder to approach faith with the openness and sincerity characteristic of a child.

sources.name: Teaching of Jesus about little children
Suffer the Little Children | Philanthropies
Suffer the Little Children | Clearly Reformed

ch_a02.evidence: While there is no direct archaeological evidence of this specific event, the cultural context supports its plausibility. Historical records indicate that children in the ancient world were often marginalized, making Jesus' actions notably counter-cultural. The consistency of this account across multiple Gospel narratives adds to its credibility. Additionally, early Christian communities' practices, such as rejecting infanticide and adopting abandoned infants, reflect the lasting impact of Jesus' teachings on the value of children.
ch_a02.happened: Around 30 AD in Judea, parents brought their children to Jesus, seeking His blessing. The disciples, perhaps believing that Jesus was too busy or that children were unimportant, tried to turn them away. Observing this, Jesus became displeased and instructed, "Let the little children come to me, and do not hinder them, for the kingdom of God belongs to such as these." He then took the children in His arms, placed His hands on them, and blessed them. This act not only demonstrated His love for children but also used them as an example of the humility and openness required to enter the kingdom of God.
ch_a02.scripture: The event is recorded in the New Testament: Matthew 19:13-15, Mark 10:13-16, and Luke 18:15-17. In these passages, Jesus rebukes His disciples for hindering the children and emphasizes that the kingdom of God belongs to those who are like them. Additionally, in Matthew 18:3-4, Jesus teaches that unless one becomes like a little child, they cannot enter the kingdom of heaven, highlighting the virtues of humility and innocence.
ch_a02.background: In the first-century Greco-Roman world, children were often viewed as insignificant until they reached adulthood. Practices like exposure and infanticide were common, especially among the Romans, where unwanted infants were sometimes left to die. In contrast, Jewish culture valued children as blessings from God, yet they still held little social status. They were expected to be seen and not heard, and their worth was often tied to their future potential rather than their present selves. This societal backdrop makes Jesus' actions and words regarding children particularly striking and counter-cultural.

ch_a03.t: The Myth of the Unloved Medieval Child
ch_a03.talk: Why do you think parents always love their children, no matter when or where they live?
ch_a03.child: Long ago, people loved their children just as much as we do today. Even if life was hard, parents felt happy when their children were born and very sad if they died. Families cared for each other then too.
ch_a03.learn: This episode teaches us that history can change when new evidence is found or old records are looked at with care. It reminds us to question claims that do not match what we know about love, family, or faith. Our love for our children is not just a tradition but a deep part of what it means to be family, in every time and place, given to us by God. Even when times are difficult, the bonds of love last through history.
ch_a03.matters: Why does this story matter? It reminds us that the love between parents and children is a part of our human story, given by our Heavenly Father, not something invented by modern people. Sometimes, even smart scholars can make mistakes, and others may follow them until someone takes time to look again at the evidence. For families who cherish their children as gifts from God, it is reassuring to know that mothers and fathers throughout history—whatever their circumstances—loved and grieved for their children as we do. Love for our children is not a new way of thinking; it is part of God’s plan for families in every time and place.

sources.name: British Library: Medieval Childhood
Encyclopedia Britannica: Philippe Ariès
Nicholas Orme, Medieval Children (Yale University Press google preview)

ch_a03.evidence: Careful research into medieval records paints a very different picture than Ariès described. Household accounts show parents buying toys and commissioning prayers for their children’s health. Wills often mention children by name with gifts or requests for their care. Medieval coroners’ rolls and church miracle stories describe families deeply mourning when children died or celebrating when a sick child recovered. Historian Nicholas Orme and others have shown that these records are full of evidence that children were wanted, cherished, protected, and truly mourned. Modern historical studies now agree that Ariès’s theory is not supported by the facts. Instead, the bonds of family love were present in the Middle Ages, much as they are today.
ch_a03.happened: In the 1960s, a French historian named Philippe Ariès made a famous claim in his book Centuries of Childhood. He argued that people in medieval Europe—about seven hundred years before he wrote—did not see childhood as a special, important part of life. Ariès said that, because children often died young, adults avoided loving them deeply, and that parents did not grieve as we do today when a child died. This idea became quite popular and was believed by many teachers and historians for decades. But when other scholars returned to the old records—like coroner’s rolls, wills, church miracle stories, and family accounts—they found heartwarming evidence of real love between parents and children. Medieval children were given names, watched over carefully, baptized with godparents, and mourned when they died. Nicholas Orme, a leading historian, showed that Ariès’s idea was mistaken in nearly every way. The truth is parents in medieval Europe cared for their children, felt deep loss if they died, and found joy in their children’s lives, much as parents do now.
ch_a03.scripture: Scriptures teach us that children are precious in the sight of God. Jesus said, 'Suffer little children to come unto me, and forbid them not: for of such is the kingdom of God' (Luke 18:16; 3 Nephi 17:21). The Book of Mormon also describes Jesus blessing the children and praying for them, showing deep love (3 Nephi 17:21–24). These verses remind us that children have always mattered, both to those who love them now and to their Maker. The principle that all are alike unto God (2 Nephi 26:33) gives us courage to see the value of every child.
ch_a03.background: Medieval Europe, around the year 1200, was a world very different from ours. Most people lived in small villages or towns. They grew their food, worked as craftspeople, and were surrounded by the church's teachings. Life could be hard: diseases were common, and many children did not survive to adulthood. Family was the center of daily life. Children were expected to help at home or in the fields, but they also played and learned skills from their elders. The church performed baptisms and kept careful records, showing that people valued names and welcomed each child. Even though health care was simpler, and life was more uncertain, the bonds of love were still deeply felt between parents and their children.

ch_a04.talk: Why do you think it’s important for everyone, even girls and younger kids, to learn to read?
ch_a04.child: Long ago, a man named Martin Luther asked leaders to build schools so every boy and girl could learn to read. He wanted everyone to read the Bible for themselves. Because of this, more kids could go to school and learn new things!
ch_a04.learn: From Luther’s letter, we learn how much it matters that everyone has a chance to read and grow in understanding. Heavenly Father wants all His children to have access to learning so they can use their talents, help others, and gain their own testimonies by reading scripture. When parents and leaders make sure every child can learn, they act as partners with God in His work. Learning blesses not just individuals, but families, communities, and even whole nations.
ch_a04.matters: Luther’s push for schools for everyone changed the course of learning in Europe and beyond. For the first time, it became a common idea that every girl and boy should be able to read, especially so they could know and choose God’s teachings for themselves. This belief helped start public education systems, where all children—not just the wealthy or the boys—could go to school. For families of faith today, this teaches us how precious the gift of learning is, and how important it is to use that gift to understand God’s words and world. It also shows that the desire to read scripture and grow closer to Heavenly Father can lead to blessings for everyone.

sources.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica - Martin Luther: Education
National Endowment for the Humanities - Martin Luther and Education
World Bank - How the Protestant Reformation Transformed Education

ch_a04.evidence: Historians have studied the growth of schools in Protestant areas after Luther’s call. Research by Becker and Woessmann found that regions in Prussia (a historic German state) that followed Protestant ideas built more local schools and had higher literacy many years later than neighboring Catholic regions; this difference was tied directly to Luther’s emphasis on reading scripture. Records from the 1500s and 1600s show city laws, school openings, and writings by Luther himself, supporting that his calls led to real changes. While not every detail can be tracked for each village, the overall pattern is clear: Luther’s push for universal schooling made a measurable difference for children then and for generations after.
ch_a04.happened: In the year 1524, Martin Luther, a German priest and reformer, wrote a powerful letter to the leaders of the cities in his country, urging them to open and maintain schools for all children. At this time, most children, especially girls and poorer children, could not go to school. Luther argued this needed to change. He believed that every child should learn how to read, so that each one could read the Holy Scriptures on their own and understand God's word personally. He wrote not just to suggest schools, but to say it was the duty of leaders to make them happen—and he included girls in this call, which was rare for that time. Later, Luther even said the leaders could require children to come to school, seeing it as important for both faith and society. His letters and sermons encouraged city councils and communities across Protestant parts of Europe to start new schools, and these schools would eventually help the people become more literate than before, planting seeds for the future of public education.
ch_a04.scripture: Scriptures encourage gaining knowledge and learning truth. In the Bible, Proverbs 4:7 says, "Wisdom is the principal thing; therefore get wisdom: and with all thy getting get understanding." Doctrine and Covenants 88:118 teaches, "Seek ye out of the best books words of wisdom; seek learning, even by study and also by faith." Though there is not a specific verse about starting public schools, these passages invite everyone to learn for themselves and value wisdom. The Restoration also teaches that all should learn, men and women alike, a principle found in Doctrine and Covenants 93:36–37.
ch_a04.background: Before Luther's call, few children in Europe went to school. Most learning happened at home or through church, and was focused mainly on boys whose families could afford it. The Middle Ages were a time when books were very expensive and written mostly in Latin, a language most people did not know. The invention of the printing press only a few decades earlier had begun to change this, making books and the Bible more affordable and available. Martin Luther lived in Wittenberg, in what is now Germany, during a time of great religious change called the Reformation. He challenged old church traditions and sparked new ideas about faith, freedom, and education. Life was very different from today—most families were farmers or craft workers, and many did not know how to read or write.

ch_a05.t: The First Picture Book for Children
ch_a05.talk: What is your favorite picture in a book, and how does it help you learn what's happening in the story?
ch_a05.child: A long time ago, a kind man made the very first picture book for children. It had words and pictures that helped kids learn about the world. Books like the ones you read today come from his good idea.
ch_a05.learn: From Orbis Pictus, we learn that even in hard times, one person’s inspired work can change many lives. Teaching can be kind, simple, and full of pictures. Heavenly Father can guide people to create tools that make learning joyful and easier for every child. When we teach with love, at the right level, and in an inviting way, we follow a tradition that honors every child as precious and capable.
ch_a05.matters: Comenius’ first picture book matters deeply in the story of childhood and learning. It was the first time a book was made just for the youngest learners’ eyes and hands—a big change from old ways. By using pictures and easy words, Orbis Pictus invited children to understand their world and begin to read and think for themselves. It helped adults see children as learners in their own right. For families of faith, this spirit of gentle teaching and including all children echoes Christ’s command to teach and bless little ones, and reminds us that learning can be a joyful, spirit-filled journey for all God’s children.

sources.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica – Orbis Sensualium Pictus
The British Library – The World in Pictures, John Amos Comenius
Smithsonian Libraries – Orbis Sensualium Pictus

ch_a05.evidence: Historians can actually see copies of the first editions of Orbis Pictus, some still kept in rare book rooms today. The illustrations and text show clearly how Comenius matched pictures to simple explanations, something not found in earlier books for children. The book’s popularity is confirmed by its continued printing and translation throughout Europe for centuries. It influenced later educational thinkers and led directly to the picture books familiar today. Scholars widely recognize Orbis Pictus as a turning point in the history of teaching children, as is shown by museum exhibits, documentary evidence, and studies of early editions.
ch_a05.happened: In 1658, in the city of Nuremberg, Germany, John Amos Comenius, a bishop from Moravia who had become a refugee, published a book called Orbis Sensualium Pictus, or The World in Pictures. This was a new kind of book, made just for children. Each page showed woodcut illustrations beside simple words and sentences in both Latin and German. The book would say, for example, 'This is a tree,' and show a picture of a tree. Comenius described things from daily life—animals, plants, numbers, family, work, and worship—in a gentle way meant for young minds. He wrote a guide for teachers and parents, encouraging them to help children learn by seeing and touching as well as hearing and reading—using their senses to understand the world. Orbis Pictus became very popular. It was translated into many languages and used across Europe for more than two centuries, opening the door for future children’s books.
ch_a05.scripture: While the scriptures do not mention picture books, the Savior Himself valued children and gentle teaching. In the Bible, Jesus says, 'Suffer little children to come unto me, and forbid them not: for of such is the kingdom of God' (Luke 18:16). He often taught with simple stories and images so all could understand, as seen in His parables. The Book of Mormon and Doctrine and Covenants emphasize teaching 'according to the understanding of the children' (2 Nephi 25:26; D&C 68:25–28), supporting the idea that learning should be plain and suited to a child’s needs.
ch_a05.background: When Orbis Pictus was published, Europe was just recovering from the Thirty Years’ War, a time of hardship, and most people were very poor. Few children went to school, and most books were small, heavy, serious, and meant for adults or older students. Knowledge was usually shared from master to apprentice or passed down in families. John Amos Comenius had spent years as a teacher and church leader. Because of religious persecution, he had been forced to leave his home, taking with him his ideas about education: that children learn best step by step, with kindness, and with things they can see and touch. Comenius dreamed that both boys and girls, rich and poor, could learn and grow through gentle teaching.

ch_a06.talk: What is your favorite storybook, and why do you like it?
ch_a06.child: A long time ago, books for kids were not very fun. Then Mr. Newbery made a book just for children, with games and pictures to make them happy. Now, we have many fun books because of his idea.
ch_a06.learn: We learn that sometimes a small, kind idea—like making a child smile through reading—can change the world. When there is courage to try something new that brings good, many can be blessed. It also reminds us that learning can be joyful and creative, and that families should cherish the times when children laugh, wonder, and grow. Encouraging a love of wholesome stories can help children see the goodness Heavenly Father wants for them.
ch_a06.matters: John Newbery’s book changed how people thought about children and learning. Instead of seeing children as small adults who needed constant instruction, it showed that children could and should find joy in reading. For a family of faith, this is important: Heavenly Father wants His children to grow in both wisdom and happiness, using their agency. Making learning delightful helps children develop a love for goodness and knowledge. Newbery’s experiment showed that enjoying a story is not only acceptable, but it can be a gift that opens doors to learning, imagination, and faith.

sources.name: British Library – A Little Pretty Pocket-Book
Encyclopedia Britannica – John Newbery
Library of Congress – Children's Book Week: John Newbery

ch_a06.evidence: Historians know of Newbery’s A Little Pretty Pocket-Book because original copies survive in libraries, including the British Library. The book is well-documented in contemporary records and advertisements from the time. Scholars consider it the first English children’s book published for pleasure, rather than only moral instruction. Many features Newbery introduced, like illustrations and bonus toys, are discussed in museum exhibits and established reference works on children’s literature. Later authors credited Newbery as the inspiration for their work, and his imprint helped birth a whole industry of writing and publishing for children. The book’s impact is confirmed by the continued use of his name in children’s literary awards.
ch_a06.happened: In 1744, a London publisher named John Newbery released a small book called A Little Pretty Pocket-Book. This book was very special because, for one of the first times in history, it was made to make children happy and not just to tell them how to behave. The book had simple rhymes and little lessons, paired with colorful pictures, and it even came with a toy: a ball for boys or a pincushion for girls. Before this, most children’s books were like sermons or textbooks, meant either to teach reading or warn children to avoid sin. Newbery’s idea was new and bold—he believed children should have books that were fun to read and could make them laugh and wonder. When parents bought the Pocket-Book for their children, they were choosing a kind of joy and delight in reading that hadn’t been common before. The book quickly became popular. This success led others to create books made for the delight of children, and soon writers like the Brothers Grimm and Hans Christian Andersen followed the path Newbery made. Over time, books for children became a special part of publishing, and today, John Newbery’s name is remembered every year when the Newbery Medal is given to the best children’s book in America.
ch_a06.scripture: While the scriptures do not discuss children’s storybooks directly, many passages encourage learning and the seeking of goodness with joy. Proverbs 3:13 says, 'Happy is the man that findeth wisdom, and the man that getteth understanding.' In the Book of Mormon, 2 Nephi 2:25 teaches, 'Adam fell that men might be; and men are, that they might have joy.' The Savior Himself welcomed and blessed children (Mark 10:14), showing that childhood is precious. Joyful learning honors both child and Creator.
ch_a06.background: In 1744, London was a busy, growing city. Most children attended little school, and those who did rarely saw books that were just for them. Most families were not wealthy, and books were precious things, often shared by everyone or kept by adults. John Newbery ran a print shop and bookstore, where he noticed there was a gap—nothing much made for children that was playful or fun. Before his time, stories and lessons for children were mostly serious, teaching them to be obedient or warning them about dangers. People believed children needed strong discipline, and even the books reflected that. With noisy streets full of carts and markets, and homes often crowded and plain, a bright, cheerful book would have been a real treasure for a child. Newbery himself was a lively man, creative and full of ideas, who understood that joy was a way to teach, too.

ch_a07.t: Sunday Schools Teach the Poor to Read
ch_a07.talk: How do you think it felt for a child to learn to read for the first time at Sunday School?
ch_a07.child: Long ago, a kind man started little schools on Sundays to help children learn to read, using the Bible. For many children, this was the first time anyone had taught them. This helped lots of children feel special and learn new things.
ch_a07.learn: We can learn that even when society does not give everyone an equal chance, caring people can step forward to help meet a need. God can use anyone who is willing to serve, no matter their job or position, to bless the lives of others. Families today can remember that the gifts of learning, reading, and teaching are not just for our own comfort, but can be shared to lift others. Persistence, kindness, and faith can together make a real difference in the world.
ch_a07.matters: The spread of Sunday Schools is important because it was a turning point in the history of learning for many children who would otherwise have been forgotten. By teaching reading (with the Bible as the main text), the Sunday School movement increased not just literacy, but also sparked hope and a sense of worth in children and their families. Today, when we read, write, and learn freely, it is good to remember that there was a time when kindness and faith filled in where governments were not yet ready to help. For families of faith, it reminds us that lifting the vulnerable and sharing the gifts we have—including knowledge—is part of following Jesus Christ, who welcomed little children and taught that everyone was precious in the sight of God.

sources.name: British Library: The Sunday School Movement
BBC: Robert Raikes and the Sunday School Movement
Encyclopaedia Britannica: Robert Raikes

ch_a07.evidence: Historians agree that Robert Raikes began Sunday Schools for the poor in Gloucester in 1780, using the Bible as the primary textbook. Newspaper articles and letters from Raikes himself, as well as reports by others like Hannah More, confirm the early work and rapid spread of these schools. Records from the period show a dramatic rise in literacy among working-class children within a generation. Later studies and censuses from England show that, by the early 1800s, around a quarter of English children attended Sunday Schools, which clearly helped increase literacy before the government opened public schools.
