Museums and educational historians continue to display and discuss these early Sunday School rooms and their lessons, confirming their important place in history.
ch_a07.happened: In 1780, a man named Robert Raikes, who worked as a newspaper publisher in Gloucester, England, noticed that many poor children were growing up without the chance to learn to read or write. These children often spent long hours working in factories during the week and had very little time for school or rest. On Sundays, the only day they did not have to work, Raikes invited the children to small schools where they could learn to read. The Bible was used as the main book because most families owned one if they owned any book at all. Raikes was soon joined by other people, including a lady named Hannah More, and together they helped to start many more Sunday Schools across England. Within just a few decades, Sunday Schools became very popular, and about one in every four children in England attended. For many families, these schools provided the only chance for their children to become literate. Over time, the Sunday School movement spread to other countries and became a major way for children, especially those from poor families, to learn not just to read the Bible, but how to read in general.
ch_a07.scripture: The Bible teaches that Jesus cared deeply about children. In Mark 10:13-16, Jesus welcomes little children, saying, 'Suffer the little children to come unto me… for of such is the kingdom of God.' The Book of Mormon also teaches the importance of teaching children, as in Mosiah 4:14-15, where parents are told to teach their children to walk in truth and love. While scripture may not speak of formal classrooms, the principle is clear: God values the learning and well-being of every child. Helping children learn—especially when it opens up the scripture to them—honors these teachings.
ch_a07.background: Before Robert Raikes began his Sunday Schools, there were very few opportunities for poor children in England to learn to read. Most schools charged money that families could not afford. Many children, especially those from working-class or poor families, were sent to work in factories, shops, or on farms from a young age to help support their families. There was no free public education and very few people considered it the government’s job to teach everyone. Church groups and a few kind-hearted individuals sometimes tried to help, but there was no organized effort on a large scale. Children’s daily lives were often filled with hard work, a little play, and sometimes very little hope for changing their situation. People like Robert Raikes saw this need and stepped in, sharing the belief that everyone deserved the gift of reading and understanding scripture for themselves.

ch_a08.talk: What is your favorite way to play, and how do you think it helps you learn new things?
ch_a08.child: Long ago in Germany, a kind teacher named Froebel made a special school just for little children where they could play, sing, and learn together. He believed that playing was how young children learned best, and his idea is now used in kindergartens all over the world. Every time you build or create, you are learning too, just like in Froebel's first kindergarten.
ch_a08.learn: We can learn from Froebel’s story that small changes, when rooted in loving concern for children, can bless many lives. Seeing children as individuals with their own needs and strengths helps us create kinder homes, classrooms, and communities. As a family, recognizing play as important work reminds us to cherish the joyful, imaginative side of childhood and to make time for learning in gentle, nurturing ways.
ch_a08.matters: Froebel’s invention matters because it changed forever how the world thinks about childhood and learning. Today, nearly every country offers kindergarten or early years education, a time and space made just for little learners. For parents of faith, his insight also echoes the belief that every child is a child of God, precious and full of promise, with a spirit meant to grow in joy. Froebel’s idea that play is the work of children encourages families and teachers to look for learning in simple, joyful moments. His approach invites us to see each child as worth patient guidance, loving care, and opportunities to discover, just as our Heavenly Father nurtures us.

sources.name: Encyclopedia Britannica: Friedrich Froebel
Smithsonian Magazine: The History of Kindergarten
National Association for the Education of Young Children (NAEYC): The Legacy of Friedrich Froebel

ch_a08.evidence: Historians have well-documented Froebel’s founding of the first kindergarten in 1837, including his writings, letters, and reports from others who visited or trained with him. His methods and “gifts” quickly caught the attention of other teachers in Germany, then spread throughout Europe and to America by the mid-1800s. Froebel's emphasis on structured play is now backed by many studies showing young children learn best through hands-on, playful experiences. Modern research has confirmed the long-term benefits of quality early childhood education, including for language, social-emotional skills, and problem-solving, findings accepted by both education scholars and governments today.
ch_a08.happened: In 1837, Friedrich Froebel, a German teacher and thinker, opened a unique school in the small town of Bad Blankenburg, Germany. He called his school a kindergarten, which means "garden of children." Froebel believed childhood was a special time with its own needs and purpose. Instead of seeing young children as little adults or idle beings, he saw them as growing and learning in ways unlike older children or grownups. Froebel argued that play was not wasted time, but the highest way children could learn and express themselves. He created a space filled with songs, movement, and special playthings he called gifts. These gifts—simple objects like balls, cubes, and sticks—were designed to help children learn through touching, doing, and imagining. In kindergarten, learning was joyful work, done with games, crafts, songs, and stories, guided gently by teachers instead of strict drills or harsh rules. Froebel's new school was a gift to children everywhere, offering a loving, structured place shaped just for them.
ch_a08.scripture: The scriptures do not mention kindergarten, but they teach us about the worth and promise of children. In Matthew 19:14, Jesus said, “Suffer little children, and forbid them not, to come unto me: for of such is the kingdom of heaven.” The Book of Mormon (Moroni 8:10–12) teaches that little children are whole and innocent before God. Doctrine and Covenants 68:25 instructs parents to teach children the basics of faith, showing the importance of early learning. These passages remind us that caring for and teaching children is sacred work, worthy of our best.
ch_a08.background: Before Froebel’s time, life was much harder for small children in most of the world, especially those who were not from wealthy families. In the early 1800s, many little ones were seen as extra hands to help at home or in fields if needed, or they were simply underfoot until they could attend regular school, which often began much later. Teachers focused on memorization and strict discipline, treating all ages much the same. Friedrich Froebel himself grew up in a busy family in Germany and worked as a teacher and school inspector. He was inspired by ideas from earlier educators and by nature, seeing children as young plants in need of careful tending to grow strong, happy, and wise. Froebel’s own life was full of both hardship and kindness, shaping how he wanted schools to feel for children.

ch_a09.talk: Why do you think learning is important for every child?
ch_a09.child: Long ago, many kids had to work all day and did not go to school. When people made a law that children must go to school, it helped kids learn and have better lives. Now, almost every child in the world goes to school and learns new things.
ch_a09.learn: We learn that protecting children means more than keeping them safe; it also means giving them chances to learn and grow. It took brave people to change old traditions and make learning a right for every child. When families, communities, and laws work together, great blessings can follow for generations.
ch_a09.matters: The shift to compulsory education may seem ordinary to us now, but it was revolutionary. It opened doors for children to value learning and gain skills no matter who their parents were. For families of faith, the idea that each child is precious and has divine potential is closely tied with helping them reach their fullest light. Having laws that protect a child’s right to learn allowed millions to read, write, and grow into people who can serve and bless their communities. It made learning a duty for society, not just a privilege for the wealthy.

sources.name: Library of Congress: Compulsory Education Laws
National Geographic: The Evolution of the American Public School
Our World in Data: Literacy

ch_a09.evidence: Historians can point to the actual laws and documents that were passed in Massachusetts and other states. Census records and school reports show how the number of children attending school grew rapidly after these laws. Over time, scientific studies have measured how rising literacy changed communities, poverty rates, and even health. The sharp rise in global literacy from the 1800s to today traces directly back to compulsory education and child labor laws. Early resistance and enforcement struggles are also recorded, showing this change was real and sometimes difficult, but now it is a well-established historical fact.
ch_a09.happened: In 1852, the state of Massachusetts made history in the United States by passing the first law that required all children to attend school. Before this, some children went to school, but many did not. The new law said that children, usually from ages eight to fourteen, had to go to school unless they already knew how to read and write well. This was part of a bigger dream called the common school movement, led by a man named Horace Mann, who believed that every child deserved a good education. He saw education as a tool that could lift people up and help them live better, freer lives. The idea did not stop in Massachusetts. Over the years, other states made similar laws, and by 1918, every state in America required children to go to school. This idea spread to many other countries, so now millions of children around the world have the right to learn in a classroom and not work in fields or factories. These changes did not happen overnight, but they slowly opened the door for generations of children to learn, read, and dream.
ch_a09.scripture: The scriptures teach that learning and knowledge are precious in the eyes of God. In Doctrine and Covenants 88:118, we are instructed to seek learning, “even by study and also by faith.” The Book of Mormon encourages parents to teach their children to read and understand the scriptures (see 2 Nephi 25:26), and Proverbs 4:7 says, “Wisdom is the principal thing; therefore get wisdom: and with all thy getting get understanding.” While the scriptures do not give laws about schools, they do teach the importance of both spiritual and earthly education for every child.
ch_a09.background: Before compulsory schooling began, many children lived very different lives. In the early 1800s, families often relied on every member working, even the youngest children. Many poor children spent long hours in factories, mines, or farms to help support their families. Most did not have a chance to learn to read or write, unless their parents had the means and time to teach them at home or send them to private schools. A few countries, like Prussia, had already begun requiring children to attend school, inspiring reformers in America. Leaders like Horace Mann believed that if every child could go to school, society would be stronger and more fair. Daily life at this time was very structured for adults and children alike, with chores and work taking up much of the day for everyone in the household.

ch_a10.t: Montessori and the Casa dei Bambini
ch_a10.talk: How do you feel when someone really listens to you and believes in you?
ch_a10.child: Maria Montessori made a special school just for kids, with small tables and tools. She let the children pick what to learn. Even kids no one else thought could learn did really well in her school.
ch_a10.learn: The story of Maria Montessori and her first school teaches us that true listening and respect can make a difference, especially for those who most need help. Instead of assuming what children cannot do, we can start by noticing what they can do and what inspires them. For parents, this means watching for your child's interests and strengths and gently guiding them, trusting that growth and learning often happen when love and freedom are present together.
ch_a10.matters: The Montessori approach matters because it reminds families and schools alike that every child holds great worth, no matter their background or ability. Montessori’s careful observation and respect for each child’s individual pace reflects a gospel principle: that Heavenly Father knows and treasures each one of His children personally. As families seek to guide their children, the example of patient watching and gentle leadership can inspire us to see what unique gifts and interests each child brings. Even today, many people find that the best learning happens when children are respected, listened to, and given real work to do.

sources.name: Montessori: The Science Behind the Genius, Angeline Stoll Lillard, Oxford University Press
American Montessori Society: History of Montessori Education and the Movement
National Public Radio/All Things Considered: Montessori Schools Gaining Popularity In The United States
Montessori: The International Montessori Index

ch_a10.evidence: There is clear historical evidence that Maria Montessori opened the first Casa dei Bambini in 1907 and that her methods spread quickly. Visitors at the time wrote detailed accounts of what they saw, and Montessori herself recorded her methods and observations. Today, Montessori schools operate in over one hundred countries. Recent randomized controlled studies show Montessori schooling can lead to real—but often modest—advantages in academic and social skills, especially when the Montessori method is faithfully followed by trained teachers. However, the strength of benefits can vary depending on how well the school implements her ideas and the needs of the students. These findings are regularly published in peer-reviewed journals and education reviews.
ch_a10.happened: In 1907, in a poor neighborhood of Rome, Italy, Dr. Maria Montessori opened a very special school called the Casa dei Bambini, or "Children's House." Maria Montessori was one of the first women in Italy to become a doctor, and her heart was especially tender toward children that others found difficult or left behind. Instead of making the children fit the adult world, she made the world fit the children. She designed small tables and chairs just their size, arranged bright and tidy shelves with real tools and objects, and let them choose what to work on during the day. Instead of always telling them what to do, she watched quietly to see what interested them and how they learned best. Many of her students had been judged as unable to learn, but under her care they flourished. Soon, these same children were writing, reading, and solving problems much sooner than anyone expected, and visitors from all over Europe came to watch, amazed by their focus and kindness to each other.
ch_a10.scripture: Scripture teaches that each child is precious in God’s sight. In Matthew 19:14, Jesus said, "Suffer little children, and forbid them not, to come unto me: for of such is the kingdom of heaven." Similarly, in the Book of Mormon, we read in Moroni 8:17 that little children are "alive in Christ." These passages support the idea from Montessori’s work that children are to be cherished, listened to, and taught gently. No scripture names her methods, but the principle of respecting agency and valuing every soul echoes in the Lord’s pattern of ministering to the one.
ch_a10.background: At the start of the 1900s, most classrooms across Europe were strict and crowded. Teachers lectured at the front, and students usually sat in rows, repeating lessons or memorizing facts. Children who struggled to keep up, especially in poorer neighborhoods, often received little attention or were labeled as hopeless cases. Maria Montessori came from a well-educated family in Italy and had trained as a physician. She was influenced by her Catholic faith and by ideas spreading across Europe about treating every child with respect. In daily life, most Roman children in poor districts had little gentleness or patience shown to them. Montessori believed deep down that every child deserved both.

ch_a11.t: Goodnight Moon and the Bedtime Ritual
ch_a11.talk: What helps you feel safe and loved when you go to sleep at night?
ch_a11.child: A long time ago, a kind story called Goodnight Moon came out to help children feel safe at bedtime. Saying goodnight to everything in the room can help us feel calm and ready to sleep. Gentle stories like this can make us happy and cozy, night after night.
ch_a11.learn: We learn that quiet, thoughtful things—like saying goodnight, softly reading together, and repeating comforting words—can have a lasting impact on children’s hearts. Sometimes what the world first overlooks becomes a treasure over time, and even the simplest routines can bless our families. Goodnight Moon shows us the beauty of regular, loving habits and invites us to see bedtime as a time to connect, comfort, and give thanks for our home.
ch_a11.matters: Goodnight Moon matters in the world because it showed that gentle, loving routines—like saying goodnight to each thing in a child’s room—can help children feel safe and peaceful as they drift off to sleep. For a family who believes God cares about our daily habits, this book is a reminder that small, repeated acts, like sharing bedtime stories and prayers, can shape a child’s heart and mind for good. By celebrating the quiet, the ordinary, and the loving, Goodnight Moon has helped parents and children build trust and warmth during bedtime, a precious time of connection.

sources.name: American Academy of Pediatrics: Bedtime Routines for Children
Library of Congress: Goodnight Moon History
Smithsonian Magazine: The Surprising Success of Goodnight Moon

ch_a11.evidence: Research now supports what Goodnight Moon encouraged: a consistent, gentle bedtime routine helps children sleep better. Studies by sleep researchers show that children who follow a predictable bedtime routine—like reading the same book each night—fall asleep faster, sleep longer, and wake less in the night. The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends these kinds of routines. Sales records and library archives confirm the slow climb of Goodnight Moon to bestseller status after a quiet beginning, showing how family practices can change over time when families find something that works. These facts are supported by sleep science and historic book sales data.
ch_a11.happened: In 1947, in New York, a gentle children’s book called Goodnight Moon was first published. The author, Margaret Wise Brown, wrote the story in a soothing, repetitive style. Goodnight Moon shows a small bunny slowly saying goodnight to everything in its cozy room, from the quiet old lady whispering hush to the moon outside the window. The illustrator, Clement Hurd, carefully drew each soft detail so children could spot familiar things, like a red balloon or a mittens set, each night. When it first came out, many book reviewers and even the New York Public Library thought it wasn’t special—some felt it was too simple or repetitive, so it didn’t become popular overnight. Yet, parents and children slowly discovered how the calm rhythm of Goodnight Moon helped make bedtime feel safe and loving. Over time, families passed the book from hand to hand, and children grew up remembering its words. Decades later, Goodnight Moon is now one of the most-loved and best-selling children’s books in the English-speaking world, welcoming little ones to sleep year after year.
ch_a11.scripture: The scriptures encourage us to create peace in our homes and value small, daily patterns. In 2 Nephi 4:34–35, Nephi prays to God in his daily troubles and trusts Him for help each day. Jesus also taught in Mark 10:14 that children are precious and deserve gentle care: "Suffer the little children to come unto me, and forbid them not: for of such is the kingdom of God." While there is no scripture about bedtime stories, these verses show how daily acts, routines, and tender care for children are pleasing to God.
ch_a11.background: The late 1940s was a time of change and hope after the difficult years of World War II. Families were rebuilding their lives, and many people wanted to focus on home and children again. Margaret Wise Brown, who loved the idea of comfort and wonder in a child’s life, chose to write stories that felt calm and real. Unlike many children’s books of the time that told fairy tales or heroes’ adventures, Goodnight Moon zoomed in on the small moments at home. Daily life for most families included simple routines, such as reading aloud to children before bed. Yet, most parents didn’t have many books with a slow, quiet atmosphere like Goodnight Moon. Brown and her illustrator, Hurd, worked closely to create images and words that honored the gentle rhythms of family life.

ch_a12.t: Attachment: The Need for One Reliable Adult
ch_a12.talk: Can you think of a time when someone you loved made you feel safe or comforted you?
ch_a12.child: Babies and little kids need to know someone they trust will come when they call or cry. Having just one loving grown-up close by helps them feel safe and happy inside.
ch_a12.learn: We learn that children are built to call out for help and comfort, and need to know someone will answer. No fancy program or toy can replace the loving presence of one reliable caregiver who patiently responds. This teaches us to treasure our place in a child’s life, even when daily routines feel ordinary or tiring, trusting that this steady love is doing Heavenly Father’s work in the quietest ways.
ch_a12.matters: This discovery changed how doctors, parents, and teachers understand the needs of children everywhere. It is now clear that the presence of even one reliable and loving caregiver gives a child a kind of foundation for life—a safe place from which to explore and learn about the world. For families who see children as gifts from Heavenly Father, the message is simple: children need more than learning toys or fancy activities. They first need the security of knowing someone they love will always be there when they call. Recognizing and nurturing this attachment is one way to follow Christ’s example of pure, steadfast love.

sources.name: Simply Psychology: Attachment Theory (John Bowlby & Mary Ainsworth)
American Psychological Association: What is Attachment?
Encyclopedia Britannica: John Bowlby

ch_a12.evidence: Over the decades, many studies around the world have confirmed what Bowlby and Ainsworth found. Researchers have seen that babies who have a steady, loving adult become more confident, handle stress better, and usually form healthier relationships as they grow. Attachment patterns have been found in many cultures, showing this need is universal. Still, experts remind us that people can heal and grow after a rough start, and early struggles do not seal a child’s fate. The science strongly supports the idea that consistent, responsive care during a child's first years is a profound gift, but there is room for hope and change at every stage of life.
ch_a12.happened: In 1958, a British psychiatrist named John Bowlby carefully observed children who had been separated from their parents during and after World War II. He noticed something very important: when young children were placed in institutions or foster care without a consistent adult to care for them, they often became sad, withdrawn, or anxious, even if their basic needs were met. Bowlby believed that all babies are born with a deep, natural need to form a close bond with one caregiver who will always be there for them. He called this special connection "attachment." In the late 1960s and early 1970s, Mary Ainsworth, working alongside Bowlby’s ideas, created an experiment called the "Strange Situation." She watched how babies and toddlers reacted when their mother left them for a short time and then came back. Some children clung to their mother or cried, while others seemed calm and trusting. These patterns helped researchers understand the different ways children feel safe—or unsafe—when they are with their main caregiver. Over time, their work showed that having just one reliable, loving adult is the most important thing a young child needs to grow strong and healthy emotionally.
ch_a12.scripture: The scriptures teach us about care, love, and the importance of family bonds. In the Book of Mormon, Mosiah 4:14-15 counsels parents to care for and teach their children, comforting them in love. The Savior’s tenderness toward children in 3 Nephi 17:11-24 also shows the importance He placed on their emotional needs. While the Bible and modern scripture do not mention 'attachment theory,' the principle of nurturing love and unbroken trust is at the heart of many teachings within both the Bible and the Book of Mormon.
ch_a12.background: The world in which Bowlby worked was still reeling from the effects of two world wars. Many families had been broken apart and many children grew up in orphanages or temporary homes. Bowlby himself had spent time without his own mother as a child, and this made him wonder how separation affects little ones. Before Bowlby’s work, people often thought that a child simply needed someone to feed, clothe, and house them, not much more. In health care and psychology at the time, there was little understanding of a child’s emotional needs. Families in London, and around the world, sometimes relied on nannies, nurseries, or even busy hospitals, where consistency wasn’t guaranteed. Bowlby’s research began to show that consistent, warm, and responsive care isn’t a luxury, but a need as real as food and shelter.

ch_a13.talk: What is something new you learned from watching a show with someone you love?
ch_a13.child: A long time ago, a TV show called Sesame Street was made to help kids learn numbers and letters. It used songs and funny puppets so learning would be fun. It worked best when someone you love watched it with you.
ch_a13.learn: Sesame Street reminds us that technology is a tool. When used with care, it can teach and uplift. But it also shows us that children learn best when adults—parents, grandparents, teachers—take time to watch, talk, and grow alongside them. Wise use of technology means choosing content thoughtfully and sharing those experiences together.
ch_a13.matters: The launch of Sesame Street taught families everywhere an important lesson: technology can lift and include those who need help the most, when guided by wisdom and love. For families of faith, this echoes the belief that all good gifts—including the tools of our time—can be used to lift others and prepare children for the future. It also gently reminds us that parents matter most in what children learn: children learn best when someone who loves them explores new things right beside them, whether in front of a book or a screen.

sources.name: Sesame Street and Academic Achievement
PBS: Sesame Street's History
National Library of Medicine – Study on Sesame Street

ch_a13.evidence: Over the years, Sesame Street has become one of the most carefully studied children’s programs. Early research, along with later studies like the 2015 work published in the journal American Economic Journal: Applied Economics, found that children who watched Sesame Street were better prepared for school, especially those from homes with fewer resources. The largest improvements were often found in reading and number recognition. Researchers also found that the effect of the show was greatest when a caring adult watched alongside the child, since discussion and encouragement deepened the learning. The studies also made clear that not all TV was equal—what mattered most was the quality of the content and the presence of an engaged adult, not simply the number of hours spent in front of a screen.
ch_a13.happened: In 1969, a new kind of television show began called Sesame Street. This program was made just for young children, and it took place in a bright, friendly city neighborhood full of songs, colorful puppets, and people who aimed to teach. Sesame Street was special because it was made by educators, child experts, and television producers who wanted to help kids, especially those whose families did not have many resources. Their main goal was to help children learn letters and numbers well before starting school. What set Sesame Street apart was its use of short, catchy segments and jingles—techniques borrowed from advertising, but pointed toward teaching instead of selling. The team paid attention to every detail, even testing episodes with real children before they aired. Right from the start, they watched closely to see if what they made truly helped kids learn. This careful, thoughtful approach made Sesame Street a program built on purpose, curiosity, and care, with the success of every child in mind.
ch_a13.scripture: While the scriptures don’t speak directly of watching television, they teach us that learning is important and that knowledge is a gift from God. Proverbs 4:7 counsels, “Wisdom is the principal thing; therefore get wisdom: and with all thy getting get understanding.” Doctrine and Covenants 88:118 also encourages us to “seek learning, even by study and also by faith.” These passages remind us that the Lord wants children and families to seek opportunities to learn and to help each other grow, using wise tools and good judgment.
ch_a13.background: When Sesame Street was created, television was one of the main ways families and children spent their time together. The 1960s United States saw many homes getting their first TVs. At the same time, there was concern that not everyone had the same chances to learn early skills, especially children from lower-income neighborhoods. Most children's TV was for entertainment, not education. Joan Ganz Cooney, a television producer, and Lloyd Morrisett, a psychologist, wanted to change that. Inspired by research on early learning and the power of TV to hold a child’s imagination, they launched a bold experiment: could television help close the learning gap? The team worked out of New York City, a place where many families from all backgrounds lived close together.

ch_a14.talk: What was your favorite part of the story we read today, and why?
ch_a14.child: Reading together helps you learn new words and understand stories better. When we talk about the book, it makes reading even more fun and helps you learn more.
ch_a14.learn: Engaging in shared book reading with children, especially through interactive discussions about the story, can significantly enhance their vocabulary and literacy skills. This practice emphasizes the importance of quality interactions over merely increasing the number of words a child hears. Parents are encouraged to read regularly with their children, ask questions about the story, and encourage their children to express their thoughts and feelings about the content.
ch_a14.matters: Understanding the factors that influence a child's language development is crucial for educators and parents alike. While the exact size of the "word gap" is debated, the consistent finding is that quality interactions, such as shared book reading, play a significant role in a child's vocabulary and literacy skills. For families of faith, this underscores the importance of spending meaningful time with children, engaging them in conversations, and fostering a love for reading. Such practices not only support educational outcomes but also strengthen family bonds.

sources.name: The effects of shared storybook reading on word learning: A meta-analysis
The impact of shared book reading on children's language skills: A meta-analysis
Language Matters: Denying the Existence of the 30-Million-Word Gap Has Serious Consequences

ch_a14.evidence: Recent meta-analyses have examined the impact of shared book reading on children's language development. A 2018 study published in Developmental Psychology analyzed 38 studies involving 2,455 children and found that dialogic reading styles and repeated story readings significantly enhanced word learning. Another meta-analysis in 2019, published in Educational Research Review, reviewed 54 studies and concluded that shared reading interventions positively affect children's language skills, though the effects were modest. These findings suggest that the quality of interactions during reading, such as engaging discussions and repeated exposure to stories, are key factors in promoting language development.
ch_a14.happened: In 1995, researchers Betty Hart and Todd Risley published a study suggesting that by age three, children from wealthier families hear about 30 million more words than those from less affluent backgrounds. This "word gap" was thought to contribute to differences in vocabulary and later academic success. However, subsequent studies have questioned the size and significance of this gap. More recent research highlights the importance of shared book reading—when an adult reads with a child and discusses the story. This practice has been consistently linked to improvements in children's vocabulary and literacy skills. Meta-analyses of dialogic reading interventions, where adults engage children in conversation about the book, show significant positive effects on language development.
ch_a14.scripture: The scriptures emphasize the importance of teaching and nurturing children. In Deuteronomy 6:7, parents are instructed to teach their children diligently, discussing God's commandments throughout daily activities. Similarly, in Doctrine and Covenants 68:25, parents are commanded to teach their children to understand the principles of the gospel. These passages highlight the value of intentional teaching and communication within the family, aligning with the benefits observed in shared book reading.
ch_a14.background: In the early 1990s, educators and researchers were seeking ways to address educational disparities among children from different socioeconomic backgrounds. Hart and Risley's study gained widespread attention, influencing early childhood education policies and programs. Their findings suggested that the quantity of words a child hears in early years could impact their language development and future academic performance. This led to initiatives aimed at increasing verbal interactions between parents and children, especially in lower-income families.

ch_a15.talk: How do you feel after spending a lot of time on your phone or tablet?
ch_a15.child: Too much time on phones and computers can make kids feel sad or lonely. It's good to play outside and talk with friends and family in person.
ch_a15.learn: This situation teaches us the importance of balance and mindfulness in our use of technology. It encourages families to engage in open discussions about screen time, set appropriate boundaries, and prioritize activities that foster face-to-face interactions and emotional well-being.
ch_a15.matters: Understanding the relationship between screen time and adolescent mental health is crucial for families striving to create a balanced environment. While technology offers many benefits, including access to information and connection with others, it's essential to be mindful of its potential drawbacks. For families of faith, this underscores the importance of fostering open communication, setting healthy boundaries, and encouraging activities that promote spiritual and emotional well-being.

sources.name: Increases in Depression, Self‐Harm, and Suicide Among U.S. Adolescents After 2012 and Links to Technology Use: Possible
Smartphones are bad for some adolescents, not all

ch_a15.evidence: Research has shown a concurrent rise in adolescent mental health issues and digital media use since the early 2010s. Studies indicate that increased screen time may be associated with declines in happiness and life satisfaction among teens. However, the strength of this association varies, and some researchers argue that the effect sizes are small. The debate continues, with ongoing studies aiming to clarify the relationship between technology use and mental health outcomes.
ch_a15.happened: Starting around 2012, there was a noticeable increase in mental health issues among adolescents, particularly in Western countries. Reports showed that more teens were experiencing depression, anxiety, and engaging in self-harm behaviors. This trend was especially pronounced among girls and young women. At the same time, the use of smartphones and social media platforms became widespread among teenagers. Some researchers, like Jonathan Haidt, suggested that the rise in digital media use might be linked to the increase in mental health problems. They proposed that excessive screen time could interfere with sleep, reduce face-to-face social interactions, and expose teens to cyberbullying. However, other experts, including Candice Odgers and Andrew Przybylski, argued that the evidence connecting smartphone use to mental health issues was not strong enough to establish a direct cause-and-effect relationship. They pointed out that while there is a correlation, it doesn't necessarily mean that one causes the other. This debate led to further studies and discussions about the impact of technology on adolescent well-being.
ch_a15.scripture: The scriptures teach the principle of moderation and balance. In Doctrine and Covenants 59:20, it states that all things are given by God for our benefit, but they are to be used with judgment, not to excess. This can be applied to the use of technology, reminding us to use it wisely and not let it dominate our lives.
ch_a15.background: Before 2012, adolescent mental health indicators were relatively stable or improving. The early 2000s saw advancements in technology, but smartphones and social media were not yet central to daily life. By 2012, smartphone ownership among teens had surpassed 50%, and platforms like Instagram and Snapchat were gaining popularity. This period also marked a shift in how young people communicated and spent their leisure time, moving from in-person interactions to digital ones. The rapid adoption of these technologies coincided with changes in adolescent behavior and mental health trends.

ch_a16.talk: What is your favorite part of our daily routine, and why do you like it?
ch_a16.child: Children need love, routines, talking, stories, sleep, and to feel safe. These simple things help them grow happy and strong.
ch_a16.learn: We learn that the most effective ways to support a young child's development are through simple, daily interactions and routines. By being present, responsive, and engaged, caregivers can provide the stability and stimulation children need to thrive. This reinforces the idea that the greatest gifts we can offer our children are our time, attention, and love.
ch_a16.matters: These findings are significant because they reassure parents that fostering a child's development doesn't require expensive resources or specialized expertise. Instead, it emphasizes the value of everyday interactions and routines. For families of faith, this aligns with the belief that the most meaningful contributions to a child's growth come from love, attention, and time spent together. It underscores that the tools given by Heavenly Father to nurture children are simple and within reach, emphasizing the importance of being present and engaged in a child's daily life.

sources.name: Child safety from the perspective of essential needs - PMC
Identifying the Needs of Prekindergarten Children: A Focus on Health, Wellbeing, and Family Environment - PMC
Nurturing care: promoting early childhood development - ScienceDirect
Supporting Healthy Brain and Behavioral Development During Infancy - Lisa S. Scott, Natalie H. Brito, 2022

ch_a16.evidence: Scientific research supports these findings. Studies have shown that consistent, responsive caregiving leads to secure attachments, which are crucial for emotional and social development. Regular routines provide a sense of security and predictability, aiding in behavioral regulation. Engaging in conversations and reading to children enhances language acquisition and cognitive skills. Adequate sleep is essential for physical health and cognitive function. Protecting children from chronic stress prevents negative impacts on brain development and overall well-being. These elements are foundational and do not require wealth or advanced technology, but rather time and attention from caregivers.
ch_a16.happened: In 2026, researchers from around the world gathered and analyzed extensive studies on early childhood development. They found that the most crucial elements for a young child's healthy growth are simple and accessible: having a few stable and responsive adults in their lives, following predictable daily routines, engaging in regular conversations, being read to, getting enough sleep, and being protected from ongoing stress. These findings emphasized that these fundamental needs are consistent across different cultures and environments, highlighting their universal importance in nurturing a child's development.
ch_a16.scripture: The scriptures teach us about the importance of nurturing and guiding children. In Proverbs 22:6, it says, "Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it." This highlights the significance of consistent guidance and teaching. Additionally, in the Book of Mormon, Mosiah 4:15 advises, "But ye will teach them to walk in the ways of truth and soberness; ye will teach them to love one another, and to serve one another." These passages emphasize the role of parents and caregivers in providing a stable, loving environment that fosters a child's growth and development.
ch_a16.background: Before these studies, there was a growing concern about the increasing reliance on technology and structured educational programs for young children. Many parents and educators believed that advanced tools and specialized knowledge were necessary to support a child's development. However, daily life for many families was becoming busier, with parents juggling work and other responsibilities, leading to less time spent on simple, direct interactions with their children. This shift raised questions about the essential components of early childhood development and whether modern approaches were overlooking fundamental needs.

sf_a01.talk: Why do you think God wants us to learn about both the world and His teachings?
sf_a01.child: A long time ago, the church started the first universities so people could learn about both God and the world. They argued ideas kindly and studied together. Because of this, we have schools and science today.
sf_a01.learn: We can learn that faith and science can work together as friends, not enemies. The honest search for answers and the careful practice of debate and study were seen as ways to honor God. Being curious, asking questions, and using our minds can be faithful acts. This makes it possible for families to see the classroom as a place where faith and learning walk together.
sf_a01.matters: This story teaches us that the places where science is taught began with people of faith. Universities did not grow apart from the church, but out of it. For families who believe that God gives us tools to learn and build, this history is a reminder that seeking knowledge is part of our faith. It also shows how ideas can grow stronger when people learn to ask hard questions in a spirit of respect and honesty. As we send our own children into today's classrooms, we can trust that learning deeply about the world is not just a modern idea, but one that faithful people have loved and defended for centuries.

sources.name: Britannica Kids – University
Oxford University – History and Heritage
Vatican Museums – Medieval Universities: A Church Invention
Church of Jesus Christ – Seek Learning by Study and by Faith

sf_a01.evidence: Historians have good records showing the founding of the University of Bologna around 1088. Documents from the time mention its special charter and its right to set its own rules. The University of Paris may have roots earlier or later, but records from the 1100s show a community of teachers recognized by both kings and popes. Oxford has evidence of teaching by the late 1100s. Scholars have found copies of charters, letters between school leaders and popes, and old course lists that included logic, philosophy, math, medicine, and law. These sources confirm that universities were church-connected, self-governing, and protected centers of learning.
sf_a01.happened: In the late 1000s, a new kind of school appeared in Europe—one that did not belong to a single church or noble family, but stood by itself. The University of Bologna, started in 1088, was the first of its kind. After Bologna, Paris and Oxford soon followed. These universities were deeply connected to the Christian church. Most of their teachers were not just masters of learning but priests or monks, and many students were training to serve in the church. Classes were not divided like today; instead, they gathered in groups to listen, discuss, and especially to debate. One key method was disputation—where everyone learned by arguing different sides of important questions, searching for the best answer together. Students learned about God, but also about nature, math, stars, medicine, and law. Soon, universities earned special charters from popes and kings, giving them the right to teach and grant degrees. By 1500, the idea had spread across Europe. This way of teaching—open, questioning, and careful—was unlike anything that had come before, and it created a new space for science to grow.
sf_a01.scripture: Scriptures encourage the pursuit of knowledge and learning. In Doctrine and Covenants 88:118, it says, “seek ye out of the best books words of wisdom; seek learning, even by study and also by faith.” The Bible, in Proverbs 4:7, reminds us, “Wisdom is the principal thing; therefore get wisdom: and with all thy getting get understanding.” While the Bible does not mention universities, these teachings reflect Heavenly Father's desire that we seek understanding of both spiritual and earthly things. The principle of gathering to learn and teach is found many times in scripture (Acts 17:11, 2 Nephi 9:29).
sf_a01.background: Before universities, most learning in Europe happened in monasteries or small church schools. Only a few people could read or write, and most books were copied by hand. The church was the main protector of learning after the fall of Rome. Life was hard for most families, who worked the land and faced dangers from illness, war, and famine. Faith was woven into every part of life. When the first universities were founded, much of Europe was rebuilding. People wanted more knowledge—as more trade, cities, and new ideas began to spread. The university grew out of a longing to organize this learning, make it safer, and to train leaders for both church and community.

sf_a02.t: Ibn al-Haytham and the Scientific Method
sf_a02.talk: Can you think of something you wondered about, and how you could do a little experiment to learn more?
sf_a02.child: A long time ago in Egypt, Ibn al-Haytham showed that light goes into our eyes to help us see. He taught people to test their ideas with real experiments, not just trust what others say. Today, scientists everywhere try to learn truth by testing things, just like he did.
sf_a02.learn: From Ibn al-Haytham we learn the importance of questioning what we hear, testing it for ourselves, and letting evidence guide us. Faith and science do not need to be rivals; both encourage careful seeking after truth. His life teaches us that every honest question and humble experiment can help us learn more about God’s world and share those discoveries with others, no matter where or when we live.
sf_a02.matters: What happened in Cairo with Ibn al-Haytham changed the world’s approach to learning. His method—test, observe, question—spread across cultures and centuries. When his Book of Optics was translated into Latin, European scholars, including Roger Bacon and later Isaac Newton, built studies on his way of thinking. His story shows that great discoveries can come from careful, humble searching, and reminds us that science can flourish when people of faith seek to understand God’s world and share with others. For families of faith, his example encourages us to welcome learning and test what we’re taught against truth, trusting that all real knowledge comes from God.

sources.name: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Ibn al-Haytham
The Met Museum: Ibn al-Haytham (Alhazen) and the Legacy of Arabic Optics
University of St Andrews: Ibn al-Haytham
Encyclopædia Britannica: Ibn al-Haytham

sf_a02.evidence: Historians have carefully studied Ibn al-Haytham’s original Arabic manuscripts, as well as early translations of his work into Latin that spread through Europe. His detailed experiments are described plainly in the Book of Optics, which survives in many versions. Researchers agree that his method was new for his time. While science has grown since then, his insistence on experimental proof rather than authority alone set a lasting example. Museums and universities hold his early works, and scientific historians credit him directly with influencing later giants like Kepler and Newton. This is considered solid history, built on many primary documents and scholarly studies.
sf_a02.happened: Around the year 1021 in Cairo, Egypt, a scientist named Ibn al-Haytham wrote a book called the Book of Optics. Ibn al-Haytham was deeply curious about how vision worked. People before him believed our eyes sent out rays to see, but he disagreed. Through careful thinking and experiments, he showed how light actually travels from what we see into our eyes. What made Ibn al-Haytham’s work extra special was his approach. He insisted that just believing what someone said—even famous thinkers like Aristotle—was not enough. He thought that every idea, even his own, should be tested with real-life experiments to see if it was true. He wrote that a seeker after truth must check everything carefully, trusting experiments over tradition. His Book of Optics wasn’t just about light and vision, but about how to seek knowledge. It invited others to test, observe, and learn from the world itself, and this way of learning would become the heart of science everywhere.
sf_a02.scripture: Scriptures teach us to seek knowledge, to ask questions, and to test all things. In James 1:5 of the New Testament, we are encouraged, “If any of you lack wisdom, let him ask of God.” Doctrine and Covenants 88:118 counsels to “seek learning, even by study and also by faith.” Alma 32:27 in the Book of Mormon compares truth-seeking to planting a seed, testing to see if it grows. These verses remind us that seeking truth—by experiment, faith, and reason—is a pattern the Lord approves, and that all good and truth can be sought courageously.
sf_a02.background: Ibn al-Haytham lived during what many call the Islamic Golden Age, a time when science, math, and learning flourished in places like Cairo and Baghdad. Scholars gathered in libraries and exchanged ideas, translating works from Greece, Persia, and India. Many of these thinkers were people of faith who believed that studying nature was a way to appreciate God’s creation. Daily life in Cairo bustled with trade, learning, and worship. Books were copied by hand, and scholars often worked for wealthy patrons or in grand public houses of learning called "houses of wisdom." Until Ibn al-Haytham’s time, much scientific thinking relied on ancient texts more than observation. He changed that by urging everyone to look at the world directly and test their ideas.

sf_a03.talk: Why do you think Heavenly Father wants us to learn about His creations?
sf_a03.child: Long ago, a man who worked in a church found out that the sun is in the middle, not the earth. He loved God, and he loved to study the stars. His work helped everyone see the sky in a new way.
sf_a03.learn: We can learn from Copernicus that faithful people can make amazing discoveries, sometimes by patiently working for years and never losing sight of either their faith or their curiosity. He teaches us that our callings, our science, and our faith can work together, just as God intended. It’s important not to rush to fear or judgment when new understanding comes, but to remember that truth grows brighter as we seek it.
sf_a03.matters: This event matters because it reminds us that seeking truth and loving God are not two separate paths. Copernicus’s story shows that sincere faith and good science can go hand in hand. For families who believe all truth comes from God, this is a comfort and a call to courage—sometimes the world changes not by setting faith aside, but by following its deepest call to learn and serve. It also reminds us to double-check our stories: history is sometimes more surprising and hopeful than we remember.

sources.name: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Nicolaus Copernicus
Encyclopaedia Britannica: Nicolaus Copernicus
NASA Solar System Exploration: Nicolaus Copernicus

sf_a03.evidence: The evidence for Copernicus’s role as a canon at Frombork, and the writing and dedication of his book, is clear from church and scientific records of the time. We have his letters, the original printed book from 1543, and letters from bishops and cardinals who encouraged him. Historians agree that Copernicus’s book was quietly accepted among many leading churchmen for decades, and it did not instantly cause trouble. Only when Galileo’s work stirred a public debate, many years later, did the Church place Copernicus’s book on a list for review, and even then, it was not completely banned but paused for corrections. His life and work are well documented in libraries and museums.
sf_a03.happened: In 1543, Nicolaus Copernicus, who was not only a skilled astronomer but also a faithful canon (church leader) at Frombork Cathedral in Poland, published a book that changed how people understood the heavens. His book, "On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres," made the bold claim that the sun, not the earth, sits at the center of the universe and that the planets—including Earth—move around it. This idea was very new and surprising at the time, because for centuries most people believed that everything revolved around Earth. Copernicus worked on his book for many years, often sharing drafts with bishops and cardinals. He dedicated his work to the Pope, showing great respect for his faith. Far from hiding his beliefs, Copernicus served his church every day while quietly changing the way people would see the sky forever. His book was printed in the last year of his life and passed quietly among scholars and churchmen for decades, becoming one of the most important works in the history of science, and only became controversial long after Copernicus had died.
sf_a03.scripture: Scripture teaches us that God is the Creator of all things and encourages us to study His works. Psalm 19:1 says, “The heavens declare the glory of God; and the firmament sheweth his handiwork.” Doctrine and Covenants 88:42–47 speaks of the laws that govern the heavens, given by God. While the scriptures don’t say how the planets move, they invite us to search for truth in all things and trust that God wants us to learn about His creations.
sf_a03.background: In the early 1500s, Europe was full of learning but also of questions. Most people believed what they saw—the sun seemed to rise and set around them—but astronomers kept careful notes and noticed things that didn't quite fit with old ideas. Before Copernicus, a wise astronomer named Ptolemy had taught that the Earth stood still at the universe's center, and this view matched what people read in their Bibles and saw with their eyes. Copernicus grew up in a world where the church was the center of learning, keeping libraries and teaching at universities. Life in Frombork, Poland, was shaped by the church, with bells ringing through the day and people gathering for worship, but curious minds like Copernicus's spent long nights measuring the stars. He was respected by church leaders and served as a canon even as he studied and taught about the stars and planets.

sf_a04.t: Kepler: Thinking His Thoughts After Him
sf_a04.talk: Why do you think it is important to tell the truth, even if it isn’t what you hoped?
sf_a04.child: Johannes Kepler loved God and wanted to understand how the planets move. He found out they go in ovals instead of perfect circles, even though he wished for circles. He taught that following the truth is important, even when it surprises us.
sf_a04.learn: Kepler’s story teaches that true faith does not fear honest questions, and that it is good to check what we hope is true against what really is. Sometimes we might want things to be a certain way, but following the truth, even if it surprises us, can lead to bigger discoveries and deeper faith. In both science and faith, Heavenly Father wants us to seek, learn, and listen—trusting that His creation will always speak what is true.
sf_a04.matters: Kepler’s discovery matters because it changed how people understood our place in the cosmos. For families of faith, his story shows that seeking truth—no matter where it leads—can be part of worshipping God. Kepler did not let his personal wishes for how God might have arranged the heavens overrule the evidence in front of him. This kind of honesty, humility, and courage is vital in both science and faith. The very laws he found later allowed scientists like Isaac Newton to explain how gravity holds the planets in their paths, showing how careful observations can reveal even greater wonders hidden in God’s creation.

sources.name: NASA: Johannes Kepler: Discovering the Laws of Planetary Motion
Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Johannes Kepler
Encyclopaedia Britannica: Johannes Kepler
The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints: Scripture—Doctrine and Covenants 88

sf_a04.evidence: Historians have many of Kepler’s writings, including his famous books, where he explained his discoveries and the thinking behind them. Exact records show how he used Tycho Brahe’s careful measurements to reach his conclusions about ellipses and planetary motion. His three laws are taught all over the world and still help scientists today. Translations of his letters and journals show his deep faith and his struggle to accept ellipses instead of circles. Scientists can use modern telescopes and math to see that his way of describing the planets’ paths is correct. There is overwhelming evidence from both his own words and the skies themselves that Kepler’s work is trustworthy and correct.
sf_a04.happened: Between 1609 and 1619, Johannes Kepler made some of the most important discoveries in the history of astronomy. Kepler lived in Prague, Bohemia, and he was deeply committed to his faith, having trained for the Lutheran ministry before turning to science. He wanted to understand the heavens because he believed nature was God’s handiwork and that by studying it, he could learn more about the Creator. Kepler worked very hard, using observations made by the Danish astronomer Tycho Brahe. He started with the belief, shared by many in his time, that the planets must move in perfect circles. As Kepler studied the data, though, he saw that nothing quite fit these circles. Instead of forcing the information to match his hopes, Kepler carefully measured and found that the planets moved in ellipses—shaped like squished circles, or ovals—around the sun. He was disappointed because he thought circles were more perfect, but he trusted what he saw. Kepler published his findings, which we now call Kepler's three laws of planetary motion. He once wrote that by studying astronomy, he was “thinking God’s thoughts after Him.” Kepler’s willingness to change his view when faced with new evidence helped pave the way for modern science.
sf_a04.scripture: While the scriptures do not talk about Kepler directly or name the planets' orbits, they do praise honest seeking and teach that God is the author of both spiritual and physical truth. James 1:5 encourages asking God for wisdom. Doctrine and Covenants 88: 42-47 speaks of God setting “all things, both in heaven and on the earth,” in order, and how the stars obey laws He has given. The process Kepler followed—seeking truth humbly, and changing his own ideas when evidence demanded—is a principle we see encouraged through scripture.
sf_a04.background: Kepler worked during a time of major change in Europe, often called the Scientific Revolution. People were just starting to question long-held beliefs about the natural world. Before Kepler, people mostly followed the teachings of ancient thinkers like Aristotle and Ptolemy, who said the heavens must be made of perfect circles. Kepler was born in 1571 in what is now Germany, in a world shaped by the Protestant Reformation and frequent religious conflict. He grew up wanting to serve God as a minister, but eventually found his calling in mathematics and astronomy. Daily life was often hard, with wars, sickness, and little privacy or comfort by today’s standards. Still, people found wonder in the night sky, and some, like Kepler, believed that learning about the heavens was a way to honor God.

sf_a05.talk: Why do you think it’s important to ask questions, even when others think differently?
sf_a05.child: A long time ago, a man named Galileo said the earth goes around the sun, but some leaders didn’t like this idea. They told him to stop saying it, so he had to stay at home. Galileo still learned and wrote wonderful things, even when it was hard.
sf_a05.learn: Galileo’s trial can teach us the importance of being willing to seek truth, even when it is hard or unpopular, and to be patient and respectful with those who disagree. We learn to listen with humility and not to fear new knowledge, trusting that all truth can come together in God’s plan. It is also a lesson in how even trusted leaders and institutions can err when they feel threatened by change, encouraging us as families to be hopeful, honest, and humble as we learn both from faith and from science.
sf_a05.matters: Galileo’s story matters for our families today because it shows that sometimes faith and science can seem to be at odds, but both are ways of seeking truth. It reminds us that even good people and good institutions can make mistakes when they are afraid to listen or change. This event does not prove the Church always opposed science; in fact, believers have often been great scientists! But it warns us that when any group refuses honest questions, it might silence people who find out new truths. For families of faith, it teaches us to be humble in what we know and brave enough to keep searching and learning, knowing all truth comes from God.

sources.name: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy - Galileo Galilei
Smithsonian - What Galileo's Telescope Reveals
Vatican News - Church's Rehabilitation of Galileo

sf_a05.evidence: Historians and scientists have many records and letters that show what happened to Galileo. His book, 'Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems', his trial documents, and his own letters have survived, letting us read some of his own words. Later, scientists were able to observe the parallax Galileo could not, confirming the sun-centered model. The Vatican itself has made these historical papers open to scholars. Modern research shows he was not tortured and continued to correspond with friends and scientists while under house arrest. The story is well established in serious histories and church records, so we have strong evidence for what occurred and why.
sf_a05.happened: In the year 1633, Galileo Galilei, a well-known scientist from Italy, stood trial in Rome before the Roman Catholic Church’s Inquisition. Galileo believed that the sun, not the earth, was at the center of the solar system—a view called Copernicanism after another scientist, Copernicus. Though the Pope had once allowed Galileo to discuss this idea as just a theory, Galileo’s book placed the Pope’s argument in the mouth of a character named Simplicio, which sounded like he called him simple-minded. This, along with the Church’s belief that no solid proof existed yet (since people of that time could not observe the tiny shifts in stars, called stellar parallax), led to trouble. Galileo was formally accused of heresy, or teaching against Church doctrine. He was forced to say he was wrong and was sentenced to live under house arrest for the rest of his life. Though never put in a dungeon or tortured, he was watched closely. Even so, he continued his work and wrote some of his most important science while at home. Over 350 years later, the Catholic Church officially said Galileo's treatment had been a mistake, admitting that he had been right and that science and faith can sometimes have honest disagreements.
sf_a05.scripture: While the scriptures do not discuss Galileo or his discoveries, there are principles that match this story. Doctrine and Covenants 88:78-79 teaches us to “teach one another the doctrine of the kingdom…and all things that pertain unto the kingdom of God, that are expedient for you to understand; of things both in heaven and in the earth.” The Lord invites us to learn about the heavens and the earth, showing that seeking science is a worthy part of faith. James 1:5 in the New Testament also reminds us, “If any of you lack wisdom, let him ask of God,” encouraging us to seek understanding both spiritually and through study. We are counseled to love truth, wherever it is found.
sf_a05.background: Galileo lived during the Renaissance, a time of great learning in Europe when old ideas were being challenged and new knowledge flourished. Most people still believed the earth was the center of the universe, as Ptolemy had taught for over a thousand years. Daily life was shaped by religion and tradition, and the Church was a great authority not just in spiritual matters but also in science. Books were mainly read by scholars, and the telescope was a brand-new tool. Galileo was a teacher, inventor, and father who believed that learning about the world helped people understand God’s creation. The Pope knew of Galileo and once supported him, but the fear that scientific ideas could challenge the Church’s authority made the situation tense. Galileo’s trial didn’t just involve science; it mixed personalities, pride, faith, and the struggle for truth in a changing world.

sf_a06.t: Newton Wrote More Theology Than Physics
sf_a06.talk: Why do you think Newton felt that learning about how the world works could help him learn about God?
sf_a06.child: Isaac Newton loved learning about how the world works and about God’s teachings. He wrote lots and lots about both science and the Bible. He believed the amazing order in the world shows how wise and powerful Heavenly Father is.
sf_a06.learn: From Newton, we learn that exploring the world and faith can go hand-in-hand. We can be curious and love to learn about how things work while still believing that all knowledge is part of Heavenly Father’s plan. Newton’s example reminds us not to put limits on faith or learning, and to be humble about incomplete understanding. Sometimes, the people who discover the most about our world are also looking hardest for God’s hand in it.
sf_a06.matters: Newton shows us that faith and science are not enemies; they are different ways of seeking the truth. His life reminds us that curiosity about the world can lead us to wonder about God and His designs. For a family of faith, Newton’s story encourages us to see science as a tool that helps us appreciate God’s power and order in creation, rather than something that takes away from faith.

sources.name: The Newton Project (University of Oxford)
Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Isaac Newton
Royal Society: Isaac Newton’s Faith

sf_a06.evidence: Many of Newton’s original handwritten manuscripts survive today and can be seen in museum collections. Scholars have carefully studied these pages and confirmed that Newton wrote much more about biblical chronology and theology than he did about science and math. Historians also know from Newton’s private letters and notes that he held some beliefs that were different from most Christians in his day. The Principia itself is clear about his belief in a Creator, especially in the General Scholium at the end of the book. Modern research has confirmed all these parts of his life through direct evidence from his own hand.
sf_a06.happened: In 1687, Isaac Newton published a book called the Principia, which described new laws for how objects move and how gravity works everywhere in the universe. This book became one of the most important scientific works in all history. But what many people don’t know is that Newton, who taught at Cambridge University in England, also wrote many thousands of pages about theology—his thoughts about God, the Bible, and how the world fits together. In fact, more of his written work was about faith and the study of scripture than about mathematics or physics. Newton tried to create a timeline of events in the Bible and spent a lot of time thinking about how God’s plan could be seen in the order and beauty of the natural world. He believed deeply in God but had some unusual beliefs for his time, especially about the nature of the Trinity, which he kept mostly private to avoid trouble with the church or government.
sf_a06.scripture: Several scriptures teach that God is a God of order and that studying His creations brings us closer to Him. For example, Doctrine and Covenants 88:47–49 explains that all things testify of God. Psalm 19:1 in the Bible says, 'The heavens declare the glory of God; and the firmament sheweth his handywork.' While scripture doesn’t mention Newton, it encourages us to seek learning by study and by faith, as taught in Doctrine and Covenants 88:118.
sf_a06.background: During Newton’s lifetime in the late 1600s, England was a place of great change and discovery. The scientific revolution was underway, and people were starting to use careful experiments and mathematics to understand nature better. Before Newton, famous scientists like Galileo and Kepler had made big advances in understanding the planets and motion, but no one had found one set of rules that could explain both an apple falling and planets moving in the sky. People in Newton’s time lived without electricity or modern technology; life centered around faith, farming, and the rhythms of the church and the seasons.

sf_a07.t: Faraday, the Preacher Who Found the Field
sf_a07.talk: What would you have done if you discovered something important and people wanted to honor you, but your faith asked you to be humble?
sf_a07.child: Michael Faraday discovered how to make electricity by moving a magnet in a coil of wire. He loved Jesus and chose to help his church instead of becoming rich or famous. Even today, the electricity in our homes comes from what he found.
sf_a07.learn: From Faraday, we learn that faith and curiosity can go together. Heavenly Father can inspire us as we study the world, and that knowledge can be used to bless others. We also learn that greatness is not about public honors or riches, but about quietly doing good, staying true to our values, and serving others. Like Faraday, we can find joy in discovery and use our talents for the benefit of those around us.
sf_a07.matters: Faraday’s discovery matters because it is the foundation of all electricity generation today. Where there is a power plant, a wind turbine, or even a hand-cranked flashlight, the same principle that Faraday found in his lab is at work. For families of faith, Faraday’s life is a reminder that the Lord can work through humble and faithful people, not just the rich or the famous. He chose to turn down offers of power and wealth to stay true to his beliefs. His example shows us that scientific discovery and faith can go hand in hand, blessing people’s lives without compromise.

sources.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Michael Faraday
Royal Institution: Faraday and Electromagnetism
BBC - History: Michael Faraday

sf_a07.evidence: Historians have thoroughly documented Michael Faraday’s experiments, letters, and public lectures. His notebooks describing electromagnetic induction are preserved at the Royal Institution in London, and replicas of his early apparatus can be found in science museums today. Scientists have repeated his experiments worldwide for nearly two centuries, always finding the same results: moving a magnet through coils of wire generates electricity. Faraday’s life and work were also recorded by those who knew him, including his lectures and faith service. There is no serious doubt among historians about what he discovered or how he lived.
sf_a07.happened: In the year 1831, Michael Faraday, a man known for his deep faith and gentle character, made a discovery that quietly changed the world. Working in his laboratory in London, Faraday showed that when a magnet moves inside a coil of wire, it can create an electric current. This principle is called electromagnetic induction. His experiment was simple: he wrapped wire into coils and moved a magnet through them, finding that electricity appeared in the wire whenever the magnet moved. This finding became the foundation for electric motors and generators—the machines that help power nearly every corner of our world today, from homes and schools to hospitals and factories. Faraday was not a man of wealth or high social standing; he began as a bookbinder’s apprentice and taught himself much of what he knew. Despite invitations to accept important government jobs or become a knight, he chose to remain humble and serve in his church as an unpaid preacher, living his faith quietly even while his discoveries sparked a revolution in science and technology.
sf_a07.scripture: While the scriptures do not mention electricity or Faraday’s work, several passages teach about the beauty of learning and the gifts God gives His children. In Doctrine and Covenants 88:118, we are told to "seek learning, even by study and also by faith." In the Bible, James 1:5 encourages us to ask God for wisdom. Faraday’s faith, humility, and desire to serve align well with these teachings—showing that one can seek knowledge and still rely on the Lord, using that knowledge for good.
sf_a07.background: England in the early 1800s was a place of rapid change. The Industrial Revolution was transforming how people worked, traveled, and learned. Gas lamps were lighting city streets, and the idea of “electricity” was just starting to move from science experiments into daily life. Michael Faraday grew up in a modest home in London, the son of a blacksmith. He belonged to a small Christian group called the Sandemanians, who focused on simplicity, humility, and living the teachings of Jesus. Most people at that time knew little about science, and Faraday himself had only a basic education, learning mainly through hard work and curiosity. Despite this, or perhaps because of it, he approached problems with fresh eyes and deep faith, believing that the world was filled with order that could be discovered and understood.

sf_a08.talk: What is something kind or helpful you have done that maybe nobody noticed, but you know was good?
sf_a08.child: A monk named Mendel grew lots of pea plants to figure out why plants look like their parents. He didn’t give up, even when no one cared for a long time. Because of his careful work, we now know how traits are passed down in families.
sf_a08.learn: Mendel’s story teaches us that discovery and faith can work side by side. True knowledge comes through both careful study and trust in God’s timing. Even quiet, patient work—sometimes done in the background—can lead to blessings for many people, even far into the future. We can remember that working honestly and faithfully matters, even when no one notices at first.
sf_a08.matters: Mendel’s discovery matters to the world, and to families of faith, because it shows that careful, honest work can bring great blessings, even if those blessings are not seen for many years. His findings are the roots of modern genetics, which influences everything from how we grow food to how doctors understand illnesses passed through families. For people who try to follow Christ, Mendel’s story reminds us that our efforts, especially in the service of others and in learning, are not wasted—even if we do not see the results right away. A garden in a quiet monastery became the starting place for knowledge that helps millions today.

sources.name: National Human Genome Research Institute – Gregor Mendel Biography
Encyclopedia Britannica – Gregor Mendel
Royal Society of Biology – Mendel’s Peas and Principles of Inheritance

sf_a08.evidence: Historians and scientists agree that Mendel’s experiments are well documented. His original papers exist, and copies can be seen in scientific libraries. Scientists have repeated his pea plant experiments many times and have found the same patterns of inheritance Mendel described. Later discoveries in biology, like DNA, have shown that Mendel’s observations were the first steps toward understanding genes, even though he did not know about DNA himself. Records from the monastery also show that Mendel’s abbot supported and encouraged his careful work, which was rare for the time. Today, Mendel is widely recognized as the father of modern genetics.
sf_a08.happened: In 1866, a gentle and curious Augustinian friar named Gregor Mendel finished years of careful work in the garden of his monastery in Brno, Moravia. Mendel spent long hours planting and watching over thousands of pea plants, noticing how certain traits, like flower color and seed shape, passed from one generation to the next. He kept notes on every plant and every cross he made, then counted the different results. Mendel did not use guesses but math: he was one of the first scientists to realize that some traits followed patterns that could be predicted. He described what he found in a paper called 'Experiments on Plant Hybridization' and even shared it with several other scientists. His monastery encouraged him, with the abbot providing land and support. Despite the value of his findings, almost no one paid attention at the time. People simply didn’t see how important Mendel’s laws of inheritance were, so his work sat quietly in library shelves, nearly forgotten.
