It took more than thirty years before scientists searching for answers to their own questions rediscovered Mendel’s notes and realized how much they explained. His patient, quiet study laid the groundwork for the new science of genetics, changing how we understand plants, animals, and even our own families.
sf_a08.scripture: While the scriptures do not describe scientific experiments or the discovery of genetics, they do teach about seeking knowledge, patience, and the importance of small things. For example, Doctrine and Covenants 88:118 encourages us to "seek learning, even by study and also by faith." The parable of the mustard seed in Matthew 13:31-32 reminds us how something tiny can grow large and bless many. The scriptures teach that knowledge is part of God’s work and that even unnoticed acts of good can bring great results in His time.
sf_a08.background: Europe in the 1800s was full of change and curiosity. People were beginning to ask more questions about the natural world using careful study and experiments. Schools and universities were growing, but many scientific discoveries still happened in homes, farms, and even in religious communities. Gregor Mendel lived in a monastery, a quiet place where friars studied, prayed, taught, and helped their neighbors. The monastery was also a center for learning, with a large garden and rooms for research. Mendel was trained at a university, but returned to the peaceful monastery to continue his work among the peas. Daily life for him meant a mix of worship, community service, and quiet observation of God’s creations. In Mendel’s world, faith and science were not enemies, but worked together to help people understand truth.

sf_a09.talk: Can you think of a time when learning something new helped you understand something in the scriptures better?
sf_a09.child: A long time ago, two men wrote books saying science and religion were always fighting. But later, people looked carefully and found this story wasn’t true. Faith and learning can work together to help us grow and do good.
sf_a09.learn: We can learn to be careful about popular stories, especially when they make grand claims about people or groups being natural enemies. Even ideas that sound sensible can be mistaken if they are not carefully studied. As families, we can teach children to look for truth in both science and faith, to treat both with respect, and to be patient with questions. When we know the real history, we are better able to build bridges between our beliefs and our learning, using all the gifts Heavenly Father has given us.
sf_a09.matters: This topic matters because the idea that faith and science must always clash was taught by just a few writers, but it has continued to affect how people talk and think today. For families who see technology as a gift and want to use truth from every source to bless their lives, it helps to know that this story of war between faith and science was an invention, not a fact. Both ways of seeking truth—asking questions about the world and seeking God in prayer—can work together to help us grow. Recognizing this helps us teach our children to value learning from every good book, including both scripture and science, and to seek how the Lord’s gifts can work together for good.

sources.name: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Science and Religion
Encyclopedia Britannica: Andrew Dickson White and the 'Warfare' Thesis
Colin Russell, British Society for the History of Science, The Conflict Thesis
churchofjesuschrist.org: Seeking Learning by Study and Faith

sf_a09.evidence: Today, nearly all historians who study the history of science agree that the story told by Draper and White is mostly false. Careful studies show that many of the clashes they described did not actually happen or were exaggerated. Scholars point out that most scientists throughout history have been religious themselves, and many discoveries happened within religious cultures or were supported by people of faith. For example, the Catholic Church supported many scientists, and great scientists such as Isaac Newton and Gregor Mendel were deeply guided by their faith. The majority of historians now teach that the relationship between faith and science is complex, including both cooperation and disagreement at times, but not a story of unending war.
sf_a09.happened: In 1874 in New York, a man named John William Draper published a book called History of the Conflict Between Religion and Science. Draper’s book painted a vivid picture of religion and science as two great forces locked in a never-ending battle. He suggested that religion had always tried to stop science from making progress, and that whenever science made a discovery, religious belief would fight back. His book was full of strong opinions and dramatic stories, and it became very popular, printed in fifty different editions. About twenty years later in 1896, another writer, Andrew Dickson White, released his own book, A History of the Warfare of Science with Theology in Christendom. White also told stories of fights between science and religion, giving example after example of supposed conflicts—many of which he took from old legends and rumors more than careful history. Both authors made the idea popular that science and faith are natural enemies. These books were read by many people and helped shape a common belief that these two ways of thinking racially oppose each other.
sf_a09.scripture: The scriptures do not talk about Draper or White or their books, but they do teach principles that apply. In Doctrine and Covenants 88:77-80, the Lord commands people to “teach one another words of wisdom” and to “seek learning, even by study and also by faith.” This shows that gaining knowledge through both spiritual and scientific means is valuable. Alma 30:44 in the Book of Mormon reminds us that ‘all things denote there is a God,’ suggesting that learning about the world and recognizing God’s hand in it go together. The scriptures encourage unity and seeking truth from all sources, not conflict.
sf_a09.background: The late 1800s were a time of great change in America and Europe. The world was being transformed by new inventions, discoveries, and ideas. Trains and telegraphs made travel and communication faster than ever. People were learning about electricity, and scientists like Charles Darwin were sharing new ideas about life and nature. At the same time, many people still attended church each week, and religion played a big role in their lives. Draper was a scientist and a professor in New York, while White was the first president of Cornell University. Both men believed in progress, and some of their own personal experiences with church leaders made them feel that religion could get in the way of science. Most everyday people, however, saw faith and discovery as parts of the same good life, and homes often held both scripture and science books.

sf_a10.t: The Flat Earth That Never Was
sf_a10.talk: Can you think of a time when something you heard turned out not to be true after you learned more about it?
sf_a10.child: A long time ago, people already knew the earth was round, even before Columbus sailed. The story that people thought the world was flat is made up. We can remember to check if the stories we hear are really true.
sf_a10.learn: We can learn that things 'everyone knows' may not always be true, and that it’s wise to check what we hear, especially about faith and history. Teaching children how to think carefully and look for good evidence helps them become wise and humble. This helps us trust that truth, wherever it is found, is part of God’s light, and that our minds are meant to grow bright as we learn what really happened in the world.
sf_a10.matters: This story reminds us to check the facts before we believe what everyone says, even about history. For families who want to learn and teach truth, it shows that faith and science can live together, and that both are blessed when we seek knowledge honestly. Believing myths about the past can make us misunderstand both the faith of earlier Christians and how science grows. Sharing real stories helps us honor those who came before, and teaches our children to love truth—an important part of Heavenly Father’s plan for learning and growing in wisdom.

sources.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Flat Earth Myth
Smithsonian Magazine: The Myth of the Flat-Earth
History Channel: Did People in the Middle Ages Think the Earth Was Flat?

sf_a10.evidence: Historical scholarship shows overwhelmingly that educated people in the Middle Ages did not believe in a flat earth. Medieval scholars and churchmen owned and read works from Greek and Roman times that taught the earth was round. Artworks, literature, and even some church writings from the period use and depict a spherical earth. The legend that medieval people thought otherwise only became popular in the 1800s through writers like Washington Irving, and has since been corrected by historians. We now have access to original documents and many studies showing the continuity of this knowledge into the Middle Ages. Modern encyclopedias and university research confirm this as settled history.
sf_a10.happened: The story that people in the Middle Ages believed the earth was flat is a myth. This tale became popular in the 1800s but has little to do with what really happened. In truth, most educated Europeans since the time of the ancient Greeks knew the earth was shaped like a sphere. Written works by respected scholars such as Bede, Thomas Aquinas, and the poet Dante Alighieri show that they took the roundness of the earth for granted. When Christopher Columbus asked for support to sail west to reach Asia, his critics did not argue that he would fall off the edge of a flat earth. Instead, they correctly pointed out that the earth was much larger than Columbus claimed, and that his journey would be too long to survive without stopping for supplies. If America had not been there, Columbus and his crew would have run out of food and water in the middle of the ocean. But by the 1800s, writers like Washington Irving, who wanted to make Columbus sound heroic, invented meetings where religious leaders warned him about sailing off the world’s edge. This story was repeated in books, schools, and speeches, even though it isn’t true. Today, historians have shown that the flat earth myth is one of the best examples of a made-up fact that everyone seemed to believe.
sf_a10.scripture: There is no scripture that says what shape the earth is, but the principle of seeking truth is found throughout. Doctrine and Covenants 88:118 teaches, 'Seek ye out of the best books words of wisdom; seek learning, even by study and also by faith.' This fits well with examining both the scriptures and honest discoveries from science and history. When we look for true knowledge, whether it comes from faithful believers or careful scientists, we are using one of the many gifts Heavenly Father has given us.
sf_a10.background: Medieval Europe was a world of kingdoms, monasteries, and bustling towns where knowledge from Greece and Rome was taught in cathedral schools and universities. Many people were farmers and craftsmen, while monks and priests preserved and copied ancient books. By the time Columbus sailed in 1492, astronomy and mathematics were important subjects, and scholars read old works by people like Aristotle, who wrote that the earth was round. Some sailors and ordinary folk surely didn’t understand how big the world was, but most educated people did. Books and art from that time even show globe-shaped earths, and the stars’ movements across the sky were explained using a round earth.

sf_a11.talk: What do you think it means to both love God and learn about His creations?
sf_a11.child: A long time ago, a teacher went to court because he talked about a science idea called evolution in school. People everywhere talked about it, and it made many people think about how we can believe in God and learn about the world at the same time.
sf_a11.learn: From this trial we see the importance of being able to talk kindly with those who believe differently, and of valuing both faith and knowledge. It shows that questions about science and faith do not need to divide us, and that seeking truth is an ongoing part of following God. Being respectful and curious about others' views can help families learn and grow together.
sf_a11.matters: The Scopes Trial became a moment when many Americans felt they had to choose between faith and science, even though most Christians in the world did not see such a sharp divide. For families of faith today, it reminds us that serious people can have honest disagreements about how to read scripture and understand science, and that loving God and learning about His creations do not have to compete. The trial’s echo is still heard in discussions about what should be taught in schools, showing why it is important to discuss how science and faith can work together.

sources.name: Smithsonian - Scopes Trial
National Center for Science Education - Scopes Trial
Church of Jesus Christ - Gospel Topics: Evolution

sf_a11.evidence: Records from the Scopes Trial are carefully preserved, including the court transcript, newspaper articles, and personal writings from the people involved. There is no doubt that the events happened as reported. Historians agree that the trial did not settle the debate about evolution and creation but instead made it national news. Scientific evidence for evolution has grown steadily since then, with discoveries like DNA and fossils helping us understand how life on earth has changed over time. At the same time, many people of faith find ways to accept both scientific discovery and belief in God's creative power.
sf_a11.happened: In July 1925, a small town in Tennessee became the center of a national debate about science, religion, and education. John Scopes, a high school teacher, was put on trial for teaching his students about evolution, which was against a new state law. This law, called the Butler Act, made it illegal to teach anything that denied the Biblical account of creation. The American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) wanted to challenge this law and arranged for Scopes to be put on trial. The case drew famous lawyers to Dayton: Clarence Darrow defended Scopes, and William Jennings Bryan, a well-known politician and Christian speaker, led the prosecution. The trial was held in the local courthouse, but it quickly grew into a nationwide event, with reporters from all over the country arriving to cover it. In the end, Scopes was found guilty and fined one hundred dollars. However, the verdict was later reversed, not because the law was changed, but on a technical detail. The trial became famous as the 'Scopes Monkey Trial,' and it showed just how deeply Americans could disagree on what should be taught in schools.
sf_a11.scripture: The question at the heart of the Scopes Trial touches on how we interpret the creation accounts in Genesis chapters 1 and 2, as well as in Moses chapters 2 and 3 and Abraham chapters 4 and 5 in the Pearl of Great Price. Doctrine and Covenants 88:78-79 encourages us to teach one another “of things both in heaven and in the earth,” suggesting that both spiritual and scientific learning are valued. While the scriptures do not mention evolution by name, they do affirm that God is the Creator of all things. Latter-day Saint leaders have often encouraged members to seek understanding in both spiritual and scientific studies.
sf_a11.background: The world in 1925 was changing quickly. Scientific discoveries about fossils and evolution were being talked about in newspapers, and some people believed these ideas disagreed with what the Bible says about God creating the world. At the same time, many Americans still lived in small towns where church teachings shaped daily life. John Scopes was a young teacher who usually taught math and coached sports, not just science. Clarence Darrow was known for defending unpopular causes, and William Jennings Bryan had run for president three times and was a respected voice for traditional Christian beliefs. Many people in Dayton, Tennessee, hoped the trial would bring attention and business to their town, and they welcomed the reporters and crowds that came. Radios broadcast pieces of the trial, making it one of the first major news stories carried live to the whole country.

sf_a12.t: A Catholic Priest Proposes the Big Bang
sf_a12.talk: Why do you think Georges Lemaître was careful to say science and faith answer different questions about how the world began?
sf_a12.child: A priest named Georges Lemaître said the universe began from a tiny, very hot point. At first, people didn’t believe him, but later evidence showed he was right. He loved both God and science and used both to learn about the world.
sf_a12.learn: We can learn to respect both faith and science, knowing each can help us learn about Heavenly Father’s creation. Lemaître’s life also teaches the value of humility. He listened carefully to both criticism and new discoveries, which made him a better scientist and a faithful believer. Families can be open to learning from both scripture and the wonders of the universe, trusting that all truth comes from God in His own time.
sf_a12.matters: The Big Bang theory changed how we think about our place in the universe. For families who believe in God, it is meaningful that the person who first described the universe’s beginning was a man of faith. Lemaître’s respect for both science and scripture reminds us not to force one to prove the other, but to value both as gifts from Heavenly Father. The way scientists slowly accepted the Big Bang also shows that truth can take time to be recognized and that humility helps us learn.

sources.name: NASA: Georges Lemaître, Father of the Big Bang
Encyclopedia Britannica: Georges Lemaître
American Museum of Natural History: Big Bang

sf_a12.evidence: Lemaître’s idea was supported by new observations showing that galaxies are moving away from each other, called the redshift, first measured in the late 1920s by Edwin Hubble. Over the years, many lines of evidence have built up for the Big Bang, including the discovery of cosmic microwave background radiation in 1965, sometimes called the afterglow of creation. Today, the Big Bang is the foundation of cosmology, and Lemaître’s early work is honored as its beginning. His careful separation of faith and science is still respected.
sf_a12.happened: In 1927, a Catholic priest and scientist named Georges Lemaître made a remarkable discovery in Belgium. Using Albert Einstein’s new ideas about gravity and space, Lemaître proposed that the universe was not static, but expanding. He went even further by suggesting that everything began from a single, incredibly dense point, which he called the “primeval atom.” This idea planted the seed for what we now call the Big Bang theory. At first, many leading scientists, including Einstein himself, pushed back against Lemaître’s proposal. Einstein once said Lemaître’s math was good but his physics was “abominable.” However, as more evidence emerged, even Einstein changed his mind and publicly praised Lemaître’s insight. This moment was not just a breakthrough in science, but an example of faith and curiosity working together, as Lemaître himself was both a priest and a physicist, deeply committed to both his faith and his work as a scientist.
sf_a12.scripture: There is no scripture that directly explains how the universe began in scientific terms, but the scriptures teach that God created the heavens and the earth (Genesis 1:1; Moses 2:1). Doctrine and Covenants 88:47–47 encourages us to study and appreciate creation, saying that all things testify of God. Latter-day Saints believe that both spiritual and scientific truths come from God and that we are encouraged to seek knowledge in all areas of life (Doctrine and Covenants 88:78–79).
sf_a12.background: When Lemaître introduced his idea, the world was still recovering from World War I. Science was changing rapidly, with physics leading the way into a new era. Albert Einstein’s theories had only recently turned old ideas about space and time upside down. Lemaître was living in Leuven, Belgium, enjoying academic life and serving as a Catholic priest. Most people in the world at the time imagined the universe as eternal and unchanging. Daily life in 1927 was shaped by new inventions like cars, radios, and planes, but people still relied on older ways too. Scientists gathered at universities in lively discussions, though faith and science often stayed in different circles.

sf_a13.talk: Can you think of a time when you learned something new and it helped you understand something at church better?
sf_a13.child: A long time ago, some people thought science and faith were always fighting. Now, historians say that’s not true. Sometimes they helped each other, sometimes they didn’t talk much, and only sometimes did they argue.
sf_a13.learn: We can learn that truth-seeking is best done with patience and humility. Not every story is simple, and it is wise to listen to different points of view. The best historians admit what is known and what is still debated. As we grow in faith and learning, we don’t have to be afraid that knowledge from good sources will threaten what we believe; often, it brings more wonder and trust in God’s plan. Families can build confidence in exploring science together.
sf_a13.matters: This matters for families of faith because it corrects an old idea that can cause confusion or worry. If we think science is always against faith, we might fear scientific learning. But if we know the real story is more complex, we can approach both faith and science with trust and curiosity. For the world, it means scholars aim for a fair, honest view of our past. Families can feel encouraged to learn science and remember that many great scientists were also people of deep faith. Understanding this helps children see they don’t have to choose between loving God and loving learning.

sources.name: Encyclopedia Britannica: Science and religion
Galileo Goes to Jail: and Other Myths About Science and Religion, Cambridge University Press summary
ChurchofJesusChrist: Seek Learning by Faith and by Study

sf_a13.evidence: Historical research since 1986 has carefully re-examined the most famous stories of science and religion in conflict. For example, it is now clear that Galileo’s case was far more about politics and misunderstandings than a simple science-versus-religion fight. Likewise, many early scientists were deeply religious, including Isaac Newton who wrote more about religion than science. Detailed studies of their letters, books, and the times they lived show many examples of cooperation or parallel growth. While conflicts did happen, they were rare and shaped by details of the time and place, not by some natural fight between faith and science. The evidence is strong that the conflict thesis oversimplified things, and today’s historians generally reject it.
sf_a13.happened: In 1986, two historians named David Lindberg and Ronald Numbers published a book called God and Nature. This book took a deep look at the history of science and religion and explained that most stories of a constant battle between the two weren’t really true. In the past, many people believed in something called the conflict thesis, which said science and religion had always been at war. Lindberg and Numbers showed with careful research that this wasn’t accurate. They found that the relationship was much more complicated. Sometimes, faith and science worked together, sometimes they stayed apart, and only occasionally did they really clash. John Hedley Brooke continued this work in 1991 with his book Science and Religion, laying out what is now called the complexity thesis. This idea says their relationship is very changeable—sometimes friendly, sometimes distant, and sometimes stressed. Later, Ronald Numbers also gathered other experts to write about these topics in a 2009 book called Galileo Goes to Jail and Other Myths About Science and Religion, showing many famous stories of conflict were misunderstood or exaggerated. Today, historians mostly agree with this complexity view, even though you still see simplifications in popular culture and news.
sf_a13.scripture: The scriptures teach us in several places to seek knowledge by study and by faith. In Doctrine and Covenants 88:118, we find, 'Seek ye out of the best books words of wisdom; seek learning, even by study and also by faith.' This principle is echoed in the Bible, where Proverbs 4:7 says, 'Wisdom is the principal thing; therefore get wisdom: and with all thy getting get understanding.' Both passages remind us to value learning both spiritual and worldly truths, and to do so with open hearts. While no scripture describes historians’ work directly, the idea of seeking truth from many good sources is a strong theme.
sf_a13.background: Before these historians wrote their books, many people took it for granted that science and religion could not get along. This was called the conflict thesis, and it became popular especially in the 1800s in Europe and America, when science was making big advances. Back then, daily life for most people didn’t include much science, so it was easier to believe stories that made religion and science sound like enemies. Historians like Lindberg, Numbers, and Brooke were trained in reading old letters, scientific papers, and church documents closely. They worked in universities and spent years checking the real story behind famous events, like Galileo’s trial or Darwin’s discoveries. Their careful digging showed that real history is hardly ever so simple.

sf_a14.t: Francis Collins and the Human Genome
sf_a14.talk: How do you think understanding our DNA helps doctors take care of us?
sf_a14.child: Scientists worked together to read all the instructions in our DNA, like a big book that tells our bodies how to grow and work. This helps doctors understand how to help people when they are sick.
sf_a14.learn: The Human Genome Project teaches us the value of perseverance, collaboration, and the pursuit of knowledge. It demonstrates how scientific endeavors can uncover the mysteries of life, aligning with our faith in a Creator who designed the universe with purpose and order. This achievement encourages us to seek understanding and wisdom, recognizing that science and faith can complement each other in revealing the wonders of creation.
sf_a14.matters: The completion of the Human Genome Project has profound implications for medicine and our understanding of human biology. It has enabled researchers to identify genes associated with various diseases, leading to improved diagnostics and targeted therapies. For families of faith, this achievement underscores the harmony between scientific discovery and belief in a divine Creator. Understanding the genetic code can be seen as uncovering the intricate design with which Heavenly Father created life, offering a deeper appreciation for the complexity and beauty of His creations.

sources.name: Human Genome Project Fact Sheet
International Consortium Completes Human Genome Project
The Finished Human Genome

sf_a14.evidence: The completion of the Human Genome Project is well-documented in scientific literature and official reports. The National Human Genome Research Institute provides detailed information about the project's goals, progress, and outcomes. The project successfully mapped 99% of the human genome with an accuracy of 99.99%, covering the euchromatic regions of the genome. This monumental achievement was the result of international collaboration and technological innovation, setting the stage for future research in genetics and personalized medicine.
sf_a14.happened: In April 2003, the International Human Genome Sequencing Consortium announced the successful completion of the Human Genome Project, a monumental scientific endeavor that mapped the entire human DNA sequence. This project, initiated in 1990, aimed to identify and map all the genes in human DNA, determining the sequences of the three billion chemical base pairs that make up the human genome. Under the leadership of Dr. Francis Collins, the project was completed ahead of schedule and under budget, providing a comprehensive reference for human genetics. The completion of this project marked a significant milestone in understanding the genetic blueprint of human life, paving the way for advancements in medicine and biology.
sf_a14.scripture: The scriptures teach us about the divine creation of life. In the Book of Moses, we read, "And I, God, created man in mine own image" (Moses 2:27). This passage emphasizes that humans are created in the image of God, reflecting His divine nature. The study of the human genome can be viewed as exploring the intricate details of that divine image, deepening our understanding of God's handiwork.
sf_a14.background: Before the Human Genome Project, scientists had limited knowledge of the human genetic code. The 1980s and 1990s saw rapid advancements in DNA sequencing technologies, but the task of mapping the entire human genome was daunting. Daily life during this period was witnessing the rise of personal computers and the internet, which facilitated global collaboration among scientists. Dr. Francis Collins, a physician-geneticist, was appointed director of the National Human Genome Research Institute in 1993. His leadership was instrumental in coordinating the international effort to sequence the human genome, bringing together researchers from around the world to achieve this ambitious goal.

sf_a15.talk: What is something you wonder about where the answers from faith and science seem different?
sf_a15.child: Sometimes people who love God and people who love science do not agree on everything, like how the world was made. That is all right. We can ask questions, listen kindly, and remember that both faith and science help us discover new things.
sf_a15.learn: We can learn that both faith and science are gifts from God, meant to help us grow in understanding. But like any tool, each has limits and strengths. Admitting there is real disagreement allows us to treat each other kindly, to honor the journey of learning, and to keep asking questions instead of shutting down discussion. This humility and curiosity can strengthen families, encourage discovery, and invite God’s Spirit as we search for greater truth, trusting He will guide us step by step.
sf_a15.matters: This ongoing disagreement matters for several reasons. For families of faith, it means there are some questions where loving God and respecting science do not give neat, matching answers. Parents must teach their children to value honest questions, humility, and careful listening—very important skills in today’s world. The debate also shows that neither faith nor science has all the answers or gets everything right all at once. This can help families pause, pray, and study out important issues together, relying on both revelation and reason. For the world, it is a call to treat people’s convictions with respect, even if we disagree, and to keep learning from both spiritual and scientific insights.

sources.name: Pew Research Center – Science and Religion
National Academy of Sciences –Science, Evolution, and Creationism
Church of Jesus Christ – Seeking Learning by Faith
World History Encyclopedia – Scientific Revolution

sf_a15.evidence: Historical and scientific evidence shows both conflict and cooperation between faith and science. For example, most geologists and biologists agree that the earth is about 4.5 billion years old and that all living things share common ancestry—a view tested and supported by many lines of evidence, from fossils to DNA. Yet, many sincere believers interpret sacred texts differently, and continue to hold to a young earth or special creation by God. Bioethical questions, like research on embryos, raise serious moral disagreements shaped by different religious backgrounds. Surveys from the Pew Research Center reveal that scientists are, on average, less religious than others in some places, but far from universally so—many scientists still believe in God. Historians like Noah Efron and Lawrence Principe show that the scientific revolution was shaped by many cultures and times, not just the western Christian world.
sf_a15.happened: In 2026, real tension remains between faith and science, not because these two ways of understanding the world must always fight, but because there are still subjects where they come to different conclusions. Some of the sharpest disagreements come up around topics like how old the earth actually is and how life came to be. Many scientists accept that the earth is billions of years old and that life slowly changed over time through evolution. But some people of faith, including members of several Christian denominations, believe the earth and its life are much younger and were created in ways different from what most scientists describe. Other areas of tension include bioethics—questions about what is right and wrong when it comes to research on embryos, when life begins and ends, and new medical technologies. These are not just technical debates, but heartfelt issues touching people’s deepest beliefs about life and what it means to be human. Surveys also show that, in some countries, people who work in science are less likely to say they are religious compared with the general population, which sometimes adds to the sense that science and faith belong to different worlds. At the same time, historians warn against claims that faith created modern science single-handedly, or that they can never get along. Instead, they find that science grew from many roots, including ancient Greeks, Muslims, and medieval thinkers. Faith and science are not natural enemies, but it is honest to admit they still sometimes disagree.
sf_a15.scripture: The scriptures do not directly address modern scientific debates, but they give principles to guide us. In Doctrine and Covenants 88:118, the Lord asks us to seek learning by study and also by faith. The Bible teaches to love God with all our heart, soul, and mind (Matthew 22:37), and to prove all things and hold fast to what is good (1 Thessalonians 5:21). The Book of Mormon tells us to ask God for guidance (Moroni 10:5), trusting that truth, whether discovered through nature or revelation, will ultimately come from Him. These verses encourage a humble, searching attitude in every area of life.
sf_a15.background: The world in which this tension is acknowledged is a highly connected, deeply scientific, but also deeply religious place. Billions of people still find meaning in faith, even as technology changes daily life in almost every country. People’s days are filled with information from the internet, advanced medicine, and a growing understanding of the universe. Yet, their traditions, stories, and values often come from sacred texts. Scientists now often work in large teams across countries, and discoveries about genes, the cosmos, and the brain spark hope and new questions. Parents and children may pray together in the morning, then read the latest news about scientific discoveries at night. Many want both truth from science and wisdom from faith but find the two do not always seem to speak the same language, especially on topics that matter a great deal to their communities.

sf_a16.talk: Can you think of something in nature that makes you feel amazed about God's creation?
sf_a16.child: Many famous scientists loved God and wanted to learn about His world. They believed that by studying nature, they could understand more about God's creation. This shows us that learning about science can be a way to get closer to God.
sf_a16.learn: Recognizing the historical collaboration between faith and science teaches us that curiosity and belief are not mutually exclusive. It encourages us to explore the world with an open mind, seeking to understand the natural laws that govern it while maintaining a sense of spiritual purpose. This perspective fosters a holistic approach to learning, where scientific discovery and religious faith enrich each other.
sf_a16.matters: Understanding the historical interplay between faith and science highlights that religious belief has often been a driving force behind scientific exploration. For families of faith, this underscores the idea that seeking knowledge about the natural world can be a way to honor and understand God's creation. It challenges the notion that science and religion are inherently in conflict, showing instead that they can coexist and even complement each other. Recognizing this harmony can inspire both scientific curiosity and spiritual growth, encouraging individuals to explore the world with a sense of wonder and purpose.

sources.name: How Christianity Led to the Rise of Modern Science | Christian Research Institute
How Christianity Gave Rise to Modern Science | Crossway
Christianity and the rise of science, 1660–1815 | The Cambridge History of Christianity

sf_a16.evidence: Historical records show that many pioneering scientists were deeply religious and viewed their scientific work as a means to understand and glorify God. For instance, Isaac Newton's theological writings reveal his belief that studying the natural world was a way to uncover divine truths. Similarly, Johannes Kepler saw his astronomical work as uncovering the geometric plan of God's creation. The case of Galileo Galilei, often cited as evidence of conflict between science and religion, was complex and involved political and personal factors beyond his scientific theories. Modern historians recognize that, while there have been instances of tension, the overall relationship between Christianity and the development of science has been largely positive. The Church's support for education and the establishment of universities provided a fertile ground for scientific inquiry.
sf_a16.happened: Throughout history, many of the world's most renowned scientists have been deeply religious individuals. Nicolaus Copernicus, who proposed the heliocentric model of the universe, served as a cathedral canon. Johannes Kepler, known for his laws of planetary motion, initially trained for the ministry. Isaac Newton, famous for his laws of motion and gravity, wrote extensively on theology, producing more works on religious topics than on physics. Gregor Mendel, the father of modern genetics, was an Augustinian friar. Michael Faraday, a pioneer in electromagnetism, was a devout Christian and served as a lay preacher. Georges Lemaître, who formulated the Big Bang theory, was a Catholic priest. Francis Collins, the geneticist who led the Human Genome Project, is an outspoken believer. Ibn al-Haytham, a medieval Muslim scientist, made significant contributions to optics and was deeply devout. Despite these strong connections between faith and scientific inquiry, historical records indicate that the Church formally prosecuted only one scientist, Galileo Galilei, for his scientific ideas. This suggests that, contrary to popular belief, the relationship between religion and science has often been collaborative rather than adversarial.
sf_a16.scripture: The scriptures encourage the pursuit of knowledge and understanding. In Proverbs 25:2, it is written, "It is the glory of God to conceal a thing: but the honour of kings is to search out a matter." This suggests that seeking to understand the mysteries of the universe is a noble endeavor. Additionally, Doctrine and Covenants 88:79 advises to learn "of things both in heaven and in the earth, and under the earth; things which have been, things which are, things which must shortly come to pass." These passages support the idea that studying the natural world is aligned with divine instruction.
sf_a16.background: In the periods leading up to the Scientific Revolution, Europe was deeply influenced by religious institutions. The Church played a central role in education, governance, and daily life. Many universities were established by religious organizations, and clerics were among the most educated individuals of the time. This environment fostered a worldview where studying nature was seen as a way to understand God's creation. The belief that the universe was orderly and governed by laws set by a rational Creator provided a foundation for systematic scientific inquiry. This perspective was not unique to Christianity; in the Islamic world, scholars like Ibn al-Haytham pursued scientific studies as a means to comprehend the divine order. Daily life was intertwined with religious practices, and the pursuit of knowledge was often considered a form of worship.

tech-pc.talk: How do you think having a computer at home helps our family learn and remember important things?
tech-pc.child: A long time ago, computers were big and only used by experts. In 1977, smaller computers were made that families could use at home. This helped families write down their stories and keep important records.
tech-pc.learn: The introduction of personal computers in 1977 teaches us the importance of innovation in making technology accessible to all. It reminds us that tools, when used wisely, can enhance our ability to fulfill spiritual and familial responsibilities, such as record-keeping and teaching. Embracing new technologies can help us preserve our heritage and strengthen our connections with one another.
tech-pc.matters: The advent of personal computers in 1977 was a pivotal moment that democratized technology, making it accessible to individuals and families. For families of faith, these computers provided new tools to fulfill spiritual responsibilities, such as keeping personal and family records. The ability to type and store family histories, prepare lessons, and manage household tasks aligned with the scriptural emphasis on record-keeping and stewardship. This technological advancement enabled families to document their stories and testimonies more efficiently, preserving them for future generations and strengthening their spiritual heritage.

sources.name: History of personal computers
Invention of the PC | HISTORY
Computers for Everybody - CHM Revolution
Bible Verses About Records: 9 Scriptures on Records

tech-pc.evidence: Historical records confirm that 1977 was a landmark year in personal computing. The Apple II, introduced by Apple Computer Inc., featured a color display and expansion capabilities, making it popular among consumers. The Commodore PET 2001 integrated a keyboard, monitor, and storage, emphasizing ease of use. The Tandy TRS-80, sold through Radio Shack, offered an affordable option that brought computing into many homes. These developments are well-documented in technology histories and reflect a significant shift towards accessible computing for the general public.
tech-pc.happened: In 1977, the landscape of computing transformed with the introduction of three groundbreaking personal computers: the Apple II, the Commodore PET 2001, and the Tandy TRS-80. These machines were among the first to be mass-produced and sold fully assembled, making them accessible to a broader audience beyond hobbyists and professionals. The Apple II, developed by Steve Jobs and Steve Wozniak in Cupertino, California, featured a color display and expansion slots, setting a new standard for personal computing. The Commodore PET 2001 combined a keyboard, monitor, and cassette tape storage into a single unit, emphasizing user-friendliness. The Tandy TRS-80, sold through Radio Shack stores, offered an affordable option for many families. Collectively, these computers marked the beginning of the personal computing era, bringing technology into homes and small businesses and laying the foundation for the digital age.
tech-pc.scripture: The scriptures emphasize the importance of record-keeping. In Exodus 17:14, the Lord instructs Moses to write a memorial in a book. Similarly, in 1 Chronicles 16:4, certain Levites were appointed to record and thank the Lord. These passages highlight the value placed on documenting experiences and teachings. The introduction of personal computers provided families with a modern means to fulfill this scriptural principle, facilitating the preservation and sharing of their faith and history.
tech-pc.background: Before 1977, computers were primarily large, expensive machines used by businesses, universities, and government agencies. They required specialized knowledge to operate and were inaccessible to the general public. The development of the microprocessor in the early 1970s paved the way for smaller, more affordable computers. Early personal computers like the Altair 8800, introduced in 1975, were sold as kits for enthusiasts to assemble. However, these early models lacked user-friendly interfaces and practical applications for everyday users. The release of the Apple II, Commodore PET, and TRS-80 in 1977 changed this dynamic by offering ready-to-use systems that appealed to a wider audience, including families and small businesses.

tech-tv.talk: How do you think watching a church meeting on TV is different from being there in person?
tech-tv.child: A long time ago, a man named Philo made a machine that could send pictures through the air to people's homes. This was the first television, and it let families see and learn about the world without leaving their living rooms.
tech-tv.learn: Farnsworth's story teaches us the value of perseverance and innovation. Despite limited resources and numerous challenges, his determination led to an invention that transformed the world. It reminds us that with faith and hard work, we can overcome obstacles and make meaningful contributions. Additionally, it highlights the importance of using technology responsibly, ensuring it serves to uplift and educate, aligning with our values and beliefs.
tech-tv.matters: Farnsworth's invention revolutionized communication and entertainment. Television brought the world into people's living rooms, allowing families to witness historical events, learn about distant cultures, and enjoy shared experiences. For families of faith, television became a tool to access religious broadcasts, including General Conference sessions, enabling them to hear the words of prophets without traveling great distances. It also provided opportunities to see the wonders of God's creations, from the depths of the oceans to the vastness of space, fostering a greater appreciation for the world He made.

sources.name: Philo Farnsworth - Wikipedia
1927 in American television - Wikipedia
Who Invented Television? | HISTORY

tech-tv.evidence: Historical records confirm that on September 7, 1927, Philo Farnsworth transmitted the first electronic television image in his San Francisco laboratory. This event is well-documented, with accounts from Farnsworth's wife, Elma, who was present during the demonstration. The success of this transmission led to further developments in television technology, with Farnsworth refining his system and demonstrating it to the public in subsequent years. His contributions are recognized as foundational in the history of television.
tech-tv.happened: In 1927, a young inventor named Philo Farnsworth achieved a groundbreaking milestone in San Francisco, California. On September 7th, in his modest laboratory at 202 Green Street, Farnsworth successfully transmitted the first electronic television image. This image was a simple straight line, but it marked the birth of electronic television. Unlike earlier mechanical systems that relied on spinning disks to scan images, Farnsworth's design used an all-electronic method, eliminating moving parts and paving the way for the modern television. This innovation allowed for clearer and more stable images, setting the foundation for the television technology we know today.
tech-tv.scripture: While the scriptures do not mention television, they emphasize the importance of spreading the gospel to all nations. In Matthew 28:19-20, Jesus commands His disciples to "go ye therefore, and teach all nations." Television has become a means to fulfill this commandment, broadcasting messages of faith and hope to people worldwide. Additionally, Doctrine and Covenants 88:79 encourages learning about "things both in heaven and in the earth," which television facilitates by bringing educational content into homes.
tech-tv.background: Before Farnsworth's invention, the world was exploring various ways to transmit images over distances. Mechanical television systems, which used rotating disks with holes to scan images, were the primary method. These systems produced low-quality images and were not practical for widespread use. Daily life in the 1920s was without the instant visual communication we now take for granted. News was received through newspapers and radio broadcasts, and entertainment was limited to live performances and silent films. The idea of seeing moving images transmitted into one's home was a distant dream.

tech-games.talk: What games do you like to play with our family, and what do they teach you?
tech-games.child: A long time ago, people made a game called Pong where you hit a ball back and forth on a screen. It was one of the first video games, and many people loved playing it.
tech-games.learn: From Pong, we learn that simple ideas can lead to significant innovations. It reminds us that play is an essential part of learning and growth. Engaging in wholesome recreational activities can strengthen family bonds and teach important life skills.
tech-games.matters: Pong's success demonstrated the potential of video games as a form of entertainment, leading to the growth of the gaming industry. For families of faith, video games can offer opportunities for bonding and learning. When chosen wisely, games can teach valuable skills such as patience, problem-solving, and teamwork. Playing together can strengthen family relationships and create joyful memories.

sources.name: Pong released | November 29, 1972 | HISTORY
Pong - Wikipedia
Pong Was Boring—And People Loved It - IEEE Spectrum

tech-games.evidence: Historical records confirm that Pong was released by Atari in 1972 and became the first commercially successful video game. The original arcade machines and documentation from that era provide tangible evidence of its existence and impact. The game's popularity led to numerous imitators and the rapid expansion of the video game industry.
tech-games.happened: In 1972, in Sunnyvale, California, a small company named Atari introduced a game called Pong. This simple game simulated table tennis, where two players controlled paddles to hit a ball back and forth on a screen. It was designed by engineer Allan Alcorn as a training exercise, but its engaging gameplay quickly caught the attention of the public. Atari placed the first Pong arcade machine in a local tavern, and it became so popular that the machine often malfunctioned due to being overloaded with coins. This unexpected success led Atari to produce more units, and Pong became the first commercially successful video game, marking the beginning of the video game industry.
tech-games.scripture: The scriptures encourage wholesome recreation and learning. In Doctrine and Covenants 136:28, it says, "If thou art merry, praise the Lord with singing, with music, with dancing, and with a prayer of praise and thanksgiving." This suggests that joyful activities, including games, can be a part of a balanced and faithful life.
tech-games.background: Before Pong, electronic games were mostly found in research labs or as novelties. The concept of interactive electronic entertainment was still new. In the early 1970s, most people had never seen or played a video game. Daily life was centered around traditional forms of entertainment like television, board games, and outdoor activities. The idea of playing games on a screen was a novel concept that intrigued many.

tech-light.talk: Why do you think Heavenly Father wants us to have both sunlight and electric light?
tech-light.child: Edison and his friends made a light in a glass bulb that turned on with a switch. Before that, houses were dark at night. Their invention helped families read, work, and be together even after dark.
tech-light.learn: We can learn that great inventions often come from teamwork, effort, and a desire to solve real problems. Electric light reminds us that God’s gifts can come in surprising ways—sometimes by inspiration, sometimes by invention. As families, we can remember to use the tools we are given to help and bless others, and to make our homes places of light, safety, and learning.
tech-light.matters: The electric light bulb matters because it changed how families and entire communities could live. Now, children and parents could read scriptures or work on projects at night in safety and comfort. Hospitals became safer, and schools could open earlier or stay later. For a family of faith, electric light is a sweet reminder that Heavenly Father uses both natural light and the inventions of His children to push back darkness and help His work go forward. It didn’t make night vanish, but it gave people more hours to grow, serve, and learn together—and to use that time wisely.

sources.name: Smithsonian National Museum of American History: Electric Lighting
Library of Congress: Thomas Edison and the Electric Light
History.com: Thomas Edison and the Invention of the Light Bulb

tech-light.evidence: The story of Edison’s invention is richly documented by his own diaries, lab notes, newspapers from the time, and thousands of surviving artifacts from Menlo Park. The Smithsonian Institution and many other museums show early bulbs and equipment. Edison’s successful test in 1879 was reported in The New York Times, and he even gave public demonstrations to show it worked. Historians agree he did not invent the very first electric light, but he created the first one that most people could use safely at home. The evidence clearly shows Edison’s bulb worked, was adopted widely, and began a new age of invention.
tech-light.happened: In 1879, in Menlo Park, New Jersey, Thomas Edison and his team created something simple but world-changing: the first practical electric light bulb. The bulb had a tiny wire, called a filament, inside a glass globe. When electricity passed through the wire, it began to glow brightly without catching fire. Before this, people had tried many ways to make a light last long and burn safely, but Edison's design lasted over 12 hours, and soon he improved it to shine for many days. Families could turn night into day simply by flipping a switch. This not only brought light into homes, but also started a wave of invention. Streets, schools, hospitals, and churches began to glow with artificial light. For the first time in history, people weren’t forced to stop reading, learning, or working when the sun went down. Edison didn’t do it all alone; his team helped improve the bulb, and many inventors had tried before. But it was his version that was sturdy and safe enough for everyone to use. His laboratory soon became known as the birthplace of modern invention, showing the power of teamwork and perseverance.
tech-light.scripture: The Bible begins with the words, 'And God said, Let there be light: and there was light' (Genesis 1:3). Light is a symbol of truth and the Savior, who said, 'I am the light of the world' (John 8:12). The Book of Mormon also uses light to represent guidance from God (2 Nephi 31:20). The principle at work is that light—whether spiritual or physical—chases away darkness and helps us see truth, make good choices, and care for others. Electric light is not sacred itself, but it can be used for sacred work, helping families read, gather, and learn of God, even after the sun goes down.
tech-light.background: Before electric light, people used candles, oil lamps, or gas lights to see after dark. These were dim, smoky, and sometimes dangerous; houses caught fire easily, and the light was often too weak to read by. Life was shaped by nature’s clock. Children learned and did chores in daylight, and families gathered near the flickering fire or lamp in the evenings. Inventors in Europe and America had been racing to make a reliable light that would shine longer and more safely. Edison was born in Ohio in 1847 and grew up curious about how things worked. By 1879, the US was a busy, growing country, building railroads and cities. Menlo Park, where Edison built his lab, was a place buzzing with new ideas. In this exciting world, the electric bulb became a symbol of what people could accomplish when they mixed curiosity with hard work.

tech-photo.talk: How do you think seeing pictures of our ancestors helps us feel closer to them?
tech-photo.child: Long ago, a man named Niépce used sunlight to make the first photograph, capturing the view from his window. This means we can now see pictures of our great-grandparents and know what they looked like.
tech-photo.learn: Niépce's invention teaches us the value of perseverance and innovation. His dedication to solving the challenge of capturing permanent images reminds us that breakthroughs often come from persistent effort and creative thinking. For families, it highlights the importance of preserving memories and connecting with our heritage, as photographs serve as bridges between generations.
tech-photo.matters: Niépce's successful creation of a permanent photograph revolutionized the way humans capture and preserve moments. It transformed personal and collective memory, allowing individuals to document their lives and the world around them with unprecedented accuracy. For families of faith, photography became a powerful tool in preserving the likenesses of loved ones, connecting generations, and strengthening family bonds. It enabled children to see the faces of ancestors who had prayed for them, making family history tangible and fostering a deeper appreciation for their heritage.

sources.name: World History Project: First Photograph Ever Taken
The Franklin Institute: Daguerreotype Photography

tech-photo.evidence: The original photograph, "View from the Window at Le Gras," still exists today and is preserved at the Harry Ransom Center at the University of Texas at Austin. This tangible artifact provides direct evidence of Niépce's pioneering work. The image, though faint by modern standards, clearly depicts the rooftops and landscape visible from Niépce's window, confirming the success of his heliographic process.
tech-photo.happened: In 1826, in the village of Saint-Loup-de-Varennes, France, Joseph Nicéphore Niépce achieved a groundbreaking feat by capturing the world's first permanent photograph. From an upstairs window of his estate, Niépce set up a camera obscura—a device that projects an image onto a surface—and placed a pewter plate coated with bitumen of Judea, a light-sensitive material. He exposed the plate to light for approximately eight hours, allowing the sunlight to harden the bitumen in the brightest areas. After the exposure, Niépce washed the plate with a mixture of oil of lavender and white petroleum, dissolving the unhardened bitumen and revealing the image. The result was "View from the Window at Le Gras," a depiction of the courtyard and buildings surrounding his home. This photograph marked the first successful attempt to capture and fix an image using light, laying the foundation for the development of photography.
tech-photo.scripture: While the scriptures do not directly mention photography, they emphasize the importance of remembering and honoring our ancestors. In Malachi 4:6, it is written: "And he shall turn the heart of the fathers to the children, and the heart of the children to their fathers." This principle underscores the value of connecting with our family history, a process made more vivid and personal through the images captured by photography.
tech-photo.background: Before Niépce's invention, capturing images relied solely on artists' skills in drawing or painting. The camera obscura, known since ancient times, was a tool that projected scenes onto surfaces, aiding artists in tracing images but unable to preserve them permanently. The early 19th century was a period of scientific curiosity and innovation, with inventors exploring ways to harness light for image creation. Niépce, a French inventor with a keen interest in lithography and optics, dedicated years to experimenting with light-sensitive materials and processes. His work culminated in the development of heliography, a method that used bitumen's light-sensitive properties to create lasting images.

tech-radio.talk: How do you think it felt to hear someone’s voice through the air for the very first time?
tech-radio.child: A man named Marconi used a kite to help send the first radio signal across the ocean in 1901. For the first time, words and music could travel through the air so everyone could listen at once. Radio helped people far away become friends and hear messages together.
tech-radio.learn: We can learn that Heavenly Father can inspire people to create tools that bless His children. Radio reminds us to use technology kindly, sharing messages of hope, music, and faith. We can remember that inventions might start small or seem strange at first, but with time and faithful purpose, they can bring families and nations closer together and help us hear each other’s hearts.
tech-radio.matters: Radio changed the world by making it possible for millions of people to hear the same message at the same time, wherever they lived. For families of faith, this meant a prophet’s voice could reach every home, uplifting hearts with words and hymns even in faraway places. Missionaries could broadcast the gospel, and people isolated by illness or distance could feel the unity of worship. In a time when communication seemed like a miracle, radio helped fulfill the dream of spreading truth to every nation, kindred, tongue, and people. Today, that same blessing carries forward in ways Marconi could hardly imagine.

sources.name: National Museum of American History – Marconi's Transatlantic Radio Experiment
BBC – Marconi and the invention of radio
The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints – Sharing the Gospel with Technology

tech-radio.evidence: Historians confirm that Guglielmo Marconi’s first transatlantic radio signal happened on December 12, 1901, in St. John’s, Newfoundland. Pictures, notes, and newspaper articles from the time back up the story. Marconi’s equipment and method—using a kite to lift the antenna and Morse code for the message—have been studied by scientists and are part of museum displays today. Though some doubted whether Marconi truly received the signal, later tests proved that radio waves could travel that distance. Marconi gave public demonstrations and quickly built radio stations, leading to the first real voice broadcasts not long after.
tech-radio.happened: In December of 1901, a man named Guglielmo Marconi stood on a cold hilltop in St. John's, Newfoundland, with a kite holding up a long copper wire. He listened carefully through a set of headphones, waiting for a sound that had never crossed an ocean before. Then, he heard three short clicks: the Morse code for the letter S. These signals had come all the way from Cornwall, England—over 2,000 miles away—without any wires. For the first time ever, voices and music could travel through invisible waves in the air, making it possible for people across great distances to share news, music, and stories at the exact same moment. It was a miracle of science that promised to bring the world closer together. Marconi's experiment was the beginning of radio, and soon after, real voices could be heard instead of just clicking Morse code. Not long later, families could gather around radios in their own homes to hear concerts, stories, and even important messages from leaders.
tech-radio.scripture: Scriptures teach about God’s desire for His word to reach ‘every nation, kindred, tongue, and people’ (Revelation 14:6; Doctrine and Covenants 90:11). While the Bible and Book of Mormon were written in ancient times, the principle of sharing truth widely is clear. The Doctrine and Covenants encourages using whatever means available to spread the gospel and to ‘study and learn, and become acquainted with all good books, and with languages, tongues, and people’ (D&C 90:15). Though there is no direct mention of radio, the scriptures support the use of technology for good, so the Lord’s word can bless as many as possible.
tech-radio.background: Before radio, people could only hear someone’s voice if they were nearby or using a wired telephone. Telegraph machines could send messages over land and sea, but only as dots and dashes, not voices or music. News usually spread slowly on printed newspapers. Guglielmo Marconi, an inventor from Italy, was fascinated by electricity and the work of earlier scientists like Heinrich Hertz and Nikola Tesla. He believed invisible waves—called radio waves—could carry signals far beyond what anyone had managed before. In the early 1900s, daily life was simpler and quieter, especially in remote places like Newfoundland. Messages from far away took days or even weeks to arrive, so the idea of hearing something instantly from across an ocean sounded almost magical.

tech-steam.talk: How do you think our life would be different if nobody had invented the steam engine?
tech-steam.child: A long time ago, a man used steam from boiling water to make a machine that did hard work. This made it easier for people to travel and helped children go to school. It helped people do more, with less work.
tech-steam.learn: We can learn from the steam engine about how creative thinking and hard work can solve big problems. Not every invention is perfect, but each one can teach us something valuable. For families of faith, it’s a reminder that technology, used wisely, can free people to serve, learn, and grow together. It also encourages us to look for ways to use our own talents to lighten others’ burdens, just as machines did so long ago.
tech-steam.matters: The steam engine matters because it started the Industrial Revolution. This was a time when machines began to change the way people lived, worked, and traveled. For families, it meant there were more jobs in towns and cities, and it became possible for some work to move from the home or farm to factories. From a faith perspective, technology like this can be seen as a gift—one that helped missionaries spread the gospel and allowed the Saints to gather from faraway lands, as they did in crossing the plains to Utah. The steam engine taught that with creativity and care, new inventions can lift burdens and open up ways for God’s work to move forward.

sources.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: James Watt
The Science Museum: James Watt and the steam engine
BBC Bitesize: The Industrial Revolution

tech-steam.evidence: The story of the steam engine is well supported by historical records. Original designs, patents, and actual engines built by James Watt can be seen in museums like the Science Museum in London. Many letters and writings from that period show how his invention changed everything from coal mining to textile factories. Steam engines from Watt’s time still exist and can be visited today, still demonstrating the principles he invented. Historians agree that the changes brought by the steam engine were enormous and can be traced through people’s stories, newspaper reports, and economic changes during the late 1700s and early 1800s.
tech-steam.happened: In 1769, a man named James Watt in Glasgow, Scotland, made a big change to the steam engine. Before Watt, engines could pump water, but were clumsy and wasted a lot of power. Watt’s special idea was to use steam—boiling water—to push a piston up and down, and then turn that motion into something useful, like turning a wheel. His clever design made engines much more efficient, meaning they could do more work with less fuel. Soon, these engines were used in factories, mines, and on trains and ships. It meant that heavy work, which used to need many strong people or lots of animals, could now be done by machines powered by steam. Trains and steamships began to move people and goods farther and faster than ever before. This new kind of power was a big reason why cities grew and the world started to feel a lot smaller, because travel and sharing ideas became much easier.
tech-steam.scripture: There are no scriptures that mention steam engines, but there are principles in scripture about how knowledge and inventions are gifts from God for the benefit of His children. Doctrine and Covenants 88:118 says, “seek learning, even by study and also by faith.” This reminds us to use our minds to solve problems and use our learning to bless others. Section 89, the Word of Wisdom, is about caring for bodies and lessening physical burdens, which echoes the way inventions can help make life safer and healthier.
tech-steam.background: Before steam engines, most work was done by hand or animal power. People used windmills to grind grain and water wheels to saw wood or make cloth, but these machines only worked where there was wind or flowing water. Britain in the 1700s was a land of many farms, but it was beginning to change. There were more people, and cities were starting to grow as people moved to work in factories. Life for most was hard, with long days of physical work. Coal mines needed to be pumped dry of water, and that was slow and dangerous work. Inventors all over Europe were searching for better ways to power machines. James Watt was a Scottish engineer who spotted how the earlier steam engines were wasteful, and with careful observation and problem-solving, he built something much better.

tech-wheel.talk: How could a simple invention you use today help someone else in your family or neighborhood?
tech-wheel.child: Long ago, people made the first wheel so they could carry heavy things more easily. It made life better for families, helping them share food and travel farther. We can use tools kindly, just like they did.
tech-wheel.learn: From the story of the wheel, we learn that small, simple ideas can make a huge difference. Even something as plain as a round piece of wood—when used wisely—can help families, communities, and even the world. We can look for ways to make burdens lighter for others and remember that every invention and discovery can be used for good when we follow God's guidance.
tech-wheel.matters: The wheel changed the way people lived forever. For families, it meant you could carry much more than you ever could before. Food could get to places where crops failed, homes could be built with bricks rolled in carts, and people could visit distant relatives. Over time, the wheel became part of every new machine—water wheels for grinding grain, spinning wheels for making clothes, and eventually, even cars and airplanes. For a family of faith, the wheel reminds us that simple gifts of knowledge can bless many lives, helping us serve and care for each other, just as we believe Heavenly Father would want.

sources.name: Encyclopedia Britannica – Wheel
Smithsonian Magazine – Who Invented the Wheel?
Encyclopedia of Ancient History – Wheel and Wheeled Vehicles

tech-wheel.evidence: Archaeologists have uncovered ancient clay tablets and evidence of wheeled carts in the region of modern Iraq, showing that people were using the wheel in pottery and transport around 3500 BC. The oldest known wheel, called the Ljubljana Marshes Wheel, was found in Slovenia and is dated to around 3100 BC, supporting that wheels were invented and spread in several places. Drawings and small models of carts with wheels have also been found in the ruins of Mesopotamian cities. While we cannot know the name of the inventor, the evidence shows the wheel was one of humanity's earliest and most important innovations, spreading quickly to other ancient cultures.
tech-wheel.happened: Around 3500 BC, in a land called Mesopotamia, people invented the wheel. Before this, people had to carry everything by hand or on the backs of animals. Someone saw that a round, flat piece of wood could roll, and soon after, they figured out how to make a wheel spin on an axle. This new piece of technology was first used to help make pottery, but not long after, people began to attach wheels to carts. These wheeled carts could carry heavy loads across the plains and rivers of Mesopotamia, helping families and traders alike. Roads changed too, becoming smoother in places, allowing these first carts to roll with food, bricks, pottery, or people from one village to another. The wheel made it possible for cities to trade easily, for armies to move quickly, and later, for chariots to race through history. While it may sound simple, the wheel quietly set many other inventions in motion by showing the power of turning.
tech-wheel.scripture: The Bible does not mention the invention of the wheel itself, but wheels appear in stories of carts and chariots in the Old Testament, such as in Exodus 14:25, where the Egyptians' chariot wheels are troubled at the Red Sea. Principles about using tools for good can be found in scriptures like Doctrine and Covenants 46:11, which teaches that gifts and tools are given to benefit God's children. The wheel is an example of a simple tool that, when used with wisdom, can help gather, serve, and uplift others.
tech-wheel.background: Mesopotamia, called the 'cradle of civilization,' was home to some of the first cities in the world, like Uruk and Ur. People here lived in mud-brick homes and grew crops along the big rivers, the Tigris and Euphrates. Daily life was busy—families farmed, cared for animals, and made tools and pottery. Travel was slow; there were no cars or bikes, just walking or riding donkeys. Before the wheel, everyone had to carry loads, sometimes with the help of simple sledges. Communities traded by boat or by foot. The people of Mesopotamia were also inventors—they created early writing, laws, and irrigation. Their world was ready for something that could help families do more and reach farther.

tech-movies.talk: What is your favorite story you have seen in a movie, and what did it teach you?
tech-movies.child: Long ago, people saw movies for the very first time in Paris. They watched pictures move and tell stories, just like a movie night with your family. That was the start of something kids and parents still love to do together today.
tech-movies.learn: We can learn that stories, shared in new ways, can bring people together and change the way we see the world. As families, we remember that every new invention can be used for good. It's wise to watch carefully and talk together about how movies make us feel and what lessons we learn. Choosing good movies and using them to teach can bring light and joy into our homes.
tech-movies.matters: Movies matter because they became one of the most powerful ways to share ideas and stories, reaching millions of people in every country. For families of faith, moving pictures can teach, inspire, and sometimes warn. Just like parables in the scriptures, a movie can help us see a lesson or remember a truth in a way that words alone might not. The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints uses film to share the teachings of Jesus and invite the Spirit into the home. But every family must choose carefully, because movies can bring good or trouble. How a family uses movies can bless hearts and teach values across generations.

sources.name: Smithsonian Magazine: How the Lumière Brothers Invented the Movies
British Film Institute: Lumière Brothers
Church of Jesus Christ: Parables

tech-movies.evidence: Historical evidence for the first movie screening is strong and well-documented. Newspapers in Paris reported on the Lumière showings, and records from the time detail the films shown and the reaction of the audience. The original Cinématographe camera and some of those early films survive and can still be seen today in museums. Scholars agree that the Lumière brothers’ 1895 event set the pattern for movie theaters and film storytelling. Other inventors, like Thomas Edison in the United States, were working on moving pictures at almost the same time, but the Lumière public showing in Paris is often cited as the true birth of cinema for the public.
tech-movies.happened: In 1895, something new and magical happened in Paris. For the first time, people gathered together in a dark room and watched pictures on a screen that moved like real life. This wasn't just a slideshow or a set of photographs. The Lumière brothers, Auguste and Louis, used their invention—the Cinématographe—to show short films to a paying audience. Their device could record, develop, and project moving images. On December 28, 1895, they held what many call the first true public movie screening. The short films, such as a train arriving at a station and workers leaving a factory, were only about a minute long. But for those first moviegoers, this new way of sharing stories was so surprising that some people even jumped out of their seats in wonder. This was the beginning of movies, which would soon become a favorite way for people around the world to see stories come alive together.
tech-movies.scripture: The Bible tells us that Jesus taught with parables, simple stories that helped people understand deep truths (Matthew 13:3-9). Stories have always been a key way God teaches His children, whether those stories are told in the scriptures or through modern tools like movies. In Doctrine and Covenants 88:118, we are encouraged to "seek learning, even by study and also by faith," which includes using the best resources of the time to learn and teach. While scriptures do not mention movies directly, their guidance on teaching with stories and using wise means to learn can help families choose worthy entertainment.
tech-movies.background: Before movies, most people got their stories from books, plays, or listening to someone read out loud. There were early experiments with moving pictures—people tried out devices like the zoetrope and magic lantern—but none could show a story to a group at once. In the 1890s, Paris was full of energy and new ideas; it was called the Belle Époque, a time of invention and hope. Everyday life was changing rapidly, with new trains, electric lights, and telephones. The Lumière brothers came from a family of photographers and worked in a photography business. Their skills with cameras and love for new ideas led them to invent new ways to capture and share what they saw.

fp01:imhotep.talk: How can paying attention and learning help us find ways to serve and help others?
fp01:imhotep.child: Imhotep was a real person who helped build the first big stone building in Egypt and was one of the first doctors. He tried to help people by watching carefully and finding the best way to heal them, not just by using magic.
fp01:imhotep.learn: We can learn from Imhotep’s example that God inspires people in every nation to seek learning and to help others. His story teaches us to use our gifts with humility and to record what we learn so future generations can be blessed. Imhotep’s careful approach to healing shows the value of combining faith with wise and thoughtful action, building a foundation for the future.
